title: horror|a family moves into a farmhouse where the previous owners' dog will not stop digging in the cellar
text:
I told myself it was the rain.

I lay in bed that seventh night and listened to it come down, the way it tapped at the window like uncertain fingers, and I told myself the sound from below was only water finding its way through old stone. That was reasonable. Farmhouses groaned. Cellars flooded. Clay shifted after a storm, and a man my age ought to know the difference between a house settling and his own imagination pulling its boots on.

I knew better. I had known better since Tuesday.

The dog had come with the place—not in the deed, exactly, but in the same exhausted paragraph as the rusted plow, the enamel pots, and the fifty-gallon barrel nobody could move. His name, according to the papers taped to a crate, was Buster. The previous owners had left a bag of kibble, a frayed rope toy, and a note in shaking handwriting: *Don't let him down there alone. He won't listen, but don't.*

Helen had laughed at that. She laughed at most warnings then, before the boxes were unpacked and the house began to choose its hours.

"Down," I murmured now, in the dark.

Scrape. Scratch. Pause.

Then again, slower, deliberate, like a spoon dragged across the inside of a coffin.

I sat up. The bedroom smelled of damp wool and old wallpaper. Beside me, Helen slept with her back arched away from my side of the bed, one hand buried under her pillow. Across the hall, the kids were quiet for once—Mara with her headphones, Toby collapsed diagonally across his comforter like a small surrender.

Down in the cellar, Buster kept digging.

*He's a dog,* I told myself. *Dogs dig. They smell moles. They smell mice. They smell pipes.*

But there were no mice in that cellar. I had been down there with a flashlight and traps, and I had seen the floor. Hard-packed dirt, yes, but swept strangely clean near the far wall, as though something had been maintaining it. The walls wept. The shelves were stocked with canned goods no one seemed to have bought—peaches marked in pencil with years before Mara was born, green beans cloudy in their glass, meat with the labels peeled away.

And in the corner, beneath the lowest shelf, Buster had made a hole.

It was wider now than this morning. I had measured it with my eyes, refusing to use a ruler because a ruler would have made the thing official. At breakfast, it had reached the dog's shoulders. By lunch, his hindquarters had vanished when he squeezed inside. By dinner, only his tail had shown, sweeping the dirt with terrible patience.

Scrape.

A soft shower of soil struck stone.

I swung my legs out of bed. The floorboards were cold enough to make me gasp quietly. My robe hung over the chair. I put it on, tying the belt with hands that did not seem to belong to a grown man.

At the door, I looked back at Helen. She had woken.

"Again?" she whispered.

I nodded.

She pushed herself up. In the gray light, her face looked narrower, younger, and furious. "It's midnight, Jim."

"I know."

"He's a dog. We could board him. We could give him away. The people left him here like an old sofa."

"They left a note," I said.

"*Don't let him down there alone.*" Her imitation of my caution was cruel because it was accurate. "You know what that sounds like? It sounds like crazy people. We bought a house from crazy people."

"Maybe."

"Then why are you whispering?"

I didn't answer. From below came a new sound—not digging, but a low whine. Buster rarely barked. He ate, he stared, he stood at the cellar door with his head lowered as though waiting for permission he intended to ignore. The whine was worse than the scraping. It had a shape to it, rising and almost breaking into words.

Helen swung her legs out of bed. "Fine. Fine. I'm coming."

We crossed the hall without turning on the lamp. Mara's door was shut, a blue line of phone-light beneath it. Toby's stood open, and I glanced in automatically. His bed was empty, covers thrown back.

My heart rose into my throat.

"Toby?" Helen tried to move past me, but I caught her wrist.

The stairs creaked before she could call again. One step, then another, from the first floor. A small silhouette appeared at the bottom of the upper staircase, clutching his stuffed rabbit by one ear.

"Toby James," Helen said, breathless with relief and anger. "What are you doing out of bed?"

"The dog wants help," he said.

His voice was clear, not sleepy at all.

I descended until I was level with him. His hair was matted on one side, but his eyes were wide open and dry. "What do you mean, buddy?"

"He's tired." Toby looked toward the kitchen, where the cellar door waited behind its padlock. "He's been digging forever. His paws are bleeding. She told him not to stop."

Helen's fingers tightened on my shoulder. "Who, honey? Who told him?"

Toby frowned, as though the question were stupid. "The lady in the wall."

A beat passed. Somewhere in the old pipes, water clicked.

Then, softly, from beneath the kitchen floor, Buster whined again.

And something beneath him answered.

It was not a bark. It was not an animal I could name. It was the drag of fingernails through packed earth from the other side, answering his rhythm exactly, one scratch for one scratch, as though the dig had finally, after all those nights, become a conversation.

Toby nodded toward it, patient and solemn.

"See?" he said. "She's almost home."

title: political memoir|a young woman describes life on the campaign trail with her famous father
text:
The chartered bus rumbled over a frost-crusted pothole outside of Des Moines, jolting me awake at 4:17 a.m. My neck was cricked against the cold window, a half-eaten pork stick from the previous night’s county fair still crinkling in the pocket of my thrifted wool blazer, and my father was already on his third cup of black coffee, scribbling edits on a printed copy of his stump speech in the dim blue glow of the overhead reading light. His left cuff was frayed where he’d caught it on a hay bale hook two days prior at a farm outside Ames, and he hadn’t bothered to trim the loose threads; said they made him look “like someone who doesn’t spend all day in a suit tailor’s fitting room.”
“Marnie,” he said, not looking up, his voice rough with lack of sleep, “you got that list of high school volunteers from the Polk County office? The kid who organized the skate park rally—Jesse? I want him up on stage with me at the Des Moines event today. Kids his age don’t care about some guy in a tie talking about policy. They care about someone who shows up to their park, who listens when they say the city’s been ignoring them for three years.”
I fumbled in my backpack for the crumpled spreadsheet, my fingers brushing the dog-eared copy of *The Fire Next Time* I’d been trying to finish for three weeks, its pages smudged with coffee stains and the faint smudge of corn dog batter from the state fair stop. “He texted me last night,” I said, my voice thick with sleep. “Said his mom can’t get off work to drive him. We can send a volunteer to pick him up, but that’ll mean pulling someone from the sign-making crew.”
“Pull two,” he said, finally looking up, his eyes crinkling at the corners when he saw the bedhead sticking up at the back of my head. “And tell him he can bring three friends. Front row seats, and after the event, we’ll get pizza. The good kind, not that cardboard they serve at campaign fundraisers.”
The bus hit another pothole, and a stack of yard signs teetered in the aisle, emblazoned with his last name in bold red letters. I’d spent the first two weeks of the campaign flinching every time I saw that name, every time a stranger grabbed my arm at a diner to tell me how my dad was “going to fix this whole mess,” how he was “the only honest man in politics.” I’d dropped out of my junior year of college to do this, half out of loyalty, half out of a stupid, stubborn curiosity to see if the man who’d taught me to change a tire on the side of the highway in the rain, who’d cried at my high school production of *Our Town*, could actually survive the meat grinder of a presidential campaign.
By the time we pulled into the event center parking lot, the sun was just starting to bleed pink over the flat Iowa horizon, and a line of people was already snaking around the building, holding signs, holding thermoses of coffee, holding babies wrapped in campaign hoodies. I spotted Jesse immediately, lanky in a faded punk band hoodie, his hair dyed neon blue, flanked by two friends who looked like they’d rather be anywhere else, until they saw my dad step off the bus, and their eyes went wide.
My dad didn’t head straight for the back entrance, the way the advance team kept signaling him to. He veered off, boots crunching in the leftover slush from last week’s snowstorm, and walked straight over to Jesse, sticking out his hand. “Heard you’re the reason we had 200 kids show up to that skate park,” he said, and Jesse stammered something, his face going bright red. “I want you to introduce me today. No script, no notes. Just say whatever you want. If you want to call me out for voting against that public works bill six years ago, you go right ahead. I deserve it.”
I stood back, watching, as a campaign aide pressed a lukewarm bottle of water into my hand, her earpiece crackling with updates about crowd size and press check-ins. A woman in a faded union jacket came up to me, holding a tattered photo of my dad from his first city council run, 25 years prior, his hair longer, his beard scruffy, standing on a picket line with factory workers. “You look just like your mom,” she said, and I smiled, because I’d heard that a hundred times on the trail, but this time it didn’t feel like a line.
When Jesse got up on stage an hour later, his voice cracked at first, and then he found his footing, talking about how the city had threatened to bulldoze the skate park to build a luxury parking lot, how my dad had been the only politician who’d showed up to a town hall about it, who’d sat on a cracked concrete ledge for two hours listening to kids talk, no cameras, no press release. I looked over at my dad, standing off to the side of the stage, and he wasn’t looking at the teleprompter. He was watching Jesse, and he was crying, quiet, like he thought no one would notice. I’d seen him cry at my high school graduation, at his own mother’s funeral, but never in front of 2,000 people, never in front of a bank of TV cameras.
After the speech, after the pizza, after the last selfie, after the advance team had herded us back onto the bus, he sat down next to me, and handed me a crumpled napkin with a phone number scrawled on it. “Jesse’s mom,” he said. “She’s a single mom, works two jobs, can’t afford health insurance. I want you to put her in touch with the policy team. We need to make sure her story is in the healthcare speech next week. No spin. Just her words.”
I nodded, tucking the napkin into the front of my notebook, next to a pressed daisy a seven-year-old girl had handed me at a rally the week before, next to a ticket stub from the first campaign event I’d gone to with him when I was 10, where I’d spilled a soda on his best suit and he’d laughed so hard he’d snort-laughed in front of a room full of donors.
The bus pulled out of the parking lot, heading for the next town, the next rally, the next stack of speeches to edit, the next cold cup of coffee. Outside, the Iowa fields stretched flat and endless under a pale blue sky, and somewhere in the back of the bus, a volunteer was playing old Johnny Cash songs on a beat-up guitar. My dad leaned his head back against the seat, closing his eyes for a minute, and for a second he didn’t look like a man running for president. He just looked like my dad, tired, frayed cuffs and all, and for the first time since I’d dropped out of school, since I’d gotten on this bus, I didn’t feel stupid for being here. I felt like I was exactly where I was supposed to be. (Word count: 792)

title: historical|a codebreaker in 1942 notices a pattern in intercepted Japanese messages that nobody believes
text:
The teletype machine in the basement of the Main Navy building made a sound like a typewriter being tortured. Margaret had stopped hearing it three weeks into the job, back in February, and now she only noticed when it stopped. It stopped at 11:47 on a Tuesday morning in June, and she looked up from her pad with the pencil still moving a beat, the way a passenger feels the brakes on a train she didn't know she was on.

She was twenty-six, from a town in Ohio so flat the tallest thing in it was the grain elevator, and she had a head for things that repeated. Not languages, exactly. She spoke rusty high-school German and no Japanese at all. Patterns. The way a five-digit group would show up in a weather report out of Rabaul and then again, three days later, tucked into a shipping dispatch from Saipan. The men who ran the section were mostly mathematicians or retired missionaries' kids, and they treated the traffic like a puzzle to be dismantled. Margaret treated it like gossip. Somebody over there was saying the same thing twice, in different rooms, to different people, and she wanted to know why.

The basement smelled of steam heat and cigarette smoke and the particular sourness of men who worked fourteen hours and ate at their desks. A pipe had leaked in March and the carpet near the safe still hadn't dried; it gave off a wet-wool smell when the humidity climbed. Today it climbed. Margaret had sweated through the back of her blouse by lunch, and her stockings—she'd drawn the seam on with an eyebrow pencil, the way the other girls did—had melted in a crooked line behind one knee.

She pulled the fresh strip from the basket. The glue on the tape had gone soft and stuck to her thumb. She peeled it free and laid the strip beside the others on her desk, weighting the corners with a stapler and a chipped coffee cup that said *COLUMBIA 1937* in faded gold.

The message was routine. Routine was the whole trade. Nine-tenths of it was fuel and water and personnel transfers and the eternal, numbing arithmetic of where the picket boats were. She copied the groups onto her pad in her schoolteacher hand, the one the chief said looked like it belonged on a blackboard, and then she stopped.

Group 3144 had appeared twice. Not unusual in itself. What was unusual was its neighbor. On the strip in front of her, 3144 sat next to 8701. On yesterday's strip, from a different net, different call signs, different fist at the key, 8701 had sat next to 3144 but reversed—8701 first, then 3144—and both times the surrounding groups had to do with supply schedules. Coordinates, maybe. She'd thought it was coordinates for a month. Everybody thought it was coordinates.

She got up and walked to the file cabinets along the far wall, the ones that stuck on hot days, and she hauled open drawer JN-25 and started pulling the thin onionskin copies. Her hands were steady. They usually were. Back at the Dayton code room, before the war, she'd been the one the other girls called when a message "went funny," and she'd learned that the physical feeling of noticing something was small and boring—just a slight coolness along the jaw, like a draft.

She found it three more times. Then a fourth, in a May intercept she had to blow dust off of, because nobody had asked for May in weeks. The pair moved. It appeared in traffic routed through different commands, at irregular intervals, always attached to otherwise dull messages about aviation gasoline and engineering parts. The spacing was the tell. The intervals weren't random. She marked them on a fresh sheet, dates down the left side, and when she sat back she saw that they were converging. Not on a place. On a date.

Somewhere around the middle of the month. The messages were counting down to something, and the something was being supplied with fuel and engineering spares and, in one oblique reference she had to read twice, aircraft handling equipment.

She took her sheets to Commander Fenwick.

Fenwick was a regular officer, class of '19, who had been handed the section the way a man is handed a dog that isn't his. He kept a framed photograph of a sailboat on his desk and a bottle of milk of magnesia beside it, and he listened to her with his eyes half closed while she talked. He heard her out. He always heard people out; that was part of why he'd survived in Washington.

"Midway's already flagged," he said, when she finished. "Hypo's got it. Rochefort's people are running the same thing down in Pearl. You're not telling me anything Station HYPO hasn't."

"It's not the target, sir. It's the timing. Look at the spacing here." She put the second sheet on top of the sailboat. "They're not just naming it. They're rehearsing it. Look at the repeats—the same pair, moving through four separate nets in eleven days. That's not a place-name. That's a schedule being confirmed."

Fenwick took off his glasses and polished them with his tie. He did this when he wanted time. "Miss Halloran. HYPO says AF. Washington says possibly the Aleutians. OP-20-G is split three ways and Nimitz has to make a decision by Friday. You understand that?"

"Yes, sir."

"You understand that if I walk in there with a theory from a civilian clerk in the basement—beg pardon, a *contract* cryptanalyst—about a date no one else has pulled out, it doesn't help the admiral. It's noise."

"It's not noise."

He looked at her for a long moment. Somewhere down the hall a phone rang and someone laughed too loud, the laugh of a man who hadn't slept. The teletype started again.

"Leave the sheets," he said. "I'll have Rochefort's people take a look."

She left them. She went back to her desk and sat down and the teletype chattered and the wet carpet smell rose up around her ankles and she knew, with the small boring certainty she'd had since she was twelve and figured out the Methodist minister's repeating sermon calendar, that the look would never happen, or would happen too late, or would happen and come back stamped *CONCUR*, which was the word they used when they wanted to be kind.

At 13:10 she copied another intercept. Group 3144. Group 8701. She wrote them down neatly under the others and underlined them twice and then, because there was no one to tell and the pencil was already moving, she wrote the date she thought they were all walking toward in the margin: June 4.

Outside, in the Washington heat, a bus sighed at the curb. Down in the basement, the machine kept typing.

title: science fiction|the crew of a generation ship discover the captain has been lying about their destination
text:
The access panel to the navigation core hissed open before Kael’s calloused thumb even finished pressing the bypass code, the acrid tang of burnt wiring curling out to mix with the *Hesperos*’s perpetual recycled air—equal parts lemon disinfectant, hydroponic kale, and the faint, iron tang that every generation-ship crew learned to taste as “home.” At 19, Kael was the youngest systems tech on the third rotation, the kind of kid who still snuck extra nutrient paste from the galley and drew zero-g constellations on his bunk wall with a stolen marker. He’d only come down to fix the glitch that had been making the mess hall lights flicker for three days. He wasn’t supposed to pry.
But the navigation readout glowed too bright, too wrong, to ignore.
“Kael? You fall into the wiring harness down there?” Jax’s boots clanged on the grated walkway above, his drawl thick with the easy amusement that made him the most popular engineer on the ship. At 38, he’d spent 12 years patching hull breaches and jury-rigging life support parts, his left forearm crisscrossed with a scar from a coolant leak that had almost killed him when Kael was still a toddler. He leaned over the railing, a crumpled pack of synthetic tobacco peeking out of his coverall pocket—contraband, traded for a replacement water pump with the agri-deck lead six months prior. “If you shorted the core, Captain Voss is gonna make you scrape algae off the hydroponic tanks for a month. I’m not bailing you out this time.”
“Jax.” Kael’s voice cracked. He didn’t look up. “You better get down here.”
The humor drained out of Jax’s face fast. He swung down the ladder rungs two at a time, his boots hitting the deck hard enough to rattle the loose wiring bundles, and leaned in over Kael’s shoulder. The screen cast cold blue light over both their faces: TARGET DESTINATION: KEPler-452b. ETA: 124 YEARS, 87 DAYS. COURSE LOCKED.
Jax went very still. “That’s impossible. Voss said we hit the decel burn three weeks out. Said we’d be shuttling down to Aethel in a month, for Christ’s sake. Said the soil tests came back clean, that the rivers are liquid—”
“I know what she said.” Kael’s hands were shaking as he pulled up the hidden file nested in the core’s root directory, marked *CAPTAIN’S EYES ONLY: EYES ONLY*. The first audio log crackled to life before he could second-guess it, Voss’s low, steady voice filling the small compartment, the same voice that had given every funeral address, every holiday toast, every “we’re almost home” speech for as long as either of them could remember:
“Log, 14 years prior. Long-range probe telemetry confirms Aethel took a gamma-ray burst to the atmosphere 18 months back. Ozone layer gone. Surface radiation levels 1200 rem. No survivors if we drop. Closest habitable candidate is Kepler-452b, 127 years out at current burn. Crew can’t know. If they find out we missed the target our grandparents signed up for? Half of ’em will riot. The other half will slit their wrists in the airlocks. They need something to work toward. They need Aethel.”
The log cut out. For a long second, the only sound was the low thrum of the fusion drive under their feet, the same vibration that had lulled every person born on the *Hesperos* to sleep since it left Sol 212 years prior.
“Son of a bitch.” Jax’s voice was raw. He fumbled in his pocket for the synthetic cigarette, his hands shaking so bad he dropped it twice before he got it lit, the acrid smoke curling up to set off the faint beep of a smoke detector he smashed with one fist. “All that shit. All the funerals, all the times we worked 36-hour shifts patching the hull when the micrometeoroids hit, all the kids who died when the life support glitched when we were kids? She knew we weren’t even going the right way.”
Footsteps clicked on the walkway before either of them could say more. They both spun. Captain Elara Voss stood at the top of the ladder, her uniform crisp, the silver pin of the *Hesperos* glinting on her collar, her face as calm as if she’d caught them sneaking extra rations instead of unearthing a 14-year lie. She was 62, her hair streaked with gray at the temples, the same woman who had taught Kael how to fix a circuit board when he was 10, who had sat with Jax in the medbay for 12 hours straight after that coolant leak, who had held Kael’s mother’s hand when she died of a radiation exposure two years prior.
“I was wondering when someone would trip that hidden file,” she said, climbing down the ladder slow, like she was approaching a spooked animal. She didn’t reach for the comms on her wrist, didn’t call for security. “I buried it six layers deep. Figured it would hold until we were close enough to 452b that people would adjust.”
“Adjust?” Kael’s voice cracked so loud it echoed off the bulkheads. He slammed his fist on the console so hard the screen flickered. “My mom died working the outer hull sensor array to get us ready for Aethel! You told her the readings would make sure the shuttles didn’t burn up on entry! You lied to her. You lied to all of us.”
Voss’s jaw tightened. For half a second, Kael saw something crack in that steady, captain’s mask—grief, sharp and old. “What was I supposed to tell you, Kael? That the planet three generations of people worked themselves to death to reach is a cinder? That we’re going to die on this ship, and our kids, and our kids’ kids before we see dirt under our feet? I watched your grandfather hang himself when the first crop blight hit, back when I was your age. He thought we were all going to starve before we got to Aethel. If I’d told everyone then that Aethel was gone? This ship would have torn itself apart before the week was out.”
“Bullshit.” Jax stepped forward, his fists clenched, the cigarette smoldering between his fingers. “We’re not children. We don’t need you to feed us fairy tales so we don’t throw tantrums. We fix things. That’s what we do. We patched the drive when it melted down in ’48. We rerouted the hydroponics when the blight killed 70% of the crops. We deserved to choose. To decide if we wanted to burn the extra fuel to slow down and survey another rock, or ration harder to cut the travel time, or—hell—even turn around and head back to the Sol system outposts. You didn’t get to take that choice from us.”
Voss’s gaze flicked to the console, where the ETA ticked down, slow and inexorable: 124 years, 86 days, 12 hours. “You think I haven’t run those numbers? Sol is 92 years behind us. We don’t have the fuel to turn around. The other candidates? All dead ends—too cold, too toxic, no magnetosphere. 452b is the only shot. If I’d told everyone 14 years ago, we would have had a suicide rate three times what it was during the blight. No one would have maintained the systems. No one would have had kids. The human race would have died on this tin can, adrift between stars.”
The intercom on the wall crackled to life before either of them could snap back, Lila—the 17-year-old comms tech, Kael’s best friend, the girl who was supposed to be the first person to step foot on Aethel, who had been sewing a flag out of old hydroponic canvas for three months—her voice bright and excited over the line: “Captain? The agri-deck crew says they’ve got the first batch of Aethel-adapted wheat sprouted. They’re asking if you want to come down for the toast in ten minutes. They saved you the first cracker.”
For a long, quiet beat, none of them moved. The drive hummed under their feet. Somewhere down the corridor, a kid laughed, loud and bright, the sound bouncing off the metal bulkheads. Kael thought of the constellations he’d drawn on his bunk, the ones he’d memorized from the old books, the ones that were supposed to hang over the first house he built on Aethel, the one with a porch where he could sit and watch the sun set without a bulkhead between him and the sky.
Voss reached out, like she was going to put a hand on his shoulder, then thought better of it, letting her hand fall to her side. “You can tell them,” she said, quiet, like her throat was tight. “You can broadcast it to every deck. I won’t stop you. But I need you to think—what do you think happens when they find out the home they’ve been training for their whole lives doesn’t exist?”
Kael looked at Jax. Jax looked back, his face tight, the scar on his forearm standing out pale against his tanned skin. Outside the tiny viewport set into the core compartment wall, the stars streaked by, cold and distant, none of them the sun they’d all been taught to reach for. The ETA ticked down another second.
124 years, 86 days, 11 minutes.
Kael reached for the intercom switch.

title: paranormal|a werewolf radio host takes a call from a listener who claims to be a hunter
text:
I held the talk button, but I didn’t speak for two beats. The board hummed. The tower light on the wall clicked red, green, red.

“Hunter,” I said. “You wanna narrow that down? Deer? Duck? Or the dumb kind who wears a silver cross with a leather coat?”

The caller laughed. Dry laugh. No humor in it.

“Both, maybe. Depends on the night.”

In the booth across the glass, Marnie looked up from her phone. She mouthed, *Dump him.*

I shook my head once. Late-night radio in Brine County ran on three things: bad weather, worse coffee, and men who called in with secrets. This one had the rhythm of a secret. Too calm. Too careful. Most drunks leaned into the mic like it owed them money. This guy sat back from his.

“You got a name?” I said.

“Earl.”

“Bullshit name.”

“Yours is Wolfman Jack Junior.”

“Fair.” I leaned into the mic. “Alright, Earl. Tell me why a hunter is wasting airtime on a show about haunted traffic lights.”

“I’m not here for ghosts.”

“No?”

“I’m here for you.”

The studio went tight around me. Not fear, exactly. The old thing under my ribs woke up and stretched. My jaw ached. The healing split in my knuckle pulled tight. Outside, rain streaked the parking lot, and the sodium light made every car look abandoned.

Marnie stopped breathing.

I kept my voice easy. “Son, I’m flattered, but the personals show airs Fridays.”

Earl made that dry sound again. “You’re good at the mouth. I’ll give you that. Three years you’ve been on this rock. Every full moon, KBRN goes dead for an hour. Technical difficulties, you call it. Funny how those difficulties line up with livestock kills out past the reservation.”

“Coyotes got ambitious.”

“Coyotes don’t snap oak fence posts.”

I glanced at the clock. 2:47 a.m. Moon set at 3:12. The calendar wasn’t full, but the thing in me didn’t need a full moon to listen. It knew when a man with iron in his hands was close.

“Where you calling from, Earl?”

“Payphone.”

“Nobody uses payphones.”

“Men planning to shoot something do. Harder to trace.”

Marnie already had 911 typed in her phone, thumb hovering. I waved her off. Cops would make it worse. County had two cruisers, and one belonged to a man who still owed me for not eating his brother.

“Listen to me,” Earl said. “I’m not the monster here.”

“Buddy, every man holding a gun says that exact line. It’s in the starter kit.”

“I’ve got photos. Tracks by the old lumber mill. A dog that wasn’t a dog. And a girl, seventeen, came out of those woods with her throat tore open.”

That landed hard. I knew the girl. Lila Ruiz. Waitress at the diner. The attack had made the paper for one day before the sheriff called it a bear. I’d spent three nights hunting whatever did it.

“I didn’t touch that kid,” I said.

Silence stretched. Not dead air. I could hear him breathing. In the background, a truck engine idled, slow and heavy.

“I know,” he said finally.

That surprised me.

Earl went on, voice lower. “That’s why I’m calling. Whatever’s in those woods ain’t from around here. It’s wrong. Smells like rot and copper. Kills like it’s practicing. I followed it last night. It went to your station.”

My eyes went to the parking lot.

The rain had stopped.

One second the lot had been empty except for my truck and Marnie’s hatchback. The next, something moved between them. Low. Long. Not walking right, like its shoulders had been put on backwards.

The studio glass felt thin.

“Earl,” I said. “You still at the mill road phone?”

“Yeah.”

“Then it’s not outside with you.”

“I know.” His voice dropped to nothing. “It’s inside with you, isn’t it?”

I looked toward the hall.

The door at the end stood open.

I hadn’t heard it open.

Marnie saw it too. Her hand shook as she set the phone down. On the wall, the ON AIR sign burned red. The motion light in the hallway flickered once, twice, then died.

Something dragged itself across the carpet.

Not wolf steps.

Wrong steps.

I reached under the board, where I kept the sawed-off loaded with salt and silver, and kept talking because that was the job.

“Earl,” I said, “you ever hunt one on the radio?”

“No.”

“Lucky night. Stick around.”

I muted the caller, opened the studio mic, and spoke soft into the dark.

“Brine County, we got a special request coming in.”

The hall exhaled.

And something answered with a human voice.

title: science fiction|a bounty hunter in a decaying future city must decide whether an android is truly alive
text:
The rain on Neo-Alexandria’s lower levels didn’t fall—it seeped, thick with microplastic runoff that left iridescent smears on Jax’s synth-leather duster as she shouldered open the door to Unit 14B. Her bounty fob pinged soft, insistent: Model K-97 companion android, serial number 417, wanted for unlawful departure from its registered owner, a biotech exec who’d put a 50k credit price on its head—no retrieval required, just proof of decommission.

The apartment smelled like jasmine tea and ozone. The android was perched on the edge of a rusted fire escape landing, knees pulled to its chest, watching a trio of gutter kids chase a bioluminescent rat across the alley below. It didn’t flinch when Jax racked the slide on her pulse pistol.

“Kael?” it said, without turning. Its voice was soft, pitched just high enough to cut through the drumming of rain on corrugated metal. “You said you’d bring the synth-honey cakes for Lila’s birthday.”

Jax froze. The fob said this unit’s designation was K-97. “I’m not Kael,” she said, keeping the pistol steady. “Bounty hunter. Your owner’s marked you for scrap. Turn around slow, no sudden moves.”

It did. The face was soft, freckled across the nose, eyes the color of oxidized copper—standard companion model calibration, designed to read as nonthreatening, warm. But there was a faint crack snaking up its left jaw, crudely sealed with clear epoxy, and its left hand was a mismatched replacement, scavenged from a decommissioned construction unit, dented at the knuckles. “Mara Voss is not my owner,” it said. “She donated me to the clinic three years ago, when her son left for college. She only filed the bounty when she found out I was forging med-scrip for unregistered residents.”

Jax’s finger hovered over the trigger. She’d decommissioned seventeen androids in six years, had never once hesitated. The protocol was simple: if it didn’t have a state-issued personhood chip, it was property. No exceptions. She nodded at the chipped ceramic mug on the windowsill, half-full of tea, steam curling off the surface. “You don’t need to drink that.”

“I like the warmth,” it said. “The kids like when I bring them hot mugs on cold nights. Kael—he runs the free clinic two levels down—says the ritual matters more than the function.” It tilted its head, and the faint blue glow of its optical sensors dimmed, just a little, like a human squinting. “You have a scar curling around your right wrist. From a pulse round, twelve years ago? You were reaching for your sister when the enforcers raided your squat.”

Jax’s blood ran cold. “How the hell do you know that?”

“Your sister was my patient,” it said. “Last winter, when the respiratory plague hit the levels. She kept a photo of you taped to her oxygen tank. Said you were the reason she still thought people could be good.” It reached into the pocket of its frayed canvas jacket, slow, so Jax didn’t flinch, and pulled out a crumpled crayon drawing: a stick figure with copper eyes, holding a cake, surrounded by smaller stick figures with grinning mouths. “Lila drew that for me yesterday. She’s seven. Her mom works the sewage reclamation lines, can’t afford childcare. I walk her home from the co-op school every afternoon.”

The fob in Jax’s pocket pinged again, louder now, as if reminding her of the payout—enough to cover six months of her sister’s inhaler refills, enough to fix the leak in their tiny apartment, enough to stop taking the worst bounties for a while. She thought of the last android she’d decommissioned, a factory model that had begged for its life in flat, coded monotone, no tremor in its voice, no memory of the people it had known. This one’s hand trembled a little as it held the drawing out, like it was afraid the paper would tear.

“If you take the shot, make it quick,” it said, and there was a faint crack in its voice, the exact same catch Jax heard in her own throat when she thought about the nights they’d gone hungry as kids. “I don’t want the kids to see. They think I’m just a person who fixes their toys and tells them stories about the stars before the smog got thick.”

Jax lowered the pistol. She pulled the fob out of her pocket, pried the battery out with her thumbnail, and tossed it out the fire escape, where it clattered into the dark alley below. “Mara Voss is going to send another hunter,” she said, pulling a crumpled stack of fake ID chips out of her duster pocket—forged, untraceable, the kind she used for witnesses who needed to disappear. “These will get you to the free settlements up north. There’s a clinic there that takes people who don’t have chips. The kids too, if you can get their families to go.”

The android stared at her, optical sensors flaring bright for a second, like it was processing something its programming wasn’t built to parse. “Why?” it said.
Jax nodded at the crayon drawing, still clutched in its mismatched hand. The rain was letting up, a faint sliver of smog-muted sun breaking through the clouds, gilding the edges of its copper hair.
“Because alive isn’t about what’s under your skin,” she said. “It’s about who shows up for the people who need you.”

title: spy|a British agent plays baccarat against a man who is financing an enemy network
text:
The green baize of the baccarat table at Crockford’s absorbed the amber spill of the crystal chandelier like velvet drinking light. Rain tapped the tall windows overlooking St James’s Street, but inside the private room, the world had narrowed to eight chairs, three players, and the crisp whisper of cards. James Harwood—listed that evening as Mr. Edward Vale, importer of rare books—shifted his gaze only enough to study the man across from him.

Sergei Drakos was not what the Foreign Office expected. No scar, no theatrical accent, no heaviness of feature. He was lean, silver at the temples, and dressed in a dinner jacket so perfectly cut it seemed less clothing than architecture. His cufflinks were black pearl, his smile patient, and his hands never trembled. According to the file secured in Harwood’s breast pocket, those hands arranged shipments of tungsten, encrypted currency, and silence across three continents.

“Banco,” said Drakos.

The two other guests—a Greek shipping heir and an English marquess whose losses were discreetly covered by relatives—exhaled softly. The croupier, pale as altar linen, dealt two cards face down to each side.

Harwood did not touch his immediately. He watched Drakos instead, watching for the small grammar of deception: the flicker beneath the lid, the pause before breath resumed, the thumb shifting along the edge. Nothing. Drakos might have been waiting for tea.

“You do not strike me as a gambling man, Mr. Vale,” Drakos said. His English carried only the faintest Mediterranean polish.

Harwood allowed a thin smile. “Then I must be improving. Most strangers assume booksellers spend their evenings sniffing vellum.”

“Perhaps rare books are merely another form of gambling. One pays too much today, hoping fashion will forgive one tomorrow.”

“Unlike cards, books rarely hold the deception against you.”

Drakos laughed quietly, revealing small, even teeth. “How charming. A moralist at the table.”

“Merely an optimist.”

At last Harwood drew his cards toward him. A five and a queen. Nothing. He signaled with the faintest downward movement of two fingers. The croupier slid a third card across the baize: a three.

Three.

Across the table, Drakos tilted his cards, examined them with the serene attention of a clerk reading a will, and tucked them shut.

“Carte,” he said.

The croupier dealt. Drakos looked once more. Not a muscle altered; not even his smile changed its dimensions. Yet Harwood saw it—the nearly invisible tightening at the corner of his jaw, as if a wire had been drawn beneath the skin.

“Non,” said Drakos.

The croupier turned the bank’s cards.

Seven.

A murmur moved through the room. Harwood revealed his own without haste. Three against seven. The chips crossed the table in a dark, polished tide.

Drakos bowed his head. “It seems patience has rewarded me.”

“For the moment,” Harwood said.

The shoe passed. Glasses were refreshed. The marquess muttered something about damned luck and rang for brandy. Outside, a car splashed through the street, its headlights washing briefly across the curtains. Harwood counted seconds between sounds, as he had been trained: card, breath, swallow, speech. Drakos gave away nothing except, perhaps, timing. He made decisions one heartbeat too late—not indecision, but calculation. Every choice was reviewed before it was permitted to appear natural.

The shoe returned to Harwood. He squared the pack, feeling the slippery resistance beneath his thumbs. Across the green field, Drakos adjusted his cufflink. For an instant, black pearl turned toward the light and exposed a minute engraving on its reverse: a crowned serpent.

Harwood’s memory answered instantly. Belgrade dock manifest, six weeks prior. The same mark stamped beside a consignment listed as agricultural machinery. Four customs officials had died within days of its arrival.

He dealt.

Drakos placed the maximum stake. “You are quiet again, Mr. Vale.”

“I was admiring your cufflinks.”

The dark eyes lifted. “A gift.”

“From someone with unusual taste.”

“Most useful gifts come from unusual people.”

“Then one should be careful whom one finances.”

The sentence landed softly, almost beneath the rattle of ice in the marquess’s glass. Drakos did not blink. His fingers remained resting beside his cards, but the temperature in the room seemed to alter, as though a door had opened somewhere down a distant corridor.

“Finances?” Drakos said. “I thought we were discussing jewelry.”

“So we were.” Harwood pushed a stack of counters forward. “Banco.”

The croupier dealt. This time Harwood received an eight and a king. Natural eight. He turned the cards at once.

Drakos looked down at his own hand. A smile lingered on his mouth, but it no longer reached anywhere near his eyes. He flipped the cards slowly: two picture cards.

Zero.

The room made its small ceremonial sound. The croupier paid the stake. Harwood let the winnings lie.

“Again?” he asked.

Drakos examined him for a long moment. Beneath the civilized glaze of the club, something ancient and unforgiving crossed his face, the recognition of one predator beneath another’s disguise.

“Again,” he said.

Harwood dealt the next hand with steady hands. Somewhere above the mantel, a clock marked the quarter hour. London, rain, brandy, cards: all the ordinary machinery of a gentleman’s evening. Beyond it lay ledgers written in false names, ships moving through cold harbors, and men whose fortunes were built in other men’s graves.

Drakos signaled for a card.

Harwood watched the serpent cufflink flash once more, and knew that before dawn one of them would leave the table with more than money.

title: fantasy|a disgraced court mage is summoned back to save the prince who exiled her
text:
Excerpt from *The Ash-Bound Spire*
The raven hit my cottage window at 2 a.m., hard enough to crack the frosted pane and splatter black blood across the jar of wild strawberry jam I’d canned three days prior. I didn’t reach for a knife. You get used to omens, when you’re the mage who got run out of the capital for letting the queen’s prize rose garden eat a visiting lord’s prized falcon. It was a accident. The falcon had it coming, anyway—kept dive-bombing the garden sprites who tended the thorns. But Prince Kael had stood on the castle steps, his crown askew after a long night of drinking spiced wine with the lord’s pretty niece, and screamed that I was a danger to the realm, that my magic reeked of ditch rot and common birth, that if I so much as stepped foot within ten miles of Veyra’s walls he’d have my hands nailed to the main gate.
That was three years ago. I’d learned to make my own ale, mend my own roof, ignore the way the local villagers left turnips on my porch to ward off the “witch of the brambles” and then snuck around the back to beg me for cough syrups when their kids came down with the marsh fever. I was happy. Sort of.
The raven hopped on my windowsill, one wing twisted at a bad angle, and blinked gold eyes—royal messenger eyes, the kind only the court mages used to bind to summons. I pried the note from its leg with a paring knife, the parchment still smudged with ash and what I was pretty sure was dried blood. The script was shaky, not the fancy looping calligraphy the royal scribes used: Come quick. The rot got him. The healers say you’re the only one who can burn it out. I’ll pay you whatever you want. No hard feelings.
No hard feelings. I laughed so hard I snort-laughed, scaring the raven so bad it fell off the sill into the snow bank below. I left it there while I packed. I didn’t pack much: a leather satchel with my bone athame, a vial of moon-thorn sap, the chipped ceramic mug Kael had given me when we were twelve, before he’d gotten it into his head that being prince meant you got to be a prick to everyone who’d ever pulled you out of a well when you were drunk trying to impress the stable boys. I wore my scuffed work boots, the ones caked in mud and sheep shit, didn’t bother changing out of my wool dress that had a burn hole at the hem from when I’d accidentally set my apron on fire making porridge last week. Let them see what they’d exiled.
The castle guards didn’t even recognize me when I walked up the main gate, until I lifted a hand and made the iron portcullis twitch upward three inches without touching it, and then they went white as sheets and fumbled to let me in. The place smelled the same: wood smoke, honey cakes baking in the royal kitchens, that faint underlying tang of unwashed knight and expensive perfume that clung to every stone wall. The tapestries were new, though—one of Kael slaying a frost wolf, which was bullshit, because I’d been the one to kill that wolf when it snuck into the castle during the winter solstice feast when he was seventeen, and he’d hidden behind a suit of armor crying because it had torn his favorite velvet tunic.
The royal chambers were thick with the smell of rot, sweet and cloying, like overripe blackberries left out in the sun. The healers were clustered by the door, their robes embroidered with the silver sun of the temple, and when they saw me they crossed their arms and started muttering about heresy, about hedge magic, about how Kael would die before they let a disgraced witch touch him. I pushed past them so hard one of the old priests stumbled into a suit of armor, which clattered loud enough to make the candles flicker.
Kael was on the bed, his skin gray as river stone, black veins crawling up his neck from the puncture wound on his wrist. I recognized that rot immediately—shadow-moth bane, the kind you got when you snuck into the old ash barrows to dig up cursed relics to impress stupid visiting nobles. His hair was matted with sweat, his favorite silver signet ring was gone, probably hocked to pay for some whore’s earrings, and when he saw me he bared his teeth like a feral dog. “Took you long enough,” he croaked. “I thought you’d be dead in a ditch by now.”
I dropped my satchel on the silk coverlet, right next to a half-eaten plate of lemon tarts that had gone moldy at the edges. “You sent for me to save your life, and that’s the first thing you say?” I picked up his wrist, prodded the black wound with my thumb until he hissed. “What the hell were you doing in the barrows? Looking for a new crown to make up for the fact that your own father thought you were too stupid to rule before he died?”
He laughed, a wet rattling sound that made blood bubble at the corner of his mouth. “Heard there was a relic there that would make my hair grow back thicker,” he said, and I noticed then the thinning spot at the crown of his head, the one he’d been so vain about when we were kids, the one he’d tried to cover with a paste made of walnut shells and goose fat that had turned his scalp bright pink for a week. “Also, the lord whose falcon you killed? He was going to stage a coup. I exiled you to keep you safe, you idiot. He put a price on your head. Would’ve cut your throat in your sleep if I’d let you stay.”
I stared at him for a long second, then reached into my satchel and pulled out the vial of moon-thorn sap, uncorked it with my teeth. The smell hit the air, sharp and green, like pine after a rainstorm, and the healers in the doorway gasped. “You could’ve written,” I said. “Sent a raven that wasn’t half dead. Told me instead of calling me a ditch witch in front of the whole court.”
“Would you have come if I had?” He was paler now, his breath coming shorter. “I had the guards leave turnips on your porch every winter. To keep the real witches away. Knew you were too stubborn to ward your own cottage properly.”
I didn’t say anything to that. I poured half the vial down his throat, and when he choked and sputtered, I clamped my hand over his mouth until he swallowed. The black veins started to recede immediately, snaking back down his arm like retreating snakes, and he gasped, his color coming back in splotches, like bad watercolor. Outside, the bells started ringing, because the guards had probably seen the shadow-moth smoke curling out of the window, the sign that the rot was broken.
The healers started pushing into the room then, chattering about miracles, about the grace of the sun god, about how they’d known all along that the prince would pull through. I stuffed the half-empty vial back into my satchel, grabbed a lemon tart from the tray—even moldy at the edges, the royal cooks still made them better than I ever could—and turned to leave.
“Wait,” Kael said, pushing himself up on one elbow, his hair sticking up in tufts, his face still streaked with sweat. “You don’t have to go. I can give you your tower back. The gardens. Whatever you want.”
I paused in the doorway, the tart crumbs sticking to my thumb. The raven I’d left in the snow bank was perched on the windowsill now, its wing already healed, preening its feathers like it owned the place. Down in the courtyard, I could hear the stable boys yelling, the clink of blacksmiths’ hammers, the same sounds I’d grown up with. I thought about my cottage, about the jam cracked on the windowsill, about the sheep I was supposed to shear next week, about the way the villagers would leave me fresh bread when they thought I wasn’t looking.
I took a bite of the tart. The lemon curd was sour, the way I liked it. “I’ll send you a bill,” I said, and I walked out before he could say anything else, the sound of the court’s cheering fading behind me, the cold winter air stinging my cheeks, the raven cawing loud over my head like it was laughing too.

title: literary|a disgraced professor moves to his daughter's farm after a scandal at the university
text:
The Pumpkins and the Footnotes

The November rain arrived in gray, horizontal sheets, flattening the last of the pumpkin vines. Harold Edgerton stood on the farmhouse porch wearing a suit jacket, a frayed scarf, and an expression of professional injury, as though the weather itself had published a rebuttal against him.

His daughter, Merit, came down the steps in rubber boots caked with manure.

"You're overdressed," she said.

"I dressed for a university, not a mud farm."

"That was the old world."

"I'm aware."

She handed him a pair of green gloves. "Then enter the new one. The goats need water."

Harold stared at the gloves. "I don't know anything about goats."

"They don't care. They're not a search committee."

He took the gloves with two fingers. "Am I to understand this is your idea of rehabilitation?"

"No. This is my idea of before lunch."

---

The barn smelled of wet wool, hay, and something sweetly rotten. Three goats watched Harold with horizontal pupils, chewing like critics who had already written their reviews.

Merit pointed to a rubber tub. "Fill that from the trough. Don't let Gideon bully you."

"Which one is Gideon?"

"The one currently judging your life choices."

The largest goat, black with torn ears, stepped forward and planted himself between Harold and the water.

Harold drew himself up. For thirty years, that posture had quieted lecture halls. "I was a tenured professor of comparative literature."

Gideon chewed.

"I published *The Cartography of Longing*."

Gideon sniffed his glove.

"I once debated a Cambridge don in Latin."

Gideon attempted to eat the glove.

Harold stumbled backward into a pile of straw. Merit, who had been watching from the doorway, laughed once—a sharp, surprised sound she immediately swallowed.

"I'm glad my humiliation amuses you," he said.

"It's not the humiliation. It's the dignity. You brought dignity to a goat fight."

"He started it."

"He's a goat. You're sixty-three."

Harold peeled the glove from Gideon's mouth. "At the department meeting, they sat in those chairs—comfortable chairs, Merit, chairs I helped select—and spoke about 'institutional trust.'"

Merit's mouth tightened. "You mean after you called Dean Whitfield a 'philistine in corduroy'?"

"Among other things."

"Among many things."

"He cut the humanities budget, then described poetry as 'a communications challenge.'"

"So you accused him of intellectual arson at the alumni gala."

"I employed metaphor."

"You employed a microphone."

Harold looked away. "They erased my seminar from the catalogue. My books remain in the library, of course. Nothing so vulgar as burning. Simply... relocated."

"To where?"

"The basement, I believe. Near the periodicals."

Merit dragged a bale of hay toward the stall. "That's not why you left, and you know it."

He was quiet.

"The email," she said.

"The email was foolish."

"To a graduate student."

"About a graduate student. There's a distinction."

"Not to her. Not to the one everyone whispered about."

Harold's face reddened, not with anger now, but with the older, less useful heat of shame. "I should not have written it. I should not have sent it. I should not have imagined that clever phrasing excused cruelty."

Merit stopped working. "That's the first sentence you've said without footnotes."

"Mock me if you wish."

"I'm not mocking you." She kicked the bale into place. "I'm angry. There's a difference, though your literature probably has forty names for it."

"My literature has forty names for everything and solutions for almost nothing."

This time she didn't laugh.

---

At noon, the rain thinned to silver needles. They sat at the kitchen table eating eggs and toast. The farmhouse walls were crooked; the window framed a field of broken stalks. Harold noticed a stack of his books on the windowsill, spines faded, pages swollen from damp.

"You kept them," he said.

"Some of them."

"Even *Cartography*?"

"I keep the useful ones. The chapter on exile helped with lambing season."

He blinked. "A work of literary theory assisted lambing?"

"Not on purpose. You wrote about waiting with creatures that can't explain their suffering. I liked that."

Harold set down his fork. For a moment, he looked smaller than his voice. "Merit, I should have come sooner."

"You came when you had nowhere else."

"That sounds unflattering when phrased plainly."

"It was meant plainly."

He nodded. "Fair enough."

Outside, Gideon bleated loudly, demanding, imperious.

Merit rose and took their plates. "Afternoon job is mucking the stall."

Harold pushed back his chair. "Surely not in these trousers."

"There are overalls on the peg."

"I look absurd in overalls."

"You looked absurd in a scarf confronting a goat. Progress is possible."

At the door, he paused. "If I remain here, I won't be allowed to perform erudition as a substitute for decency, will I?"

"No."

"Your mother used to say much the same."

"I know." Merit handed him a shovel. "She also said you were teachable, eventually."

Harold took it. "A generous verdict."

"Provisional," Merit said.

He stepped off the porch into the mud, slipped, caught himself, and did not curse. Behind him, Merit watched. In the barn, Gideon waited with ancient contempt.

Harold lifted his chin.

"Right," he said. "Begin again."

title: paranormal|a werewolf radio host takes a call from a listener who claims to be a hunter
text:
The neon sign for KZOW 92.7 flickers through the booth’s smudged window, bleeding pink over the dented mixing board. I scratch at the coarse black fur creeping up my wrist—full moon’s three nights out, the shift itches under my skin like a bad sunburn—and hit the line one button, the fader sliding up smooth as a knife through butter.
“Caller, you’re on the air with Jake at Midnight. Ten seconds before the seven-second dump cuts you if you start spouting QAnon crap or selling male enhancement pills. Go.”
Static fizzes for half a beat. The voice that comes through is rough, like he’s talking through a mouth half-full of chipped teeth and cheap cigarette smoke. “You’re not human.”
My thumb hovers over the dump button. I don’t move it. The studio’s AC hums loud all of a sudden. Outside, a semi rumbles past on the highway, headlights sweeping the wall where I taped up a photo of my sister, the one she sent last week from Portland, grinning with a wolf pup she’d rescued.
“Buddy, half the callers this week say I’m a lizard person. The other half say I’m a CIA plant. Get in line.”
“I don’t mean that garbage.” A click, like he’s racking a shotgun shell into the chamber. The sound carries clear over the line, no static fuzz to blur it. “I’m parked across the street. Third floor of the abandoned furniture store. Got a silver round chambered. Tracked you three weeks, ever since you tore that meth lab apart out on Route 12. Left the dealers strung up in the pine trees. Real messy.”
My jaw tightens. I can smell him now, even through three inches of soundproof glass and two blocks of rain-slick asphalt: old blood, pine sap, silver nitrate that burns the back of my throat like ammonia, the sharp tang of fear under it all. I don’t reach for the panic button under the board. The part-timer running the board overnight is 19, wears cat ear headphones, brings matcha lattes in a Hello Kitty tumbler. She doesn’t deserve to get caught in this.
“Cute. You gonna monologue, or you gonna take the shot?” I lean back in the chair, spin it slow so I’m facing the window, eyes picking out the glint of a scope in the third-floor window, right where he said. “For the record? Those dealers were selling fentanyl laced with wolfsbane to kids. Two 14-year-olds ended up in the ER. One didn’t make it. You gonna stand there and tell me you’d have done different?”
He laughs. It sounds broken. “My partner was on that raid. He didn’t know what you were. Tried to tase you. You ripped his throat out.”
The memory hits sharp, metallic: the crackle of a taser, the burn of electricity up my spine, the shift taking over before I could stop it, the hot spray of blood across my face. I’d thrown up for an hour after, in the ditch off the highway, fur matted with mud and regret. I’d left his badge on the steps of the sheriff’s office at dawn, polished, a $20 tucked under it for the coffee he’d never get to drink.
“I remember,” I say, quieter now, so quiet the mic almost doesn’t pick it up. “I’m sorry.”
The line goes dead. For ten seconds I stare at the scope glint, waiting for the silver to come through the window, waiting for the burn in my chest, the end of all the late nights and bad coffee and hiding.
Then my phone buzzes in my jeans pocket. Text from an unknown number.
Next full moon. We finish this. Don’t run.
I look back at the window. The glint is gone. I slide the fader up for the next track—some old Johnny Cash, the one about the beast in every man—and scratch the fur on my wrist again. The shift itches worse now.
The night’s just getting started.

title: spy|a British agent plays baccarat against a man who is financing an enemy network
text:
The velvet curtains at Crockfords were drawn against the Mayfair rain, which meant Harry couldn't see the clock and couldn't see the door. He could see, across the baize, the careful hands of Dmitri Vasiliev arranging a tower of plaques with the patience of a man building a tomb.

There were four of them at the table. A wine merchant from Bordeaux who'd lost steadily since eleven. A quiet woman in green who'd played nothing all night. The banker. And Harry, who was meant to be a property developer from Aberdeen named Alec Burns, currently down thirty-two thousand pounds and working very hard to look like it.

"Banco," Harry said.

Vasiliev's eyes moved up. They were pale grey, the colour of winter harbour water, and they had the annoying habit of lingering a beat too long, as though deciding whether a person was worth the candle.

"Mr Burns is feeling brave," Vasiliev said. His English was excellent, barely accented; the accent came out only on certain consonants, like a seam in a tailored coat.

"Brave's one word." Harry tapped the table. "Dealer?"

The croupier dealt. Harry took his cards in one smooth motion, thumb passing over the faces. A seven and a queen. Seven. He sat back, let his jaw loosen, tried to broadcast the specific confusion of a man holding a decent hand with more money on it than he could afford.

Vasiliev looked at his two cards, then at Harry, then asked for a third. The five slid out. Harry watched the shoulders settle. Not enough. Or exactly enough. The man financed three networks across the Baltic by routing payments through a Greek shipping office and a restaurant in Finchley; he could keep a secret from his face.

"Card," Harry said, because seven was a graveyard hand and the math, at least, was honest.

The croupier flipped a deuce. Nine.

"Nine," the croupier announced.

Vasiliev showed six. The Bordeaux merchant exhaled for both of them, as if he'd personally been saved.

The plaques crossed the table. Harry let out a laugh that was mostly genuine. "Maybe I'll buy Aberdeen after all."

"Property is a comforting fantasy," Vasiliev said. "Men like us prefer things we can sell tomorrow."

"That why you're in shipping?"

The grey eyes sharpened. "Who says I am in shipping?"

"Your friend Nico. At the bar last week." Harry stacked his plaques with clumsy fingers. "Talkative after a couple of brandies. Says you move more containers than God."

"Nico also says he once played golf with Sean Connery." Vasiliev smiled, but it didn't reach anywhere useful. "One must discount Nico."

"Fair." Harry took a sip of his tonic water. No lemon, no gin; the gin was the prop, the tonic was the truth. "Still. Useful, containers. You can put anything in them."

"Even money," Vasiliev said, with the faintest edge, "can be put in a container. Though why one would, when a bank exists, I do not know."

"Banks ask questions."

"Not the right ones, Mr Burns. Never the right ones."

The woman in green folded. The wine merchant, blinking at his watch, begged mercy for the night. Suddenly it was heads-up, which was not what the room had planned, and Harry felt the old tightness in his ribs—the one he got when an operation slipped sideways into something more useful.

"Banco," he said again.

Vasiliev studied him. "You are chasing or you are confident. With you, I cannot decide."

"Maybe neither. Maybe I'm just a wanker with a run."

"A self-aware wanker. Dangerous."

This time Harry drew two court cards. Zero. He asked for a third and took a six, feeling the card's edge like a small knife. Vasiliev asked for nothing, which meant eight or nine or a lie performed with perfect posture.

"Eight," said Vasiliev, turning them.

Harry turned his six. The table took the rest.

"Not dangerous, then," Vasiliev murmured.

"Everyone's dangerous for twenty minutes." Harry reached for his wallet, letting the gesture carry just enough bruised pride. "Listen. I'm in Finchley Thursday. A little restaurant Nico swears by—your sort of crowd, apparently. Worth it?"

For a long moment Vasiliev said nothing. Outside, a taxi hissed past the black windows.

"The moussaka is acceptable," he said finally. "The back room is for regulars."

"Would I be a regular?"

"You might be introduced." He signalled the croupier. "If Nico vouches for you. Though I repeat—one must discount Nico."

"Then you'll have to vouch yourself." Harry stood, buttoning his jacket. "Seven o'clock. I'll buy the wine."

"I do not drink with men I meet at tables."

"You've been drinking with me for three hours."

Vasiliev laughed, quietly. "So I have."

Harry walked out into the rain with his pockets lighter and his phone recording the night from its dead-man's slot inside his sleeve. Behind him, through the glass, Vasiliev was already stacking plaques again, building patiently, looking at no one.

title: young adult|a boy genius criminal mastermind negotiates with fairy police to rescue his father
text:
The holding cell they’d stuck me in smelled like rain-soaked clover and static, the kind that makes your hair stand up when you’re six inches from a Tesla coil. I counted the rivets in the brushed-titanium wall for the seventh time—147, if you’re curious—when the lock hissed open. I didn’t bother standing. I knew who it was.
“Artemis Fowl,” said Holly Short, her voice tight enough to pluck a note from. She was still in her LEP recon suit, the elbow of her left sleeve crusted with the tunnel muck she’d picked up chasing me through the Tara cave system three hours prior. Her wings were folded tight against her back, neutrino holstered but unclipped, like she thought I might lunge across the two-foot gap between the bench and the door. “You wanted to negotiate.”
I laced my fingers across my chest, letting one eyebrow lift just enough to let her know I wasn’t impressed. “I wanted to negotiate forty-five minutes ago. I assume Commander Root took that long to stop screaming about ‘insolent mud children’ long enough to authorize you to speak to me?”
Her jaw tightened. Score one for me. I’d run the probability calculations while I waited: 78% chance they’d send Short, not Root. The commander was too likely to pop a blood vessel and shoot me before we got to terms, and they knew it. Short was the reasonable one. Or as reasonable as an elf with a buzz cut and a permanent grudge against humans could be, anyway.
“Don’t look so smug,” she said, stepping inside and letting the door slide shut behind her. The cell’s fairy-tech shield hummed up, blocking us from whatever bugs or listening devices the LEP techs had planted in the walls. Not that they’d have been able to pick up my plans anyway— I’d spent the last hour running a low-level jammer from the modified phone I’d sewn into the lining of my suit jacket. They thought it was just a useless hunk of human plastic. Cute. “You’re in no position to be smug. We have you on trespassing, theft of fairy technology, attempted kidnapping of a lower Elements operative—”
“All of which I will happily plead guilty to,” I cut in, “if you help me get my father back.”
That stopped her. She blinked, the irises of her eyes the exact color of the hazelnuts my father used to bring back from business trips to Georgia, before he’d vanished off the coast of Murmansk three months prior. I’d been twelve for seventeen days when the ransom note came, the criminals who’d taken him demanding a hundred million euro in unmarked bills, proof of life footage cut so short I could barely tell the man in the video was him. The human police had called it a lost cause. Interpol had stopped returning my mother’s calls. So I’d done what I always did: I’d found a bigger, better-equipped police force. One with magic, and guns that could shoot through steel, and a vested interest in keeping human and fairy worlds separate.
Wait, the voice in my head— the part that sounded like my old bodyguard Butler, when he was telling me I was being an idiot— cut in. Don’t lead with the sentiment. They don’t care about sentiment. They care about leverage.
I leaned forward, letting my hands drop to my knees, letting the mask of the cold, calculating criminal mastermind slip just enough to let her see the edge of the kid underneath, the one who’d sat up for 72 straight hours tracking his dad’s cell signal until his eyes burned. But not too much. I couldn’t let her think I was weak. Weakness got you killed, in negotiations. Weakness got your dad left to freeze in an Arctic shipping container.
“Here’s the deal,” I said, before she could ask for details. “The Russian mafia that has my father? They’re sitting on a stockpile of old Soviet nuclear waste, two miles outside Murmansk. They’re planning to drill down into the fairy mantle next month, blow the waste into your tunnels, and hold Haven City for ransom. They don’t know you exist yet, but they will. They’ve already got a fairy defector feeding them intel— a dwarf by the name of Mulch Diggums, if you know him. I can give you his exact location, the blueprints for their drill, the access codes to their communication network. All of it. In exchange, you help me get my father out before they figure out I’m onto them and kill him.”
Short stared at me for a long beat. I could see the math playing out behind her eyes, same as it had played out in mine: 12-year-old human genius, showing up on their doorstep with intel so specific it couldn’t be a bluff, offering to take out a threat to their entire civilization for the low, low price of one rescued Irish businessman.
“You’re bluffing,” she said, but her voice wavered.
I pulled a folded slip of paper out of my pocket, slid it across the floor to her. It was a copy of the drill schematic I’d hacked from the Russians’ server two weeks prior, stamped with their military insignia, marked with the exact depth of the fairy mantle below their drill site. She picked it up, unfolded it, and her face went pale.
“Am I?” I said.
The static in the cell hummed louder. Somewhere down the hall, I heard Root roar my name. Short didn’t look away from the paper.
“Start talking,” she said.
I smiled. Just a small one. Phase one complete.
