title: mystery|a Venetian police commissario questions a widow who seems relieved rather than grieving
text:
The Widow at Caffè Florian

The rain came down in thin gray needles over the Piazza San Marco, turning the stones the color of old bone. Commissario Marco Trentin pulled his coat tighter and watched the widow through the café window before going in. She was sitting with her back to the glass, one hand resting easy on the tablecloth, the other turning a demitasse in slow circles. Not the hand of a woman who'd buried her husband fourteen hours ago.

He pushed through the door. The café was nearly empty—a German couple arguing in low voices near the bar, a waiter polishing silver with the resigned concentration of a man who'd done it for thirty years. The music from the small orchestra had stopped for the season, leaving the room too quiet, too ornate, all gilt and faded velvet like a theater between shows.

"Signora Zanon."

She looked up. Middle-forties, dark hair pulled back with a tortoiseshell clip, a small scar at the corner of her left eyebrow. Her eyes were dry. More than dry—they were *present*, the way people's eyes are when they've stopped waiting for something.

"Commissario." She gestured to the chair across from her. "Please. I ordered coffee, but I can ask for another cup."

Trentin sat. He set his notebook on the table but didn't open it. "I'm sorry for your loss."

A flicker crossed her face, gone before he could name it. Not grief. Something closer to embarrassment, as though he'd congratulated her by mistake.

"Are you?" she said.

It wasn't sharp. That was the strange part. She said it mildly, almost kindly, the way you'd correct a child who'd thanked you for a gift you hadn't given.

The waiter came over. Trentin shook his head at the offer of coffee. When they were alone again, he said, "Your husband was found at the bottom of the stairs leading to the canal entrance. Near the Ponte dei Sospiri. You know this."

"I know what you told me on the telephone."

"Had he been drinking?"

"Enzo?" The faintest smile. "Only wine at dinner. He wasn't a man for excess."

"Except when it came to business, perhaps."

She turned the cup again. Outside, a gull cried, harsh and stupid. "You've been talking to people."

"It's my job to talk to people, signora. His partner, Signor Bellini, seemed quite shaken. Kept saying something about documents. About a shipment from Murano that didn't arrive."

"Bellini is a frightened little man who sees trouble in every fogbank." She lifted her coffee, drank, set it down precisely. "Enzo handled the books. I didn't involve myself."

"Then you won't mind telling me where you were between ten and midnight."

"Here. More or less." She glanced around the café. "I walked. From the apartment in Dorsoduro, across the Accademia—before the rain started, or just as. I sat here for a while. Then I walked home."

"Alone?"

"Alone."

"Someone would remember."

"Perhaps. The waiter at the bar, maybe. I don't know his name." She paused. "I wasn't keeping track, Commissario. I had no reason to think I'd need an alibi."

He opened the notebook then, mostly to give his hands something to do. He wrote *Accademia, 10-ish* and knew even as he formed the letters that it was useless. The city kept no honest time after dark. A hundred bridges, a thousand narrow calle, fog coming off the water like it owned the place.

"Your husband was a strong swimmer," Trentin said.

It was a guess. The medical examiner hadn't finished, and the canal at that hour was cold enough to stop a man's heart whether he could swim or not. But he watched her.

"He hated the water," she said. "Funny, for a Venetian. He took the vaporetto like everyone else, but he never learned. He'd have drowned in a bathtub if he could." She said it flatly, then added, as if remembering herself, "It's a terrible thing to say."

"Did you love him?"

The question landed without echo. She didn't recoil. She studied him for a long moment, and in it he saw something he recognized—not calculation, but weariness, the tiredness of a person deciding whether to keep performing or finally stop.

"We were married nineteen years," she said. "I was twenty-three when we met. He sold my father's glass, back before the war, before everything. My mother thought I'd landed well." She looked past him, toward the window where the rain made streaks against the light. "You ask if I loved him. I think I did, at the start. Or I thought love was supposed to feel like that—quiet, a little dull. Like being given a house you didn't choose and learning to live in its rooms."

"And later?"

"Later I learned the house had locks on the inside."

Trentin waited.

She didn't go on. Instead she picked up her handbag—a plain black thing, scuffed at the corners—and set it in her lap. "He wasn't a monster, if that's what you're after. He never struck me. He never shouted, even. He just… made the world smaller. One friend at a time. One trip, one letter, one hour outside the apartment. Until the world was exactly the size of whatever he permitted." Her voice hadn't risen. "So if you're waiting for me to cry, Commissario, I should tell you I tried last night. I sat on the edge of the bed and I tried, and what came instead was—" She stopped, pressed her lips together. "It wasn't grief. I'm not a good enough liar to pretend it was."

The waiter dropped a spoon somewhere. It rang against the tile.

Trentin closed the notebook. "Did you kill him, signora?"

"No." She met his eyes. "But if I tell you I'm sorry he's dead, I'll be lying, and I think we've both had enough of that for one day."

He believed her. About the lying, anyway. The rest—the walk, the rain, the alibi that dissolved like sugar in water—he'd have to find out the hard way, the way you found everything in this city: slowly, and against the current.

He stood up, put on his hat. "Don't leave Venice."

"Where would I go?" she said, and for the first time she almost smiled. "For the first time in twenty years, I can stay."

Outside, the rain had thinned to mist. Trentin lit a cigarette and stood looking out at the flooded edge of the piazza, where the water made a false second city beneath his feet. Somewhere a bell began to ring, off by half a minute, and no one bothered to correct it.

title: young adult|a boy genius criminal mastermind negotiates with fairy police to rescue his father
text:
The rain soaked through Artemis Fowl’s tailored charcoal blazer before he even reached the moss-choked stone circle at the edge of the fairy ringfort, but he didn’t shiver. At twelve, he already knew that displays of discomfort were leverage handed to your opponent. The redcap guards flanking the clearing had pikes tipped with iron, their knuckles crusted with old blood, but they tensed when he tossed a crumpled black velvet pouch at their feet. It clinked with solid gold ingots, smelted to fairy purity standards.
“Tell Commander Root I’m here to trade. Not to fight.”
Ten minutes later, the ground rippled like disturbed water, and Holly Short materialized first, her LEP patrol suit streaked with mud, Neutrino 3000 holstered but unclipped at her hip. Behind her, Julius Root’s face was the color of overripe beetroot, his cigar clamped so tight between his teeth the end flared bright enough to cast orange light on the ferns.
“Fowl,” Root barked, smoke curling out of his nostrils. “I ought to lock you in a goblin cell for the ATM hack you pulled last month. You’ve got ten seconds before I order my men to put a sleep round in your shoulder.”
Artemis adjusted his wire-rimmed glasses, his expression so neutral it bordered on bored. “You won’t. Because you know I’m the only person on this planet who can trace the missing shipment of solar batteries your goblin task force lost last week to the B’wa Kell smuggling ring. I already have the coordinates. They’re buried under a disused sheep pen in County Kerry, rigged to blow if anyone without goblin blood gets within ten feet.”
Holly stepped forward, her pointed ears twitching. “You set that up. You tipped the smugglers off to the raid route three days ago, didn’t you?”
“Of course I did.” Artemis didn’t blink. “I needed leverage. You have my father. Held in the lower levels of Howler’s Peak, if my sources are correct. The goblins grabbed him three months ago when he tried to cut a deal to trade fairy tech for the release of their imprisoned clan chief, and you’ve been holding him as a material witness ever since. You’re not charging him. You’re just keeping him locked up because you’re scared he’ll tell human authorities the People exist.”
Root’s jaw tightened. “Your father’s a thief, Fowl. He broke every fairy secrecy law on the books the second he set foot in our tunnels.”
“He’s an idiot.” The words came out sharper than Artemis intended, and he saw Holly’s eyebrows lift, so he softened his tone just enough to sound human, not cold. “He thought he could make a deal with goblins without getting double-crossed. That’s his mistake. But he’s my idiot. And I’m not leaving here without him.”
He pulled a slim silver hard drive from his pocket, held it up between two fingers. “On here: every smuggling route the B’wa Kell has used in the last two years, the names of every LEP officer on their payroll, the disarm code for those batteries in Kerry, and a virus I wrote that will wipe every fairy-related file off every human law enforcement server on the planet within 72 hours—including the ones your rogue dwarf informant sold to Interpol last spring. If I walk out of here with my father in one piece, you get the drive, the disarm code, and I will never step foot in a fairy tunnel or trade fairy technology for as long as I live. If you don’t?”
He smiled, thin and sharp, the kind of smile that made even battle-hardened LEP officers take a half-step back.
“I’ll remotely trigger those batteries in two hours. The blast will take out three miles of farmland, blow a hole straight through the top of your smuggling tunnel network, and every news crew in Ireland will be there filming it before your shield generators boot up. Secrecy will be gone. You’ll spend the next hundred years running from human scientists with nets and lab coats. And I’ll be long gone, sipping hot chocolate in my private jet, watching the whole thing on CNN.”
Holly’s hand flew to her Neutrino. “You wouldn’t.”
“Try me.” Artemis held her gaze, no trace of bluff in his pale blue eyes. “I’m twelve years old. I don’t care about your rules. I care about my father. You have ten minutes to bring him to the surface. If he has so much as a scratch on him, the deal’s off. If you try to trick me, the deal’s off. If you waste time posturing? The deal’s off.”
Root stared at him for a long, silent minute, then spat his cigar into the mud, grinding it under his boot. “You’re a little monster, Fowl.”
Artemis’s smile didn’t waver. “I’m a businessman. And right now, you can’t afford to turn down my offer.”
The air hummed with magic for three minutes before the grass rippled again, and two elves dragged a disheveled man in a tattered suit to the surface, his wrists bound with fairy rope, a bruise darkening his left jaw. Artemis Fowl Sr. blinked against the rain, squinting at his son like he thought he was hallucinating.
“Arty?”
Artemis slipped the hard drive back into his pocket, tossing a small vial of memory-wipe serum at Root’s feet as he stepped forward to cut his father’s bonds with a pocket knife. “Standard dose for the guards who saw him. No loose ends. Pleasure doing business with you, Commander.”
As he slung his father’s arm over his shoulder and turned toward the treeline where his driver waited, he heard Holly mutter under her breath, loud enough for his enhanced hearing to pick up: “That kid’s going to be the death of us.”
Artemis didn’t look back. He just adjusted his father’s collar against the rain, and kept walking. For once, he’d won fair and square. Well. As fair as negotiations with fairy police ever got.

title: fantasy|a disgraced court mage is summoned back to save the prince who exiled her
text:
The iron door groaned on rusted hinges. Maren didn't look up from the stew she wasn't eating.

"You've got nerve coming here," she said.

Captain Rill stepped into the hovel, mud-caked and breathing hard. He'd been handsome once. Court life had sanded him smooth. Now something harder showed through, like grain in worn wood.

"The prince is dying."

Maren's spoon scraped the bowl. "Lots of people are dying. Mostly because of him."

"The wasting curse. Black veins at the throat, fever that won't break. His own mages can't touch it." Rill hesitated. "He asked for you. By name."

That got her attention. She lifted her head. Three years in this hole had carved her face thin, and the exile's brand had faded to a silver knot between her thumb and forefinger. She flexed the hand out of habit.

"Kael asked for me." She almost laughed. "The man who called my work rot. Who stood silent while they burned my books and marched me out barefoot in winter."

"I'm not here to defend him." Rill's jaw tightened. "I'm here because the healers give him two days. And whatever he did to you, he's still the heir. The kingdom without him—you know what comes after. Vane holds the eastern army. You think Kael was cruel?"

She did know. She'd treated refugees from Vane's border campaigns. Farmers missing hands. Children who didn't speak anymore.

Maren pushed the bowl away and stood. Her knees ached. Everything ached out here, where the damp got into the walls and the walls got into you.

"What's in it for me?"

"A full pardon. Restoration of rank."

"Don't want rank." She crossed to the shelf where a single locked box sat, gray with dust. "I want the charter back. The one permitting independent practitioners. The one he revoked to make an example of me."

Rill blinked. "That's a council matter."

"Then go wake the council. I'm not lifting a finger for another funeral unless every hedge-witch and hedge-wizard in this kingdom can work without looking over their shoulder." Her eyes held his. "Your prince can sign it on his sickbed. Or he can die on it. Either works for me."

The silence stretched. Rain ticked the thatch.

"Done," Rill said at last. "I'll answer for it."

"You'll answer for a lot before this is over." She opened the box. Inside, wrapped in oilcloth, lay her old implements—knife, needle, a clay vial stoppered with wax. And beneath those, something she'd never shown the court: a blackened shard of bone that hummed faintly even through its wrappings.

Rill saw it and paled. "That's grave-work."

"It's curse-work. There's a difference, and the difference is why your polished mages are useless right now." She rewrapped the bundle and slung it into a worn satchel. "A wasting curse doesn't grow on its own. Somebody planted it. Somebody close enough to feed it every day."

"You're saying it's someone in the palace."

"I'm saying your prince made a lot of enemies, and at least one of them knows what they're doing." She shouldered past him into the rain. It hit cold and hard, plastering her gray hair to her neck. "Now move. Two days is generous, and I want to see the color of those veins before dawn."

The horses were miserable, half-wild things kept at the edge of the village. Maren mounted without grace and didn't care. Behind her, Rill gathered his reins.

"Maren," he said quietly. "If this works... he may not remember it kindly. Being saved by the person he ruined."

She heeled her horse forward, hooves sucking in the mire of the single road. Over her shoulder, her voice came flat as a blade.

"Then he and I have something in common."

They rode east as the last light failed, toward the glow of a city that had forgotten her name, and the dying man who'd had three years to regret learning it.

title: historical|a codebreaker in 1942 notices a pattern in intercepted Japanese messages that nobody believes
text:
The linoleum in Station HYOP’s basement stuck to the rubber soles of Dot Voss’s shoes as she carried her third mug of burnt coffee back to her desk, the overhead fluorescent buzzing so loud it had started to match the throb behind her eyes. It was 2:17 a.m. on October 12, 1942, three months since she’d left her math PhD program at Radcliffe to lie about her typing speed and talk her way into the Navy’s codebreaking unit, where the men who ran the shop still thought the women in the back room were just there to file intercepts and fill coffee cups.
Her desk was stacked three feet high with flimsy yellow intercept slips, smudged from carbon paper, each one a fragment of Japanese naval radio traffic pulled from the airwaves over the Pacific. For three weeks, she’d been picking at a thread no one else had bothered to tug: every reference to a target the cryptanalysts had written off as a ruse, a fake buildup to draw the Pacific Fleet away from the Solomons, carried the same tiny, unremarkable detail.
She leaned in, flipping between slips, her pencil hovering over the grid she’d scribbled on a scrap of graph paper. There it was: the weather report appended to each message referencing “AF”—the designation the team had spent months arguing over—cited a barometric pressure reading that matched nothing in the central Solomons, nothing in the Aleutians, where the brass insisted the next Japanese strike would land. It matched the three-day-old readings she’d cross-referenced from the old Pan Am clipper weather logs she’d dug out of a storage closet, the logs the pilots had used to refuel at a tiny atoll 1,200 miles northwest of Hawaii.
“Dot. If you squint at those slips any harder you’ll burn holes right through them.”
Lieutenant Joe Harlow leaned against the edge of her desk, his uniform crumpled, a half-smoked cigarette hanging from his lip. He was one of the better ones, the ones who didn’t automatically dismiss her out of hand, but he’d pulled three straight shifts too, and his patience was frayed thin.
“It’s Midway,” she said, not looking up, tapping the graph paper. “Everyone’s saying AF is a feint, that the Japs are going for Alaska, but look—every message tagged AF has a pressure reading 10 millibars lower than the Solomons front, wind out of the northeast at 12 knots. That’s not Alaska in October. That’s the edge of that stationary low sitting 300 miles east of Midway right now. The commercial pilots used to log those exact readings on the Hawaii run, I checked the old Pan Am files.”
Joe sighed, tapping ash into her empty coffee mug. “We’ve been over this. The weather codes are too garbled to cross-reference, OP-20-G ran their models last week, they’ve got the strike force mapped to the Aleutians. The brass up at Pearl are already moving three destroyers north to meet them.”
“The models are wrong because they’re treating the weather tags as noise.” Dot pushed her chair back, grabbing a stack of intercepts, and followed him to the bank of code machines where the senior analysts clustered around a map of the North Pacific. “Look at this one, from the 10th: the refueling coordinates for the strike group’s screen are 700 miles east of the AF marker. If AF was in the Aleutians, that puts them in the middle of the Bering Sea, where there’s no fuel caches, no resupply. But if AF is Midway? That coordinate is exactly where the fleet tankers were spotted by a patrol plane last Tuesday. The Japs aren’t faking it—they’re committing their whole carrier group.”
The room went quiet for half a second before Ted Rowe, the senior civilian cryptanalyst who’d spent 20 years in the Navy before the war, snickered, leaning back in his chair. “Nice work, sweetheart. You run that by your girls in the typing pool before you brought it up here? We don’t plan battle strategy off barometer readings. The Japs are deliberately seeding garbage into the traffic to throw girls like you off the scent.”
Heat crawled up Dot’s neck, but she didn’t step back, slamming the intercepts down on the map. “Then what about the water desalination report? Last week the Midway garrison sent a fake message in the clear saying their distillation plant was broken, that they were down to two days of fresh water. Forty-eight hours later, there’s an intercept from the Jap submarine picket line reporting the target was short on water. That wasn’t a feint. They were watching Midway.”
Joe froze mid-drag on his cigarette. Rowe’s smile dropped. For a long moment the only sound was the buzz of the lights, the clatter of a teletype machine in the other room.
Before anyone could speak, the teletype operator stuck his head around the door, his face pale. “Flash from Pearl. Patrol plane just spotted a Japanese carrier strike group 600 miles out from Midway, bearing southeast. They want every analyst on the line five minutes ago.”
Dot stood there, her pencil still in her hand, as the room erupted into movement, men scrambling for phones, knocking over coffee mugs, shouting for coordinates. Joe looked over at her, his eyes wide, and nodded at the map.
“Better grab your intercepts,” he said. “You’ve got a call with Nimitz’s staff in ten minutes.”
She didn’t move for a second, staring at the little pin she’d stuck in the atoll three nights before, the one everyone had told her to take down. Outside, the first gray light of dawn was seeping through the basement’s high, barred windows, and somewhere far down the hall a siren started to wail.

title: legal thriller|a public defender realises her client's alibi witness is lying to protect someone else
text:
I knew before the words reached across the table that the witness was lying. Not because of a tell, exactly—there was no dramatic tic, no sudden fascination with the scuffed linoleum. It was smaller than that. It was the way Marcus Beale settled into his story like a man who had rehearsed it in a mirror until it fit.

“You sure this is the room?” I asked.

He glanced around the attorney–client meeting room as if seeing it for the first time: cinder blocks, metal table, camera in the corner blinking red to tell us we were being recorded. The jail had no interest in making anyone comfortable. Comfort made clients talk. Comfort made witnesses honest.

“I’m sure,” Marcus said. “Back booth at Mabel’s. Eleven, maybe eleven fifteen. He sat down across from me, ordered coffee, complained the pie was stale. Your boy was there, Counselor. All night, far as I know.”

My boy was Damon Quill, twenty-one, charged with felony murder for the shooting of a convenience store clerk. The security footage was grainy, the getaway car had been stolen, and the person who’d called 911 remembered a hoodie, not a face. The case was thin enough to snap, which meant an alibi should have felt like rain after drought.

Instead, my stomach turned over.

I made myself write it down anyway. *Mabel’s Diner. Back booth. 11:00–1:00 a.m.* My pen scratched too loud in the little room.

“Describe the booth,” I said.

Marcus’s eyebrows drew together. “Why?”

“Humor me.”

“Vinyl. Red, maybe. One of them lights hanging over the table.” He shrugged. “It’s a diner.”

Mabel’s booths were blue. I knew because I’d eaten there Sunday with my investigator, grease congealing on my eggs while she showed me photos of the place. Blue vinyl, neon beer signs despite no liquor license, and a front counter where every seat faced the door. There was one back booth, but it sat beside a shattered gumball machine that had been empty for years.

Maybe he hadn’t noticed. Maybe adrenaline made people careless.

Maybe I wanted to believe him because Damon was facing life in prison, and I was tired of standing in courtrooms while kids became numbers on a docket.

“Did you talk to anyone else?” I asked.

“Nah.”

“Waitress?”

“Some girl.”

“Name?”

“I don’t know. Blonde, I think. Short.”

The only server on shift that night was a gray-haired man named Hector. I had his timecard in my bag, along with Mabel’s statement that Damon had not been in the diner.

I kept my face still. That was the first lesson in this job after the idealism wore off: don’t flinch when the story rots underneath you.

Marcus leaned forward, earnest now. “Look, Ms. Reeves, I get why you’re pressing. But I was there. So was he. Ain’t no confusion about it.”

There it was again—not hesitation, but performance. He answered too cleanly, as though each sentence had been sanded free of the edges that make memory believable. Real witnesses contradict themselves. They say, “I think,” then, “No, wait,” then, “Why does that matter?” They don’t hand you a block of polished prose.

I thought of Damon in the holding cell that morning, hollow-eyed, his knee bouncing beneath the table.

*He’ll come through,* Damon had said. *Marcus owes me.*

“Owes you what?” I’d asked.

Damon had pressed his mouth shut so hard his lips whitened. “Just talk to him.”

Now, watching Marcus fold his hands on the table, I understood what my client couldn’t say.

“Who asked you to do this?” I said.

His jaw tightened. “Nobody asked me.”

“Damon?”

“I’m telling you what happened.”

“Marcus.” I closed the notepad. “Hector was the server. The booths are blue. Mabel swears Damon wasn’t there. If I put you on that stand and you say this, the prosecutor is going to carve you into pieces. Then she’ll use the pieces to bury my client.”

For the first time, anger flashed across his face. “So that’s it? You just gonna let him take this charge?”

“I’m going to defend him. I’m not going to suborn perjury.”

“Perjury.” He laughed, but it had no humor. “Y’all got words for everything until it’s somebody you love sitting in that cage.”

Love, then. Not debt. Not loyalty to Damon.

I studied him: the ink-dark prison tattoo peeking from his cuff, the frayed cuff of his coat, the fear held stubbornly behind his eyes. This wasn’t a man protecting himself. If it were only him, he’d have bolted by now. He’d have slurred the details, admitted uncertainty, given himself an exit.

But there was no exit in his story.

“Who is it?” I asked quietly.

“Don’t.”

“Brother? Cousin?”

His silence answered.

“Your son,” I said.

Marcus looked away.

The room seemed to shrink, the walls pressing in with all the quiet weight of it. If Marcus was lying to protect his son, then the son mattered to the night of the murder. Maybe he was the shooter. Maybe he was the driver. Maybe he’d run to his father with blood on his shirt and a desperate, impossible request.

And Damon knew.

That was the thing that sickened me most. Damon knew the alibi was false, and he’d let me walk toward it anyway because some loyalties ran deeper than fear.

“Where was your son between eleven and one that night?” I asked.

Marcus’s voice dropped. “I’m not saying another word.”

“You could be charged.”

“Then charge me.”

“That won’t save him.”

He stood, chair scraping against the floor. “Neither will you.”

The guard opened the door a moment later, and Marcus walked out with his shoulders squared, already carrying the secret like a sentence. I stayed seated, staring at my notes, the neat blue lines suddenly useless.

Somewhere in the building, Damon was waiting for hope.

And I had just learned the truth wore someone else’s face.

title: literary|an old woman tells a police officer the true story of the night her husband died
text:
The rain had turned the gravel drive to slurry by the time Officer Hale pushed through the screen door, its rusted spring whimpering a complaint that matched the hunch of the woman in the ladder-back chair by the cold hearth. Elspeth Voss was seventy-eight if she was a day, her hands knotted around a chipped ceramic mug that held nothing but rainwater she’d caught an hour prior, when the gutters finally gave out. The coroner had ruled Tom Voss’s death a hunting accident three weeks prior—slip on wet leaves, shotgun misfire, closed casket, the whole tidy small-town verdict—but Hale had driven out twice already, nagged by the way the slug had entered Tom’s chest at an angle no man could manage tripping over his own boots.

“You didn’t drive out here in this to ask if I remembered to lock the gun cabinet,” Elspeth said, not looking up. Her voice was like crumpled linen, soft but frayed at the edges, sharp enough to catch if you pulled too hard. Hale pulled off his dripping cap, set it on the edge of the oak table where a half-carved wren sat next to Tom’s whittling knife, the blade still crusted with pine resin.
“Coroner’s report came back amended,” he said. “Powder burns say the gun was fired from three feet away. Not point-blank. Not a fall.”
Elspeth’s thumb stroked the chip in her mug, the crack that ran from rim to base, glued shut with pine sap the winter Tom got snowed in for twelve days and they’d burned the kitchen chairs to stay warm. “You want the truth that fits in your report, or the one that stays in this house when you drive back down the mountain?”
Hale pulled out the chair across from her. The seat still had the indent of Tom’s broad frame, worn smooth over fifty-two years of sitting there to lace his boots, to shell pecans, to hold her hand when their son’s helicopter went down in Kuwait. “I want the one that doesn’t keep you up at night.”
She laughed then, a thin, reedy sound that made the tabby cat curled on the windowsill lift its head. “Tom was up that night long before the rain started. Knew it was coming, said his knee ached like the devil himself was twisting it. He pulled his old hunting coat out—the one with the tear in the elbow I mended with feed sack fabric, the frayed cuffs he refused to let me replace—said he had to go check on the henhouse, said a fox had been circling for three days. I knew he was lying. Could always tell, when he lied. He’d scratch the left corner of his mouth, same as he did when he told me he’d quit chewing tobacco, same as he told me the tumor in his lung wasn’t nothing but a smoker’s cough.”
She paused, lifted the mug to her lips, sipped the rainwater like it was bourbon, and didn’t flinch. “I followed him out ten minutes later, boots caked in mud, the flashlight he’d given me for our twentieth anniversary flickering so bad I could barely see the path up to the oak stand. He wasn’t at the henhouse. He was standing at the edge of the bluff, the shotgun propped against his hip, and for a second I thought he was just watching the storm roll in, the way he liked to, said lightning over the valley looked like God striking matches. Then I saw his hand shake. I saw him fumble the safety off. I yelled. I yelled so loud the crows took off from the treetops, and he turned, and his boot slipped on that slick moss he’d been meaning to scrape off the rock for two years, and the gun went off.”
Hale leaned forward. “Mrs. Voss, the angle—”
“I was three feet away,” she said, and finally lifted her eyes to his. They were the color of storm clouds, not faded, not watery, sharp as the shards of a canning jar she’d dropped the summer they put up forty quarts of peaches. “When he slipped, he didn’t fall backward off the bluff. He fell forward, right toward me, and the gun was still in his hand, and I grabbed for the barrel. I grabbed it hard, and I pushed. Not hard enough to hurt him. Just hard enough to keep him from tumbling right into me, hard enough to make sure he didn’t pull the trigger again when he hit the ground. But the moss was slicker than I remembered. His boot slid out from under him again, and he went down, and the gun went off, and the sound was so loud my ears rang for three days after.”
Her fingers uncurled from the mug, and Hale saw the faint burn scar snaking across her left palm, still pink at the edges, the kind of scar you get when you grab a hot gun barrel. “You thought he was going to shoot himself,” he said, quiet, like he was afraid to break the hush that had fallen over the room, the only sound the rain lashing the windows and the cat’s soft purr.
Elspeth nodded, slow. “The doctor told him two weeks prior the cancer was in his bones. Said he’d be bedridden by Christmas, in so much pain morphine wouldn’t touch it. He didn’t tell me. Thought I couldn’t handle it, after Jamie. Thought if he did it out in the woods, they’d call it an accident, and I’d get the insurance money, and I wouldn’t have to watch him waste away. I didn’t tell the coroner I was there. Because he wanted that story. He wanted me to have that easy, soft story, the one where he went out quick, doing what he loved, not the one where he was so scared of being a burden he’d walk up a mountain in the rain with a gun he hadn’t cleaned in a year.”
She reached across the table, brushed the half-carved wren with her knuckle. “When I grabbed that barrel, I didn’t push it away from me. I pushed it toward him. Because I knew. I knew if I didn’t, he’d pull the trigger again, once he got his balance, and he’d do it right, and I’d have to walk back down this mountain alone without even the chance to tell him I’d have sat by that bed for every last minute of the pain, if it meant I got one more day of him scratching that left corner of his mouth when he lied about burning the toast.”
Hale sat there for a long time, the rain drumming on the roof, the scar on her palm pale in the faint gray light seeping through the window. He thought of the coroner’s report, of the way the whole town had talked about what a good man Tom Voss was, how he’d helped every neighbor rebuild their barn after the tornado, how he’d left jars of honey on every porch in the holler every fall.
“Your boot prints,” he said finally. “They were all over the rock. I saw them the first day I came out.”
Elspeth smiled, a small, wobbly thing, and pushed a chipped jar of peaches across the table toward him, sealed with wax, the label scrawled in Tom’s messy handwriting. “I know. I waited for you to ask. You want a slice? We put these up the day before he went to the doctor. He ate half a jar straight from the pot, said store-bought never tasted half as sweet.”
Outside, the thunder rumbled closer, and the screen door whined on its hinge as the wind picked up, and for a second Hale swore he could smell pine and tobacco and peaches, like Tom was still sitting there in that worn chair, whittling his wren, waiting for the storm to pass.

title: horror|a family moves into a farmhouse where the previous owners' dog will not stop digging in the cellar
text:
The Cellar Dog
The moving truck’s brakes screamed like a wounded thing as it rumbled up the gravel drive. Mara pressed her forehead to the car window, staring at the weathered gray farmhouse hunched under a sky bruised with storm clouds. “It’s… charming,” she said, though the word tasted like ash.

Her husband, Ethan, slammed the car door and pumped a fist. “Charming? It’s a steal. Three bedrooms, ten acres, and the cellar? Perfect for my home brewery.” He was already halfway up the porch steps, toolbelt slung over one shoulder, grinning like a kid on Christmas.

Twelve-year-old Jax didn’t look up from his handheld game. “It smells like wet dirt and regret.”

“Jax,” Mara chided, but she couldn’t argue. The air clung thick and earthy, even through the closed windows.

A sharp, frantic scrabbling sound cut through the quiet. Scratch. Scratch-scratch. Thud.

Ethan paused, hand on the doorknob. “You hear that?”

The sound came again, faster now, desperate. It was under the house.

They found the cellar door tucked under the back stairs, its wood warped and crisscrossed with deep gouges. The scratching was deafening here, accompanied by a low, whimpering growl.

“Raccoon?” Mara whispered, reaching for Ethan’s arm.

“Realtor said the previous owners left something behind.” He hefted a crowbar. “Said they couldn’t catch it.”

“Catch what?” Jax had finally looked up, his game forgotten. His eyes were wide.

Ethan jammed the crowbar under the door. With a shriek of rusted metal, it flew open. Cold air billowed out, thick with the stench of turned earth and something older, something metallic.

At the bottom of the rickety wooden stairs, a dog sat.

It was a large, shaggy thing, matted black fur caked with mud. It wasn’t a raccoon. It wasn’t a stray. It looked like an old English sheepdog, or what one might look like after digging its way through a grave. It wasn't growling at them. It was growling at the floor.

Its paws were a blur, tearing at the packed dirt of the cellar floor. Clods of mud flew. Scratch-scratch-scratch. It paused only to whine, a high, keening sound, before diving back in, teeth bared in a rictus of effort.

“Hey, boy,” Ethan said softly, taking a step down. “Easy now.”

The dog froze. Its head snapped up.

Mara gasped. Its eyes weren't right. They were filmed over, milky white, entirely blind. But its head tracked Ethan's movement perfectly, as if it could see the heat coming off his skin. It let out a low, rumbling warning, then immediately returned to digging, faster, more frantic, as if their arrival had put a timer on its terrible work.

“Is he blind?” Jax breathed from the doorway.

“Looks like it,” Mara said. “Poor thing. He’s probably starving. Let me get the leftovers from the cooler.”

She retrieved a paper plate of cold cuts and descended slowly, holding it out. “Here, boy. Hungry? Look, ham.”

The dog didn't even twitch. Its claws scraped against something hard. Wood.

Ethan frowned. “There's something down there. A box, maybe.” He took the last two steps and moved toward the dog. “C'mon, buddy. Let us see.”

He reached for the dog's collar. The animal’s reaction was explosive. It spun, jaws snapping, a feral, unearthly snarl ripping out of its throat. Ethan stumbled back, tripping over a loose stone, and landed hard in the dirt.

“Ethan!” Mara screamed.

But the dog didn't press the attack. It immediately turned back to the hole, digging with a terrifying, renewed frenzy. A low, rhythmic thumping sound began to emanate from the hole. Not from the dog. From below.

Thud. Thud. Thud.

Jax clapped a hand over his mouth. “Dad. Dad, what is that?”

Ethan scrambled back up the stairs, his face the color of paper. He grabbed a flashlight from his toolbelt and shone it into the hole the dog had made.

The beam caught a rotting wooden plank. The dog's claws had torn through it, revealing a narrow, black void beneath. The thudding was louder now, deliberate. It sounded like a fist hitting wood from the inside.

“The previous owners,” Mara whispered, her blood turning to slush. “The realtor said they just… walked away. Left everything. She said they wouldn't talk about why.”

The dog suddenly stopped digging. It sat back on its haunches. It tilted its blind, white head up toward the ceiling, toward the living world above.

And then it spoke.

It wasn't a bark. It wasn't a howl. The sound that rumbled out of the dog's chest was deep, gravelly, and horribly, unmistakably human. A single, exhausted word, spoken in a perfect mimicry of a man's baritone.

“Finally.”

Jax broke. He turned and ran, his sneakers slapping the kitchen floor. Mara grabbed Ethan's arm, her nails digging into his flesh. “We have to go. Right now.”

But Ethan wasn't moving. He was staring at the dog. The blind dog was staring right back at him. Its lips were pulled back in something that looked almost like a smile.

The thudding stopped.

In the sudden, suffocating silence, the dog's tail began to thump against the dirt.

Thump. Thump. Thump.

A new sound drifted up from the void. A soft, relieved sigh, right beneath their feet. And then, a woman’s voice, gentle and warm, whispering up through the cracks in the plank.

“Good boy, Rufus. Good boy. You found us new hands to dig with.”

The cellar door above them slammed shut.

In the absolute darkness, the scratching began again.

But this time, it wasn't just the dog.

title: literary|a disgraced professor moves to his daughter's farm after a scandal at the university
text:
The muck sticks to his work boots thick as regret. He prods the rusted edge of the trough with a broken pitchfork handle, doesn’t flinch when a glob of slop splatters his faded tweed cuff—last good shirt he brought from the city, the one he wore to defend his dissertation once, back when people leaned in to hear him talk instead of crossing the street to avoid the stink of his name.
His daughter Lila doesn’t tiptoe. She slams a dented pail of feed at his feet an hour back, said, “Pigs don’t care if you fudged study data. They just care if you show up.” She hasn’t asked about the emails, the hearings, the way his old department head sent his office books in cardboard boxes marked *PERSONAL EFFECTS* like he’d died instead of getting run out on a rail. Good. He doesn’t want to talk about it. Doesn’t want to explain how the grant money got siphoned to pay for his ex-wife’s third rehab stint, how he’d faked three months of soil toxicity readings because he was too tired, too scared, too broke to start over at 58.
The sow in the far pen grunts, shoves her snout through the slats. She’s got a gash over her left eye, crusted black with mud and old blood, and she stares at him like she knows. He reaches for the feed scoop, his wrist aching—arthritis flaring from three straight days of mending fence in the October rain—and spills half the pail over the edge. The piglets come skittering, squealing, tiny hooves skidding on muck, and one nips the tip of his work glove hard enough to make him yelp.
“Y’know, I used to teach grad students who couldn’t pour a cup of coffee without asking for an extension,” he mutters to the sow, who just blinks slow. The wind picks up, carries the sharp tang of wood smoke from the house, the distant rattle of Lila’s beat-up pickup coming up the drive. He knows she’s got a stack of his unopened mail on the passenger seat: the certified letters from the academic ethics board, the divorce papers his ex finally got around to filing, the alumni magazine with his face crossed out in Sharpie on page three, someone sent it to the PO box last week.
He doesn’t move when the truck crunches to a stop. Just leans on the pitchfork, lets the muck cake higher on his boots. The sun dips low behind the oak line, paints the mud pink and bruised purple, and for a second he can almost forget the sound of the provost’s voice saying *You have disgraced this institution*, almost forget the way his former research assistant called him a fraud to his face in the hallway, spittle hitting his cheek.
Lila hops out of the truck, tosses him a cold can of beer from the cooler in the bed. He fumbles it, catches it against his chest, cold aluminum seeping through his shirt. “Trough’s still leaking,” she says, nodding at the slow drip of murky water seeping into the mud at his feet. “Fix it tomorrow.”
He pops the tab. Beer foam runs down his wrist, mixes with the muck. Doesn’t wipe it off. “Yeah,” he says. “Tomorrow.”
(Word count: 598)

title: romance|a widowed veterinarian and a stubborn rancher are snowed in together during a blizzard
text:
The wind screamed against the cabin windows like something alive and furious.

Dr. Elena Marquez pressed her palm flat against the frosted glass and stared out at the whiteout swallowing the Colorado valley. Ten minutes ago, she'd been able to make out the gabled roof of the barn across the yard. Now she could barely see her own reflection in the darkening pane.

"Well," she said, turning back toward the stone fireplace, "that's not letting up."

Cole Barrett crouched before the hearth, feeding another split log into the flames, and didn't look up. His broad shoulders strained the faded denim of his shirt, and a day's worth of dark stubble shadowed a jaw that seemed chiseled from the same stubborn granite as the mountains surrounding his ranch.

"Told you not to come out," he said.

Elena's jaw tightened. "Your mare was in dystocia, Cole. Breech, with a leg back. You called me."

"I called the clinic. Figured they'd send Trent."

"Trent's in Denver with a fractured pelvis from a skiing accident." She kept her voice level with an effort. "I'm the on-call vet for the entire county this week. Whether you like it or not."

He finally looked up, and something flickered in those deep-set hazel eyes—something that might have been contrition if she'd believed him capable of it. He rose to his feet in one fluid motion, towering over her by a good six inches. "Didn't say I didn't like it."

"You've said plenty over the years."

It was true. In the three years since she'd moved to Willow Creek and bought out old Doc Patterson's practice, Cole Barrett had treated her with a gruff wariness bordering on hostility. He'd questioned her diagnoses, second-guessed her treatments, and on one memorable occasion, driven forty miles to seek a second opinion after she'd prescribed antibiotics for his prize quarter horse. The second vet had prescribed exactly the same thing.

Now he had the decency to look away. "I was out of line with the Redford thing."

Elena blinked. An apology. From Cole Barrett. Maybe the blizzard had frozen the hinges on whatever armor he wore.

"How's Daisy?" she asked, softer now.

"Sleepin'. Colt's already tryin' to stand on those fool long legs." The ghost of a smile crossed his face, there and gone so quickly she might have imagined it. "You did good work, Doc."

"She did good work. I just helped." Elena moved closer to the fire, holding her hands out toward the blaze. Her coat was still damp at the cuffs, and her boots were soaked through. She'd left in such a hurry when the emergency call came that she'd grabbed only her medical bag. "How long do you think we're stuck?"

"Road'll be impassable until morning at the earliest. Maybe longer if it keeps dumpin'." He nodded toward the kitchen. "Coffee's fresh. You look like you could use it."

She followed him through the archway into the rustic kitchen of the ranch house, trying not to notice the way he moved—coiled, deliberate, like a man comfortable in his own body in a way that made her own skin feel too warm. The cabin was small but immaculate, decorated with Western landscapes in rough-hewn frames and a single framed photograph on the mantel that she'd glimpsed on her way in: a young woman with a bright smile, a wedding dress, Cole beside her looking younger and happier than she'd ever seen him.

Maya Barrett. She'd died four years ago in a car accident on an icy road much like the one currently disappearing under snow. Elena knew because the whole county knew. Grief like that didn't stay private in a town of eight hundred people.

Cole poured two mugs of black coffee and handed her one without asking how she took it. Black, as it happened. She sipped it carefully, feeling the heat spread through her chest.

"Thank you," she said. "For letting me wait it out."

One dark eyebrow arched. "Hardly gonna turn you out into a blizzard, Doc. I'm stubborn, not a monster."

"I never thought you were a monster."

He studied her over the rim of his mug, and this time she held his gaze. Outside, the wind rattled the shutters, but inside, the fire crackled and the coffee steamed between them, and suddenly the small kitchen felt much too small.

"Elena," he said, and it was the first time he'd ever used her first name. It sounded different in his low voice—slower, almost careful. "I owe you an apology for more than the Redford thing."

She set her mug down. "Cole, you don't—"

"I do." He stepped closer, and she caught the scent of him—woodsmoke and hay and something clean beneath it. "You've been nothin' but professional since you got here, and I've been an ass. It wasn't about you. Not really."

"I know." Her voice came out quieter than she intended. "Grief makes people cautious."

Something raw crossed his face. He looked away first, toward the window where the snow fell in thick, relentless curtains.

"She would've liked you," he said, almost to himself. "Maya. She always said I needed someone who'd tell me when I was bein' a damn fool."

Elena's throat tightened. "And do you? Have someone telling you that?"

The fire popped. Cole turned back to her, and the distance between them seemed to shrink without either of them moving.

"Not until tonight," he said.

Somewhere in the barn, the newborn colt whickered. The storm held them captive in its white, frozen grip, and for the first time in three years, Elena thought that being snowed in with the most stubborn man in Willow Creek might not be such a bad thing after all.

title: crime|two small-time crooks argue in a parked car about whether to go through with a kidnapping
text:
The rain hit the Vauxhall’s windscreen so hard I swear I could see the metal flex under it, wipers slapping back and forth like a dying man gasping for air. It was 2:17 a.m. according to the cracked dashboard clock, the kind that ran three minutes fast no matter how many times Jimmie banged on it, and we’d been parked at the end of Beechwood Close for forty-two minutes. My left foot had gone numb from the cold seeping up through the rusted floorboard, the half-smoked roll-up between my fingers was dead, and I still couldn’t stop replaying the way the kid had waved at us when we’d cased the place yesterday, pigtails flying, holding a stuffed rabbit so matted its ears looked like old rope.
Jimmie picked at a split in the vinyl passenger seat, pulling out chunks of yellow foam and dropping them on the floor mat that was already caked in mud and old takeaway wrappers. “You’re overthinking it,” he said, for what had to be the dozenth time. “Mack said the old man’s got the cash. No cops, no fuss. We grab her when she comes out for the paper at seven, drive her to the lockup, make the call, we’re out by sundown. Five grand split down the middle. Easy.”
Easy. I stared at the terraced house at the end of the close, the one with the pink bike chained to the front railings, the glow of a nightlight seeping through the curtains of the upstairs front room. Five grand sounded like a king’s ransom when you owed two grand to a guy who’d broken your cousin’s hand over a missed payment on a three-hundred-quid loan, when you’d spent the last three months sleeping on Jimmie’s couch because you couldn’t keep up the rent on your bedsit, when the last “job” we’d pulled was nicking a crate of Irn-Bru from the back of a corner shop that netted us forty quid between us. But easy didn’t usually involve a seven-year-old. Easy didn’t involve the way my throat had gone tight when she’d waved, like she thought we were just some blokes parked waiting for a mate, not a pair of pricks planning to yank her off her own doorstep.
“Mack’s a lying prick,” I said, and my voice came out rougher than I meant it to. I fumbled in my jacket pocket for the Bic lighter, flicked it three times before it caught, held it to the dead end of the roll-up until the tobacco glowed. “Remember when he said that warehouse in Salford was full of unguarded tellies? Turned out it was full of guard dogs and a bunch of blokes with crowbars. We spent three hours hiding in a skip full of rotten cabbages.”
“That was one time.” Jimmie’s jaw tightened, the way it always did when I brought up the skip. He leaned over, jabbed a finger at the house. “This is different. The old man’s a accountant, right? Does the books for half the firms in town, including Mack’s. He won’t call the cops. He can’t. Too much dodgy shit he don’t want dug up. We don’t even have to hurt her. Just keep her in the lockup for a few hours, give her a packet of crisps, let her watch that shite cartoon she likes, boom. Cash in hand, we’re off to that caravan in Rhyl we talked about, yeah? No more skips, no more nicking Irn-Bru, no more Mack breathing down our necks.”
I thought about the caravan, the one with the sea view we’d seen advertised in the newsagent’s window, chipped blue paint, a little deck where you could sit and smoke and not have to listen to Jimmie’s mam yelling at the telly all day. It sounded nice. It sounded like the kind of thing people who weren’t total fuckups got to have. But then I thought about the lockup, the one with the concrete floor and the single bare bulb that flickered so bad it gave you a headache, the smell of old paint thinner and rat shit. I thought about the kid crying for her mam, the way her rabbit’s ear was half chewed off, like she carried it everywhere, even to bed.
“What if she screams?” I said. The smoke burned my lungs when I inhaled, and I coughed, hard, until my eyes watered. “What if someone sees? What if—”
“What if you stop being a little bitch?” Jimmie snapped, and he reached down to the footwell, hefted the crumpled canvas sack we’d brought, the one with the holes cut in it for air. It looked stupid, like a Halloween costume someone had thrown together five minutes before a party. “We already paid for the burner phone. We already got the lockup for the day. You wanna go back to Mack and tell him we bailed? You think he’s gonna let that slide? Remember what he did to Kev when Kev fucked up that coke run?”
I remembered. Kev had three fingers missing on his left hand now, and he couldn’t talk right because his jaw had been wired shut for six weeks. I stared at the sack in Jimmie’s hand, then back at the house. The rain was letting up a little, the wipers moving slower now, smearing water across the glass instead of slapping it away. Somewhere down the street a dog barked, sharp and loud, and I jumped, like the cops were already there, like they could read the stupid, desperate thoughts bouncing around my skull.
The dashboard clock ticked over to 2:19. Four hours and forty-one minutes until she came out for the paper. I could taste the stale tobacco on my tongue, the cold metal of the car door under my hand. I could turn the key right now, I thought. I could put the car in drive, peel out of here, drive to Rhyl by myself, never look back. But I knew I wouldn’t. Jimmie was right about one thing: Mack didn’t let people bail. And I was tired of running. I was tired of being the guy who hid in skips, who slept on couches, who couldn’t even afford a pack of fags without scrounging change off his mate.
Jimmie must have seen the look on my face, because he grinned, the gap between his front teeth showing, the one he’d got when we were sixteen and he’d tried to jump a fence on a stolen BMX. “There we go,” he said. “Knew you’d see sense. We’ll take turns watching her, yeah? I’ll even bring the Mars Bars she likes. She won’t even be scared.”
I didn’t say anything. I took another drag of the roll-up, watched the nightlight glow in the kid’s window, and tried not to think about how the last time I’d told myself something was going to be easy, I’d ended up in a skip full of rotten cabbages, stinking for three days. The clock kept ticking. Somewhere, a bird started singing, like it didn’t know what kind of shit we were about to pull.
