title: military science fiction|mercenary tank crews defend a mining colony against a much larger invading force
text:
The ferrocrete balcony groaned under Kade Voss’s weight as he lowered the magnoculars. Dawn painted the Kestrel Range in bruised oranges and violets, turning the convoy crawling through Ironheart Pass into a procession of black beetles glinting against rust-colored scree.

“Count’s confirmed,” he said, lowering the glass. “Twenty-eight chassis. Four are Typhoon-class. Six are Thor heavy battle tanks. The rest are Apollos, plus infantry support crawlers.”

Behind him, Mira Chen spat a stream of stim-coffee over the railing. “Rennick promised us a brigade. Our three tanks are supposed to stop that?”

“Our three *Ironclad* main battle tanks,” Kade corrected, turning back. Below, in the prefab motor pool, the vehicles sat squat as sleeping megafauna: sloped composite armor scarred by previous contracts, long-barreled 120mm railcannons, automated turret pods sprouting from their hulls like mechanical horns. “And Rennick paid half in advance. The other half buys the new lungs Jessa needs.”

Mira’s jaw tightened. She glanced toward the colony’s habitation spires, where atmospheric recyclers droned behind radiation shielding. “Then we’d better earn it.”

They descended the gantry as the other crew chiefs gathered. Big Halvarsson, Vulcan’s loader, was methodically sharpening a trench knife he’d somehow kept through three corporate inspections. “Deploying in the bulldozer cut?” he asked.

Kade nodded. “The pass narrows there. We hull-down behind the tailings piles and let them funnel. Mira, you take Wraith to the east shelf—higher position, overwatch the Typhoons. Hal, Vulcan anchors the west ridge. I’ll hold center in Ares. We don’t stand and trade; we shoot, reposition, shoot again. Active camouflage until the first shot.”

“Against twenty-eight?” Halvarsson said, but he was already turning toward his tank.

The cockpit of Ares smelled of recycled air, ozone, and old sweat. Kade settled into the commander’s couch and linked his neural interface. Diagnostics bloomed behind his eyelids: reactor steady, rails charged, APU humming. His gunner, young Petrov, cycled the targeting array while Lira, the driver, fed power to the treads.

“Contact in six kilometers,” Petrov said. “Their vanguard’s pushing fast.”

“Let them get comfortable.” Kade switched to the commons. “All crews, hold fire. I repeat, hold fire until my mark.”

Ares rumbled down the service road, dust rising fine and gray around her hull. The miners had spent weeks piling crushed ore into staggered revetments; from above, the defenses looked like nothing more than excavation spoil. Kade’s tank nestled into the central berm, active camouflage rippling across her armor in patterns of rock and shadow. Through the periscope, he watched the invasion vanguard spill into the valley: four Apollos fanning into wedge formation, turrets sweeping.

Farther back, a Typhoon crested the ridge. Kade’s mouth went dry. The enemy tank was twice Ares’s length, its twin railcannons housed in a slab-sided turret, missile racks armored like plate mail. *Corporate expeditionary force*, he thought. *Rennick lied about who was attacking.*

“Command element’s with the second Typhoon,” Mira murmured over encrypted comms. Her Wraith was a ghost on the eastern shelf. “I can see their antenna array.”

“Priority remains the vanguard,” Kade said. “We gut the front and make the column think the whole pass is fortified.”

The first Apollo crossed the painted range line.

“Mark.”

Ares’s railcannon roared—a crack like thunder folded inside lightning. The sabot round crossed two kilometers in a breath and punched through the Apollo’s glacis. The tank lurched, hatches blew open, and flame vomited from its engine deck before the ammunition brew detonated in a white-hot gout.

Simultaneously, Wraith’s gun flashed from the east shelf. A second Apollo slewed sideways, track links unspooling across the road. Vulcan joined a heartbeat later, her round striking a third vehicle beneath the turret ring. Metal screamed. Black smoke curled toward the pale dawn sky.

“Reloading!” Petrov shouted.

The valley exploded into motion. Enemy turrets traversed, seeking muzzle flashes, but the mercenaries had already shifted. Lira threw Ares into reverse, sliding the tank behind a second tailings pile as hypervelocity rounds gouged the berm where she’d rested. Shrapnel rattled against the hull like demonic hail.

“Typhoon acquiring Wraith!” Halvarsson barked.

Mira’s voice came tight and calm. “I see him.”

Wraith lunged from one rock shelf to another, camocloak flickering between stone patterns. The Typhoon’s first shot missed by meters, vaporizing a boulder. Its second sent granite shards scything across the ridge. Mira fired down at the rear deck; the round sparked and failed to penetrate.

“Dammit—their top armor’s upgraded!”

“Then go for sensors,” Kade said. “Petrov, center mass on the lead Thor. Lira, forward ten, angle us thirty degrees.”

Ares surged up again. Kade watched the targeting reticle settle over the heavy tank’s optical array. “Fire.”

The railcannon slammed. The Thor’s left sensor block disintegrated, and the great vehicle staggered as though blinded. Halvarsson put a second round through its exposed turret joint. Flame licked from the cracks; then the crew hatches opened and figures tumbled out, burning.

But the column was recovering. Infantry fighting vehicles disgorged power-armored troops who scattered behind ore conveyors, their rifles spitting blue coherent beams. Two Apollos had pushed through the smoke and were advancing directly on Ares.

“Infantry in the trench line,” Lira warned.

“Canister on the left,” Kade said. “Then back us—now.”

The anti-personnel blast scythed through the nearest squad, but a missile team launched from behind a crusher. It struck Ares’s frontal armor and detonated with a concussive roar that slammed Kade against his restraints. Alarms wailed.

“Damage report!”

“Armor holding, reactive plating spent on that panel,” Lira said through gritted teeth. “Reactor’s fine.”

“Won’t hold a second one,” Petrov said.

On the tactical display, the remaining Typhoons were pushing forward, using the Apollos as a screen. Behind them, more vehicles kept pouring through the pass—a river of steel no contract had prepared them for.

Mira’s voice cut across the channel. “Kade, their command tank just exposed its flank. I can take the shot, but the second Typhoon’s got my line. I need thirty seconds.”

Kade looked at the two Apollos closing to point-blank range, at the infantry crawling through the rubble, at Vulcan’s icon blinking as Halvarsson fought his own duel to the west.

“Hal,” he said, “suppress everything on the east approach. We’re buying Mira thirty seconds.”

“With what, prayers?”

“With whatever’s left.”

Ares roared forward, bursting from the berm directly into the enemy’s face.

title: historical|a codebreaker in 1942 notices a pattern in intercepted Japanese messages that nobody believes
text:
Station HYPO, Pearl Harbor, May 1942
The coffee tasted like burnt shell casings and bromine. Joe Rochefort’s slippers had a hole in the toe, the one he’d been meaning to patch since March, and the linoleum stuck to his wool socks every time he shifted in his chair. The ventilation system had died three days prior, so the air hung thick with cigarette smoke, sweat, and the sharp, briny reek of the harbor that seeped through the cinder block walls every time the tide came in. It was 0317 hours. The rest of the watch had stumbled off to the bunks an hour prior, leaving only Joe and the hum of the IBM machines, their punch cards fluttering like dead moths into the wire bins.
He’d been staring at the same intercept for twelve hours straight, his eyes burning so bad he’d doused them with Visine twice, the stuff running down his cheeks in streaks that looked like tears if you were dumb enough to look close. The message was partial, garbled, picked up by a radioman on Midway who’d been half-asleep when he keyed it, static eating half the characters: *AF* scheduled for resupply, 1200 drums aviation gas, 300 cases rice, medical detachment attached.
AF. For three weeks the brass at Pearl and DC had been screaming that *AF* was the Aleutians. Or Johnston Atoll. Or the West Coast, for Christ’s sake—some idiot in Navy Intelligence had sent a memo last week warning of a strike on San Francisco, citing “enemy chatter about coastal fog.” Joe had spit coffee all over that memo when he read it.
He flipped through the stack of old intercepts, the edges soft from being handled by a dozen men, his thumb smudging the pencil marks where they’d scribbled tentative code groups. There. March 4, a patrol plane out of Wake reporting bad weather 100 miles northeast of *AF*. March 18, a submarine commander requesting updated charts for the approaches to *AF*, noting “shallow reefs, high surf, civilian construction crews present.”
Wait.
Civilian construction crews. The Aleutians had no civilian construction crews. Johnston had a Marine detachment, no contractors. Midway—Midway had a crew of 120 Seabees and civilian workers out there building a new runway, had since February. The reefs? Midway’s fringing reef was the reason the landing craft had a bitch of a time getting supplies ashore when the surf was up, every supply memo for the last six months complaining about it. The aviation gas? Midway’s tanks only held 800 drums. They’d been begging for a resupply since the end of April.
His heart started thumping so hard he could hear it over the IBMs. He fumbled for his red pencil, the one he only used for confirmed correlations, and started scrawling across the intercept, his handwriting slanted and messy, the lead breaking twice: *AF = MIDWAY. TARGET DATE JUNE 3. STRIKE FORCE 4 CARRIERS.*
He ran up the stairs two at a time, his slipper flapping, the paper crumpled in his fist, and banged on the door of the watch commander’s office. Captain Layton was asleep on his cot, his uniform unbuttoned, a half-empty bottle of bourbon on the desk next to a framed photo of his daughter in a Brownie uniform. He blinked when Joe flipped the light on, squinting like he was staring into the sun.
“Joe, it’s three in the goddamned morning.”
“It’s Midway. They’re hitting Midway.”
Layton sat up, rubbed a hand over his face. He’d heard this before. “Washington says Aleutians. OP-20-G ran the frequency analysis last week—”
“To hell with OP-20-G’s frequency analysis. Look.” Joe spread the intercepts across the desk, his finger jabbing at the construction line, the reef note, the gas request. “They sent a message two days ago about a water distillery breaking on *AF*. Remember? The garbled one about potable water shortages? We tell Midway to send a plaintext message, unencrypted, saying their desalination plant’s busted. We sit back and wait. The Japs will pick it up, and they’ll radio their command saying *AF* is short on water. Then we’ll know.”
Layton stared at him for a long minute. He reached for his coffee, took a sip, made a face. “You’re sure.”
“I’m sure.”
“Washington will call this a stunt. They’ll say you’re fudging the intercepts to make your call look right, after you missed the Pearl traffic.”
Joe’s jaw tightened. He still got the letters, every so often, from mothers whose sons had died on December 7, calling him a fool, a coward, a man who’d slept at his post while the bombs fell. He didn’t blame them. Some nights he thought they were right.
“I don’t care what they call it. If we pull every carrier north to the Aleutians, they’ll take Midway, and then they’ll be in Hawaii by August. You know that.”
Layton sighed. He reached for the phone, cranked the handle, asked for the Midway cable station. While he waited, he looked up at Joe, and nodded at the hole in his slipper. “You ever gonna fix that thing?”
Joe looked down. His sock was sticking out, gray and frayed at the toe. “Probably not.”
The cable went out at 0458 hours, plain as day: MIDWAY ISLAND DESALINATION PLANT EXPERIENCING CATASTROPHIC FAILURE. POTABLE WATER RESERVES AT 50 PERCENT. REQUEST IMMEDIATE RESUPPLY.
They waited. Joe went back down to the code room, poured another cup of that terrible coffee, sat down. The sun came up over the harbor, gilding the sunken hull of the *Arizona*, the oil still seeping up to make rainbow slicks on the water. He lit a cigarette, stared at the bank of radios, their dials glowing soft green.
At 0742, the radioman on duty, a 19-year-old kid from Iowa named Parker who still had acne across his cheeks, looked up from his headset, his eyes wide. “Sir. We got it. Jap naval intelligence just broadcast to their combined fleet: *AF reports water shortage. Supply units to carry extra potable water for landing parties.*”
Joe didn’t yell. He didn’t jump up and down. He just nodded, took a drag off his cigarette, and looked down at the red pencil marks on the intercept, smudged where his sweat had run onto the paper. Somewhere down the hall, a man laughed. The IBM machines kept humming, spitting out punch cards.
He thought of his ex-wife, back in DC, who’d left him in ’39 because he spent more time talking to code groups than he did to her. He thought of the kid from the *Arizona* he’d pulled out of the water on December 7, his leg blown off, who’d kept asking if his buddy was okay, who’d died before they got him to the hospital. He thought of the way the water looked in Hawaii when the trade winds blew, bright blue, so clear you could see the fish 30 feet down.
There was no grand feeling. No rush of triumph, no sense that he’d just changed the course of the whole goddamned war. He was tired. His eyes burned. His toe was cold where the hole in his slipper let the air conditioning hit it.
He picked up his pencil, started scribbling the next set of coordinates, when the phone rang on his desk. It was Layton. “Washington just called. They still think it’s a feint. They’re ordering two of the carriers north to the Aleutians.”
Joe stared at the wall for a second. He took another sip of coffee. It was cold now, tasted even worse than it had hot.
“Okay,” he said. “Tell ’em I said they’re wrong.”
He hung up. Outside, a gull cried, wheeling over the harbor. The next intercept was already coming in, the dots and dashes tap-tap-tapping through the speaker, sharp and fast, like someone knocking on a door. He leaned forward, squinting, his pencil hovering over the paper. Somewhere out there, across four thousand miles of ocean, the Japanese fleet was sailing straight for them, and no one who mattered believed him.
He wrote *AF* at the top of the fresh sheet of paper, underlined it twice. The pencil broke again.
(Word count: 698)

title: mystery|a Venetian police commissario questions a widow who seems relieved rather than grieving
text:
Chapter 7 (continued)
The rain lashed against the leaded windows of the palazzo, streaking the canal light into gray smears. Commissario Marco Rizzo leaned forward in the velvet chair, the smell of damp wool and old money clinging to his throat. The widow, Signora Elena Moretti, twisted a pearl earring between her thumb and forefinger. No puffy eyes. No crumpled handkerchief. Just that odd, tight smile—like someone who’d just paid off a debt.

“Your husband fell from the roof at two in the morning,” Rizzo said, flipping open his notebook. The paper was already warping from the humidity. “He was in his pajamas. Barefoot. The roof access latch was rusted shut from the outside. You expect me to believe he climbed up there to check the gutters during a storm?”

Elena’s smile twitched. She poured herself another glass of prosecco, the bottle half-empty already though it wasn’t yet noon. “Giovanni was a creature of habit. He heard a tile rattle. He had to fix it himself—couldn’t bear to pay a workman.”

“At two a.m.”

“At two a.m.”

Rizzo studied the room. Oil paintings of stern ancestors. A marble bust missing its nose. On the sideboard, a stack of unopened condolence letters still bound with ribbon. He’d seen widows before. The screamers. The silent ones. The ones who kept setting a second plate at dinner. This woman looked like she was planning a vacation.

“He owed money,” Rizzo said. It wasn’t a question.

The prosecco glass stopped halfway to her lips. “Who told you that?”

“Nobody had to. The ledgers in his study. The calls from creditors. Your husband’s construction company was bleeding cash for three years. The Calatrava bridge job ate him alive.” Rizzo paused. “Then last week, he takes out a life insurance policy. Two million euro. Beneficiary: you.”

Elena set the glass down hard. A bubble slid down the side. “You think I killed him for money?”

“I think you had reason to want him gone. Money’s only the start.” Rizzo pulled a photograph from his jacket, slid it across the mahogany table. A younger man, dark-haired, grinning on a beach. “Francesco Lotto. Your lover. He booked a flight to Buenos Aires yesterday. One way.”

The color drained from her face, but the relief didn’t vanish—it sharpened into something harder, cornered. “Francesco had nothing to do with this.”

“Then why run?”

“He wasn’t running from you.” Her voice dropped. “He was running from them.”

“ Them who?”

Elena stood abruptly and walked to the window. Below, a gondola slid past, the gondolier hunched under a yellow poncho. She pressed her palm to the cold glass. “Giovanni borrowed from the wrong people. The men who don’t send letters. They came here, Commissario. Two weeks ago. They sat right where you’re sitting and told him if he didn’t pay by the end of the month, they’d make an example of him.” She turned, and for the first time Rizzo saw something genuine in her eyes—not grief, but fear. “They said they’d throw him in the canal. But the roof… that wasn’t their style.”

Rizzo’s jaw tightened. “You know a lot about their style.”

“I know Giovanni begged them for more time. I know he slept with a knife under his pillow.” She laughed, brittle and hollow. “And do you know what I thought when the carabinieri knocked on the door at dawn? I thought, *finally*. At least it’s over. The waiting. The lies. Watching my husband drink himself into a stupor every night because he was too proud to tell anyone his empire was dust.” Her voice cracked, just a little. “Does that make me a monster?”

Rizzo didn’t answer. Outside, a siren wailed over the water, drawing closer. He thought of the rusted latch. Of a barefoot man on a wet roof in the dark. Of two million euro and a lover bound for Argentina.

“It makes you a suspect,” he said quietly.

A door slammed somewhere in the palazzo. Heavy footsteps on marble. Elena’s head snapped toward the hallway, her breath catching.

The footsteps stopped outside the study.

Rizzo’s hand drifted to the holster beneath his jacket.

The door swung open.

It wasn’t his officer.

---
*Word count: ~598*

title: mystery|a wedding planner finds the best man dead in the hotel's walk-in freezer the night before the ceremony
text:
Clara Voss’s loafers stuck a little to the commercial kitchen’s epoxy floor as she shouldered open the heavy metal door of the Rosewood Hotel’s walk-in freezer, the blast of frigid air stinging her cheekbones hard enough to make her eyes water. It was 11:17 PM, the night before Lila and Ethan’s wedding, and the pastry chef had sworn three of the hand-piped sugar peonies for the five-tier vanilla bean cake were stashed on the top shelf, left over from a luncheon earlier that week. She’d already fended off a crisis with the groomsmen’s custom bow ties (one had been used as a beer pong net, now soaking in club soda) and a last-minute demand from the mother of the bride to swap the processional for a Taylor deep cut, so tracking down edible flowers felt like small potatoes.
The shelves were stacked high with tubs of artisanal ice cream, vacuum-sealed tenderloin for the reception, crates of champagne chilling for the toast. She reached up, fumbling for the cake box she’d marked with a neon pink sticky note, when her boot connected with something solid that wasn’t a crate.
She yelped, fumbling for her phone to flip on the flashlight. The beam landed first on scuffed white cowboy boots, the pair Jesse Marlow, the best man, had bragged he was going to wear down the aisle “to give the old-money in-laws something to side-eye.” It panned up to his fraternity hoodie, the fabric stiff with frost, his face blue, eyes half-open, a crumpled silver flask clutched in his frozen fist.
Clara stumbled back, slamming into a shelf of sorbet, the tubs clattering to the floor as she scrabbled for the door handle, her fingers already numb. She half-fell into the kitchen, gasping, and collided with Manny, the night sous chef, who was carrying a tray of caramelized canapés.
“Whoa, easy,” Manny said, steadying her, then his smile dropped when he saw her face. “You look like you saw a ghost. The peonies gone bad? I told Maria not to stack them next to the salmon—”
“It’s Jesse,” Clara said, her throat tight, the cold still clinging to her bones. “He’s in there. He’s dead.”
Manny set the tray down so fast a few of the canapés slid off. “What? Jesse was in here ten, fifteen minutes ago? Grabbed a bag of ice for the groomsmen’s suite, yelled something about a prank he was gonna pull on Ethan—said he swapped the ring bearer’s pillow for whoopee cushion. Seemed fine. Annoying, but fine.”
Clara fumbled for her radio, her hands shaking so bad she almost dropped it. “Security? This is Clara, event services. I need you in the main kitchen, walk-in freezer, now. And call 911. Tell them—tell them we have a deceased guest.”
The radio crackled back, a harried confirmation. A second later, Ethan stumbled into the kitchen, his tux shirt unbuttoned, a half-empty beer in his hand, his hair sticking up like he’d been running his hands through it. “Clara, thank God, have you seen Jesse? He bailed on the poker game twenty minutes ago, said he was gonna go grab something from his truck, and we were gonna—”
He cut off when he saw the freezer door propped open, Manny’s ashen face, the way Clara couldn’t meet his eyes.
“Wait,” Ethan said, his voice dropping, the beer sloshing over the edge of the bottle onto his shoe. “Wait, no. What happened?”
“I’m so sorry,” Clara said, stepping forward, but he was already moving past her, pushing the freezer door open wider. She heard his sharp, ragged gasp, the clatter of the beer bottle hitting the floor, amber liquid pooling across the epoxy.
She followed his gaze. The flashlight on her phone was still on, casting a harsh white beam across Jesse’s hand, the one curled tight around the flask. Tucked under his other arm, half-crushed where he’d fallen, was a manila folder, its edges already frosted over, the words *PRENUP* scrawled across the tab in thick red marker.
The cold seeped through Clara’s blazer as she stared, the hum of the freezer’s compressor loud in the sudden silence, the distant wail of a siren starting to bleed through the kitchen walls. The wedding wasn’t just off the rails, she realized. It was never going to happen the way anyone had planned. (Word count: 698)

title: romance|a widowed veterinarian and a stubborn rancher are snowed in together during a blizzard
text:
I’d convinced myself the silence between us was only the storm.

The wind threw itself against the ranch house as if the blizzard had a personal grudge against every nail and windowpane. I stood at the kitchen counter with both hands braced against the edge, staring at a coffee mug I’d already emptied, while behind me Cole adjusted the same fireplace log for the third time in ten minutes.

We were being ridiculous.

At least, I hoped we were both being ridiculous. It was easier than considering the alternative: that after six years of carefully keeping every feeling locked behind a wall of work and widowhood and competent, steady loneliness, I was snowbound with the one man in Redpine County who could make me forget the shape of the lock.

“Fire’ll hold,” Cole said, gruff enough to sound like he expected an argument.

“Good.”

“Generator’s running.”

“I heard it.”

“Bathroom faucet’s dripping.”

I closed my eyes. “That usually means water, Cole, not impending disaster.”

He made a low, annoyed sound. “Could freeze.”

“It’s dripping inside a heated house.”

“Pipes can be stubborn.”

Of course he’d sympathize with the pipes.

I turned around. He stood near the hearth in worn denim and a dark Henley, snow still melting dark into the cuffs of his boots, though he’d stomped it off on the porch what felt like hours ago. Broad-shouldered, weathered, impossible. Cole Harmon had the kind of face that looked carved by the same wind that battered his land, and the disposition to match.

He also had a barn full of rescued horses, a cattle dog that slept on his pillow, and a habit of calling me at two in the morning when one of his animals was sick and pretending he wasn’t worried.

I knew better.

“Say it,” I told him.

His jaw tightened. “Say what?”

“Whatever is making you rearrange that fire like it personally insulted you.”

“I don’t—”

“Cole.”

His name came out softer than I intended. That seemed to bother him more than frustration would have. He drove his fingers through his black hair, leaving it disordered, and glanced away toward the snow-choked window.

“You should be home.”

“My home is currently under the same whiteout as your driveway.”

“You know what I mean.”

I did. Unfortunately.

My little house on the edge of town was twenty minutes away in fair weather. In this, it may as well have been on another planet. The plows wouldn’t reach his ranch road until morning, maybe later. The phone service flickered in and out. The veterinarian who’d come out to check on a mare with a retained placenta—fine now, thank God—was stuck for the night.

And the rancher who’d been bickering with me since the day I’d told him his prize bull was overweight clearly found that fact intolerable.

“I’m not angry about being here,” I said.

His gaze snapped back. “Aren’t you?”

“No.”

“Most people don’t choose to spend a blizzard sleeping on a stranger’s couch.”

“Then it’s fortunate you’re not a stranger.”

The words landed between us, smaller and warmer than I meant them to. The fire popped. Outside, the siding rattled.

Cole stared at me. “I’m not?”

There it was. The question beneath every argument, every loaded silence, every time his hand had hovered near my elbow and then fallen away as though touching me might burn him.

I should have laughed. I should have deflected, listed the ways we knew each other through animals and emergencies and small-town errands. You bring me injured owls. I yell at you for wrapping barbed wire too low. We’ve shared bad coffee in your barn at dawn.

Instead I leaned my hip against the counter and said, “You know my coffee order.”

“Black, no sugar.”

“You remembered Daniel’s birthday.”

Something flickered across his face. Daniel, my late husband, had been gone six years, but his name still had the power to rearrange the air in any room. Cole rarely said it. When he did, it was careful—not reverent exactly, but respectful, the way a man handled a fence line that wasn’t his to mend.

“Kids talk about him at the feed store,” he said.

“You put flowers on his grave in November.”

His silence answered.

I’d seen them once. Winter pansies, unlikely and stubbornly alive, no card. I’d thought perhaps a relative, an old friend. Then I’d noticed the same calloused thoroughness in the way he mended a hurt bird’s wing and tried to pretend he hadn’t.

“Why?” I asked.

He looked toward the fire again. “Seemed wrong for the marker to be bare.”

“That’s not all of it.”

“Elsie.”

My name on his mouth was almost a warning.

I should have heeded it. My heart certainly did; it stumbled, then raced like a foolish thing that had forgotten how to run. Six years. Six years of black clothes and medical charts and frozen dinners eaten standing over the sink. Six years of telling myself that surviving was enough.

But Cole didn’t ask for more than I could give. That was the danger. He didn’t knock down doors. He simply stood on the other side, patient and immovable, waiting for me to open one myself.

“The couch is fine,” I said, because it was the safest sentence I could find.

“It’s too short.”

“I’m not.”

His mouth twitched, almost a smile. “You’re also not sleeping under one blanket while the fire dies.”

“I survived veterinary school on two-hour naps.”

“That’s not the same and you know it.”

“Then tell me what it is.”

He crossed the kitchen in two long strides before I could brace for it. He didn’t touch me. He stopped close enough that I could smell woodsmoke and hay and cold air caught in wool, close enough that I saw the fleck of amber in one brown iris.

“It’s me,” he said, low and rough, “not wanting to pretend there’s nothing in this room but weather.”

I stopped breathing.

Outside, the blizzard screamed. Inside, the whole world narrowed to the space between his hand and mine.

And for the first time in six years, I didn’t look away.

title: cozy mystery|a doll collector stumbles onto a murder at a county fair antiques show
text:
The sawdust under Clara Bennett’s scuffed leather boots still held the sharp, sun-warmed scent of pine from the morning’s 4-H livestock show, cut through with the sticky sweetness of cotton candy drifting from the midway three tents over. At sixty-two, her silver bun skewered with a vintage porcelain hatpin shaped like a blue jay, she’d been coming to the Maple Creek County Fair antiques show for twenty-seven years, her canvas tote slung over one shoulder already weighted with a chipped 1920s porcelain teacup and a set of hand-stitched doll aprons she’d haggled down to twelve dollars from a retired schoolteacher from Millersburg.

“Last call for the Kewpie doll display, folks!” Marty Hargrove, the show’s paunchy, flannel-shirted organizer, called from the end of the row, his voice muffled by the candy apple he was crunching. “We’re locking the tent up in ten for the midday pie contest, so grab your finds before then!”

Clara’s fingers itched for the bisque-head Kewpie she’d spotted an hour earlier, perched on the edge of Wendell Pike’s display table—the doll had original rosebud lips, a faint smudge of factory paint on its left cheek, and a tiny hand-sewn romper that hadn’t been bleached by decades of sun. Wendell, a sharp-nosed dealer who’d once tried to pass a mass-produced 1980s Cabbage Patch off as a 1950s soft-sculpture original, had told her it was “firm at seventy-five” when she’d asked earlier, but she’d watched him sneak a flask out of his coat pocket twice since then, and figured he’d be malleable once his lunchtime bourbon hit.

She wove between folding tables stacked with rusted canning jars, faded quilt blocks, and a set of cracked carnival glass bowls that glowed amber in the slanted light streaming through the tent’s canvas seams, heading for the curtained-off storage nook at the back where vendors stashed their unsold inventory. Wendell had ducked that way ten minutes earlier, she’d seen him, muttering about “getting his best stock out before the rush” and shoving a crumpled envelope into his tweed coat pocket.

The nook was dim, strung with a single bare bulb that swayed slightly in the cross-breeze from the tent’s open flap, and the air here smelled like old mothballs and lemon Pledge instead of cotton candy. Clara pushed aside a hanging wool blanket printed with 1976 bicentennial stars, and her boot caught on something soft and heavy on the floor.

She stumbled, catching herself on a stack of vintage hatboxes, and looked down.

Wendell was splayed half-propped against a stack of steamer trunks, his tweed coat splotched with something dark and sticky that glistened in the dim light, his eyes wide and fixed on the canvas ceiling. Protruding from the base of his throat was the carved wooden handle of a 1950s doll repair awl—she recognized it immediately, had seen him use it a dozen times to restring bisque heads, the handle worn smooth where his thumb had rested for decades. The Kewpie doll she’d been coveting was clutched in his stiffening right hand, its rosebud lips smudged with a faint streak of blood.

“Clara? You back there? I got that lemon bar you said you wanted, the ones with the shortbread crust—”

Marty’s voice cut off as he pulled the blanket aside, the half-eaten candy apple slipping from his hand to thud into the sawdust. His face went the color of sour milk. “Holy hell. Is that Wendell?”

“Don’t come any closer,” Clara said, her voice steadier than she felt, her gaze darting across the nook. The crumpled envelope she’d seen him tuck into his pocket was gone, but a tiny, hand-painted porcelain doll shoe—cobalt blue, with a minute pearl button at the ankle—lay half-buried in the sawdust by Wendell’s left boot, the kind that only came on the ultra-rare 1890s French Bru dolls collectors would kill for. Literally, it seemed. “Go call the sheriff. And don’t let anyone leave the tent, okay? Not a single person.”

Marty nodded so hard his jowls wobbled, fumbling for his flip phone in his overalls pocket and stumbling back toward the tent entrance. Clara knelt slowly, careful not to step in the dark pool seeping into the sawdust, and leaned in to look at the Kewpie in Wendell’s hand. Tucked under its tiny romper collar, folded so small it was almost invisible, was the edge of a pawn shop receipt—for that very Bru doll, sold three days prior by a name she knew well: Verna Mae Tucker, the soft-spoken retired librarian who’d sold her that chipped teacup not an hour earlier, who’d told her she was selling off her mother’s doll collection to pay for her granddaughter’s leukemia treatments.

Somewhere outside the tent, a cheer went up from the pie contest, and a child’s laugh carried on the breeze. The bare bulb swayed, casting long shadows over the trunks and the doll parts stacked on the shelves, and Clara’s fingers closed gently around the tiny porcelain shoe in the sawdust. She’d never much liked Wendell—he’d cheated her out of a rare Ginny doll at the 2019 fair, after all—but nobody deserved to be stabbed with a doll repair awl over a pile of old porcelain. She tucked the shoe into her cardigan pocket, next to her reading glasses and the peppermint she always kept there, and settled onto an upturned crate to wait for the sheriff. The fair’s blue ribbon apple pie would have to wait this year. She had a murder to solve.

title: legal thriller|a public defender realises her client's alibi witness is lying to protect someone else
text:
The Quiet Room

The fluorescent light in Interview Room 3 buzzed like a dying wasp, and Dana Reyes had been staring at the same smudge on the table for ten minutes—a dried coffee ring shaped like Florida, complete with panhandle. Across from her, Marcus Cole sat with his hands folded so tight his knuckles had gone white, and beside him, Latisha Eubanks adjusted her glasses for the fourth time since sitting down.

"Tell me again," Dana said, keeping her voice flat. The way she did when she knew someone was lying. Flat made people nervous. Flat made them talk too much.

Latisha cleared her throat. She was twenty-three, wore scrubs with little sunflowers on them, and had chipped burgundy nail polish. "Like I said. Marcus was with me that night. The whole night. We ordered Chinese, watched that show about the—"

"Which show?"

"The one with the dragons. You know." She waved a hand. "He was on my couch from seven until maybe two in the morning. Didn't leave."

Dana wrote nothing. She'd learned that trick from her first supervisor, a man who ate breath mints like candy and hadn't lost a bench trial in eleven years. When people are lying, silence scares them more than questions.

Marcus stared at the wall. He was nineteen, charged with armed robbery of a liquor store on Pico, facing twenty-five years. The surveillance stills were grainy but not that grainy. The guy in the hoodie had Marcus's lanky build, his slouch, the way he held his left shoulder a little forward like he was protecting an old football injury. Dana had seen the stills forty times. She kept coming back to the hands. The robber's hands were small. Marcus had hands like shovels.

"You two work together?" Dana asked.

"Same hospital," Latisha said quickly. "I'm a CNA, he transports. We been friends a while."

"A while."

"Since like March."

It was October. Dana nodded slowly, drew a circle on her legal pad, then another inside it. Outside, a door slammed somewhere in the courthouse and somebody laughed, the sound muffled through cinder block.

"Ms. Eubanks. Can I ask where you were between nine and ten p.m. on September fourth?"

"Home. With Marcus." She answered too fast, then corrected, slower. "I mean—he came over around seven, like I said."

"Your building has cameras in the lobby, doesn't it? The one on Mariposa."

A flicker. Just a small one, a tightening at the corner of her mouth. "I guess. I don't pay attention to that stuff."

"Uh-huh." Dana flipped a page though she didn't need to. "Because here's the thing. I subpoenaed the lobby footage. Not because I wanted to. Because the DA's office will, and I'd rather know first." She looked up. "Marcus isn't on it. Not at seven. Not at all that night."

The room got smaller. The buzzing light seemed louder.

Latisha's mouth opened, closed. Marcus finally moved, turned to look at her, and Dana saw something cross his face she couldn't read—not surprise exactly, more like resignation, the look of a kid who'd been waiting for the other shoe to drop since he was old enough to know shoes dropped.

"I must've got the day wrong," Latisha said.

"No. You didn't." Dana leaned forward, just an inch. "You're lying. And I need to know why, because if you get on that stand and say this under oath, they're going to charge you with perjury, and you're going to lose your job, and whatever you're trying to do here? It won't work anyway. The footage exists."

Latisha's eyes went shiny. She blinked hard, picked at the chipped polish on her thumb. "I can't—" Her voice cracked. She tried again. "I can't tell you."

"Can't, or won't?"

"She asked me to," Marcus mumbled.

Dana's head snapped toward him. "Who did?"

He didn't answer. He was looking at Latisha now, and she was shaking her head, almost imperceptibly, jaw set.

"Marcus. Who asked her?"

"Nobody. It doesn't matter."

"It matters a great deal. You're looking at twenty-five years. Do you understand that? Twenty-five. You'll be middle-aged when you get out." Her voice rose despite herself, and she reined it in. "Somebody asked this woman to invent an alibi for you. Either you're protecting them or she is. So which is it?"

Latisha stood up so fast the chair scraped the floor. "I should go. I have a shift."

"Sit down, Ms. Eubanks."

"No. I—I don't have to talk to you." She was already reaching for her bag, a faded canvas thing with a hospital logo peeling off the side. "I'm sorry. I can't."

She was at the door when Dana said, quiet, "It's your brother, isn't it?"

Latisha froze with her hand on the handle.

Dana didn't know how she knew until she said it. But there it was—the scrubs, the hospital job, the way Marcus had gone so still. "The hands in the video. They're small. The build's wrong. I've been looking at the wrong client since the day I got this file." She stood up too. "Your brother robbed that store. And Marcus here is willing to take the fall for it. Why?"

Latisha's shoulders shook. She didn't turn around.

"Because he was there," Marcus said softly. "Because it went bad and the clerk got hurt and Devin panicked. Because Devin's seventeen. Tried as an adult, he's gone forever. I'm nineteen. I got—I got nothing on my record, they'll go easier, maybe—"

"They won't," Dana said. But her stomach had dropped, because she could see the shape of it now, the whole terrible machine. "And Devin? Where is he?"

Latisha turned. Tears had cut two clean lines through her makeup. "You don't understand. Our mother's dying. Stage four. Devin's all she's got left. If he goes in before—" She stopped, swallowed. "She asked me. My mother asked me. From her hospital bed. What was I supposed to do?"

Dana looked at the two of them—the girl with the chipped nail polish, the boy with the shovel hands and the bad shoulder—and thought about the lobby footage, and the DA who ran on being tough, and the judge who'd once given a kid eighteen years for a sandwich. Outside, the intercom crackled with someone's name.

She closed her legal pad.

"I need a minute," she said. "With my client."

title: romance|a widowed veterinarian and a stubborn rancher are snowed in together during a blizzard
text:
The wind howled like a scorned coyote, hurling snow against the cabin windows so hard the panes rattled in their frames. Dr. Elara Voss, widowed three years come spring, wiped the last smudge of antiseptic off her calico cat Mabel’s paw and glanced up at the rancher leaning against her kitchen doorframe.
“For the last time, Hale, you are not driving back to your place tonight.”
Jake Hale’s jaw set, the scar along his left cheek—from a run-in with a spooked stallion when he was 19—pulling tight as he glowered at the drifts already piling three feet high against her porch. “I got 12 head of heifers due to calve any day. Can’t leave ’em to fend for themselves.”
“Your ranch hand Javi texted ten minutes ago saying he battened down the barn, turned on the heat lamps, and locked the feed shed.” Elara tossed the paper towel in the trash and crossed her arms, her worn vet scrubs dotted with dog hair and a faint coffee stain on the cuff. “Your truck’s already buried to the wheel wells. You’d freeze solid before you hit the county line.”
Jake pushed off the doorframe, boots thudding on her pine floor as he strode to the window. He was broad-shouldered, worn flannel stretched tight across his back, work gloves crumpled in one calloused hand. He’d showed up at her door two hours prior, half-frozen, carrying a limp border collie puppy that had wandered off his ranch and gotten caught in barbed wire. Elara had stitched the pup’s hind leg, wrapped it tight, and set him up in a dog bed by the wood stove, where he now snored softly, Mabel curled purring against his side.
“That storm came out of nowhere.” Jake’s voice was gruff, like he was angry at the sky itself for trapping him here. “I shoulda checked the forecast before I rode out to the north pasture.”
Elara huffed, turning to the cast-iron stove where a pot of chili simmered. “You never check the forecast. You’re the most stubborn man in three counties. Last winter you tried to break ice on the trough in the middle of a whiteout because you ‘didn’t have time to wait for the thaw.’ You ended up slipping and cracking your rib, remember? You showed up here refusing to let me drive you to the clinic, said you ‘didn’t need no doctor fussing over you.’”
A faint flush crept up Jake’s neck, visible even under the stubble dusting his jaw. “That was different.”
“Sure it was.” Elara ladled two bowls of chili, sliding one across the kitchen table to him along with a spoon and a hunk of sourdough she’d baked that morning. “Sit. Eat. You’re not going anywhere till this blows over, which the weather app says won’t be till tomorrow afternoon at the earliest.”
Jake hesitated for a long moment, staring at the bowl like it might bite him, before finally pulling out a chair and sitting down. He took a bite of chili, and his eyebrows shot up in surprise. “This is good.”
“Comes from spending three winters snowed in alone with nothing but old cookbooks and Mabel for company.” Elara sat across from him, blowing on a spoonful. “You get good at making food that sticks to your ribs when there’s no pizza delivery for 40 miles.”
Silence fell between them, broken only by the wind outside and the pop of the firewood. Jake’s gaze drifted to the framed photo on the windowsill: Elara and her late husband Liam, grinning with a golden retriever puppy between them, taken the summer before the car crash that killed him.
“You ever get lonely out here?” Jake’s voice was quieter now, the gruff edge softening.
Elara followed his gaze, her fingers tracing the rim of her bowl. “Sometimes. But I’ve got the animals. The clinic. It’s enough.” She looked up at him, sharp. “Don’t you? All that land, all those cattle. Big old empty ranch house?”
Jake stared into his chili, jaw working. “Got the dogs. The horses. Work keeps me busy.” He paused, then added, almost mumbled, “Ain’t the same, though.”
The puppy whimpered in his sleep, and both of them turned to look. Mabel lifted her head, blinked at them, then tucked her face back against the pup’s fur.
“Thank you.” Jake said it so quietly Elara almost didn’t hear it over the wind. “For patching up Bo. I… that pup’s the best herding dog I’ve had in years. Thought I’d lost him when I found him tangled up in that wire.”
Elara smiled, a small, soft thing she didn’t show many people. “It’s my job. Besides, he’s a sweet thing. Knew he was yours the second I saw that white patch on his chest—all your border collies have that same mark.”
Jake blinked, like he was surprised she’d noticed. “You pay attention to that?”
“I pay attention to everything about the animals in this county.” Elara leaned back in her chair, watching him. “Even the ones owned by stubborn ranchers who’d rather walk through a blizzard than admit they might need help.”
A faint, lopsided smile tugged at the corner of Jake’s mouth, the first real smile she’d seen from him all night. “You’re never gonna let me live that rib thing down, are you?”
“Not as long as I live.” Elara stood, grabbing their empty bowls and taking them to the sink. “I’ve got extra blankets in the hall closet. The couch pulls out into a bed. It’s not the Ritz, but it’s warm.”
Jake stood too, moving to stand beside her at the sink, close enough that she could smell pine and hay and the faint, sharp scent of winter on his flannel. “Elara…” he started, then trailed off, like he didn’t know what to say.
Outside, the wind picked up again, sending a gust of snow slamming against the window. Inside, the fire crackled, Bo snored, and for the first time in three years, Elara didn’t feel the cold, empty quiet of the cabin pressing in on her.
She turned to look at him, and that soft smile was back on her face. “Stay, Jake,” she said, quiet enough that it was almost lost to the storm.
For a long second, he just looked at her, brown eyes steady on hers, and then he nodded.
“Yeah,” he said. “I’ll stay.”

title: horror|a family moves into a farmhouse where the previous owners' dog will not stop digging in the cellar
text:
The first week in the farmhouse smelled like fresh paint and old secrets. Mara stood at the kitchen sink, watching her husband, Eddie, wrestle a flat-packed bookshelf across the living room while their daughter, Lily, chased a moth with a cereal bowl. Outside, the August fields rolled gold and indifferent, the nearest neighbor almost two miles down the cracked county road.

They had gotten the place cheap. The real estate agent’s smile had tightened when Eddie asked why. “Older couple,” she’d said. “The husband passed. The wife moved into town. They left a few things behind.”

Including the dog.

He was half shepherd, half shadow, gray-muzzled and thin, waiting on the porch when the moving truck arrived. A tag on his collar read BUDDY in stamped letters. He let Lily kneel beside him and scratch behind his ears, but his eyes kept sliding toward the cellar door.

“Probably misses them,” Mara said.

By the second night, he was digging.

Scratch. Scratch-scratch. Pause. Then the slow, deliberate tear of claws into packed earth.

It came from under the kitchen floor, deep and rhythmic, loud enough to pull Mara from sleep at two in the morning. She found Eddie sitting up in bed, jaw set, listening.

“Moles?” she whispered.

“Moles don’t work eight-hour shifts.”

He pulled on jeans and took a flashlight. The cellar door was a warped oak slab set into the floor near the pantry, fitted with a brass latch that looked newer than it should have. Eddie lifted it. A smell rose from the black stairs: wet dirt, rot, and something metallic, like pennies left in rain.

Buddy stood at the bottom, illuminated in the weak cone of light. His front legs were dark to the shoulders. Behind him, along the far stone wall, he had torn open a trench beneath the shelving. Dirt fanned across the concrete.

“Hey,” Eddie said. “Buddy. Quit it.”

The dog did not turn. He dug faster, claws scraping, chest heaving with a low whine that wasn’t quite a growl.

Mara backed up when Eddie hauled him out by the collar. Buddy’s eyes were wild, rimmed white. He twisted, scrambled, and made a sound she had never heard from an animal—a thin, human-like sob. The instant Eddie released him, he bolted for the open door and nearly made the stairs before Mara slammed it shut.

They locked him in the mudroom. He threw himself against the door until dawn.

By morning, reason returned. “Separation anxiety,” Mara told Eddie over coffee, though she didn’t fully believe it. “Boredom. We’ll buy him toys. Maybe a crate.”

Lily fed him bacon and whispered to him while he ate, but his attention kept fixing on the floor, head tilted, as if listening to something beneath their feet.

That afternoon, Eddie filled the trench with two bags of topsoil and hammered boards over the gap. Buddy watched from the top of the stairs, trembling.

By dusk, the digging started again.

Not through the fresh dirt alone. The boards creaked and split in the dark, accompanied by desperate, huffing breaths. Mara went down with Eddie this time. The flashlight shook in her hand. The new soil had been hurled aside. One plank jutted crookedly from the wall. Buddy was buried to the shoulders in the hole, hind legs braced, tearing at the earth in frantic spasm after spasm.

Then his claws clicked against something white.

Mara’s stomach turned. “Eddie.”

It was smooth at first, curved, streaked with clay. Eddie reached down, grabbed Buddy’s collar, and dragged him backward. The dog snapped—not at him, but at the hole, teeth clicking in the empty air. When Eddie shone the light inside, the beam caught a row of yellowed shapes set in the dark like broken dishes.

Not dishes.

Mara stumbled up the stairs. She could hear Lily in the kitchen, humming to herself, and the ordinary sound made the horror sharper.

Eddie emerged white-faced, shut the cellar door, and latched it. “Animal bones,” he said quietly. “That’s all. Livestock. Old farm dump.”

Buddy disagreed. He planted himself before the door and barked once, sharp and cracking. Then he went still, ears forward.

From below, soft and muffled, came the sound of digging.

Not from where Buddy had been.

From somewhere deeper.

Slow. Steady. Coming up.

Lily appeared in the hallway, hugging her stuffed rabbit. “Mommy?” she said. “Why is the dog barking at the floor?”

Mara opened her mouth, but no answer came.

At their feet, the brass latch twitched.

Once.

Then again.

Buddy backed away, hackles ridged along his spine, and for the first time since they had found him on the porch, he tucked his tail and hid behind Lily.

The digging stopped.

Something on the other side of the door inhaled.

title: comic|a holistic detective tries to explain to a sceptical client why a horse is in the bathroom
text:
The first thing you have to understand about holistic detection is that people will look at a horse in a bathroom and immediately jump to the most uncharitable conclusions possible. It’s the problem with linear thinking. Everyone sees the horse, sees the claw-foot tub full of peppermint polos, sees the chipped tile where the horse tried to scratch his left hindquarter at 2:17 a.m., and goes “why is there a horse in my bathroom?” instead of asking the far more pertinent question: why wouldn’t there be?

I was perched on the edge of Mrs. Harrington’s vanity, dabbing at a smudge of horse slobber on the cuff of my second-best tweed jacket, when she appeared in the doorway, curlers still in, silk dressing gown pulled so tight across her chest I was half-convinced the buttons would take out my left eye. Her mouth opened and closed three times, like a goldfish that had just wandered into a particularly baffling episode of Grand Designs.

“Mr. Pebble,” she said, voice so cold it could have kept her weekly grocery delivery fresh for a month, “why is there a horse in my bathroom.”

It wasn’t a question. It was the kind of statement that comes with a pre-attached invoice for emotional distress and a lifetime ban from the village WI. I held up a hand, the universal gesture for give me ten seconds to come up with something that doesn’t sound like I snuck a draft horse into your en-suite for a prank, and glanced over at the horse. He was a nice bay, fourteen hands, white sock on his off fore, name tag around his neck that read *BARRY*. He gave me a slow, unblinking look, like he was also waiting for a good explanation, the little traitor.

*Think*, I told myself, *think holistically*. It’s not about the horse. The horse is just the node. Last week Mrs. Harrington had called me because her prize-winning marrow seeds kept vanishing from the greenhouse, and her cat had taken to leaving whole, perfectly intact mackerel on her pillow instead of dead shrews, and the church bells three villages over kept ringing *Dancing Queen* at 3 a.m. for no discernible reason. Linear detectives would have treated those as three separate problems. Fools. All things are connected. The great web of the universe doesn’t have loose ends, just things people haven’t bothered to trace back to the spider yet.

“Mrs. Harrington,” I said, leaning forward as earnestly as I could without knocking over her bottle of lavender bubble bath, “let me ask you this. When was the last time you wrote a thank-you note to your postman?”

Her jaw tightened. “What on earth does that have to do with—”

“Humor me.”

“Three weeks ago? He left a parcel on the step in the rain and my copy of *The Beekeeper’s Annual* got water damaged. I told him I’d be making a formal complaint.”

I nodded, like this confirmed everything. Which it did, sort of, if you squinted and tilted your head far enough to the left. “Right. And your great-aunt Mabel, the one who left you this cottage? She kept horses, didn’t she? She always said a house that didn’t have a horse in it at least once a generation was cursed to have bad jam for a hundred years.”

“That was a joke she told at my wedding!”

“Was it?” I raised an eyebrow. Barry chose that moment to nudge the tap with his nose, sending a trickle of cold water down the back of Mrs. Harrington’s dressing gown. She yelped, jumping a foot in the air. “Now, hold on—before you get cross. The seeds? Barry ate them. He’s got a terrible thing for marrow seeds, wandered over from the livery yard two miles up the lane when the postman left the side gate unlatched on Tuesday—he was distracted, see, because he was upset about your complaint, and he’d stopped to chat to the livery yard owner about it, and Barry made a break for it. The mackerel? Your cat’s been bringing them to Barry as offerings. They’re mates. Sees him as a very large, very slow cat who lives in the bathroom now. The bells? Turns out the vicar’s teenage son has been sneaking in to practice ABBA covers for his school talent show, and he said he saw a horse trotting down the high street on Wednesday night and got so flustered he accidentally set the timer for 3 a.m. instead of 3 p.m. It all ties together.”

Mrs. Harrington stared at me. She stared at Barry. Barry blinked, and lipped a polo mint out of the tub, crunching it so loud the sound echoed off the tile.

“You are telling me,” she said, very slowly, “that there is a horse in my bathroom because I was rude to the postman.”

“I’m telling you,” I said, “that there is a horse in your bathroom because the universe is a series of tiny, domino-sized choices, and you knocked over the first one when you decided that a slightly damp beekeeping magazine was worth making a man who walks six miles a day in all weather feel like garbage. Also, Barry likes your underfloor heating. Says it’s better than the stable at the yard. He’s very particular.”

She took a deep breath. I could see the fight draining out of her, the way it always does when people realize that fighting the interconnected web of all things is less productive than just making a cup of tea and accepting that sometimes horses end up in bathrooms. She reached into her dressing gown pocket, pulled out a polo mint of all things— leftover from her granddaughter’s pony party last weekend, I’d bet—and held it out. Barry craned his neck over the shower rail to take it, very gently, like he was handling fine china.

“Fine,” she said. “But if he leaves a pile on my bath mat, you’re cleaning it up. And you’re explaining to the vicar why his son thinks there’s a ghost horse haunting the village.”

I grinned, sliding off the vanity. “Holistic detection, Mrs. H. Full service. Now—do you have any sugar? He takes two lumps, and he’s promised he knows where your missing silver teapot is.”

Barry nodded. Obviously. Horses don’t lie. Not about teapots, anyway.
