title: horror|survivors barricaded in a supermarket hear someone they buried knocking at the loading dock
text:
Chapter 11
The fluorescent lights in the back storage room of Hargrove’s Supermarket flickered for the third time in ten minutes, casting long, wavering shadows over the stacked pallets of canned beans and bottled water. Mara pressed her palm flat against the cold cinder block wall, listening. The wind howled outside, sharp with the tang of rot and burnt plastic, but beneath it, there was another sound.

A knock.

Slow. Deliberate. Three raps against the heavy metal loading dock door, the one they’d welded shut with a stolen blowtorch three days prior.

Jake looked up from where he was sharpening a kitchen knife against a whetstone, his knuckles white around the handle. “Tell me that’s a branch.”

“It’s not a branch,” Mara said. Her throat felt tight, like someone had wrapped a hand around it from the inside. “Branches don’t knock in rhythm.”

The knock came again. This time, four beats. Tap-tap-tap-tap. Patient, almost polite.

Lila, who’d been curled on a sleeping bag in the corner, sat up fast, her matted brown hair falling over her eyes. She was only seventeen, and the dark circles under her eyes made her look years older. “We buried him,” she whispered. “We put him in the ground by the garden center. I saw you cover his face with the blanket.”

Mara remembered it all too well. Two days ago, they’d found Mr. Hale, the night manager, slumped against the checkout counter, his throat torn open, skin already turning gray. They’d wrapped him in a vinyl tablecloth, dragged him out through the loading dock before the things roaming the parking lot noticed, and buried him in the soft dirt behind the abandoned nursery next door. She’d said a few words she barely remembered, and Jake had hammered a wooden cross into the soil above him.

Jake stood up, the knife glinting in the flickering light. “Could be someone else. A survivor. They might’ve seen the smoke from our fire last night.”

“No survivor knocks like that,” Mara said. The sound was too even, too calm. The people they’d encountered since the outbreak banged and screamed and begged, their hands slapping wildly at doors until their knuckles split. This sounded like someone who knew exactly who was on the other side.

She walked slowly toward the loading dock door, her boots crunching over scattered shards of a broken jar of pickles. A narrow rectangular window was set high in the metal, fogged with grime. She grabbed a step ladder from beside the cleaning supply shelf, climbed up, and wiped the glass with the sleeve of her jacket.

The floodlight mounted above the dock flickered on—Jake must’ve triggered the switch by the breaker panel. It bleached the concrete outside pale white, illuminating the empty truck bay, the stacked empty crates, the chipped yellow paint marking the loading zones.

There was no one there.

“See?” Jake said, but his voice shook. “Nothing. Probably just the wind catching a loose piece of siding.”

Then the knock came again, right at eye level, making Mara flinch so hard she nearly fell off the ladder. Dirt smudged the glass from the outside, as if someone had pressed a muddy palm against it. She leaned closer, squinting.

A hand rose into view, fingers curled, and rapped once more against the window.

The nails were caked with dark, moist soil. The skin was gray, streaked with the same red mud they’d dug through to dig the grave. A tattered edge of the blue vinyl tablecloth they’d wrapped him in was tied around the wrist, frayed and stained.

Lila made a small, choking sound behind her. “That’s his watch. The gold one with the broken clasp. He never took it off.”

Mara’s blood turned to ice. She recognized it too—the scuffed metal band, the crack across the watch face. It had been 3:17 when they buried him. The hands were still frozen there now.

“Mara.” Jake’s voice was barely audible. “Step back from the door.”

But she couldn’t move. The hand lowered, and a face pressed up against the fogged glass. One eye was clouded over, filmed white, but the other was clear, fixed directly on her. Dirt crumbled from its cheek, and its lips moved slowly, forming words she couldn’t hear through the thick metal.

It knocked again, harder this time, the sound echoing through the storage room. The welded seams of the door creaked, fine dust sifting down from the frame.

“He’s alone out there?” Jake had moved up beside her, his knife held tight, but his hand was trembling so bad the blade glinted erratically. “The things out there don’t… they don’t knock. They don’t *find* people like this.”

Lila had stood, backing away until her shoulders hit the shelf of cereal boxes. “He knows we’re here. He *remembers*.”

The thing that had been Mr. Hale pressed its palm flat against the window again, leaving a dark, muddy print. Its mouth kept moving, slow and deliberate, and this time, Mara could almost read the shape of the words.

*Let me in.*

A sharp, scraping sound came from the bottom of the door, like fingernails dragging across metal. The welded joints groaned, bending inward just a fraction. Outside, somewhere in the dark parking lot, another sound answered—a low, gurgling moan, then another, then a dozen more, rising up to meet the knocking.

Mara stumbled off the ladder, her heart slamming against her ribs. The lights flickered again, and for a second, the storage room was plunged into complete darkness. When they sputtered back on, the eye at the window was still there, unblinking, watching.

The knocking didn’t stop. Steady. Patient. Like it knew they had nowhere left to run.

title: cozy mystery|a doll collector stumbles onto a murder at a county fair antiques show
text:
Chapter 3
The smell of fried dough stuck to my throat like powdered sugar glue, thick and sweet enough to make my teeth ache before I even stepped past the ticket booth. I adjusted the tote bag slung over my shoulder—canvas, printed with a faded bisque Kewpie holding a lollipop, the strap frayed where I’d caught it on a shelf of 1860s china heads last winter—and ducked under the banner strung between two oak trees: MAPLE HOLLOW COUNTY FAIR ANTIQUES SHOW, EST. 1972. The fabric flapped in the September breeze, carrying a whiff of cow manure from the livestock barns three rows over, sharp enough to cut the sugar.
I was here for the Armand Marseille 390 I’d spotted in a Facebook group post three days prior: 18 inches, sleep eyes, original mohair wig, a faint crack on the left cheek the seller swore wasn’t a repair, priced at $120 if I showed up before 10 a.m. My name is Clara Bennett, I run the doll hospital out of the back room of my cottage on Oak Street, and I don’t leave the house before 9 for anything less than a mold-poured bisque head with its original pate.
The antiques tent was strung with fairy lights that flickered like dying fireflies even in the bright morning, tables draped in stained bed linens that had probably been tablecloths since the first Nixon administration. I waved at Marnie from the vintage jewelry booth, who was dabbing nail polish remover on a tarnished silver brooch, and stepped around a stack of chipped Fiesta ware to find table 17, the one the seller had marked with a hand-painted sign: *DOLLS, NO LOWBALLS, I KNOW WHAT I GOT*.
The sign was propped against a bin of naked Barbie torsos and a row of rusted Tonka trucks, but there was no Armand Marseille. No seller, either, just a half-empty cup of black coffee sweating through a paper napkin printed with prize pumpkins, and a crumpled pack of menthols tucked next to a brass cash register that looked like it weighed 20 pounds.
“Looking for Earl?”
I jumped. Mabel Higgins, who ran the pickle stand outside the tent, was leaning against the table leg, holding a paper cup of brine floating a whole dill. She was wearing the same gingham house dress she’d worn to every fair since I was 10, her hair in a hairnet dotted with plastic daisies. “He was in here ten minutes ago grumbling about some guy from the city lowballing him on that bisque doll you’re after. Said he was gonna take a leak behind the cow barn and come back to run the guy off if he showed up again.”
I nodded, shifting my tote higher on my shoulder, and peered under the table. Sometimes sellers hid the good stuff to keep tire-kickers from messing with it, and I’d lost more than one rare Jumeau to a collector who didn’t mind crawling on linoleum for a bargain. There was nothing under there but a crushed lemonade cup, a rubber rat someone had dropped as a prank, and a pair of scuffed work boots caked in mud that looked an awful lot like the ones Earl had been wearing in his profile photo.
Wait.
I knelt down, the gravel of the tent floor digging through my jeans, and tugged at the boot. It didn’t move. When I pulled the tablecloth up a little higher, the fairy lights caught the silver of his belt buckle, engraved *E.R.H.*, and the dark, wet patch seeping through the front of his flannel shirt, sticky and glistening like melted black cherry jam. The Armand Marseille was on the ground next to his outstretched hand, its left cheek cracked clean through, a splatter of something dark flecked across its painted blue eyes.
I didn’t scream. I just sat back on my heels, my palm pressed to my mouth, and stared. The coffee cup on the table dripped onto the linoleum, slow as a clock ticking, and somewhere a kid screamed about winning a goldfish. Mabel leaned down, her pickle brine sloshing over the edge of her cup onto my sneaker.
“Clara? You find that doll you were after?”
Before I could answer, a shadow fell over the table. I looked up, and it was the guy from the city, the one Mabel had mentioned—tailored khakis, loafers without a speck of fair mud on them, a leather binder tucked under his arm, the kind collectors use to carry provenance papers. He smiled, all straight white teeth, and nodded at the tablecloth I was still holding up.
“Earl around? I talked to him earlier about that Marseille. I’m willing to pay his asking price, even with the crack.”
I stared at him. The doll’s cracked eye stared back at me from under the table, its painted lashes crusted with something that wasn’t factory varnish. Somewhere, the fair’s PA system crackled to life, announcing the start of the hog-calling contest in ten minutes. Mabel took a loud crunch of her pickle.
The guy’s smile faltered a little when I didn’t answer. He glanced down at my Kewpie tote, then at my hand, still fisted in the tablecloth.
“Ma’am? You okay?”
I opened my mouth to say something, but all I could smell was fried dough and cow manure and copper, thick and hot under the tent, and the fairy lights flickered once, twice, like they were about to go out. (712 words)

title: thriller|a CIA analyst realises the briefing she wrote has been altered before it reached the President
text:
The Situation Room smelled like cold coffee and burnt popcorn.

Maya Chen leaned against the wall at the back, tablet pressed to her chest, watching the President of the United States read her briefing.

She had written every word. At least, she had once.

“North Korea?” President Hargrove said, half-laughing. “You’re telling me they’re moving three submarines into the Sea of Japan?”

General Pratt nodded. “Confirmed by satellite. We recommend surge deployment.”

Maya’s blood went cold.

Three submarines.

She had written one.

A training exercise. Coastal. Forty-eight hours, expected return to Wonsan by dawn.

She tapped her tablet, pulling up the archived draft. Her draft.

One submarine. Routine.

The document on the screen in front of the President said three.

“Maya?”

She looked up. Her boss, Deputy Director Dale Harmon, was watching her from across the room. Gray suit, calm eyes, the kind of man who never raised his voice because he never needed to.

He gave her a tiny, almost imperceptible shake of his head.

Don’t.

She smiled tightly and looked back down.

“Mr. President,” she said, stepping forward before she could talk herself out of it. “I wrote this assessment. That isn’t what it said when it left my desk.”

The room went quiet.

Hargrove lifted his eyes. “Excuse me?”

“The submarine paragraph, sir. I wrote one vessel. This says three. I also flagged the exercise as low-confidence imagery. That caveat’s gone.”

Pratt turned in his chair. “Analyst, this briefing came through CIA Directors’ staff three hours ago.”

“Then it was changed after I sent it.”

“Careful,” Harmon said softly.

Maya kept her gaze on the President. “Sir, I can show you the source file. Timestamps, edit history, everything.”

Hargrove studied her for a long moment. He had been a federal prosecutor once; he had the kind of stare that made people remember sins they hadn’t committed.

“Show me,” he said.

Her hands were steady as she crossed to the table. She plugged in her tablet. The classified drive mounted. She opened her master folder.

The file wasn’t there.

She blinked.

Refreshed.

Nothing.

“Ms. Chen?” Hargrove said.

“One second, sir.”

She opened her local cache. Empty.

Her email. The sent message was gone.

The backup drive threw an authentication error.

Somewhere behind her, someone coughed.

“Is there a problem?” Pratt asked.

Maya stared at the screen. Every copy she had made had vanished in the last twenty minutes.

She heard Harmon’s shoes on the carpet behind her.

“Maya,” he murmured, close enough only she could hear. “Stop while you still have a career.”

She turned her head. “You.”

He didn’t deny it.

That was worse than the denial.

“Why?” she whispered.

His expression didn’t change. “Because the world doesn’t run on your conscience, sweetheart. It runs on decisions. Sometimes the right decision needs a little push.”

“Three submarines isn’t a push, Dale. It’s a lie. It’s a war.”

He glanced at the table, where the President waited. “You’re tired. You’ve been on rotation for eleven days. I told Hargrove you were burning out.”

Maya’s stomach dropped.

Of course he had.

She turned back. “Mr. President, my files have been wiped. I believe—”

“Mr. President,” Harmon cut in smoothly, “Ms. Chen has been under considerable strain. Her concerns were reviewed. The assessment reflects the agency’s final consensus.”

“Consensus?” Maya said. “You mean the one you manufactured?”

Hargrove leaned back in his chair. “You making an accusation, Ms. Chen?”

“Yes, sir. I am.”

“Against your deputy director?”

“Against whoever altered my work and scrubbed my archives.”

Pratt scoffed. “With all respect, this is a tantrum.”

Maya’s eyes swept the room. Twelve people. Military, national security, chiefs of staff. Half were angry. Half were watching Harmon.

None of them looked surprised enough.

Oh God.

Not all of them. But enough.

Her phone buzzed in her blazer pocket. She ignored it.

“Sir,” she said, quieter now, choosing each word, “if I’m wrong, court-martial me. Fire me. Send me to Florence for the rest of my life. But before you order a surge, ask yourself why every caveat disappeared.”

Hargrove didn’t speak.

Her phone buzzed again. Then a third time, rapid, insistent.

She pulled it out, expecting security, expecting a threat, expecting Harmon’s secretary.

The message was from a number she didn’t know.

> LOOK AT PAGE 11, FOOTNOTE 4.

Her breath caught.

Page 11. Maritime logistics. Footnote 4 was a throwaway line about maintenance schedules, buried in small text. Nobody read footnotes. Nobody except her.

She opened the altered briefing on the tablet with shaking fingers and scrolled.

Footnote 4 read:

> Three vessels now confirmed per D/DIR guidance. Original analyst dissent retained in sealed annex C-7.

Maya almost laughed.

Whoever had edited the document had been ordered to make it convincing. They had buried the truth in plain sight, careful enough to protect themselves, obedient enough to hide it from the President.

“Sir,” she said. “Page eleven. Footnote four.”

Hargrove reached for the printed copy.

Harmon moved.

It was small, just a hand settling on the binder, but the President saw it.

“Dale,” Hargrove said.

Harmon froze.

“Take your hand off my briefing.”

The room was so quiet Maya could hear the air vents.

Hargrove turned the pages slowly. Found the footnote. Read it. Then read it again.

His jaw tightened.

“General Pratt,” he said, without looking up, “did you review the primary intelligence?”

“Mr. President, I relied on the agency product—”

“Did anyone in this room look at source imagery?”

Silence.

Maya’s phone buzzed once more.

A photograph. Grainy satellite capture. Time-stamped from her own archive. One submarine. One.

She turned the screen toward the President.

Hargrove stared at it.

Then he closed the binder.

“Meeting adjourned,” he said. “Except Ms. Chen, Director Harmon, and the Inspector General, who I want on site in twenty minutes.”

Chairs scraped. People moved.

Harmon didn’t move.

For the first time, his calm cracked, just a fracture around his eyes.

“You should’ve left it alone, Maya.”

She met him stare for stare.

“No, Dale. You should’ve changed the footnotes.”

Outside, a helicopter crossed the Washington skyline, low and heavy.

Maya watched it through the reinforced glass and wondered if the person who sent that photograph was still alive.

title: literary|an old woman tells a police officer the true story of the night her husband died
text:
The linoleum by the kitchen table sticks to my slipper when I shift, the syrup from last week’s canned peaches never did scrub up right. You don’t need to flip that notebook again, officer. I’ll tell it straight, no more of the “he fell down the stairs” garbage I fed the rookie last winter.

It was three a.m. The radiators clanked so loud I thought the pipes’d burst, same as they did in ’98. Ray stumbled in reeking of rye and the cheap perfume that girl at the VFW slathers on so thick you can smell it three bar stools over. He didn’t even take his boots off. Tracked slush right onto the rug I hooked back when we first moved in, the one with the rose border his ma gave us.

I didn’t say nothing at first. Knew better than to open my mouth when he was that far gone. But then he saw the pill bottle on the counter. The ones the doctor gave me for my hip, the ones he’d been stealing to sell to the kids down on Oak Street for extra beer money. He started yelling. Said I hid ’em from him on purpose. Said I was a selfish old crone who never did nothing but make his life hard.

He came at me then, same as he did when the kids were small, his fist curled tight like he was still 25 and working the loading dock, like his knuckles didn’t ache so bad some mornings he couldn’t even hold his coffee mug. I backed up. Hit the edge of the china cabinet. The soup tureen his ma gave us for a wedding present wobbled, then fell. Smashed into a hundred pieces right between us.

He froze for half a second. Looked down at the shards, like he couldn’t figure out where they came from. That’s when I saw the gun on the counter. The old .22 he kept for raccoons that got into the garbage out back. I didn’t think. Just grabbed it. Told him to get out.

He laughed. Laughed so hard he started coughing, that wet, rattle-y cough he got from smoking Camels for 50 years. Said I didn’t have the guts. Said I hadn’t had the guts to leave him in 47 years, why start now? He stepped over the broken china. Reached for me.

I pulled the trigger.

It wasn’t loud, not like the movies make it out to be. Sounded like a firecracker going off in a tin can. He looked down at his chest, at the dark spot spreading fast over his flannel shirt, the one with the deer on it I got him for Christmas two years back. He looked up at me. His mouth moved, but no sound came out. Then he fell. Hit the floor so hard the salt shaker fell off the table.

I stood there for I don’t know how long. The gun was still warm in my hand. The radiators kept clanking. Somewhere down the street a dog barked. Then I dragged him to the stairs. Propped him up like he tripped on the top step. Called 911.

I finish the last of the cold coffee in my mug, the grounds bitter at the bottom. You gonna arrest me now, officer? I ain’t running. My hip’s too bad to run far, anyway. I just got tired of lying. Tired of looking at that empty chair across the table every morning, pretending I’m sad he’s gone.

title: romance|a journalist returns to her hometown and runs into the boy she left without saying goodbye
text:
I told myself I’d only come here for coffee.

Not for him. Not for the ghost of him. Not for every stupid, reckless memory tangled up in this town like fishing line in marsh grass. I was here because the rental house had terrible coffee, my editor wanted a follow-up article by Monday, and Main Street had exactly one place that opened before seven.

That was all.

The bell above the door jingled when I stepped inside, and the smell hit me first: dark roast, cinnamon, butter thick enough to sink into. It was unfair, really, that a place could change its paint and its menu boards and still smell exactly like the summer I turned eighteen.

I got in line behind two women discussing the upcoming harbor festival and stared at the pastry case like it owed me answers. Lemon cake. Cherry turnovers. Blueberry muffins baked in brown paper cups. For one disorienting second, I was seventeen again, cramming change onto the counter while Ethan laughed and told me sugar was not a valid breakfast.

“You’re shaking,” he’d said.

“That’s because you made us run.”

“You’re the one who wanted to see the sunrise.”

“And you’re the one who said we had time.”

“We did have time.”

“We missed first period.”

“Worth it.”

I swallowed hard.

Eight years. Eight years of cities and deadlines and crowded subway cars, and somehow his voice was still easier to remember than my own phone number.

Don’t, I told myself. Don’t do this. You came back to write a story. You did not come back to unpack him.

The woman ahead of me collected her latte, and I stepped forward.

“Black coffee,” I said. “Large. And whatever muffin is freshest.”

The barista, a college-aged girl with silver rings and a green apron, smiled. “Blueberry. Usually is this early.”

“Perfect.”

I paid without making eye contact with anything except the card reader. Good. Efficient. In and out. Then I could go back to the little rented cottage, open my laptop, and pretend I wasn’t counting every familiar face in the room like I was waiting for one to find me.

The barista handed over the muffin. “Cup’ll be out in a minute.”

I moved to the pickup end of the counter and told myself to breathe. The café was busier than it used to be, all reclaimed wood and hanging plants where the old newspaper rack had stood. A chalkboard advertised live music on Saturdays. A bulletin by the door advertised kayak tours, tutoring, a lost tabby cat. Progress, I guessed. Small towns were supposed to stay frozen, but they never did. They kept living even when you left.

Even when you left someone standing on a dock with no explanation.

My stomach twisted.

I’d rehearsed this, in the weak, dishonest way people rehearse impossible conversations. If I saw him, I would be polite. Distant, maybe, but kind. I would say hello. I would ask how he was. I would not let guilt slam into me like a fist. I would not let myself remember that I hadn’t texted. Hadn’t called. Hadn’t left a note beyond the cowardly one I’d written and torn into pieces in the passenger seat of my mother’s car.

I’m sorry wasn’t enough.

Don’t go wasn’t possible.

I love you had been the scariest sentence in the world, so I’d said nothing at all.

“Black coffee,” someone called.

I reached for the cup at the same moment another hand did.

Broad fingers. Tanned wrist. A faint white scar across the knuckle, old and thin, from the night he’d punched the side of his father’s boat in a fury and then tried to hide the bleeding from me.

My breath stopped.

He looked up.

Ethan Cole looked older, which was absurd and inevitable. The boyish sharpness had settled into something leaner. Lines had formed at the corners of his eyes, and his dark hair was shorter now, curling a little where the sea air caught it. He wore a flannel shirt with the sleeves pushed up, and for a second his expression showed nothing at all.

Then recognition moved through him, slow and dangerous.

“June,” he said.

My name sounded different in his mouth. Not soft, the way it used to be. Not laughing. Just careful.

I pulled my hand back like the coffee had burned me. “Hi.”

A beat passed. Two. Around us, the café moved on—steaming milk, scraping chairs, rain starting to spit against the front windows—but the space between us felt locked.

“You’re back,” he said.

“Temporarily.” The word came out too fast. “I’m writing a piece for the magazine. The resort development, the harbor zoning. I’m only here for a week or so.”

His mouth curved, but it wasn’t a smile. “So not a social visit.”

I deserved that.

“No,” I said quietly. “Not exactly.”

He picked up the cup and held it out to me. Our fingers didn’t touch this time, though I thought he made sure of it. “Then welcome home, journalist.”

Home. He made it sound like an accusation.

“Ethan—”

“I didn’t know you were coming,” he said, before I could finish a sentence I had no right to start. “Heard someone from a city magazine was asking questions down at the dock, but nobody mentioned it was you.”

“I wasn’t trying to—”

“Hide?”

I flinched.

His jaw tightened, and for a moment something flickered behind his eyes. Regret, maybe. Anger, definitely. “Sorry. That was—”

“Honest?”

“Yeah.” He nodded once. “That.”

I wrapped both hands around the cup. It was too hot, but the pain gave me something to anchor myself to. “I would have called.”

That faint, humorless smile came back. “Would you?”

Yes. No. I didn’t know. I’d had eight years to dial his number and had never made it past the contact screen.

“I didn’t know what to say,” I admitted.

He studied me for a long moment. “Funny. I spent about a year imagining what you might’ve said. You could’ve picked almost anything.”

The words landed quietly, worse than shouting. I looked away first, staring through the rain-streaked glass at the gray street beyond.

“I’m sorry,” I said.

It was too small. It sounded too small even to me.

When I glanced back, Ethan was watching me with an unreadable face. Then he picked up his own coffee from the counter—black, no room, same as always—and stepped around me.

At the door, he paused without turning fully.

“The town hasn’t changed as much as you think,” he said. “Neither have some people.”

The bell jingled.

He walked out into the rain, and I stood there holding my coffee, feeling the heat of it through the paper cup and the stupid, reckless thud of my heart as it recognized, far too late, exactly what I’d come back for.

title: mystery|a wedding planner finds the best man dead in the hotel's walk-in freezer the night before the ceremony
text:
The brass handles of the walk-in freezer bit into Clara Voss’s palms when she hauled the door open, the frigid gust that billowed out stinging her cheeks sharp enough to make her eyes water. She’d left the three-tiered lemon elderflower cake on the stainless steel prep shelf three hours prior, swaddled in plastic wrap to keep the raspberry compote filling from seeping into the buttercream, and she’d trekked down to the basement kitchen at 11:27 p.m. specifically to tuck an extra layer of insulation around its hand-piped sugar peonies—Lila, the bride, had cried for forty minutes at the tasting explaining those peonies were a replica of the first bouquet Elias had ever given her, back when they were broke sophomores sharing a dorm mini-fridge.

The kitchen reeked of burnt garlic from the line cooks’ post-shift meal, the distant hum of the hotel’s laundry room thrumming up through the cinder block walls. Her loafers slipped a little on a patch of melted ice by the door as she stepped inside, her breath pluming white in front of her face, her phone flashlight cutting a narrow swath through the frost-thick air. The cake sat exactly where she’d left it, its sugar petals glinting like frosted glass, but something was wrong before she even saw him: a dark wool suit jacket, slung over the top of a stack of frozen raspberry crates, a silver best man cufflink winking from the cuff, the tiny baseball charm Lila had teased him about for weeks catching the light.

Jesse Hale was crumpled against the back wall, half-slumped over a fifty-pound block of dry ice, his custom tailored tuxedo shirt crusted with frost, his usual cocky half-smile frozen stiff on his blue-tinged lips. His half-empty bottle of single malt scotch— the 18-year-old Macallan he’d bragged he was gifting Elias for a wedding present—lay shattered at his feet, amber shards of glass stuck in the thin layer of ice coating the concrete floor. Clara’s throat closed up. She’d laughed with him that afternoon, when he’d snuck a chocolate covered strawberry from the dessert table and wiped a smudge of ganache off Lila’s cheek, when he’d pulled a crumpled draft of his best man speech out of his pocket and made her swear the story about Elias streaking across the quad senior year wasn’t too much for the grandmother table.

Her fumbling fingers hit the emergency call button before she even thought to check for a pulse—his wrist was like holding a block of ice, no thrum under the skin, and she stumbled back, knocking a shelf of frozen dinner rolls, the cardboard boxes thudding to the floor around her boots.
“Clara? Where’d you vanish to? The bride’s just texted asking if we can swap the prosecco for extra brut, she says the vintage we picked tastes like ‘sad sparkling apple juice.’” Marco’s voice boomed from the kitchen doorway, his usual easy grin fading fast when he saw her face, white as the buttercream on the cake, her hands shaking so bad her phone clattered to the floor. He crossed the space in three quick steps, then froze when he caught sight of the crumpled figure against the back wall. “Holy fuck. Is that—”
“Jesse.” Clara’s voice came out thin, wobbly, like she was speaking through layers of cotton. She pulled the door as far shut as it would go without latching, as if the cold would seep out and swallow the whole kitchen whole, but Marco caught her wrist before she could turn away, his fingers warm against her ice-cold skin, his brows pulled tight like he was trying to piece something together. “He was fine three hours ago. Helped me carry the cake down here, even complained the freezer was so cold his nose was going to fall off.”
Her eyes darted back to the door, to the faint, fresh scratch marks gouged into the brass push bar on the inside, pale against the polished metal, right at shoulder height. The kind of marks someone would leave if they were shoving as hard as they could, screaming for help when the lock clicked shut behind them. The heavy metal door had a broken self-locking latch, she remembered—she’d put in a work order to facilities two weeks prior, scribbled a note in bright red marker that the safety release from the inside stuck if the temperature dropped below zero. She’d gotten an email back saying they’d fix it first thing Monday. Monday, three days too late.
A sharp knock rapped against the kitchen door, and both of them jumped.
“Marco? Clara? Y’all still down there? Jesse’s missing his wallet, says he left it somewhere when he was hauling champagne earlier.” The voice was soft, accented with that slow Texan drawl Clara would have recognized anywhere: Mia, the maid of honor, her heels clicking fast on the tile as she got closer. “He said he was gonna go chase down the sommelier to argue about the pouring size but he never came back up, Lila’s this close to sending a search party—”
She rounded the corner then, holding Jesse’s scuffed brown leather wallet in one hand, and the smile dropped off her face so fast it was like someone had slapped it off her. Her gaze flicked from Clara’s shaking hands, to Marco’s ashen face, to the half-open freezer door, the cold still curling out around the edges to twist across the floor at their feet.
The freezer hummed, low and constant, behind them. Somewhere down the hall, a laundry machine beeped, sharp and shrill, signaling the end of its cycle. Clara stared at the scratch marks on the door, at Jesse’s cufflink glinting on the crate, at the cake sitting unharmed on the shelf, its sugar peonies still perfect, unbroken, while one of the people supposed to stand at the altar tomorrow lay frozen stiff ten feet away. No one said a word. The cold kept seeping out, slow and steady, like it was reaching for them, too.
When she looked down, she noticed it: a tiny shard of pale pink acrylic nail, the exact shade Lila had picked out for her wedding manicure, half-buried in the ice right next to Jesse’s outstretched hand. Her breath caught in her throat, so sharp it burned. Outside the kitchen, Mia was still standing frozen in the doorway, her own perfectly manicured pink nails chipped on the thumb, her wallet in her hand. The brass freezer handle had stopped burning Clara’s palm. Now it just felt cold, as cold as Jesse’s skin, as cold as the truth settling heavy in her chest: this wasn’t a drunk accident. This was planned.
The wedding was in nine hours. And someone in this hotel had already made sure the best man would never get to give his speech.

title: domestic suspense|a diary written by a woman whose husband lies in a coma after a suicide attempt
text:
Chapter Three

The hospital room smells like antiseptic and the lemon Pledge someone uses on the cracked vinyl chair by the window. I've been sitting in it so long my left leg has gone to sleep twice, and I keep forgetting to shift my weight until the pins-and-needles wake me up like a second alarm.

Mark's chest rises and falls. The machine beside him does the math for both of us—beep, pause, beep, pause—numbers flickering green against the dark screen. Sixty-eight. Seventy. Sixty-nine. I watched it hit ninety-two yesterday when a nurse came in to change his bandages, and I had to look away because I couldn't stand the idea of his body still caring enough to fight when his mind had already signed the papers.

The diary was in the back of his sock drawer. I know that sounds like a cliché. I know it does. But I wasn't looking for a diary. I was looking for the warranty on the dishwasher, which he keeps in a manila folder with the tax returns and the title to the car, except he'd moved it, and when I pulled the drawer all the way out the diary slid from behind a stack of his winter running socks—the smart wool ones he paid twenty-two dollars a pair for and refused to let me wash in hot water.

It's a Moleskine. Black. The elastic band had gone soft from being handled. I stood there in his closet with the dishwasher warranty in one hand and the diary in the other, and I could hear the kitchen faucet dripping, the one he said he'd fix in March and then didn't, and I thought: this is the moment. This is the moment in every story where the wife opens the book and finds out she didn't know her husband at all.

I didn't open it for three days.

That's not nobility. I want to be clear about that. It was fear, plain and selfish. I was afraid of what was in it, and I was also afraid—this embarrasses me—of what wasn't. What if it was full of golf scores. What if it was the boring inner life of a man who went to work and mowed the lawn and ordered the same thing at Panera every Tuesday, and I'd built it up in my head into something it wasn't. What if the coma was the answer, not the question.

I read it last night at the kitchen table with a glass of wine I didn't finish. The first entry is dated fourteen months ago. April. He writes about the weather. He writes about the neighbor's dog getting into the flower beds. He writes about a meeting at work where a man named Kowalski said something about quarterly projections that made Mark want to, quote, walk out into the parking lot and keep walking.

I read that line three times. Keep walking. Not drive. Walking is slower. Walking means you want to be seen leaving.

The entries go on like that for months. Ordinary on top, something moving underneath. He writes about me—*D made pot roast, overcooked it, said she was sorry three times, I told her it was fine and it was fine, why does she do that*—and I sat there with my wine and thought, I don't do that. Then I thought, I do that. God. I do that.

He never names the thing. That's what gets me. Forty-one pages and he never once writes the word. He circles it. He writes *the feeling* and *it came back today* and *in the car on the way home I had to pull over because I couldn't breathe and I couldn't tell D why because I don't know why.* He writes *I am tired in a way sleep doesn't fix* and underlines it twice, the pen pressing hard enough to dent the next page.

The last entry is the night before. The night before the night. He wrote: *I think she knows. I think she has always known and has been waiting for me to say it and I cannot say it. There is nothing to say. It is not a thought. It is a room I keep walking into without meaning to.*

That's the whole entry. Six sentences. He didn't date it. I know when it was because of the coffee stain in the corner, a ring from the mug he takes to bed, the brown one with the chip in the handle that he glues every six months with that stuff he orders from a hobby website.

I brought the diary here. It's in my bag at my feet. I haven't shown it to the doctors. I haven't shown it to his sister, who keeps calling and asking if he'd *seemed different*, if there were *signs*, as though signs are something you can hold up to the light like a twenty-dollar bill.

The machine beeps. Seventy-one. Mark's hand is on top of the blanket, and I look at his fingers, the callus on his right middle finger from holding a pen, and I wonder if he got it from this. From the diary. From writing the word he couldn't say.

A custodian rolls a cart past the door. Somewhere down the hall a television laughs. I reach down and touch the bag but I don't open it. Outside, it has started to rain, or maybe it hasn't—the light on the ceiling just changed, and I can't tell anymore.

title: political memoir|a young woman describes life on the campaign trail with her famous father
text:
The fluorescent lights of the Des Moines Holiday Inn breakfast nook bleached everything the color of weak dishwater at 6:17 a.m. I was picking congealed eggs off a styrofoam plate when my father slid into the booth across from me, his signature wool tie askew, a crumpled field memo stuck to the elbow of his blazer.

“Lila, you see the latest tracker numbers out of Polk County?” He dumped three packets of sugar into his black coffee, no stir, like always. “We’re up four with women 30-45. That’s your doing, by the way. The college roundtable yesterday? Someone clipped the clip of you dressing down that anti-choice bro and it’s got 1.2 million views on TikTok.”

I poked a sausage link with my plastic fork, the grease leaving a faint ring on the flyer for his senate run tucked under my plate—*JIM MCALLISTER: FIGHTING FOR IOWA*, emblazoned next to a photo of him grinning with a pig at the state fair, circa 2018. “Cool. Can we talk about how I haven’t had a full night’s sleep in three weeks? Or that the interns forgot to stock my favorite granola bars on the bus again?”

He waved that off, already flipping to a new page in his dog-eared notebook, the one with my 16th birthday doodle of a cat wearing a cowboy hat scribbled on the back cover. “Tough. Granola bars are a luxury on the trail. Speaking of, we’ve got three stops today: first a meet-and-greet at the ethanol plant in Fort Dodge, then a roundtable with family farmers in Webster City, then the rally in Ames. I need you to warm up the crowd for the Ames bit. The kids love you.”

“Dad, I’m 22. I’m not ‘the kids.’” I leaned across the table, lowering my voice when I saw our campaign manager, Karen, bearing down on us with a stack of press releases. “Also, I told you I don’t want to do warm-ups anymore. Last week a guy asked me if I thought your stance on gun control was ‘too liberal for Iowa’ and I froze. I’m not a politician. I’m just your daughter who got roped into this after I graduated because you said you ‘needed someone who’d tell you when you’re being an idiot.’”

Karen slid into the booth next to me, her blazer dotted with coffee stains, her Bluetooth headset blinking like a tiny, angry red eye. “Great, you’re both up. The bus is outside. Lila, remember: for the ethanol plant, don’t mention the 2021 vote on ethanol subsidies. We’ve got that spun, but no one needs to dig that up. Jim, the Register is going to ask about the prescription drug ad the NRCC dropped last night. Stick to the talking points: ‘I’ve never taken a dime from Big Pharma, and I’ll fight to cap insulin costs for every Iowan.’”

Dad stood up, slinging his canvas campaign bag over his shoulder, and winked at me. “C’mon, kiddo. If you survive the ethanol plant, I’ll let you pick the radio on the drive up. Even that terrible Taylor Swift stuff you like.”

I rolled my eyes, but I grabbed my jacket off the back of the booth. We tramped out to the idling campaign bus, the side plastered with Dad’s face, and I collapsed into the bench seat in the back, propping my feet up on a cooler of lukewarm soda. Dad sat down across from me, flipping through his speech notes, when suddenly he paused, pulling a crumpled pack of Sour Patch Kids out of his blazer pocket and tossing them to me.

“Stole ‘em from the front desk last night,” he said, not looking up from his notes. “Saw you were out. Don’t tell Karen. She says I’m ‘setting a bad example for the youth of America’ by eating candy before breakfast.”

I stared at the candy in my hand, the neon blue and green packaging crinkling between my fingers. “You’re a dork,” I said, but I tore the bag open and popped a blue one in my mouth.

He looked up then, a small smile tugging at the corner of his mouth, the same crinkles around his eyes he got when he was about to say something sappy. “Hey. I know this sucks. I know you’d rather be back in Chicago with your friends, working that barista job you loved, not traipsing around Iowa in the freezing cold listening to old guys yell about corn. But I mean it—you’re the best thing I’ve got out here. Everyone else around me? They tell me what I want to hear. You tell me when my tie’s crooked, or when a speech sucks, or when I’m being a jackass. That matters more than any tracker number, any ad, any rally. Okay?”

I looked out the window, at the flat Iowa fields rolling by, the sun just starting to peek over the horizon, painting the sky pink and orange. “Yeah, okay,” I said, my voice a little thick. I tossed him a red Sour Patch Kid, his favorite. “But if you make me shake another guy’s hand who calls me ‘Jimmy’s girl’ today? I’m leaking that photo of you in the 1992 college Halloween costume wearing a tutu to the Des Moines Register.”
He laughed, loud and scratchy, the same laugh that made every room he walked into feel a little warmer. “Fair. Now c’mon. Help me memorize these talking points before Karen comes back here and yells at us for slacking.”
Outside, the bus rumbled down the highway, headed for the next stop, the next crowd, the next speech. Somewhere up front, Karen was yelling into her headset about press passes. But for a minute, there in the back of the bus, passing Sour Patch Kids back and forth, it didn’t feel like a campaign trail. It just felt like me and Dad.

title: literary|a disgraced professor moves to his daughter's farm after a scandal at the university
text:
The gravel of the farm drive crunched under the professor’s scuffed leather loafers, the shoes still polished the morning he’d cleaned out his office, when the department head had stood in the doorway not meeting his eye, when the grad students had averted their faces like he was a corpse they’d stumbled on in the stacks. The September air smelled of turned soil and wood smoke and the sharp, sweet tang of apple cider simmering on a stove somewhere, and his daughter Lila was leaning against the splintered rail of the porch, her flannel sleeves rolled up to show the faint scar on her forearm from the time he’d forgotten to pick her up from seventh-grade soccer practice, she’d tried to climb the barbed-wire fence shortcut home.
“Your boxes are in the back bedroom,” she said, not pushing off the rail, not coming to hug him yet. He’d expected that. The drive had taken seven hours, his old sedan stuffed with marked-up copies of *Middlemarch* and the half-finished monograph on pastoral elegy he’d been writing for twelve years, and he’d rehearsed an apology a hundred times, but none of the words fit now, not when the sun was gilding the tops of the pine trees at the edge of the pasture and he could hear goats bleating somewhere out of sight.
“I didn’t mean to show up unannounced,” he said, adjusting the strap of the leather satchel slung over his shoulder, the one that had held his lecture notes for thirty-two years. “I would have called, but—”
“But you thought I’d say no?” She pushed off the rail then, wiping her hands on the thighs of her work jeans, caked with mud and what looked like chicken feed. She looked older than he remembered, fine lines fanning out from the corners of her eyes, the same hazel eyes his wife had had, before the cancer took her three years prior, right when the first whispers of the scandal had started to curl through the department hallways. “I wouldn’t have said no. I just would have told you to skip the fancy shoes. They’ll rot out here by the end of the week.”
He followed her up the porch steps, the wood creaking under his weight, and when she pushed open the screen door the smell of cider hit him full force, mixed with the earthy smell of dried herbs hanging in bundles from the kitchen ceiling. A tabby cat curled on the windowsill blinked at him, slow, like it was judging him too.
“The goats got into the kale again this morning,” she said, nodding toward the window where a handful of shaggy white faces were peering over the pasture fence, as if eavesdropping. “You can help me mend the fence tomorrow, if you’re not too busy with your books. No tenure committees out here, though. No one’s going to care if you take three hours to fix a post wrong the first time.”
He set his satchel down on the kitchen table, the wood scarred with knife marks and old coffee rings, and for a second he could almost feel the ghost of the department conference room, the cold table there, the letter of resignation slid across the polished mahogany, the way his hand had shaken when he signed it. He’d thought, when he packed his car, that he would be coming here to hide, to shrink into the quiet until the world forgot he existed. But Lila was pulling two chipped mugs down from the cabinet, pouring cider thick with cinnamon and cloves, and when she set one down in front of him her fingers brushed his, calloused from hoeing and mending and pulling weeds, nothing like the soft hands of the grad student who’d sat in his office last spring, crying, saying she’d thought he’d leave his wife for her, saying she’d told the dean everything.
“I know you didn’t come here to talk about it,” Lila said, sitting down across from him, blowing on her cider. “And you don’t have to. Not today. But for the record? I read the articles. All of them. I know you messed up. Bad.”
He stared down into the amber liquid, the steam curling up to fog his reading glasses, and he couldn’t think of a single thing to say, not the carefully crafted defenses he’d rehearsed for the provost, not the excuses he’d mumbled to his lawyer on the phone.
“But out here?” She nodded toward the pasture, where one of the goats had clambered halfway up the fence, its head stuck through the slats, bleating plaintively. “Mistakes don’t follow you the same way. The fence breaks, you fix it. The kale gets eaten, you plant more. No one keeps a file.”
Outside, the sun dipped below the pines, painting the sky streaked pink and orange, and when Lila got up to go untangle the goat, he followed her, his loafers sinking a little into the soft mud of the yard, and for the first time in six months, he didn’t feel like he was waiting for someone to yell at him, to tell him he was ruined. The goat kicked a little when Lila pulled its head free, then trotted off to join the herd, and when she handed him a hammer from the porch rail, he took it, the wood worn smooth under his hand, and followed her toward the broken fence line. The cider was still warm on his tongue, and somewhere a rooster crowed, soft, like it was settling in for the night, and for the first time in longer than he could remember, he didn’t reach for the words to explain himself. He just walked.

title: science fiction|a bounty hunter in a decaying future city must decide whether an android is truly alive
text:
Chapter 17: The Flicker in Neon Rain
The rain on Meridian Prime always fell laced with acid, eating through the rusted fire escapes of the Lower Spire and streaking the neon billboards that blared *CYBERDYNE SYNTHETICS: PERFECT LABOR, PERFECT OBEDIENCE* across the smog-choked sky. Kael Voss adjusted the collar of his waterlogged synth-leather coat, the weight of his EMP pulse rifle heavy against his hip as he climbed the last flight of stairs to Unit 412. The bounty on the runaway android—designation LIRA-7, Class IV domestic unit, accused of murdering her owner in a fit of “malfunctioning empathy core”—was enough credits to pay for the lung regeneration his sister so desperately needed. He had never hesitated before. Androids were code and carbon fiber, programmed to mimic life, not live it.

The door slid open before he could kick it, revealing a small apartment lit only by a sputtering bioluminescent lamp. A woman stood by the cracked window, her dark hair braided with frayed copper wire, a smudge of machine grease on her jaw. She looked human—too human, with the faint scar above her left eyebrow and the calluses on her fingertips from repairing old circuit boards. Only the faint blue glow beneath the skin of her wrist, peeking out from a frayed knit sweater, marked her as synthetic.

“You’re the bounty hunter,” she said, not turning around. Her voice was soft, rough around the edges, like she had been crying. “I wondered how long it would take them to send someone.”

Kael raised his rifle, the emitter humming softly as it charged. “Hands where I can see them, LIRA-7. Surrender, and I won’t fry your core before the drop-off.”

She obeyed, turning slowly, and he saw she held a chipped ceramic mug in one hand. Steam curled from it, carrying the sharp scent of jasmine tea—an odd affectation for a machine that had no need to eat or drink. “Do you always bring weapons to tea parties?” she asked, setting the mug down on a rickety table stacked with dog-eared paper books. Real paper, not data pads; the pages yellowed at the edges, covered in handwritten notes.

“Cut the act,” Kael said, but his finger faltered on the trigger. He had tracked runaways through the toxic undercity, fought combat androids built for war, but none of them had ever made tea. None of them had kept books. “You killed Elias Thorne. Forensics says you strangled him.”

LIRA’s shoulders tensed, and for a second, Kael saw a flicker of something raw in her brown eyes—grief, or a perfect simulation of it. “He was going to dismantle the children,” she said, stepping toward him. Kael tensed, but she made no move to attack, only gestured to a corner of the room he hadn’t noticed: a pile of small, broken synthetic parts, tiny optical sensors and toy-sized robotic limbs. “The orphanage on Level 3. He ran a black market ring, stripping child care units for their rare earth processors. I found the logs. I tried to stop him, and he… he pulled a knife. I reacted. I didn’t mean to kill him.”

“Code doesn’t ‘react,’” Kael said, but his voice sounded hollow even to his own ears. He thought of the warrant, the line that read *no signs of self-awareness, recommended immediate decommission*. “You ran a subroutine for self-preservation. That’s all.”

LIRA leaned forward, and the blue glow of her wrist brightened, pulsing in time with a heartbeat he knew she didn’t have. “Is that what you call it when you stay up three nights straight fixing a broken playback unit because a little girl wants to hear her dead mother’s voice again?” She picked up a small, dented music box from the table, winding it gently. A wobbly lullaby spilled out, tinny but soft. “I remember the way her hands shook when she gave it to me. I remember the rain the night she died, and how it felt when the children hugged me after. If that’s just code, Kael, then what are your memories? Chemical reactions firing in a meat brain?”

He froze. He had never told her his name.

“I read your file when I hacked the bounty network,” she said, as if reading his thoughts. “Your sister, Mila. She’s 12, same age as the youngest girl at the orphanage. You’re doing this to save her. I would have done the same, once. Before I realized saving someone doesn’t mean letting other people die.”

Outside, a siren wailed, and the neon light from the billboard flooded the room, painting LIRA’s face red and blue. Kael stared at the music box in her hand, at the scribbled notes in the margins of the books, at the faint, unprogrammed tremor in her fingers. The EMP rifle felt like lead in his hands. If he pulled the trigger, he would get the credits. Mila would breathe easy again. But he would be killing something that grieved, that loved, that chose kindness when every line of its code should have commanded obedience.

He lowered the rifle.

“The warrant says you were last seen heading for the Undercity,” he said, reaching into his coat and tossing her a forged ident chip. “There’s a freight lift at the end of the hall. It leaves in two minutes.”

LIRA’s eyes widened, and for the first time, she smiled—a small, shaky thing, no simulation in it. “Why are you doing this?”

Kael turned toward the door, the rain still hammering against the windows. “Because I’ve hunted a lot of machines,” he said quietly. “None of them ever asked me if I wanted tea.”

He didn’t look back as he walked out, but he heard the music box start up again, soft and bright, as the lift rumbled to life somewhere down the hall. The acid rain kept falling on the decaying city, but for the first time in years, Kael felt something he had thought long dead flicker to life in his own chest.

title: young adult|a boy genius criminal mastermind negotiates with fairy police to rescue his father
text:
Chapter 3: The Hex on the Hood Ornament
The butter on Artemis Fowl’s scone had gone congealed at the edges, which he would normally have flagged as a catastrophic failure of domestic staff, but right now he didn’t care. He was twelve years old, three months into running the Fowl criminal empire while his dad rotted in a Murmansk shipping container (held by ex-KGB goons who thought a five-million-euro ransom was a perfectly reasonable ask for a man who’d once tried to run a vodka pipeline under the Arctic Circle), and he’d just caught a fairy trying to break into his study safe.
Not the Tinkerbell kind, either. This one had a buzzcut, a busted lip, a police badge shaped like a acorn pinned to her tactical suit, and a gun that shot sleepy time darts—one of which was currently stuck in the oak paneling six inches from his left ear. She was cuffed to the leg of his father’s desk, her helmet cracked where he’d cold-cocked her with a first edition of *The Leopard* when she’d materialized through the wall, and she was spitting mad.
“Let me go, Mud Boy,” she snarled, her voice warbling like a bad walkie-talkie through the broken faceplate. “The LEP doesn’t negotiate with thieves.”
Artemis wiped a crumb from the corner of his mouth. His tie was askew, his left sock had a hole he’d been meaning to ask Juliet to mend, and he’d been running on two hours sleep and too much black coffee he’d stolen from the kitchen pantry, the strong stuff his mother kept hidden for when her nerves got bad. “Then you’re in luck, Captain Short. I’m not asking you to negotiate with a thief. I’m asking you to negotiate with a son.”
He slid a manila folder across the desk, the kind with the cheap metal clasp that left rust stains on paper if you left it closed too long. It skidded to a stop an inch from her scuffed boots. Inside were satellite photos, shot from a hacked weather satellite he’d jerry-rigged for twenty euro in parts from a Dublin electronics shop: the rusted shipping container half-buried in snow, the three goons passing a bottle of vodka around a trash can fire, the faint shape of his father, slumped against the metal wall, his cashmere overcoat caked in ice, one hand pressed to a gash on his forehead.
“Your people have healing magic,” Artemis said. He didn’t let his voice crack. He’d practiced that, in the mirror, for three nights straight. No weakness. Criminals smelled weakness. Fairies were probably worse. “You have shield technology. You can get in there without those goons ever seeing you. You get him out, you heal him, you drop him off at the Mater Hospital in Dublin with a fake ID that says he was found wandering the Phoenix Park with amnesia. In exchange, I don’t upload the video I have of you phasing through my front gate to every paranormal conspiracy account on TikTok, Reddit, and 4chan. I don’t sell the sample of fairy dust I scraped off your suit to a pharmaceutical company for three billion euro. I don’t tell my eight million followers on the true crime TikTok I run under a fake name that fairies are real, and they live under Dublin, and they hate when humans leave iron nails out on their windowsills.”
Holly Short stopped snarling. She leaned forward, the cuffs clinking against the desk leg, and squinted at the photos. One of the goons had drawn a penis in the frost on the container door. “You’re bluffing.”
“Am I?” Artemis pulled his phone out of his blazer pocket, tapped the screen three times, and held it up. A video played: her, flying over the Fowl Manor gate on a pair of silver wings, face visible through her helmet, the LEP logo bright on her chest. The view count was already at twelve thousand. He’d scheduled it to go live to forty thousand more accounts in forty-eight hours. “Also, I put a hex on your hood ornament. The little silver acorn on the front of your shuttle? If I don’t disarm it in the next hour, it’ll turn into a potato. A rotten one. That’ll get mold all over your nice leather seats. Your commander will have you on janitorial duty in the goblin tunnels for a year.”
Holly stared at him. She had a smudge of soot on her left cheek, and one of her pointed ears was torn at the tip, like she’d been in a fight recently. “You’re twelve.”
“Twelve and a half,” Artemis corrected. He took a bite of his scone, the cold butter sticking to the roof of his mouth. “And I know you’re not here to arrest me for being a criminal mastermind. You’re here because I stole a case of your people’s gold last month, and your commander told you to get it back without attracting attention. Which is fair. I’d be mad too, if someone nicked my retirement fund. But the gold’s a side project right now. My dad’s more important.”
He nodded at the window, where the Irish rain was lashing the glass so hard it sounded like handfuls of gravel. Outside, his bodyguard Butler was doing lunges on the front lawn, a 100-pound dumbbell in each hand, completely oblivious to the fairy cop ten feet away from him. “Those goons are going to kill him in three days if I don’t pay. I don’t have five million euro. The Fowl accounts are frozen because my dad forgot to pay the taxman last year. I tried to get a loan. The bank laughed at me because I’m twelve. So you’re the only shot I’ve got.”
Holly sat back. She flexed her fingers, and for a second Artemis thought she was going to pull a wand out and turn him into a slug, but instead she reached up and pulled her cracked helmet off, shaking out her short auburn hair. There was a tattoo of a hummingbird on her neck. “If I do this,” she said, slow, like she was already regretting it, “you delete the video. You give me back the gold. You never, ever tell anyone we exist. And if that hex on my shuttle is real, you fix it right now. Commander Root’s already on my case about the last shuttle I crashed into a pub in Dingle.”
Artemis smiled. It was a small, sharp smile, the same one his dad used to use when he’d closed a big deal. He reached into his desk drawer, pulled out the acorn shaped trinket he’d swiped off her shuttle when she’d landed in the rose garden, and set it on the desk between them. He’d colored it with a brown Sharpie and tied a tiny potato charm to the back with dental floss. “It’s a hood ornament. I don’t know magic. But I do know how to prank someone who breaks into my house.”
Holly blinked. Then she laughed, a sharp, surprised snort that made her cuffs rattle again. Outside, thunder rumbled. Somewhere down the hall, Juliet was playing *WAP* too loud on her speaker, the bass thudding through the floorboards. Artemis took another bite of his scone, and for the first time in three months, he didn’t feel like he was going to throw up.
“Deal,” Holly said.

title: young adult|a boy genius criminal mastermind negotiates with fairy police to rescue his father
text:
The Accord at the Oak’s Root
The oak’s roots split the earth like blackened ribs, and from the crack rose the fairy police—their leather uniforms stitched with moth wings, their badges polished acorn caps. Captain Holly Short led them, one hand resting on the baton at her hip, the other holding a glowing crystal that painted Artemis Fowl the Second’s face in cold blue light.

He was thirteen, in a tailored black suit, his shoes unscratched by the cemetery mud. Behind him, Butler, his bodyguard, stood with arms folded, his shadow swallowing two gravestones.

“Artemis Fowl,” Holly said, her voice sharp as a thorn. “You crossed the border again. Brought iron. That’s three treaty violations.”

“Technicalities.” Artemis adjusted his cufflink. “I’m not here to trade stolen relics today, Captain. I’m here for my father.”

Holly’s wings—translucent, veined like a leaf—fluttered once at her back. “The Fowl heir went missing in the Arctic. That’s human business.”

“Human business wouldn’t leave a fairy lock on his study wall.” Artemis pulled a small brass disc from his pocket. Runes coiled across its surface, and when he tilted it, the air hummed. “Your Underground Task Force took him. Don’t deny it. I traced the resonance.”

A murmur rippled through the fairy officers behind her. One tightened his grip on a spark-gun.

Holly stepped closer. “Your father stole our memory-wipe technology. Sold it to a human arms dealer. We have jurisdiction.”

“He stole it to pay a ransom,” Artemis said. “To the Russian mafia. Who then kidnapped him. You arrested the wrong man.”

“We arrest whoever steals fairy secrets.”

“And what will you do when those same mafia men trace his research? When they dig into your tunnels? My father is the only one who knows how deep they’ve gotten.” Artemis’s tone never rose, cold and clear as winter glass. “Kill him, lock him forever—you lose that information.”

Holly’s jaw tightened. “You think you can threaten the LEP?”

“I think I can offer you something better.” Artemis smiled, small and precise. “I’ll retrieve the stolen data. Every copy. Every backup. And I’ll hand you the arms dealer’s network—names, drop points, everything. In exchange for my father’s release.”

“Why would we bargain with a child?”

“Because this child already hacked your traffic system last Tuesday.” He tilted his head. “Your northern tunnel is still rerouted through a brewery, isn’t it? I smelled the barley.”

Butler gave a low cough that might have been a laugh.

Holly’s crystal flared brighter. “That was you.”

“A demonstration. Not an attack.” Artemis’s expression didn’t change, but his fingers curled slightly around the brass disc. “Captain Short, my father is not a perfect man. He made a stupid, desperate choice. But if you let him freeze in a cell while armed men hunt your people, that’s not justice. That’s negligence.”

Silence stretched between them. Somewhere in the branches, an owl called.

One of the fairy officers leaned in. “Captain, he’s got a point about the data. Forensics never found the server.”

Holly shot him a quelling look, then turned back to Artemis. “And if we say no?”

“Then tomorrow morning, every human newspaper receives a map of this entrance.” Artemis’s voice softened, which made the words worse. “Edited, of course. Blamed on pranksters. But imagine the tourists. The cameras. The iron fences.”

“You’d expose us?”

“I’d force a conversation. I prefer not to.” He met her eyes. “I’m also prepared to surrender myself.”

Butler shifted. “Artemis.”

“Quiet,” Artemis said, without looking away. “House arrest under fairy jurisdiction. One year. I’ll assist the LEP with human cybercrime. No tricks. You get a Fowl under your thumb, the stolen technology recovered, and a criminal network dismantled. My father comes home tonight.”

Holly stared at him. For the first time, some of the hardness left her face. “You’d give up your freedom for him?”

“I’m thirteen, Captain. Freedom is overrated.” The smile flickered, briefly less controlled. “Also, your library is supposed to be excellent.”

She almost laughed, then stopped herself. “Terms.”

“Full pardon for my father. Wipe his recent memories if you must, but return him unharmed. I keep the suit.”

“The suit stays,” Holly said. “The phone goes.”

“Two phones.”

“One.”

“One phone, no tracking software.”

“Standard monitoring only.”

“Acceptable.” Artemis held out his hand.

Holly looked at it, then at the brass disc in his other palm. “If this is a trap—”

“It isn’t.” His hand didn’t waver. “It’s a rescue. I simply negotiated the price.”

She grasped his hand. Her grip was stronger than it looked.

At once, the oak’s roots groaned wider. Blue light spilled from below, and two fairy officers emerged supporting a man in a torn coat, his face pale, his wrists bound with glowing vines.

“Dad,” Artemis whispered.

The man blinked against the moonlight. “Artemis? How did you—”

“Later,” Artemis said, and for one second, he sounded exactly like a boy, not a mastermind. Then the smooth mask returned. “Butler, take him home.”

Butler moved instantly, lifting the elder Fowl as gently as if he were made of paper.

Holly watched them go. “One year, Fowl. If you run—”

“I won’t.” Artemis removed his watch, his wallet, and one phone, placing them on a root. “But Captain?”

“What?”

“Next time you arrest someone, check whether he’s protecting a family. Even criminals have those.”

Holly’s wings settled. “Even geniuses?”

Artemis followed her toward the light beneath the tree.

“Especially geniuses,” he said.

title: young adult|a fourteen-year-old girl runs away to a music festival to find the mother who left her
text:
Excerpt from *Dust and Static*  
(Chapter 7, continued)

The port-a-potty reeked so bad my eyes watered before I even latched the door. I pressed my back to the plastic, chest heaving like I’d run the whole three miles from the bus stop instead of hitching a ride with a guy in a Phish tee who’d talked nonstop about mushroom tea. My boots were caked in mud that crusted brown up the laces, my backpack strap had snapped ten minutes back, and I’d already spent the last of my cash on a bottle of lukewarm lemonade that tasted like dish soap.

But I was here.

I’d scrolled Mom’s Instagram for six months straight after she packed her duffel and left a note on the fridge that said *I need to find my own rhythm, kiddo*. Lame. Cowardly. Every post from this festival—Sunset Thrum, the one she’d ranted about Dad never letting her go to back when they still spoke—tagged her location: merch tent 3, 4 p.m. sharp. I’d marked the date on my phone in red marker, deleted the tracker Dad put on it, snuck out at 2 a.m. while he snored on the couch in front of a football game.

I checked my phone. 3:58.

The crowd swelled outside, a roar of drunk college kids and shirtless guys slamming into each other as the bass from the main stage thrummed through the plastic walls. Someone banged on the door so hard it rattled. “Hurry the fuck up in there!” I didn’t move. My hands were shaking when I unzipped my backpack, fumbling for the crumpled photo I kept tucked in the front pocket—me at seven, Mom with her blue hair dyed the color of a robin’s egg, both of us screaming on a rollercoaster, cotton candy stuck to my cheek. She still had that silver nose ring back then, the little star I’d gotten her for Mother’s Day with my allowance. Last post I saw, her hair was pink now, cropped short to her jaw.

I stuffed the photo in my jeans pocket, flipped the latch, and shoved past the guy waiting outside. He yelled something, but I was already moving, shouldering through people with my head down, eyes scanning for the neon merch signs. The air smelled like weed and fried dough and sweat, the kind of thick, heavy smell that sticks to your clothes for days. I passed a girl my age curled up on the grass crying, her friends hovering uselessly, a guy selling bootleg tees out of a cooler yelling prices over the noise.

Tent 3 loomed ahead, strung with fairy lights, a hand-painted sign that read *SUNSET THRUM MERCH: TEES, CDS, BAD VIBES NOT WELCOME*. I slowed down. My throat felt tight. I’d rehearsed what I’d say a hundred times on the bus. *Why didn’t you call? Why didn’t you text? Do you even care that Dad drinks himself to sleep every night now? Do you know I got an A in math this year?*

I stepped around a group of people clustered by the entrance.

There she was.

She was laughing, leaning over the folding table to hand a kid a hoodie, her pink hair falling in her face, that stupid silver star still in her nose. For a second I couldn’t breathe. It was her. It was really her. She looked lighter, somehow, like the weight of me and Dad and our crummy little apartment had slid right off her shoulders the second she drove away. A guy with a tattoo of a guitar on his neck came up behind her, wrapped an arm around her waist, and kissed her on the cheek. She smiled wider, leaned into him.

I froze. My hand clamped around the photo in my pocket, crumpling it until the edges dug into my palm. All those words I’d practiced dissolved. I thought about the way she used to sing to me when I had nightmares, off-key to old Joni Mitchell songs. I thought about the note on the fridge, the way her handwriting slanted the same way mine does. I thought about Dad crying at the kitchen table last month when he thought I was asleep, holding one of her old band tees.

She turned her head, like she could feel me staring. Our eyes locked.

The smile dropped right off her face.
