title: thriller|a CIA analyst realises the briefing she wrote has been altered before it reached the President
text:
Chapter 14 (continued)

Maya stared at the screen until the pixels burned. The sentence sat there in twelve-point Times New Roman, same font, same margins, same classified header she'd formatted herself at two in the morning. But the words weren't hers.

*"The Kremlin's posture is defensive. No imminent threat to Baltic airspace."*

She'd written the opposite. She'd written it three times, argued with her deputy about it, then put it back. Russia was moving assets into Kaliningrad at a pace she hadn't seen since 2014. The President needed to know that before he sat across from Petrov in Helsinki.

Somebody had swapped the meat and left the skeleton.

Her office was a glass box on the seventh floor, lights off, the city bleeding gray through the blinds. She pulled the draft history. Nothing. The file had been checked out under her credentials at 4:17 a.m. She'd been in bed at 4:17 a.m. Or at least she thought she had. Twelve hours was a long time now. She couldn't swear to it.

She pulled up the login records. Her badge had swiped the building at 3:52. She'd been asleep. She remembered the alarm, the coffee, the Metro. She remembered all of it because none of it had happened here.

A keycard could be cloned. A password could be phished. But her workstation used a palm-reader, and the log showed a clean biometric match.

Maya looked down at her right hand. Turned it over. The lines looked the same. They always did.

She pulled the final version again and started at page one, forcing herself to read slow. Most of it survived intact. Source names redacted, her hedges intact, the dry analytic voice she'd spent fifteen years perfecting. Then, buried on page nine, a second change. A line about the Chinese fuel contract had been softened from *"probable default within sixty days"* to *"uncertain near-term outlook."*

Two edits. Two specific downgrades. Both in the same direction — reassurance. Nothing that would get anyone fired, nothing dramatic, just enough fog that the President would walk into the room believing the world was calmer than it was.

This wasn't a hack. Hacks stole things. This was surgery, and the patient was American foreign policy.

Her desk phone rang. She nearly jumped out of her skin.

"Voss."

"It's Garrick." Her division chief. He sounded tired, or maybe he always sounded tired now. "You still up there?"

"Yeah."

"Come down to my office. Leave the machine. Don't print anything, don't message anyone, and don't ask the help desk about file integrity. I mean it, Maya."

She held the phone a beat too long. "How'd you know?"

"Because the same thing happened to three other products this week, and you're the first analyst who caught it. That makes you useful." A pause. "It also makes you a problem. Move."

The line went dead.

Maya pocketed her phone but didn't stand. She looked at the monitor one more time, at the sentence that wasn't hers, and thought about how easy it would be to close the file and go home. Nobody would blame her. The briefing was already in the binder. Helsinki was tomorrow. The machinery didn't stop for one GS-14 with a bad feeling.

She copied the altered paragraph into a note, encrypted it to her personal email, and hated herself while she did it because that was the exact move people made right before they got fired, indicted, or disappeared. Then she wiped her search history, locked the workstation, and stepped into the hallway.

The seventh floor was too quiet. Somewhere a printer hummed. A camera she'd never noticed before tracked her as she walked toward the elevator, its little red eye steady as a pulse.

Garrick's office was two floors down. She pressed the button and waited, watching the floor numbers tick.

The elevator opened on five.

A man she didn't know got on. Suit, no badge, hands empty. He smiled at her like they were old friends.

"Ms. Voss," he said. "Garrick sent me. We'll take the garage."

The doors closed.

She didn't move. Her reflection in the brushed steel looked back at her, calm as anything, while her hindbrain screamed that she had just run out of floors to trust.

title: mystery|a wedding planner finds the best man dead in the hotel's walk-in freezer the night before the ceremony
text:
The industrial hum of the hotel’s basement seeped through Clara Bennett’s steel-toe boots as she hefted the dented catering bin against her hip, her clipboard crammed with seating charts and a crumpled note from the bride insisting the peony centerpieces be “exactly three shades pinker than blush.” It was 10:47 PM, twelve hours before Mia and Ethan’s wedding, and the walk-in freezer was the last stop on her list: she needed to confirm the three-tiered salted caramel cake, the 200 mini lobster rolls, and the backup case of vintage champagne the groom had smuggled in against hotel policy.

She swiped her keycard, and the freezer door whooshed open, a wall of frosty air stinging her cheeks hard enough to make her eyes water. “Miguel?” she called, expecting the night pastry chef to be restocking the macaron towers. “If you hid the cake toppers again, I swear I’ll tell the bride you ate the test batch—”

The words died in her throat.

A man in a tailored navy suit was propped against the stacked cases of ice cream, his loafers caked in slush from the evening’s rain, a half-crushed cigar still clamped between his frozen fingers. His face was waxy, eyelashes frosted white, and Clara knew instantly it was Leo Voss, Ethan’s best man since college. The same man who’d grabbed her elbow at the rehearsal dinner two hours prior, sloshing bourbon on her cream blazer, slurring that he had “a little wedding present everyone was gonna lose their minds over.”

She fumbled for her phone, dropping her clipboard with a clatter that sent seating charts skittering across the frost-covered floor, when a voice came from the doorway behind her.
“Clara? You said you needed a hand hauling the champagne up?”
She spun to find Jake Marlow, the hotel’s night manager, holding a dolly, his easy smile dropping the second he saw past her shoulder. He stepped inside, boots crunching on the thin layer of ice, and let out a low, sharp whistle. “Jesus. That’s the best man, right?”
Clara nodded, her throat too tight to speak for a second. She’d dealt with drunk groomsmen, collapsed cake tiers, a runaway ring bearer who’d hidden in a laundry chute last spring, but never this. “He was fine at the rehearsal. Bragging about a speech that was gonna ‘blow the roof off.’” She edged closer, careful not to touch anything, and nodded at the cigar in Leo’s hand. “Miguel runs a nut-free kitchen, no exceptions. No one smokes in here. Ever.”
Jake pulled his own phone out, thumb hovering over 911, then paused. “You think he wandered in drunk? Got locked in?”
“Look at the door.” Clara nodded at the heavy metal latch, propped open three inches with a cinder block she’d seen by the service elevator an hour prior, the one the valets used to block wind gusts. “That wasn’t there when I came down here at 8 to check the salad course. Someone wanted to make sure it didn’t swing shut by accident.” She leaned in, squinting at Leo’s suit pocket, where a crumpled manila envelope peeked out, its seal broken. “He was going on and on about that present. Said Ethan had a secret no one knew about, something from his old job in Chicago.”
Jake’s jaw tightened. He’d worked at the hotel for six years, knew every regular, every closet, every glitch in the security system. “The camera out here? It’s been on the fritz since Tuesday. Maintenance was supposed to fix it before the wedding.”
A faint, slurred shout echoed down the basement hall: “Leo? Dude, where’d you go with the good tequila?”
It was Ethan, the groom, stumbling toward the freezer in his rehearsal dinner suit, tie loose around his neck, holding an empty shot glass. He stopped in the doorway, squinting like he couldn’t process what he was seeing, the shot glass slipping from his hand to shatter on the concrete.
“Leo?” His voice cracked, all the drunken slur gone sharp with panic. “What the hell is he doing in there? He said he was going to get his laptop, he had to show me—” He cut himself off, his gaze locking on the manila envelope peeking out of Leo’s pocket, and his face went so pale Clara thought he might pass out.
Clara stepped between him and Leo’s body, the cold seeping through her blazer, the hum of the freezer suddenly too loud, too close. The peonies, the cake, the seating charts—none of it mattered now. She’d spent seven years planning perfect days, gluing broken moments back together before anyone saw the cracks. But this crack ran deep.
“Ethan,” she said, keeping her voice steady, “what was on that laptop?”
Outside, the first siren wailed, faint but getting closer. Somewhere upstairs, a bride was probably touching up her skincare routine, counting down to the moment she walked down the aisle. Down in the freezer, the frost was already starting to settle on Leo’s shoulder, and no one answered.

title: horror|a family moves into a farmhouse where the previous owners' dog will not stop digging in the cellar
text:
I told myself it was only a dog.
That first week in the farmhouse, I kept saying it the way you say prayers in the dark—only a dog, only a dog, only a dog. Mara laughed at me for it. Jesse said dogs dug, that was the whole story, and if I needed a villain, I could blame the moles. But the dog wasn’t ours. The dog had belonged to the Hargroves, the people before us, and when the moving trucks pulled away, he was sitting on the porch like he’d been waiting for us to arrive.

Nobody mentioned him at the closing. Not the realtor, not the lawyer, not the old neighbor who watched from the road with his hat pulled low. One life ends in a house, another begins, and somehow the dog is the thing that stays.

His name, according to the tag matted into the fur under his chin, was King. He was old, gray-muzzled, thin in the way things get when they’ve forgotten hunger except as a kind of company. He didn’t bark. He didn’t beg. He watched us carry boxes through the kitchen with patient, bloodshot eyes, and when night came, he went down into the cellar.

And he dug.

“Listen,” Mara said on the seventh night.

We were in bed. The farmhouse made its usual noises—pipes knocking, old wood settling, wind worrying the shutters—but under all of it was that sound. Scrape. Pause. Scrape-scrape. Slow. Steady. Deliberate, the way a man works when he knows exactly what he’s after.

“I hear it,” I said.

“Has he stopped at all since dinner?”

“Dogs sleep,” I said. “They must.”

But I’d checked at midnight, shining Jesse’s flashlight down the cellar stairs, and King had been there at the far wall, dirt kicked up around his chest, his paws moving without hurry. He didn’t look at the light. He didn’t even lift his head.

Jesse appeared in the doorway with a comic book folded against his chest. “Mom says it’s moles.”

“Your mother’s asleep.”

“Then she said it earlier. Moles, Dad. Or groundhogs. It’s a farm. Farms have stuff under them.”

“Not usually inside the foundation.”

“He’s hunting. It’s, like, his purpose.” Jesse said this with the grave certainty of an eleven-year-old who has watched one nature documentary and considers the matter closed. “You should just let him finish.”

“Finish what?”

But he only shrugged and went back to his room, and the digging continued.

By the second week, the cellar smelled like turned earth and rain and something sweeter underneath, something I didn’t want to name. I kept the door closed. I nailed a latch over it, low, where King couldn’t hook it with his paw. That lasted half a day. Mara found him on the other side anyway, standing at the top of the stairs, breathing hard, dirt crusted black on his legs.

“The latch’s on the outside,” she said quietly. “I checked.”

“Then he didn’t go through the door.”

“Sam.”

“I don’t know.” I set down the hammer harder than I meant to. “Maybe I didn’t set it right. Maybe one of us let him in and forgot.”

“Nobody forgot.”

She was right. We both knew it. That was the worst thing about the new house—not the dark, not the isolation, not the way the phone service died whenever fog came off the fields. It was the small, impossible knowledge that something in the place didn’t obey the rules we’d agreed the world obeyed.

I went down that afternoon with a shovel, meaning to fill in the hole. King had dug deeper than I expected, a narrow trench running along the stone foundation, the earth black and damp. At the end of it, my blade struck something soft.

I froze.

For a second I thought cloth. Leather. Something folded into the soil a long time ago. I knelt, my heart hammering, and reached in with my bare hand—and pulled out a child’s shoe. Small. Blue. Buckled. The leather was stained, but it hadn’t rotted. It looked almost new.

“Jesse never had shoes like that,” Mara said behind me.

I jumped. She stood on the bottom stair, her arms crossed, watching the shoe in my hand.

“I know,” I said.

“The Hargroves didn’t have children.”

“How do you know?”

“I asked. In town. Everybody made sure to tell me. No children. Just the couple and the dog.” She swallowed. “And then just the dog.”

King had stopped digging.

I became aware of the silence the way you become aware of a stopped alarm—suddenly, guiltily, after the noise has been inside you so long you mistook it for your own pulse. The dog stood at the end of the trench, and for the first time he looked directly at me. His eyes were not animal eyes, or maybe they were more animal than I could bear. There was no madness in them. There was patience. There was an old, exhausted relief.

He stepped aside.

Behind him, the hole was deeper than the foundation should have allowed. Deeper than the cellar floor. The darkness in it didn’t look like dirt. It looked like space, like an opening into somewhere light had never reached, and from that opening rose a smell I recognized from the hospital in the last hour of my mother’s life—warm flowers, wet stone, and breath held too long.

“Sam,” Mara whispered. “What did he dig up?”

I looked at the little shoe in my hand.

And from the hole, soft as a question, something moved.

title: thriller|an ex-military drifter is cornered in a small-town diner by men who mistake him for someone else
text:
The linoleum under Cole’s boots stuck tacky, crusted with three layers of syrup and forgotten cherry pie filling, when the bell above the diner door jingled wrong. It was 2:17 a.m., the kind of small-town hour where the only sound should be Mabel the waitress refilling coffee and the pop of the pie case’s heat lamp, but the four men who stepped in didn’t smell like diesel or rain off the highway. They smelled like gun oil and pine, the sharp, unwashed reek of men who’d been parked in the treeline across Route 12 for three hours, waiting.

Cole didn’t look up. He kept his fork moving through the last of his meatloaf, the edge worn smooth from four years of bouncing around his pack, his left hand resting loose on the Formica table where he could reach the KA-BAR sheathed at his hip fast enough if he needed to. He’d drifted through 17 states in the two years since he mustered out, never staying longer than it took to fix a fence or bale hay for gas money, never giving anyone a name beyond “Cole,” and he’d thought he’d outrun the last of the people looking for him 200 miles back.

Mabel’s coffee pot clattered when the biggest of the men slid into the booth across from him, blocking the exit to the parking lot. The other three fanned out, one leaning against the pie case, one blocking the kitchen door, one hovering by the payphone by the restrooms, all of them with their jackets zipped high enough to hide the holsters on their hips.

“Long way from the Arkansas border, Jesse,” the man across from him said. His nose was crooked, broken twice at least, and there was a faint white scar snaking up from his jaw to his earlobe, the kind you got from a knife fight in a bar where no one called the cops. He slid a crumpled wanted poster across the table, the edge smudged with mud, a blurry photo of a man with the same sharp jaw, the same cropped brown hair, the same faint scar slashing through his left eyebrow that Cole had gotten when a piece of IED shrapnel nicked him outside Kandahar. “You thought we’d stop looking after you ran off with that eighty grand?”

Cole took a slow sip of coffee, bitter, burnt just the way he liked it, and didn’t reach for the poster. “Got the wrong guy.”

The man laughed, a dry, rasping sound that didn’t reach his eyes, and nodded at the scar on Cole’s brow. “Got that same little cut, same tattoo peeking out your wrist.” He jabbed a finger at the faded ink on Cole’s right wrist, the 10th Mountain insignia he’d gotten drunk and inked the night before his first deployment. “Jesse had that exact same tattoo. Joined the Army right after he ripped us off, thought we wouldn’t track a grunt? Cute.”

Out of the corner of his eye, Cole saw Mabel edge her hand toward the baseball bat she kept propped behind the counter, and he gave a tiny, almost imperceptible shake of his head. She was 62, had a granddaughter in 4-H, didn’t need to get caught in crossfire over a case of mistaken identity that was about to turn ugly. The guy by the kitchen door shifted his weight, his jacket riding up just enough to show the grip of a Glock, and Cole calculated the distance: three steps to the guy by the pie case, four to the door, if he moved fast enough he could flip the table before any of them cleared leather.

“I don’t know any Jesse,” he said, keeping his voice low, even, the same tone he’d used when he talked jumpy privates down off ledges after mortar attacks. “I rolled into town an hour ago. Never been to Arkansas in my life.”

The man across from him pulled a revolver from his waistband, slow, like he was putting on a show, and pressed the barrel hard against the edge of the table, pointed straight at Cole’s gut. “Nice act. You got two choices. Come out to the truck quiet, we’ll put a bullet in your head fast out in the woods where no one has to clean up the mess. Or we do it right here, and the old lady behind the counter gets it too for harboring a thief. Your call.”

The bell above the door jingled again. All four men turned, just a fraction, just enough, and Cole moved. His boot slammed into the leg of the table, sending it crashing into the guy across from him, the revolver going off with a deafening crack that blew a hole in the linoleum right where his boot had been two seconds earlier. He was out of the booth before the echo died, his KA-BAR in his hand, and he heard Mabel scream, heard the clatter of salt shakers hitting the floor, saw the flash of headlights through the diner window as a state trooper’s cruiser rolled into the parking lot, drawn by the gunshot.

The guy with the crooked nose was already scrambling to his feet, blood pouring from his nose where the table had caught him, and for half a second Cole thought about staying, about explaining the mix-up to the cops, about not running for once. But then he saw the second wanted poster the guy dropped when he reached for his gun, this one newer, this one with Cole’s real name on it, the one he’d thought was buried under all the discharge papers and the VA forms he’d never filled out, the one that said he was wanted for questioning in the death of his staff sergeant, the death he’d run from for two years.

He didn’t hesitate. He dove through the broken window by the booth, the glass slicing through his flannel shirt, cutting a thin line across his forearm, and hit the asphalt running, the sound of shouting and sirens fading behind him as he disappeared into the pine treeline, the dark swallowing him whole before anyone could get a clear shot. The rain started to fall then, cold and sharp, washing the blood off his arm, and he didn’t look back. There was another town 12 miles west, another diner, another stretch of highway where no one knew his name, and he’d be long gone before the sun came up.

title: mystery|a Venetian police commissario questions a widow who seems relieved rather than grieving
text:
The Quiet Canal

The rain had stopped by the time Commissario Marco Brunetti reached the house on Rio della Salute, leaving the stone steps slick as black glass and the air thick with the smell of wet plaster and something sweet drifting from a pasticceria two canals away. He counted three boats tied to the palina before the door—one police launch, one plain wooden sampietro he recognized as the medical examiner’s, and a low, polished motorboat with the name *La Puttana* hand-painted across its stern in peeling gold. Someone had a sense of humor, or had stopped caring what the neighbors thought.

He let himself in through the unlocked water gate and climbed the exterior staircase, his shoes making no sound on the worn brick. On the second-floor landing, a young officer he didn’t know well—Foa, maybe, or Boa—stood with his cap in his hands. “She’s in the kitchen, Signore. Asked if she could make coffee. We didn’t think—”

“Of course she did,” Brunetti said. He handed the man his damp raincoat. “Where’s the body?”

“Study. Across the hall. Dottor Rizzardi’s with him now.”

Brunetti nodded and went the other way, toward the light and the smell of burning sugar.

The kitchen was large, low-ceilinged, the kind of room that belonged to a house that had once held a family of ten and two servants and now held, apparently, a married couple who didn’t speak to one another. Copper pans hung in graduated sizes above a stove that looked old enough to have cooked for the Austrians. At the wooden table in the center, a woman sat with her back straight, watching an old-fashioned stovetop moka pot begin to tremble.

She was perhaps fifty-five, handsome rather than pretty, with graying dark hair pulled back and the kind of lined, un-made-up face that looked as though it had spent years outdoors. She wore a navy cardigan over a white shirt, and on her feet were a pair of frayed leather slippers, the sort sold near the Rialto to tourists who thought they looked authentic. Her hands were folded on the table in front of her, and they were not shaking.

“Signora Fontana?” Brunetti said.

She turned, and he saw it before she spoke—not grief, not shock, but something he had learned over twenty years to recognize and never to name aloud. A loosening. The particular stillness of a person who has just set down something very heavy.

“Commissario,” she said. “You’ll take coffee? The water’s bad here, but I buy bottled. It’s drinkable.” Her voice was low, a little hoarse, as though she had been talking recently, or singing.

“Thank you, yes.” He pulled out the chair across from her and sat, setting his notebook beside a chipped ceramic bowl containing three lemons and a single brown egg. “I’m sorry for your loss.”

It came out automatically, and he watched her receive it the way people receive a religious card at the door—politely, without belief. “Yes,” she said. She rose and took two cups from a shelf, neither matching. “Everyone says that. The carabiniere who came first, then the doctor. Even the man from the *agenzia funebre*, though I suppose he’s paid to. Would you like sugar? Maurizio always said I used too much.”

“Black is fine.”

She poured. The coffee came out dark and thick, with a pale crema that trembled and broke. She sat again, wrapped both hands around her cup, and looked at Brunetti directly. “He’s in the study, then. You’ve seen him.”

“Not yet. I wanted to speak with you first.” He opened the notebook but didn’t pick up his pen. “Can you tell me what happened, Signora? In your own time.”

She took a sip of coffee, then another, and for a moment he thought she was going to keep him waiting, the way people did when they were constructing a story. But when she spoke it was without calculation, almost without interest, as though she were describing the plot of a film she’d half watched on television.

“I came home around seven. I’d been at the Giardini—a friend’s opening, bad photographs, mostly wine. Maurizio said he wasn’t going. He never went anywhere anymore. The study door was closed, and the light was on. I knocked, because sometimes he was on a call with his brother in Padova and didn’t want to be disturbed. He didn’t answer. I knocked again, and then I opened it.” She paused, turned her cup a quarter turn on the table. “He was at his desk. He looked like he’d fallen asleep. He did that, after lunch, over his ledgers. I went over to wake him, and I saw the bottle was empty. The glass, too. And then I saw that his mouth was the wrong color.”

“What bottle?”

“His heart medicine. The drops. Lanoxin, I think. He took them every morning. The bottle was new on Monday—three days ago, and there should have been almost all of it left.” She said this flatly, watching Brunetti’s face. “He didn’t spill it, Commissario. I looked. There wasn’t a mark on the desk.”

He made himself not glance toward the hall. “Did you touch anything?”

“The bottle. I picked it up. Stupid of me. I watch the television, I know better. But I thought maybe I could read the label, see how much—” She stopped herself. “I put it back where it had been. More or less.”

“More or less?”

She gave a small shrug, and there it was again, that flash beneath the surface—not quite amusement. “I’m not a criminal. I didn’t measure.”

Brunetti wrote that down, partly because it was true and partly to give himself time. Outside, a gull cried, and somewhere on a neighboring canal a boat engine sputtered to life and died. He thought of the dead man in the next room, of a three-day bottle emptied into a glass, and of the woman across from him who had not cried once and who was now finishing her coffee with the calm of someone who had finished all her crying years before.

“Had your husband been ill, Signora?”

“His heart. Badly, for two years. The doctor gave him six months last autumn, then changed his mind. Maurizio said the man couldn’t decide anything.” Her thumb moved once along the rim of her cup. “He wasn’t kind, toward the end. Pain makes some people sweet, did you know that? It made him precise. He remembered every slight, every bill, every name of a boy who’d laughed at him in school in 1958.” She looked up. “That sounds cruel of me, saying it now.”

“You don’t have to—”

“No. Let it be cruel.” She set the cup down with a small, definite click. “He’s dead. It won’t hurt him.”

Brunetti closed the notebook. He would speak to Rizzardi, he thought, and to the brother in Padova, and to the bad-photographer friend at the Giardini who might or might not remember what time Signora Fontana had poured her second glass of wine. There would be an autopsy, and a toxicology report in a week if they were lucky, and a great many questions about prescriptions and access and the precise meaning of a marriage that ended in a locked room with an empty bottle.

But all of that was later.

Now he sat across from a widow whose husband had been dead perhaps four hours and whose only visible grief, so far, was that she had not yet offered him a second cup.

“Would you like more coffee, Commissario?” she asked, already reaching for the pot.

He hesitated. Rain began again, faint against the leaded window.

“Yes,” he said. “Thank you. I would.”

title: horror|survivors barricaded in a supermarket hear someone they buried knocking at the loading dock
text:
The fluorescent lights above Aisle 7 flickered so hard Jessa’s split knuckles whitened around the crowbar she’d pried off a hardware shelf three days prior. The smell of rot seeped through the loading dock’s steel roll-up door, thick and sweet, curdling over the stacked pallets of canned beans and bottled water they’d wedged against it as a barricade.
“Quit bouncing your leg,” she snapped at Ty, who was perched on a case of off-brand soda, his hunting knife twisting in a nervous circle between his fingers. “You’re gonna shake the whole damn fort down.”
Ty didn’t look up. His jaw was tight enough to crack a molar. “You hear that, right? I’m not crazy. That’s not a walker slamming into the side of the building. That’s knocking. Rhythmic.”
Marnie didn’t even glance up from the first-aid kit she was restocking at the checkout counter, her movements sharp, precise, the same way she’d sutured Jessa’s arm two days prior without flinching when the needle pulled skin. “Walkers don’t knock. It’s a looter. Or a raccoon. Raccoons make all kinds of racket when they’re going for the trash out back.”
“Raccoons don’t knock three slow, then two fast, then three slow again.” Ty’s voice cracked a little, and he gestured at the door with his knife. “That’s the code. The stupid code we made up when we first holed up here, remember? So we wouldn’t shoot each other through the door. Jessa? You remember.”
Jessa’s throat went dry. She did remember. She’d made the code up herself, back when they still thought the army would show up, back when there were five of them instead of three. She forced a laugh, sharp and brittle, and prodded the nearest pallet with her crowbar. “It’s the wind. The seal on that door’s shot. It rumbles when the gusts hit off the highway.”
The knock came again, clear as day: three slow, two fast, three slow. Marnie’s hands stilled mid-tuck of a gauze roll. For the first time all night, her steady composure slipped, just a fraction. “That’s not wind.”
“Told you!” Ty surged to his feet, nearly sending the soda case clattering. “It’s him. It’s Cole. We—we didn’t check close enough. We thought he was bit, but he wasn’t, he made it back—”
“Shut up.” Jessa’s voice was ice. She stepped between him and the barricade, crowbar held loose at her side, the way she’d held it when they’d fought off the group of raiders who’d tried to break in two nights prior. “Cole’s dead. We buried him. I drove the crowbar through his skull myself before we put him in the hole out by the garden center. Remember? You held his legs still for me.”
Ty’s face went ashen. He’d thrown up after, she remembered, had cried for an hour because Cole had been his college roommate, the kid who’d driven three hours to pick him up when the first outbreaks hit the dorms. “He was warm when we put him in the ground,” he mumbled, like he was trying to convince himself. “He was still warm, Jessa.”
“He was fevered from the bite.” Marnie stood, sliding a box cutter into the waistband of her scrub pants, her voice flat, no room for argument. “The bite on his calf was oozing black. He stopped breathing for ten minutes before we dragged him out. You felt for a pulse. You said it was gone.”
The knocking grew louder, more insistent, followed by a muffled voice, warped through the steel, familiar enough to make Jessa’s stomach drop. “Let me in. C’mon, guys, it’s freezing out here. You left me.”
Ty made a strangled sound. He lunged for the pallets, shoving at the top one hard enough to send cans of beans clattering to the floor. “We have to let him in! He’s alive, he’s out there alone—”
Jessa slammed the crowbar down on the concrete hard enough to send a chip of it flying, the crack echoing through the silent store. He froze. “You think that’s him? You think whatever’s out there is the kid who shared his last granola bar with you when we ran out of food on the highway? That thing knows the code because it listened. It listened to us talk about him, it listened when we cried over him, and now it’s wearing his voice to get in. And if you move one more can, I will hit you before it gets the chance.”
The voice came again, softer now, cracking, exactly the way Cole had when he’d begged them not to leave him as the fever spiked, when he’d sworn he wasn’t going to turn. “I can hear you in there. Ty? Tell them I’m not bit. I promise. I just wanna come home.”
Tears were running down Ty’s face now. His knife hung limp at his side. Marnie had walked over to the barricade, pressing her ear to the cold steel for a second before pulling back, her face paler than Jessa had ever seen it. She mouthed two words: It’s his voice.
Jessa didn’t move. She could smell the rot getting stronger, seeping through the cracks under the door, could hear the faint, wet gurgle under the words, the sound that no living human made. She raised the crowbar again, holding it tight, her eyes locked on the roll-up door as the knocking started up again, slower this time, like the thing on the other side knew they were listening.
“Home’s where we buried you,” she said, loud enough for it to hear. “Stay there.”
Outside, the knocking stopped. For three long seconds, the only sound was the hum of the dying lights, Ty’s ragged breathing, Marnie’s quiet, shaky exhale.
Then something heavy slammed against the door so hard the top pallet shifted, and Cole’s voice rose to a snarl, raw and inhuman, loud enough to rattle the windows: “I’m not staying out here alone.”

title: literary|an old woman tells a police officer the true story of the night her husband died
text:
Ruth kept the photograph on the kitchen sill, face-down, as though the image might otherwise witness what she was about to say. The officer was young enough to be her grandson, though he carried himself like a much older man, careful with the chair he pulled out, careful with the notebook he laid flat. Rain brushed the window. Beyond it, the garden had turned to black water and skeletal roses.

“You’ll want tea,” she said.

“I’m fine, Mrs. Calloway.”

“Nobody’s fine at this hour. Tea’s not a cure.”

She filled the kettle anyway. Her hands did not shake now. For thirty-one years they had shaken at the wrong moments—while peeling apples, while signing forms, while waking from dreams in which the lake spoke in a man’s voice. Tonight they were steady, which frightened her a little.

The officer opened his notebook. “You mentioned on the phone that the original statement wasn’t accurate.”

“It wasn’t.”

“Take me back.”

Ruth set two mugs between them, though he did not touch his. “November third, 1992. There was a storm, much like this one. Arthur came home late. He had been at the pub, but not drunk. People remembered drunk because it made things neat. He was angry. He’d found out the marina sale was fraudulent. His partner, Hollis, had signed Arthur’s name to documents. If Arthur exposed it, Hollis would go to prison. If he didn’t, Arthur would lose everything.”

“Was Hollis Fenn at the house?”

“No. Not then.”

She turned the photograph over. Arthur stood squinting in sunlight, one hand on the bow of a boat named Marisol. He looked kind; he had often been kind. Kindness and cruelty could live in a man like two tenants who never met on the stairs.

“We argued,” Ruth said. “Not about Hollis. About me. I’d known for six weeks and said nothing. Arthur thought I was protecting him. I was protecting myself. I wanted to leave. I had a suitcase in the boot of the car. I’d packed two sweaters, my mother’s ring, and the good scissors, as if any of that could make a new life.”

The officer wrote without looking up. “What happened next?”

“He went to the lake. He often did when he couldn’t bear being inside his own head. I followed with a torch. The path was mud. The water was high, almost over the jetty. I told him I wasn’t going to stay if he buried this. He laughed—not cruelly. He said I had nowhere to go. He was right enough to make me furious.”

Ruth paused. The kettle’s tick sounded like footsteps in an empty hall.

“He turned from me,” she went on. “I didn’t push him. I have said that to myself every day, and it’s true. I didn’t push him. But I wanted him gone. Not dead. Gone. When the board cracked, I saw him slip. He caught the edge. His fingers were there, white in the torchlight. He called my name.”

The officer’s pen had stopped.

Ruth looked at the rain rather than the young man’s face. “I could have taken his hand. I was close enough. The torch was in my left hand. He was clinging with both of his. If I had put it down and lain flat, I believe I could have pulled him back. I didn’t move.”

“Mrs. Calloway—”

“For four seconds. Perhaps five. Long enough to know what I was doing. Then I knelt, but the rotten wood gave way more, and he couldn’t hold. The lake took him. I screamed then. I suppose that was real. Grief can be real even when it’s also relief.”

The silence changed shape. It became something with weight, settling over the table.

“Why did you wait so long?” the officer asked.

“Because Hollis saw me.”

The officer looked up sharply.

“He came after Arthur,” she said. “He parked by the boathouse and watched from the trees. Later, he found me on the jetty. He said if I told anyone I’d hesitated, he’d say I pushed Arthur. And if I exposed the fraud, he’d make sure everyone believed it. So I gave him the clean story. Accident, storm, rotten timber. He gave me silence. It was a bargain between two guilty people, though our guilt wasn’t the same size.”

“You have evidence?”

She slid a folded envelope from her cardigan. “His letter. He wrote it when cancer made him afraid of judgment—not God’s, I think, just mine. Names, dates, what he saw. What he did with the accounts. And what I did.”

The officer took it as though it might burn. “You understand this changes the death investigation. It may not meet the legal threshold for homicide.”

“I know what the law calls things. I’m not asking it to call me innocent.”

At last he touched the tea, only to move it a half-inch closer to himself. “What do you want?”

Ruth turned Arthur’s photograph face-down again, gently, as if covering a sleeping child.

“I want to stop being the widow the storm made,” she said. “And become, for whatever time I have left, the woman who stood there and chose not to reach.”

Outside, the rain kept falling, indifferent, endless, washing nothing clean.

title: science fiction|a bounty hunter in a decaying future city must decide whether an android is truly alive
text:
The rain on Neon Line 7 tastes like burnt copper when it seeps through the cracked visor of my rain slicker. I’m pressed up against a rusted bulkhead, pulse pistol digging into my ribs, watching the noodle stall across the way where my mark’s been stirring the same pot of synth-ramen for forty-seven minutes. The bounty chit in my pocket says this is unit Kael-9, serial number 417, escaped from GenSys’s off-world pleasure coliseum three weeks back, charged with killing two handlers before he bolted. Dead or alive, payout’s enough to fix the leak in my apartment ceiling, cover my little sister’s lung filter refills for six months. No brainer, right?
That’s what I kept telling myself when I tracked him here, when I sat through two bowls of over-salted noodles across from him an hour ago, when I noticed he slipped extra protein cubes to the feral street kid who hangs around the stall begging scraps.
He looks up like he can feel me staring, and for a second I freeze—GenSys androids have motion sensors sharp enough to pick up a rat’s heartbeat three alleys over. But he just nods, wipes his hands on his stained apron, and calls across the rain-slicked tarmac. “You gonna stand there getting soaked all night, or you gonna come get the free miso I promised you? It’s gonna curdle.”
I hesitate for half a second before I push off the bulkhead, boots squelching through puddles that glow neon pink from the holo-ads bleeding down the building walls. The stool across from him is cold when I sit, the miso he slides me steaming so hard it fogs the cracked lenses of my glasses. “You knew I was there the whole time,” I say. It’s not a question.
He nods, prodding a lump of synthetic pork in the pot with a wooden spoon. The serial number tattooed on his wrist—417, same as the chit—is faded, like he’s been scrubbing at it with steel wool. “Knew you were following me since the mag-lev station yesterday. You don’t walk like a junkie looking for a fix, don’t walk like a Corp goon looking to shake down stall owners. You walk like someone who’s got a price on my head.”
I don’t reach for the pistol. Not yet. The miso tastes better than it has any right to, like actual seaweed, not the lab-grown crap they sell in the ration packs. “GenSys says you killed two handlers. Tore their throats out with your bare hands before you stole a transport.”
He snorts, flipping a noodle into the air and catching it in his mouth like he doesn’t have a care in the world. The kid he fed earlier peeks around the edge of the stall, and he tosses her a dried fruit bar without looking, like he’s done it a hundred times. “One of those handlers was gonna sell that kid—Lila, the one with the braid full of old wire—to a flesh broker down in the Undercity. The other tried to put a bolt through my chest when I stopped him. You gonna tell me that makes me a monster?”
My throat goes tight. I know that flesh broker. I turned down a contract on him last month, because the payout was half what they were offering for Kael, and I needed the money for Mia’s filters. The chit in my pocket feels like it’s burning a hole through my coat. The Corp manual says androids don’t feel fear, don’t feel loyalty, don’t care if some street kid gets sold off to the worst people in the city. They’re code, right? Wires and plastic and pre-programmed responses, designed to look human, to act human, but no more alive than the vending machine down the block that shorted out last week and started dispensing free soda.
But I’ve been tracking him for three days. I watched him sit with an old drunk veteran for two hours in the rain last night, listening to him ramble about the war on Mars, even gave him the last of his cash for a bunk at the flop house. I watched him fix a broken prosthetic leg for a single mom who couldn’t pay the mechanic, no charge, stayed up half the night soldering the wiring while her kid slept on a crate behind the stall. The Corp says that’s all subroutines, empathy algorithms designed to make them more palatable for the rich folks who buy them. But when he looks at me now, his eyes don’t look like code. They look tired. Same as mine.
“I’m not gonna run,” he says, like he can read the thoughts bouncing around my skull. He slides a crumpled data chip across the counter, smudged with noodle grease. “That’s all the evidence you need to take down GenSys’s coliseum ring, the stuff about the kids they’re snatching off the streets to fight in the pits. You can turn me in, take the payout. I know you got a sister, right? The one with the bad lungs, lives up in level 12? I’ve seen you visit her on your days off. I won’t fight you. But if you do? Those kids? They’re gonna end up dead, same as those handlers you heard about.”
The rain picks up, drumming so hard on the stall’s tin awning I can barely hear the holo-ad blaring two blocks over for GenSys’s new line of “obedient, non-sentient” companion androids. My hand rests an inch from my pistol, and for a second I can’t breathe. The chit says dead or alive. The manual says he’s a machine. But the miso is warm in my hands, and the kid is staring at me from behind the stall, eyes wide, and I can still remember the way Mia coughed up blood last week when her filter shorted out, the way the doctor said if I didn’t get the refills soon, she wasn’t gonna make it to next winter.
I don’t know what alive even means, anymore. Not in this city, where the Corp sells people the same way they sell toasters, where the rain poisons you if you stay out in it too long, where half the folks walking around have more wiring in their bodies than the androids they hunt. I pick up the data chip, turn it over in my fingers. Kael doesn’t flinch. He just goes back to stirring his pot, like he’s already made peace with whatever I decide.

title: romance|a journalist returns to her hometown and runs into the boy she left without saying goodbye
text:
The greyhound bus exhaled a breath of diesel and cooling metal as it lurched to a stop before Haven’s Rest’s only diner. Elara Vance pressed her palm to the smudged window, the October glass sharp enough to bite through her glove, and stared at the flickering neon “EAT” sign. It drooped in the exact same crooked arc, the ‘A’ dark as a missing tooth. Five years. Five years of city smog, shouted editor deadlines, and rental walls so thin she’d learned the rhythm of her neighbor’s sobs. Five years since she’d folded a single note into the seam of her suitcase and boarded a bus at 2:17 a.m., not daring to glance at the tree line where the old tire swing hung.

The bell above Molly’s Diner jingled as she stepped inside, and the scent engulfed her first—burnt maple syrup, bacon grease, and the cinnamon potpourri Mrs. Hale simmered every autumn. Red vinyl booths patched with electrical tape winked under fluorescent lights. A handful of faces turned, strangers softened by familiarity, their gazes sliding past the tailored wool coat she’d saved three months to buy, settling instead on the scar slicing through her left eyebrow, the one she’d gotten climbing the water tower at sixteen.

She slid onto the cracked cushion of the farthest booth, shoulders loosening despite herself, and reached for a sticky menu. The coffee mug set down before her was chipped along the rim, blue cornflowers faded almost to white.

“Elara?”

Her fingers locked around the ceramic. The mug shifted, coffee sloshing over the edge to bloom dark across the paper placemat. She knew that voice. Had heard it in a hundred half-dreams, always calling from the other side of a closing train door, always dissolving before she could answer.

She lifted her head.

Kael Rainer stood beside the Formica table, a pot of coffee in one hand. The boy she remembered had been all sharp, sun-bleached angles—grass stains permanently ground into the knees of his jeans, calluses roughening his fingertips from guitar strings, a smile that tilted higher on the left when he was about to lie about not stealing a kiss. The man before her had broader shoulders beneath a faded flannel shirt, sleeves rolled to show forearms dusted with dark hair and a thin, silvery scar winding around his wrist. His hair was shorter, curling damply at his temples as though he’d walked through rain, but his eyes were the same: the deep, unreadable brown of river mud after a storm, ringed with gold at the edges.

A muscle in his jaw ticked. He didn’t smile.

“Hi,” she said. Her voice came out thin, stripped of the polished broadcast lilt she’d drilled into herself during journalism school. She cleared her throat. “You work here now?”

“Own the place,” he said. He set the coffee pot down with deliberate care, as if his hand had tightened around it. “Bought it from Molly last spring. Fixed the roof last month. You?” His gaze flicked over her—her leather tote embossed with the *Boston Chronicle* logo, the faint ink stain beside her thumbnail, the way she held herself like someone braced against wind. “Back for a story? Or just passing through?”

The old defensiveness rose, automatic as breathing. “My mother’s house. She’s selling it. I came to pack.”

“Right.” He nodded slowly. “Saw the listing. Figured you’d show up eventually.”

The words hung between them, heavy with all the things she’d never written in that note. *I got the scholarship. I couldn’t wake you. If I’d looked at you, I would have stayed.*

“I—” Elara began, but her throat closed. She stared at his hands, at the chipped black polish he used to wear replaced by clean, blunt nails, at the faint tremor in his index finger when he reached for the coffee pot again. “Kael, I should have—”

“Don’t.” The word was quiet, sharp as a shard of the ceramic they’d once broken in this very booth, laughing so hard milkshakes spilled. His expression didn’t soften, but something cracked behind his eyes, brief and raw, like lightning swallowed by clouds. “You don’t owe me a speech in a diner, Elara. You made it out. That’s what you always wanted, isn’t it? Out.”

Out of the mill town. Out of the life where futures were measured in hourly shifts at the lumber yard. She had wanted it so badly it had burned. She just hadn’t known, at eighteen, that leaving would carve a hole shaped exactly like the boy sitting across from her in stolen moments, teaching her chord progressions on a guitar with a cracked neck, promising they’d drive west until the Atlantic became the Pacific.

“I didn’t know how to say it,” she whispered.

The bell above the door jingled. A gust of cold air swept in, carrying the sharp, clean scent of pine. Kael stepped back, his face closing like a book she was no longer allowed to read. “Your usual?” he asked, and his voice was polite now, the voice he used for tourists who stopped on their way to the ski slopes. “Blueberry pancakes. Extra syrup.”

Elara looked down at her hands. Her engagement ring sat cold and heavy in her coat pocket, where she’d twisted it off an hour before the bus crossed the town line.

“Yes,” she said. “Thank you.”

He walked away. Through the steam rising from her coffee, she watched him pause behind the counter, his back to her, and press both palms flat against the linoleum. The rain began to tap against the window then, slow at first, then steady, as if the town itself had decided she wasn’t allowed to leave again without getting wet.

title: political memoir|a young woman describes life on the campaign trail with her famous father
text:
Excerpt from *Bleeding Signs*  
They say the first real lesson of politics is that the candidate is never the one who smells like regret. It’s the advance team, or the interns who forget the hand sanitizer, or the kid who hands him a melted vanilla Dairy Queen cone at a county fair and doesn’t think to wipe the sticky streak that runs down his wrist to the cuff of his tailored white shirt. That was my job, mostly, in the summer of 2018—wiping regret off my dad before the cameras caught it. I was 22, fresh out of Sarah Lawrence, where I’d written a 42-page thesis on gendered disenfranchisement in rural Iowa that I’d handed in with a coffee stain on the title page and a B+ scrawled in red pen. Dad called two days after I moved back to our empty house in McLean, the one where the dog had died the winter before and no one had bothered to replace the rug she’d chewed by the back door, and said, “I need someone who won’t lie to me when my fly’s down.” I said yes before I thought to ask if he’d pay me. He didn’t, not really—just a $500 a week stipend that went mostly to gas station energy drinks and the occasional motel room where I could cry without his field director, Marge, knocking on the door to say we were 12 minutes behind schedule.  
The first rally I went to was in a VFW hall outside Des Moines, the kind of place where the walls are lined with yellowed photos of boys who never came home from Vietnam and the beer taps stick if you don’t jiggle them just right. Dad was running for Senate then, still playing up the “small-town kid who made good” schtick even though he’d left Iowa for Yale when he was 18 and hadn’t been back for longer than a long weekend in 30 years. I stood off to the side of the stage, holding his favorite black Sharpie and a bottle of room-temperature water he insisted tasted better than cold, and watched a woman in a faded Trump 2016 hoodie push through the crowd to hand him a jar of pickled beets. “My ma made these,” she said, her voice cracking like she was talking to a movie star, not a man who still burned toast every time he tried to make breakfast. Dad took the jar, smiled that smile—the one that crinkles the corners of his eyes just enough to make people forget he once voted to cut food stamps—and said, “These’ll be gone by Friday, darlin’.” I knew for a fact he hated pickled beets. We left them on a bus seat an hour later, next to a half-eaten bag of Cheetos and a stack of yard signs that said *SENATOR TOM HALE: FOR THE FOLKS WHO SHOW UP*.  
The bus was a beat-up 2004 Fleetwood Bounder that Marge had bought off a retired preacher in Ames for $12,000, with a broken AC that only worked if you banged on the vent above the driver’s seat three times and a couch that smelled like old cigarette smoke and regret. I slept on that couch more nights than I slept in a bed, my head propped on a hoodie I’d stolen from my ex-boyfriend, the one who’d dumped me over text the week before the campaign started because he said I was “choosing dynastic politics over our future.” He was right, probably, but I didn’t have the energy to say so. Most nights on the bus, Dad would sit up front with Marge and the driver, a quiet guy named Ray who chewed tobacco and kept a photo of his grandkid taped to the dashboard, going over talking points until his voice went hoarse. Sometimes he’d wander back to where I was pretending to sleep, sit on the edge of the couch, and talk about when I was little, how he’d take me to get ice cream after Little League games and I’d always get sprinkles all over his suit. He never apologized for missing my high school graduation to vote on a farm bill, or for forgetting my 21st birthday because he was at a fundraiser in the Hamptons. I never asked him to.  
The worst night was in Davenport, two weeks before the primary. We’d just wrapped up a town hall at a community college where a kid with a nose ring had called Dad out for taking $200,000 from a pharmaceutical PAC, and Dad had stammered through a non-answer about “bipartisan solutions” until Marge cut the Q&A short. We got back to the bus to find someone had keyed *CORPORATE WHORE* into the side, the letters deep enough to scratch through the red, white, and blue vinyl wrap we’d paid some kid in Des Moines $800 to put on. Ray cursed under his breath and kicked a tire, Marge started yelling on the phone to the state party, and Dad just stood there staring at the words like they were written in a language he didn’t understand. I pulled a can of silver spray paint out of the supply bin—we kept it for touching up yard signs—and started spraying over the letters, the fumes burning my eyes. After a minute, Dad knelt down next to me, took the can from my hand, and started spraying too, his tie dragging in the gravel of the parking lot. We didn’t talk while we did it. When we were done, the side of the bus looked like it had a weird silver scar running from the door to the back wheel well. Marge came over, looked at it, and sighed. “Looks like shit,” she said. Dad laughed, a loud, rough laugh I hadn’t heard since before Mom left, and said, “Yeah, well. So does this whole damn thing.”  
We won the primary by 17 points. That night, we got drunk on cheap bourbon in a hotel room in Des Moines, the kind of place where the carpets are sticky and the TV only gets three channels. Dad gave a speech to the volunteers, talking about “fighting for the heartland” and “remembering where we come from,” and then he came back to the room, sat on the edge of the bed, and cried. I sat next to him and handed him a crumpled napkin from the pizza place down the street, and he said, “I don’t know if I’m doing this for the right reasons, kiddo.” I didn’t say anything. I didn’t know either. Later that night, I snuck out to the bus and found the jar of pickled beets, still sitting where we’d left it, the lid sealed tight. I opened it and ate one, just to see what all the fuss was about. It was sour, and it made my eyes water, and it tasted exactly like every summer I’d ever spent waiting for my dad to notice I was in the room.
