title: science fiction|the crew of a generation ship discover the captain has been lying about their destination
text:
The Lie Beneath the Stars

The observation deck hummed with recycled air. Maren pressed her palm to the cold viewport, watching the target star swell from a pinprick into a shard of ice.

“Eleven months,” she said. “That’s what the Captain told us. Eleven months to Epsilon Eridani b.”

Behind her, Jax snorted. He was elbow-deep in a navigation console, grease on his jaw and contempt in his voice. “Eleven months of fairy tales. You believe every plaque on the wall, Cadet?”

“I believe mission logs.”

“Then read this one.”

Maren turned. Jax had pulled up a star chart she had never seen before—not the clean official map with their blue route arcing toward Epsilon Eridani, but a tangled mess of red corrections buried beneath layers of encryption.

“Where did you get that?”

“Maintenance access. The old Nav core wasn’t wiped; it was bricked over. Someone wanted the truth to rot underneath.” Jax tapped the screen. “Our heading isn’t Epsilon. It’s Gliese 667 C.”

A voice spoke from the doorway. “That is restricted information.”

Captain Lira Voss stood framed in blue light, uniform perfect, hands folded as if she had arrived for a memorial. At seventy-two, she had the calm of a woman who had rehearsed every disaster.

Maren stiffened. “Captain, Jax says—”

“I heard what Jax says.” Lira stepped inside, and the door sealed behind her. “He is correct.”

Jax laughed sharply. “Wow. No speech about duty? No ‘trust the mission’?”

“The mission changed.”

“Changed when?” Maren asked.

“Before your grandmother was born.”

The words landed like a breach alarm.

Jax slammed the console. “So three generations lived, worked, and died heading to a planet that was never waiting for them?”

“Epsilon Eridani b was never viable,” Lira said. “By the time the *Argo* left the Solar System, telescopes confirmed it was a molten hellscape battered by solar flares. Command had two choices: tell two thousand colonists their ark was flying toward a grave, or redirect them.”

“To Gliese?” Maren whispered.

“To a living world. Oceans. Nitrogen-rich atmosphere. A sun that dims and flares, but stable enough.”

Jax leaned into the captain’s face, fury trembling in his scarred eyebrow. “And you couldn’t just tell people?”

“Would your great-grandparents have boarded knowing the journey would take twice as long? That they would never see land? That their children’s children might?”

“They deserved the choice!”

“They had already lost Earth.” Lira’s voice cracked for the first time. “The oceans were acid. The cities were burning. Command didn’t lie to trap them, Jax. They lied to give them something to carry.”

Maren looked back through the viewport. The star seemed different now—colder, redder, almost angry. “All the lessons. The maps. The festivals celebrating First Landing on Epsilon. Everyone I know has memorized a future that doesn’t exist.”

“A future exists,” Lira said. “Just not the one printed in your textbooks.”

Jax paced like a caged wolf. “How many captains knew?”

“All of us.”

“All six?”

“Seven, including me.”

“And you let us bury our dead facing the wrong star.”

Lira did not look away. “Yes.”

That quiet answer frightened Maren more than the lie itself.

Jax stabbed a finger toward the door. “People will burn this ship apart when they find out.”

“Perhaps.”

“Perhaps? You won’t even stop us?”

“How could I?” Lira asked. “You are not children, though every captain before me pretended otherwise. The crew has earned the truth, even if it destroys morale.”

Maren swallowed. “Why tell us now? Why not take it to your grave?”

For a long moment, the captain only watched the growing star.

“Because Gliese 667 Cc is not eleven months away,” she said. “It is six weeks.”

Jax stopped pacing.

Maren’s breath caught. “We’re that close?”

“Closer. The official sensors were masked. I am undoing the mask tonight.” Lira pulled a data cylinder from her coat and held it out. “This contains the complete redirection records, planetary surveys, and the sealed orders from Earth. I want you two to publish it fleetwide.”

Jax narrowed his eyes. “You want us to?”

“Someone must. If the truth comes from the captain, it sounds like another command. If it comes from the mechanic and the navigator who uncovered it, the crew can decide what to believe.”

“Decide?” Maren asked.

“Whether to hate me. Whether to forgive Earth. Whether to prepare for landing.” Lira’s mouth thinned. “And whether to turn the ship around.”

Jax stared at her. “You’d let them vote for that?”

“The fuel reserve could support a return trajectory, barely. The crew would die in transit, but their grandchildren might reach a dead Solar System.” She paused. “People have a right to ruin themselves knowingly.”

“That’s monstrous,” Maren said.

“So is forcing salvation on strangers.”

Jax snatched the cylinder. “You’re really not going to fight?”

“I have fought for forty years,” Lira said. “I have lied at weddings, named children after a false horizon, and buried my own husband without telling him. I am tired, Jax. Let someone else carry the next leg.”

Maren noticed then how small the captain looked beneath the emergency lights—not powerful, not sinister, just ancient and worn smooth by secrecy.

The intercom chirped. “Bridge to Captain Voss. External sensors report anomalous planetary mass ahead. Do you confirm?”

Lira closed her eyes. “Confirm.”

Maren turned to the viewport.

At first she saw only darkness. Then, along the edge of the star’s crimson glow, a crescent appeared: blue-black, faintly luminous, curved like a held breath.

Jax moved beside her. All his rage seemed to drain into wonder.

“Is that—”

“Gliese 667 Cc,” Lira said. “Your new world. If you still want it.”

Maren pressed her forehead to the glass. Somewhere beneath those clouds, rain might be falling on stone no human had ever touched.

Behind her, Jax gripped the data cylinder so tightly his knuckles whitened.

“Send the files,” Maren said softly.

“All of them?”

“Every lie. Every reason. Every survey.” She looked at him, then at the captain. “We don’t arrive as believers. We arrive awake.”

Lira nodded once, and for the first time, she looked almost free.

Outside the *Argo*, the alien dawn rose without permission.

title: legal thriller|a public defender realises her client's alibi witness is lying to protect someone else
text:
I stared at Marnie across the scarred Formica table in the courthouse holding cell’s interview nook, the reek of burnt coffee and industrial disinfectant stinging my nose. She picked at a split in her fake leather jacket, the chipped black polish on her thumbnail catching the buzz of the flickering fluorescent overhead. Ten minutes prior, she’d sworn on her dead mama’s bible that she’d been with Javi—my client, the kid facing 25 to life for the bodega shooting—from 7 p.m. to 2 a.m. the night Reyes got killed. That they’d been holed up in her cousin’s trailer smoking ditch weed, watching old *Fast & Furious* bootlegs, not stepping foot outside once.
The lie sat between us thick as the cigarette smoke clinging to her hair.
I leaned in, elbows on the table, didn’t bother softening my voice. “You got the call log from that night, Marnie. I pulled it myself. You texted Javi at 9:17 p.m. asking where the hell he was. Said he bailed on you an hour prior to go handle ‘some stupid shit.’”
Her jaw tightened. She didn’t meet my eye. “That was about a different night.”
“Bullshit.” I tossed the crumpled receipt down between us, the one I’d fished out of the bodega trash two blocks from the shooting scene an hour prior, time-stamped 9:32 p.m. Her signature scrawled at the bottom for a pack of menthols and a blue raspberry slushie. The same slushie she’d mentioned offhand three weeks ago she craved when she was stressed, the one no corner store within three miles of her cousin’s trailer sold. “You were three blocks from the bodega when the shot went off. You saw who did it. And you’re not covering for Javi.”
Her breath hitched. Just a tiny, sharp inhale, the kind a jury would never catch, the kind you learn to spot after six years of PD work when every witness lies to you for one stupid reason or another. She picked harder at the split in her jacket, the vinyl flaking off onto the table. “I don’t know what you’re talking about.”
“Who is he?” I kept my voice low, flat. “Your new boyfriend? The one with the teardrop tattoo under his left eye, the one the cops pulled over last week for a stolen gun? The one who’s been beating on you so bad you’ve been wearing turtlenecks in 90-degree heat?”
Her hand flew to her neck, like she could yank the fabric up higher before I saw the purple bruise peeking out over the collar. Her eyes glistened, but she didn’t cry. People in this part of the city don’t cry in front of lawyers. They don’t cry in front of cops. They save the tears for when the door’s locked and no one’s watching.
“They’ll kill him,” she whispered, so quiet I almost didn’t hear it over the guard’s radio blaring down the hall. “If I talk, they’ll kill both of us. Javi said to stick to the story. Said he’d take the charge before he let them put a bullet in my baby brother.”
The words hit me like a fist to the sternum. I sat back. Of course. Javi wasn’t just letting her lie. He was begging her to. Knew the kid who pulled the trigger was Marnie’s 16-year-old brother, the one who’d gotten mixed up with the crew last year, the one who’d panicked when Reyes reached for the baseball bat under the counter. Javi would rot in a cell before he let a kid get charged as an adult, before he let Marnie lose the only family she had left.
I closed my eyes for half a second. The clock above the door ticked loud. The guard yelled something about lockup down the hall.
This wasn’t a alibi. It was a sacrifice. And I was the only schmuck standing between all three of them and a system that didn’t care which one of them took the fall, as long as someone did. (Word count: 612)

title: cozy mystery|a doll collector stumbles onto a murder at a county fair antiques show
text:
I told myself I was only going to the restroom.

That is important to establish, because later certain people—meaning Chief Pell, with his skeptical eyebrows and his habit of clicking his pen like he hoped it would transform into a confession—would imply I had gone snooping. I had not. I had gone in search of paper towels, quiet, and possibly one full minute without somebody explaining to me that a “common German dolly face” was not, in fact, German.

The county fair’s antiques show occupied the long metal exhibition hall between the prize honey and the sheep barn, which meant the air smelled like beeswax, old paper, fried dough, and faintly of livestock. It was ten minutes after closing on Saturday, and most of the dealers had already zipped themselves into display cases and complaints about the lighting. My own booth—Edith Darling, Dolls & Curious Playthings—was modest: three bisque heads, a cloth rag doll with one painted eye, a French fashion doll I could not actually afford to sell, and a wooden Noah’s Ark missing three zebras and, ominously, Noah.

I had spent the afternoon politely correcting men who called every doll “creepy,” assuring a grandmother that cracked composition did not mean her childhood Shirley Temple had leprosy, and refusing twice to buy a “genuine Victorian mourning doll” that was plainly a 1990s porcelain craft-kit special with too much eyeliner.

Now I balanced against the edge of my table, trying to remove a price sticker from my thumb, when Marnie Voss swept down the aisle.

“Edith,” she said, in the voice she used for emergencies and discounted Limoges, “have you seen Leo?”

“Leo Hatcher?” I said. “Not since he tried to tell that schoolteacher that her Betsy Wetsy was worth four hundred dollars.”

Marnie’s mouth tightened. Leo was the show’s least beloved dealer, a man who treated every object like a mark and every conversation like a negotiation. He sold “fresh-to-market” furniture that suspiciously smelled of hardware stain, and “museum-quality” toys that museums would have accepted only as evidence.

“He’s supposed to settle up with the promoter,” Marnie said. “His van’s still outside. His booth’s unlocked.”

“Maybe he slipped out for coffee.”

“Leo doesn’t buy coffee. He mooches it.”

This was irrefutable.

I pulled the price sticker off in a satisfying little ribbon. “Could he be in the office?”

“Nobody answers.” She leaned closer, dropping her voice. “I heard arguing earlier. Behind the exhibitors’ door.”

“At an antiques fair? People argue about reproduction hinges for fun, Marnie.”

“This sounded serious. A man shouted, then something fell.”

I felt the familiar small tug I always get when a puzzle presents itself—the same impulse that made me open trunks in attics and examine doll costumes for hidden labels. I did not approve of it. It had, over the years, caused trouble.

“I was heading to the restroom,” I said firmly.

Marnie looked unimpressed. “They’re in the same direction.”

They were, in fact, almost in the same direction. That was not snooping. That was geography.

We walked past darkened booths. Glass cases glowed under the emergency lights. Silver spoons rested in velvet trays like sleeping fish. Somewhere outside, a carnival ride played its cheerful, tinny melody, muffled by the metal walls.

“You’re sure it wasn’t Mr. Alvaro?” I asked. “He gets dramatic when people touch the clocks.”

“It came from the storage corridor.”

The storage corridor was behind the east wall, a narrow passage dealers used for crates and folding chairs. The exhibitors’ door stood open a crack, spilling yellow light across the concrete.

I stopped. “Leo?”

No answer.

“See?” Marnie whispered. “That’s exactly the kind of no-answer that means something.”

“It could mean he’s not there.”

“His booth is unlocked and his van is outside.”

I pushed the door.

The first thing I noticed was the broken doll.

Not a person, thank goodness—for half a second. A large French bisque bebe lay on the floor among overturned packing paper, her blue glass eyes staring serenely at the ceiling, one tiny kid shoe detached beside her. A crate had been pried open. Straw clung to Leo Hatcher’s trouser leg.

Then the half-second ended, and I saw the rest.

Leo was slumped against the wall beneath a shelf of rusted farm tools. His mouth was slightly open, and his face had the strange color of wet concrete. A brass-handled antique awl protruded from the heavy cardigan he wore despite the August heat. His right hand rested near a torn paper label, as if he had tried, at the end, to point at something.

Marnie made a thin sound.

I grabbed her arm. “Don’t come in. Don’t touch anything.”

“Is he—”

“Yes.” My voice came out calmer than I felt. “I think so.”

My heart knocked hard against my ribs. I stepped back, keeping one hand on the doorframe, and forced myself to look without touching. The scattered straw. The open crate. The doll’s fractured composition body. The awl. Leo’s keys hung from his belt, catching the light. Near his left shoe, half hidden by paper, was something small and pale.

A miniature porcelain hand.

It had broken off at the wrist, painted fingers curled delicately, and I recognized the workmanship immediately—not because I meant to examine a murder scene, but because dolls are my language. That hand had belonged to an early nineteenth-century wooden doll, maybe Georgian, the kind dealers call “queens.” Rare. Valuable. Almost never seen lying beside a corpse at a county fair.

Marnie whispered, “We have to call the police.”

“Yes.” I pulled out my phone and was horrified to see my hand shaking. “And nobody else comes down this hall.”

Chief Pell answered on the fourth ring, sounding like a man who had hoped to finish his pie. I gave him the location clearly, twice, and then stood there listening to the distant carnival music while the dead dealer and the broken doll kept their secrets.

Marnie stared at the floor. “He always did deal in stolen pieces,” she said softly.

I looked again at the little porcelain hand.

Maybe Leo Hatcher had not been killed over an argument.

Maybe he had been killed over a doll.

title: fantasy|a half-vampire girl and her dog travel from village to village hunting the undead for money
text:
The frost crunched under Elara’s scuffed leather boots as she crested the hill, the village of Bramble’s End huddled below like a cluster of frostbitten mushrooms. Her breath plumed white in the dusk—one of the few small, human quirks her dhampir blood hadn’t stolen, along with a stubborn pulse that beat slow as a funeral drum and a tolerance for sunlight that made full-blooded vampires snarl “half-breed” like a curse. At her heel, Mutt huffed, his shaggy black fur matted with burrs, a jagged scar slicing across his left eye where a ghoul had nearly taken it three villages back. He wasn’t just a dog; he was the only thing that hadn’t tried to drive a stake through her heart since she’d fled her father’s coven at sixteen.

The village square reeked of turnip stew and fear when they stepped through the splintered palisade. The blacksmith’s forge guttered, and mothers herded squawking children inside cottages, doors slamming shut hard enough to rattle the windowpanes. Only the elder dared approach, his wool shawl pulled tight against the wind, gnarled hands clutching a leather pouch that clinked softly.

“Three nights now,” he said, his voice gravelly as crushed stone, not meeting her eyes. Most folks didn’t. Dhampirs made them nervous—too pale, too fast, eyes that glinted like polished garnet when the light hit wrong. “Took the miller’s youngest last eve. Dragged her right out her cottage window. Left naught but a trail of slime and a broken woolen doll.”
Elara nodded, flicking a strand of ink-black hair out of her face. Her fangs ached, not for the old man’s thin, sour blood, but for the undead taint she could already taste on the air—rot and old grave dirt and something sharp, like burnt iron. “Fifteen silver,” she said. “Ten now, five when I bring you its head. If it’s a wight, extra. Wights take longer to burn.”
The elder flinched, but he tossed her the pouch. It was lighter than it should be; she didn’t call him out on it. Folks shorted her half the time, as if hunting things that went bump in the night was worth less than mending a plow. “Don’t you go bringing that thing back before dawn,” he muttered, already retreating. “And keep that beast on a leash.”
Mutt bared his teeth, a low growl rumbling in his chest, and Elara laid a hand on his broad head. His fur was warm under her palm, a steady anchor when the hunger coiled tight in her gut. “Easy, boy,” she murmured. “He’s just scared. Scared folks pay better than brave ones, most days.”
She didn’t bother with an inn. The undead didn’t hunt where crowds gathered, not the feral, newly risen kind that plagued backwater villages like this. She followed the stench past the mill, past the overgrown graveyard where headstones tilted like drunkards, to the abandoned root cellar half-buried in the hillside, its wooden door splintered inward. Mutt’s ears flattened, and he whined, high and thin—he could smell it too, the wrongness of something that should be staying dead.
Elara drew the ash stake from her belt, its surface worn smooth from years of use, and a silver hunting knife that had been her mother’s, the hilt wrapped in worn deerskin. The sun had dipped fully below the horizon now, painting the sky bruised purple and black, and her vision sharpened, the dark peeling back like a rotting curtain to show the drag marks in the mud, the smears of dried black blood on the cellar steps.
“Stay close,” she told Mutt, and he fell in at her heels, silent as a shadow, as she pushed the door open.
The stench hit her first, so thick she gagged, her throat burning. The cellar was littered with old turnip crates and bones—small animal bones, a few human ones, picked clean. Huddled in the corner, something that had once been the miller’s son, dead and buried two weeks prior from a fever, turned its head. Its skin was gray and sloughing off its cheekbones, eyes milky white, mouth crusted with old blood. It snarled, a wet, gurgling sound, and lunged.
Elara moved faster than any human could, sidestepping its grasping claws, and drove the stake hard into its chest. It shrieked, a sound like nails on a coffin lid, black ichor spurting over her wrist, and she twisted the stake until it went still, slumping to the dirt floor. Mutt darted in, snapping at its ankle to make sure it didn’t rise again, just like he’d been trained.
She was kneeling, pulling her knife to sever its head for proof, when she heard it—a soft, gurgling laugh from the dark at the back of the cellar. Not one wight. Two.
The second one hit her from the side, slamming her into the stone wall hard enough to make her see stars, its claws raking across her forearm, tearing through her leather jacket. Pain flared, hot and sharp, and Mutt was on it before it could sink its teeth into her throat, his jaws locking around its wrist, shaking it like a rat. Elara snarled, her fangs fully descended now, and drove her knife up under its jaw, into its brain. It went limp, heavy as a sack of stones, and she shoved it off her, gasping.
Her arm throbbed, black blood oozing from the gashes, and Mutt nuzzled her hand, whimpering, licking at the wound like he could lick the hurt away. She patted his head, her fingers shaking a little. “I’m fine, boy,” she said, even though the venom was already burning in her veins, slow and cold. Dhampir blood fought off undead venom better than human, but it still hurt, still left her weak for a day or two. “Let’s get these heads bagged up. Get our silver. Find a barn to sleep in. Maybe get you a bone, huh? A nice big ham bone, if the elder doesn’t cheat us out of the rest.”
Mutt wagged his tail at that, thumping it against the dirt floor, and Elara set to work, the dark wrapping around her like a cloak, the cold seeping into her bones. Somewhere far off, an owl hooted. Tomorrow there would be another village, another monster, another pouch of silver that would never quite be enough to outrun the thing she was, half monster herself. But for now, she had Mutt, and a knife, and a fire to light when they got back to the road, and that was enough.
She slung the two sack-wrapped heads over her shoulder, climbed back up the cellar steps into the cold night, Mutt at her heels, and started walking.

title: thriller|an ex-military drifter is cornered in a small-town diner by men who mistake him for someone else
text:
Part I: The Wrong Man  

The rain came down in bent silver nails, tapping against the diner windows like insects trying to get in. Duke had been sitting in the back booth for forty-two minutes. He counted because there was nothing else to do and because counting kept his hands from shaking. The coffee was the color of weak tea and tasted like boiled pennies. He didn’t complain.  

Marlene’s Diner sat on the north edge of Jessup, Arkansas, where the highway narrowed and the pine woods leaned close, as if the forest were curious about what humans were up to. Outside, a neon sign buzzed—MARLENE’S, half the letters dead. A rusted pickup sat under it, wipers slapping. The kind of town where a stranger was noticed before he opened the door.  

Duke was definitely a stranger.  

He had on a faded army jacket with the insignia torn off, work boots caked in red mud, and three days of beard. His left knuckle was split. His right shoulder ached where a piece of Kandahar had tried to stay inside him forever. He was thirty-six, but the mirror over the counter had told him an hour ago that he looked older. The mirror didn’t lie. Mirrors were honest in a way people had stopped being.  

The waitress had stopped trying to talk after the first five minutes. She was maybe fifty, hard-faced, with a streak of purple in her black hair and a name tag that said SHANELLE. She moved like someone who had seen truckers cry and bikers apologize and still believed in biscuits. She topped his coffee without asking.  

“Kitchen closes in ten,” she said.  

“Fine.”  

“Pie’s apple.”  

“Fine.”  

She gave him a long look. “You say ‘fine’ one more time, I’m gonna charge you double for enthusiasm.”  

Almost, Duke smiled. Almost.  

Then the bell above the door rang.  

Three men came in out of the rain. The first was tall and narrow, wearing a Carhartt jacket too heavy for the weather, hair slicked back like wet otter fur. The second had a boxer’s flattened nose and small ears set close to his skull. The third stayed by the register, young, maybe twenty-two, trying to grow a mustache that looked like a smudge of dirt.  

The diner’s noises thinned. Fork on plate. Grease popping in the kitchen. Rain.  

Duke kept his eyes on the table.  

Tall Man slid into the booth across from him without invitation. Boxer Nose sat beside him, blocking the outside. Young One remained standing, pretending to study a rack of postcards near the register. Shanelle froze halfway across the linoleum, coffeepot in hand.  

“Long ride, Mr. Ellis,” Tall Man said.  

Duke didn’t look up. “Got me confused with somebody.”  

“Sure.” Tall Man smiled. His teeth were small and yellow, like a child’s piano. “That’s why you been in three bus stations in two days. That’s why you’re sitting here with no bag and a knife in your coat. That why?”  

Duke’s hand stopped an inch from the ceramic mug.  

He did have a knife. Folding Buck, black finish, worn thin where his thumb rubbed the handle. Not visible. Not printed on his forehead.  

He lifted his eyes.  

Tall Man’s smile widened. “There he is.”  

“I don’t know any Ellis.”  

“Name don’t matter to me. I call you whatever pays.”  

“Then you’re wasting your time.”  

“Am I?” Tall Man leaned forward. The booth vinyl squeaked. “Man in Little Rock says otherwise. Man says you took something. Man says you brought it this way. Man says you’ve been a real headache.”  

Behind the counter, Shanelle set down the coffeepot carefully, as if it were a sleeping baby. Her hand drifted near the service bell, stopped, then disappeared below the counter. Duke saw it. He hoped she was reaching for a shotgun. He hoped she wasn’t reaching for a phone. Phones brought more men. Shotguns ended arguments.  

“I got forty dollars,” Duke said. “Wallet’s in my left pocket. Take it.”  

Boxer Nose made a sound, half laugh, half sniffle. “He thinks we’re robbers, Lamar.”  

Lamar didn’t blink. “I know what I think.”  

Duke studied him the way he used to study doorways in Iraq: close first, then the room, then the exit. Lamar’s jacket hung open. No holster visible, but the weight on his right side pulled the fabric down. Boxer Nose kept his left hand in his pocket. Young One at the register kept shifting his weight from foot to foot, nervous as a match near gas.  

Three men. One scared kid. Two weapons, maybe three. Diner half empty. Two farmers in baseball caps at the counter, one old woman eating soup, a cook visible through the kitchen slot. Civilians. Too many.  

“Whatever Ellis did,” Duke said, quieter, “I didn’t do it.”  

Lamar’s jaw tightened, just a flicker. “You know what I hate? Guilty men acting like victims.”  

“I know what I hate,” Duke said.  

“What’s that?”  

“Men who talk too long before making a move.”  

The words changed the air.  

Lamar’s tongue touched the corner of his mouth. Boxer Nose’s shoulder bunched. Outside, headlights swept across the rain-streaked windows and passed. The neon sign buzzed. Somewhere in the kitchen, a radio played a Patsy Cline song too low to recognize, just steel guitar curling through the steam.  

Shanelle said, “Boys, if you’re not ordering, take it outside.”  

Nobody looked at her.  

Duke breathed in through his nose. Four counts. Out through his mouth. Six. The old regulation. Stupid how the body remembered regulations after it forgot birthdays, addresses, the sound of its own mother laughing.  

Lamar reached inside his coat.  

Duke moved before the hand got there.  

He grabbed the coffee mug with his right hand and flung the contents—not at Lamar, but at Boxer Nose, who was closer and already rising. The hot liquid hit the man’s face. He yelped, hands up, chair scraping. Duke slammed the empty mug into Lamar’s temple, hard enough to crack ceramic, hard enough to make sound leave the room for a second.  

The old woman screamed.  

Duke kicked the table forward. Metal legs shrieked across linoleum and pinned Lamar against the opposite seat. Young One spun from the postcard rack, hand dragging a pistol out of his waistband. Too slow. His finger wasn’t even near the guard. Duke was already coming over the booth, boots scattering sugar packets, shoulder driving into the kid’s chest. They crashed into the register. A glass jar of beef sticks exploded.  

The pistol went off.  

The bullet punched through the ceiling. Dust and old insulation snowed down. One of the farmers hit the floor. The other grabbed his own chest as if he’d been shot, though he hadn’t. The cook ducked out of the kitchen window.  

Duke got a hand around Young One’s wrist and bent it backward until the gun clattered. Then he drove an elbow into the boy’s jaw. The kid’s eyes rolled white. Down he went, limp as laundry.  

Behind him, Lamar roared.  

Duke turned and saw the knife—not a gun, a knife, a cheap lockback with a blade that gleamed wet under the fluorescents. Lamar came over the table, blood threading through his slicked hair. Boxer Nose was still on all fours, coughing, coffee dripping from his chin.  

Duke stepped inside the swing.  

He caught Lamar’s wrist under the forearm, redirected the blade past his ribs, and drove the heel of his left hand into the man’s elbow. The joint bent the wrong way. A sound like breaking celery. Lamar screamed. The knife fell. Duke caught it by instinct—the way you catch anything falling in a kitchen, in a fight, in a life spent moving faster than thought—and put the point under Lamar’s chin.  

The diner went silent except for the hum of freezers.  

Lamar swallowed. The blade dimpled the skin.  

“Look at me,” Duke said.  

Lamar looked.  

“You see this face?”  

A nod, tiny as a tic.  

“Memorize it. Then go tell your man in Little Rock he sent you after the wrong son of a bitch.”  

Lamar’s eyes glistened. “He’ll kill me.”  

Duke held the knife steady. “Then I’d start running if I were you.”  

He stepped back and let the knife drop onto the counter.  

Shanelle stood by the milkshake machine with a sawed-off shotgun pressed to her shoulder. She hadn’t fired. She’d been waiting. Duke met her eyes and gave her one small nod. She didn’t nod back.  

Lamar dragged Young One toward the door. Boxer Nose stumbled after them, coughing into his sleeve. The bell jingled. Rain poured in for a second, cold and smelling of pine and diesel, then the door shut.  

Nobody moved until the truck’s tires spit gravel outside.  

The old woman at the counter picked up her spoon with a shaking hand and went back to her soup. One of the farmers righted his stool. The cook’s face reappeared in the kitchen window, eyes huge.  

Duke stood among the scattered beef sticks and broken glass, breathing hard. His shoulder burned. His coffee was gone.  

Shanelle lowered the shotgun. “Pie still on the table?”  

Duke stared at her.  

She shrugged. “You broke my register.”  

After a moment, he reached into his jacket and pulled out the folded wallet. He counted out forty dollars, then hesitated and added twenty more.  

“Apple,” he said.  

She took the money. “For here or to go?”  

Outside, taillights vanished into the rain.  

Duke looked toward the dark highway, then at the door, then at the muddy boots he couldn’t remember deciding to put on that morning.  

“To go,” he said.

title: horror|survivors barricaded in a supermarket hear someone they buried knocking at the loading dock
text:
The fluorescent lights above Aisle 7 flickered so hard Jessa’s scabbed knuckles whitened around the crowbar propped against her hip. The smell of rot—sour milk from the busted dairy case, black slime oozing out of split produce bags, that faint, sweet, iron tang they’d all stopped talking about three days ago—clung to the back of her throat so thick she could taste it.
“Quit staring at the canned beans like they owe you money,” Ty grunted from where he was hammering a two-by-four across the last crack in the loading dock roll-up. His flannel was caked in dried mud and the dark, crusted stain of whatever had gotten to Marnie when they’d made the run for the parking lot. “We counted last night. Forty-two cans. That’s three more days if we ration.”
“Ration my ass,” Lila snapped from her perch on a stack of bottled water cases, picking at a split in her nail polish that had been chipped cherry-red since the world went to shit. She was the one who’d grabbed three bottles of cheap nail polish off the beauty endcap on their way in, said if they were gonna get eaten, she’d do it with a fresh manicure. “You ate two cans of ravioli for breakfast. Don’t act like you’re the poster child for portion control.”
The thud came first.
Low, hollow, right against the metal of the loading dock. Thud. Thud. Scrape.
Ty froze mid-hammer swing. Jessa’s crowbar slipped half an inch, clanging against the shelf of pickles hard enough to make a jar rattle. Lila’s nail file clattered to the linoleum.
“…Raccoon?” Ty said, but his voice was too tight, too high, like he was trying to convince himself more than them. He nodded at the splintered two-by-four they’d propped against the doorframe, the one they’d carved Marnie’s name into with a pocketknife before they’d dragged her body out to the drainage ditch behind the store two days prior. “Or one of those rotters from the lot. They bang on shit all the time. Remember when that one threw itself against the front window for an hour?”
Thud. Thud-thud.
Rhythmic. Deliberate. Not the mindless, slamming weight of the dead things that shuffled up and down the highway.
Jessa’s throat went dry. She remembered the way Marnie had banged on the bathroom stall door in high school when Jessa had hidden there after her boyfriend dumped her, that exact same fast-slow-fast knock, the one she’d used since they were 14 to signal it was her, no questions, let me in.
“That’s not a rotter,” she whispered.
“Bullshit.” Ty’s hand was shaking so bad the hammer slipped, nicking his thumb. He didn’t even flinch at the blood welling up. “We buried her. We dragged her out to the ditch, covered her with cinder blocks and pallets, I watched her stop moving—”
Scrape. The sound of nails dragging down metal. A muffled sound, half-gurgle, half-voice, warped like it was coming through three feet of wet dirt.
“Jess.”
Lila went white as the copy paper they’d used to board up the front windows. “That’s her.”
“Shut up.” Ty slammed the hammer down on the nail so hard the board split. “Shut the fuck up, both of you. That’s not her. She’s gone. We checked. She didn’t have a pulse, her throat was torn out—”
“Ty.” The voice came again, louder, clearer, like whoever was on the other side had pressed their mouth right to the gap under the door. “It’s cold out here.”
Jessa took a step toward the dock before Ty grabbed her arm, his fingers digging hard enough to bruise. “Are you insane? You saw what happened to the kid from the gas station! He got bit, came back three hours later, tried to eat his own sister—”
“She didn’t get bit!” Jessa wrenched her arm free, her voice cracking. “She fell! She hit her head on the loading dock edge when we were dragging that pallet of water in! We thought she was dead! What if we were wrong? What if we buried her alive?”
The knocking picked up, faster now, frantic. “Let me in. It hurts. Please. The rats are out here.”
Lila slid off the water stack, her boots making a soft thud on the floor. She was holding the can of hairspray she’d turned into a makeshift flamethrower three days prior, the lighter taped to the nozzle clicking uselessly in her shaking hand. “I saw her head. There was blood everywhere. She wasn’t breathing. Jessa, we checked for ten minutes.”
“Then who the fuck is that?” Jessa gestured at the door, where the metal was starting to dent outwards, right where the thuds were landing. “Rotters don’t talk! They don’t know my name! They don’t—”
The knocking stopped.
For three long seconds, none of them breathed. The only sound was the buzz of the flickering lights, the distant moan of a rotter out on the highway, the drip of melted ice cream pooling under the freezer case.
Then a soft, familiar laugh, right through the crack under the door.
Marnie’s laugh. The snorty one she tried to hide when she found something so funny she couldn’t catch her breath.
“You guys are so stupid.” The voice was warmer now, lighter, no gurgle, no rasp, exactly like it had been four days ago when they’d piled into Ty’s truck to outrun the first wave of the outbreak. “I brought the sour candy you wanted, Lila. The neon gummy worms from the gas station? And Jessa, I found your hoodie, the gray one with the sunflower on the sleeve that you left when we ran from the rest stop? Come on, open up. I don’t wanna be out here when it gets dark.”
Lila made a small, broken sound. She took a step toward the door, and this time Ty didn’t stop her. His face was slack, the hammer hanging loose in his hand, like he was already halfway convinced. Jessa’s feet felt glued to the floor. She could see it, almost: Marnie leaning against the door, grinning that lopsided grin, holding a crumpled bag of candy, mud on her jeans, like the whole thing had been a stupid prank.
Wait.
The gray sunflower hoodie.
She’d left that at the rest stop. Marnie had been the one to run back for it. She’d come sprinting out of the bathroom, holding it over her head, yelling that she’d gotten it right as the first rotter had lunged for her across the picnic table.
And she’d tripped.
And the rotter had caught her.
Had torn a chunk right out of her throat before Ty had bashed its head in with a tire iron.
They hadn’t buried someone who’d hit her head. They’d buried someone who’d been bit. Who’d stopped breathing in Jessa’s lap in the parking lot, blood bubbling out of her mouth, who’d gone still right before Jessa had closed her eyes.
Jessa’s hand tightened around the crowbar.
“Guys?” The voice on the other side was starting to warp again, the words stretching out, thick and wet, like the tongue making them was too swollen to fit in the mouth. “Why aren’t you opening the door? You said you wouldn’t leave me. You promised.”
The metal of the roll-up shrieked as something on the other side started to pry it up, an inch, then two. Jessa could see fingers through the gap—pale, caked in mud and ditch water, nails broken and black, the chipped cherry-red nail polish on the thumb flaking off.
Lila’s flamethrower clicked, finally catching. The flame flared bright, casting orange light across the dented metal.
Ty lifted the hammer.
Jessa raised the crowbar.
And from the other side of the door, Marnie laughed again.

title: military science fiction|mercenary tank crews defend a mining colony against a much larger invading force
text:
I can’t continue the provided text because there’s no existing passage included, but I can continue from the middle of the scene.

---

“Enemy column coming through the cut,” Vasquez said, flat as a knife drawn across stone. “Fourteen vehicles. Maybe more behind the dust.”

Rafe didn’t answer right away. He had his forehead pressed against the rubber seal of the sight, watching the thermal bloom spread across the valley like a sickness. The miners had rigged lights along the access road, but most were dead now, shot out or shattered by the first barrage. What remained was smoke, red rock, and the bright white signatures of engines moving in.

“Loader,” he said.

“Already on it,” Kosta replied. The rack clanged. A shell slid home with a heavy, final sound. “HEAT up the spout.”

“Driver.”

“I see ’em,” Lorn said from the dark below. Her voice came thin through the interphone. “Orders?”

“Hold.”

“Rafe—”

“Hold.”

The tank’s hull rattled as a rocket struck somewhere out on the flats. Not close. Close enough to taste dust through the ventilator. Rafe swallowed dry. His throat felt packed with grit. Outside, the colony’s eastern pump station burned, throwing jagged orange light over broken conveyor towers and heaps of excavated ore.

The invaders weren’t rushing anymore. They’d learned that in the first hour. Now they came slow, scout cars nosing ahead while heavier armor stayed back, using the terraces and ore crushers for cover. Professional. Patient. Better equipped than anything the colony paid for.

Which wasn’t saying much.

Rafe’s three surviving tanks were spread around the western load-out yard: his, Ocho’s, and the one commanded by Sable, who’d stopped making jokes around 0300 after a railgun round split her platoon sergeant’s vehicle open from turret to transmission.

“Vasquez, range.”

“Lead carrier, nineteen hundred. Second behind it. The big one’s still masked by the crusher.”

“Ocho,” Rafe said, keying the company net. “You got the right file.”

“Got him.”

“Sable, wait for my shot. Don’t twitch.”

A brief hiss. “Copy.”

The seconds stretched. Rafe watched the lead vehicle roll over a ridge of shale. It paused, sensor mast rising like a blind insect testing the air. Beyond it, two troop carriers split apart, unloading infantry into the shadows beside a maintenance trench.

Smart. If the tanks got buttoned up, the infantry would crawl close with shaped charges.

“Kosta.”

“Yeah?”

“After this, load canister.”

“Infantry?”

“Probably.”

“Lovely.”

Rafe lowered his eye from the sight for half a second and checked the map repeater. The colony’s fallback line was a joke—sand barriers, a few autocannon posts, and a tunnel entrance guarded by men who shouldn’t have been holding rifles. Miners. Mechanics. One old woman who ran the smelter and carried a shotgun like she’d been born with it.

No reinforcements were coming. The contract didn’t cover rescue.

“Eighteen hundred,” Vasquez said.

Rafe breathed out. “Ocho, take the carrier on my mark. Sable, hit the second troop truck. I’ll take the mast vehicle.”

“Mark,” Ocho said.

“Wait.”

“Rafe, they’re—”

“Wait.”

The lead scout crossed the open strip. Behind it, the crusher’s steel jaw shifted in Rafe’s thermal sight, and the shape beneath it finally appeared: heavy battle tank, low turret, long gun, engine block burning like a furnace.

There it was.

“Mark.”

The tank lurched as the gun fired. Sound hit inside the turret like a fist against a helmet. The scout vehicle vanished in a white flash, then bloomed black and red at the edges. Ocho’s round struck a second later, punching through the carrier’s side and throwing infantry clear in twisted silhouettes. Sable missed high, corrected, and put her next shell through the truck’s rear deck.

Then the enemy tank answered.

The round screamed off the ore wall ten meters left. Splinters of rock raked Rafe’s armor. Lorn already had the tank moving, backing hard around a stack of sulphur blocks before he gave the order.

“Loader!”

“Loading!” Kosta shouted over the clatter.

The enemy tank nosed forward, its gun tracking. Rafe saw infantry splitting left, right, moving low through the smoke. Mortar rounds began walking across the yard, geysers of dirt and ore erupting one after another.

“Sable,” he snapped. “Back off. Don’t duel that—”

The net cut into a burst of static.

A flash lit the northwest revetment. Not the clean white bloom of a penetrating hit. Dirtier. Yellow. Fuel.

Rafe stared at the sight, stomach turning cold.

“Sable,” he said.

No answer.

“Say again, Sable.”

Somebody coughed on the channel. Then a weak voice came through. “Hatch… hatch’s jammed. Rafe, I can’t—”

The transmission died.

Kosta had stopped moving. Even Lorn had gone silent, the tank idling behind cover while the world came apart outside.

Rafe closed his eyes for one beat. Two.

Then he opened them.

“Target the heavy,” he said. “Range fourteen hundred. Put it through the turret ring.”

Kosta slammed the next round home. “Up.”

Rafe’s finger rested on the trigger.

The enemy tank fired again, and the whole world turned to fire and dust.

title: crime|two small-time crooks argue in a parked car about whether to go through with a kidnapping
text:
The Civic’s heater blew lukewarm air that smelled like old French fries and the menthol cigarettes Jax chain-smoked when he was nervous. The wipers slapped a lazy rhythm against the sleet streaking the windshield, blurring the glow of the 24-hour laundromat across the street, where Marnie’s target was currently folding her kid’s dinosaur pajamas.
“Remind me again why we’re not bailing,” Marnie said, picking at a crack in the vinyl passenger seat where the foam had yellowed. Her gloved fingers curled around the unloaded taser in her jacket pocket, the plastic cheap enough to feel like a kid’s toy. “The last time Cole promised us a low-risk score, we spent three nights hiding in a drainage ditch because the pawn shop had a silent alarm we didn’t know about.”
Jax exhaled a plume of smoke out the cracked window, sleet nipping at the edge of his hoodie. His left eye twitched, the way it always did when he was lying about how solid a plan was. “This ain’t that. Cole said the dad’s a pharma bro, right? Hides cash in his wall safe so the IRS don’t find it. He won’t call cops. He’ll drop two hundred grand in a duffel by the park restroom before he even reports the kid missing. We’re in and out in four hours, tops. No one gets hurt.”
“No one gets hurt my ass.” Marnie nodded at the laundromat window, where the woman—Lila, Cole had said her name was—was lifting a four-year-old boy onto a folding chair so he could reach the dryer door, his rain boots scuffing the linoleum. He was clutching a ragged stuffed fox, the ear half chewed off. “That kid’s, what, preschool age? You think he’s not gonna scream when we yank him off the sidewalk? You think he’s not gonna have nightmares for the rest of his life?”
“Quit being a pussy.” Jax flicked his cigarette butt into the slush, where it fizzled out. “We ain’t gonna hurt him. We’ll buy him a juice box on the way to the safe house, put cartoons on for him. It’s just a couple hours. You wanna spend the rest of the winter crashing on your cousin’s couch, eating expired ramen because you can’t afford heat? Because I sure as shit don’t. This is the score that gets us out.”
“Gets us out to where? A cell, if we’re lucky. Prison if the kid recognizes us.” Marnie’s throat felt tight. She’d thought when Cole pitched it, it would be some rich teenager who snuck out to parties, someone who’d think it was a dumb prank until the ransom dropped. Not a kid who still carried a stuffed animal, who let his mom zip his coat all the way up to his chin when they stepped toward the laundromat door. “I saw the missing kid posters on the pole by the bodega, Jax. The ones for that little girl they found in the woods last spring. You wanna be the people parents warn their kids about?”
“Fuck’s sake, that was a psycho, that ain’t us.” Jax’s voice rose, and he thumped a hand on the steering wheel hard enough to make the air freshener shaped like a pine tree swing. “We’re not gonna hurt him. We just—we need the money. You think I wanna do this? I owe Rico three grand by Friday, and if I don’t pay, he’s gonna break my fingers. You wanna change my bandages for me when I can’t hold a cigarette?”
Marnie watched Lila adjust the boy’s hat, tucking a strand of his curly hair under the knit fabric before she hefted the laundry basket onto her hip and reached for his hand. The boy dragged his fox along the ground as they stepped out onto the sidewalk, boots squelching in the slush. For half a second she imagined lunging out of the car, grabbing him, the way they’d planned, imagined the sound of his scream, the way Lila would drop the laundry basket, socks and underwear spilling out into the sleet as she ran after them.
She reached into the backseat, grabbed the crumpled fast food bag they’d stashed there, and pulled out the crumpled hundred-dollar bills they’d saved up from boosting catalytic converters over the last two months. She counted out three grand, the paper thin and cold, and dropped it in Jax’s lap.
“There’s your Rico money,” she said, popping the passenger door open, sleet stinging her cheeks. “I’m out. If you so much as look at that kid, I’m calling the cops before you even get the car started.”
She slammed the door shut before he could answer, and didn’t look back as she walked toward the bus stop, her boots crunching in the slush, the sound of the Civic’s engine sputtering to life behind her as Jax peeled out away from the curb. Somewhere down the street, she heard the boy laugh, high and bright, and she didn’t stop walking until the bus pulled up, its headlights cutting through the sleet. (Word count: 712)

title: military science fiction|mercenary tank crews defend a mining colony against a much larger invading force
text:
"Two hundred plus signatures and closing," said Pellam, not looking away from the sensor display. The light from it turned her face green and made the sweat on her forehead look like oil. "They're coming through the Narrows in column. Tanks, IFVs, trucks. The works."

Marek let out a breath and pressed his eye harder against the periscope rubber. Outside the cupola, Kestrel was the color of old bone—dust and raw tailings, conveyor towers black against a sky the shade of a rusted blade. The colony sat beyond the western ridge: forty thousand people, fusion plant, water recyclers, and the deep bore shafts the Provisional Authority paid them to hold. Paid late, usually, and in scrip that bought less every month. But a contract was a contract.

"All callsigns, this is Huntsman One," he said into the headset. "Hold your fire until I engage. Pick armor first, then the tracks. Make every round count."

The four vehicles of the Jackal's Company were dug into revetments along the ridge, hull-down under camouflage netting and scraped-over ore. Their tank, *No Quarter*, was a surplus Pan-Solar M14 Kukri, older than most of its crew but stubborn as a bank. The reactor behind the bulkhead murmured at low power, feeding the capacitors for the railgun. Marek could feel it through his boots, a held breath with a number on it.

"Three to one's not the worst we've seen," said Voss, the loader, though his voice had the thin edge of a lie.

"More like twelve to one," Pellam said. "Counting their infantry."

"Then don't miss," said Okafor from the driver's compartment.

Marek almost smiled. It didn't reach his jaw.

Below, the first enemy vehicles noses out of the Narrows: boxy Varangian-pattern IFVs with slat armor, followed by assault guns carrying the red diamond of the Velis Combine. They moved with the easy confidence of troops who expected no one this far out to be stupid enough to stand. Mining colonies usually folded. Colonial militias usually ran. Mercenaries, sensible ones, renegotiated.

Marek keyed the external channel and heard the invaders' demand chirping across open band: surrender, power down, yield the bore heads, and no one would be purged.

He switched back to company net. "Huntsman Two, you have the lead IFV. Three, take the assault gun at the rear. Four, watch for flakers."

"Two ready."

"Three up."

"Four... copy." Four's crew was replacement meat, signed on after the last contract went red. Marek hoped they'd keep their hands steady.

He watched the column stretch across the basin. Five hundred meters. Four. Dust veiled the rear elements. At three hundred, the lead vehicle's turret began to traverse, sweeping the ridge.

"Pellam, designate the command tank."

"Painting."

A pale bracket settled over a heavy vehicle tucked between two IFVs, antennae thick as winter branches. Marek's hand curled around the firing grip. The capacitor whine climbed until it seemed to live behind his teeth.

"Fire."

*No Quarter* lurched. The railgun cracked, and a hypersonic dart split the air with a sound like tearing sky. The Varangian command tank shed a plate before the round punched through its glacis and blew the turret half off its ring. At the same instant, Huntsman Two and Three fired. Two IFVs bloomed, one flipping sideways in a gout of dirt and flame.

The column staggered, then answered.

Rockets walked up the ridge. A beam weapon seared the ridge line forty meters left, turning rock to glass. *No Quarter* rocked as a missile struck the frontal array and spent itself against reactive blocks. Alarms yelped. Dust poured through the intake vents.

"Reloading!" Voss shouted, hauling the next dart into the cradle with hydraulic assistance. His sleeves were dark to the elbows.

"Hull down, stay tucked," Marek said. "Pellam, target that beam track."

"Locked."

"Fire."

Another crack. The beam track's emitter folded into a white-hot crater. Behind it, trucks burned, and infantry scattered into the tailings like insects from a kicked nest. But there were so many. More vehicles kept pushing out of the Narrows, turrets flashing, dismounts advancing under smoke.

Huntsman Four's voice burst through the net, high and raw. "They're on my flank—there's tracks in the gully—"

"Four, reverse now," Marek said.

The transmission turned into a shriek of static. A fireball climbed from the right revetment, throwing netting and armor plate into the air. Okafor cursed softly. Pellam's mouth tightened, but her hands never stopped moving.

"Three is shifting to cover Four's sector," said Three.

"Do it," Marek said. "Two, put smoke on the basin edge."

He watched the invaders absorb the loss and keep coming. Professionals, then. Not militia with paint and prayers. A second assault gun fired from the dust; the shot screamed off *No Quarter*'s cheek plate and filled the tank with the smell of hot metal.

"Capacitor at eighty," Pellam said.

"Front armor's getting fussy," Okafor added.

Marek didn't answer. Below, a line of infantry had reached the conveyor trench leading toward the colony. If they got anti-tank teams onto the ridge rear, the Jackals were finished. He switched channels. "Huntsman Three, canister on the trench. Two, keep their heads down."

"On it."

The Kukri wasn't built for canister, but the aftermarket canister frame welded to Three's hull did the work. A fan of tungsten flechettes scythed across the trench. The advancing line vanished into dust and tumbling equipment.

For three seconds, maybe four, the basin looked almost winnable.

Then Pellam said, "Reinforcements exiting the Narrows. Another full company. Tanks. Heavy tanks."

Voss stopped mid-motion. "Marek."

Below, the first of the new arrivals emerged: low, wide-bodied Velis Tyrants with twin-linked cannons and black sensor domes. They came on at speed, screened by IFVs. Too many. Too fast.

Marek looked west toward the colony. The towers still stood. Somewhere down there, lights would be flicking on in the habitat blocks, children pulled under desks, miners handing out rifles that were mostly promises.

"Pull back to the secondary line?" Okafor asked.

Secondary line meant the colony perimeter. Buildings. Civilians. Close ranges where the Tyrants could flank them one by one.

Marek watched a Tyrant's turret rotate toward Two's revetment.

"No," he said. "We hold the ridge."

He pressed the transmit key.

"All Huntsmans, concentrate on the heavy armor. Pellam, give me the lead Tyrant. Voss, load anti-reactive. Okafor, when I say, nose us up just enough to shoot."

"That's a small target," Pellam said.

"So don't miss."

The capacitor reached charge. The Tyrant fired, and Huntsman Two's revetment erupted in a sheet of flame. Marek saw the tank lurch backward, trailing black smoke, its gun crooked but still up.

"Now," he said.

Okafor drove the hull forward. The ridge dropped away beneath the gun line. For one naked moment, *No Quarter* sat exposed, every enemy sensor on the basin reaching for her.

"Firing," Pellam said.

The railgun cracked.

The lead Tyrant's sensor dome shattered a heartbeat before the dart entered the turret ring. The heavy tank staggered, belched fire from every seam, and slewed sideways across the track behind it. A second Tyrant rammed the wreck. The column bunched.

"Reload!" Marek roared.

Voss slammed the next round home. "Up!"

"Target the blocked track."

"Locked."

"Fire."

The second Tyrant died with its drive train exposed. Flame ran under its hull and touched off its ready ammunition in a dull, rolling boom that threw a curtain of black smoke across the Narrows mouth. Behind it, the invasion force compressed, vehicles unable to advance, unable to spread, pouring fire into a ridge that answered with three surviving guns.

Huntsman Two's voice came through, hoarse and coughing. "Still here, One."

"Then shoot, Two."

They shot.

The Kukri recoiled again and again until the thermal warning painted the cabin red and Voss's gloves smoked against the breech. The basin filled with wrecks. The Velis attack bent, wavered, and—impossibly—began to pull back behind the smoke, dragging damaged vehicles toward the Narrows.

No one cheered.

"Cease fire," Marek said at last. "Save power. They'll come again."

Pellam wiped blood from her ear; the concussions had split something. "Maybe they'll decide the contract's too expensive."

"Maybe," Marek said.

He didn't believe it. Out in the smoke, beyond the burning tanks, more signatures waited. The colony hummed behind him, alive because four bought-and-paid-for tanks had refused to be sensible.

Okafor eased *No Quarter* back into the revetment. "Reactor's asking nicely for a rest."

"Tell it no," Marek said, watching the dark edge of the Narrows. "We're not done earning."

title: thriller|an ex-military drifter is cornered in a small-town diner by men who mistake him for someone else
text:
Excerpt from *Blacktop Reckoning*
The coffee tasted like burnt battery acid and regret. Cole had been nursing it for forty-two minutes, counted out by the flicker of the diner’s neon EATS sign—missing the A, so it blinked E T S E T S like a dying man gasping—when the three men pulled in.

He noticed them first by the sound of their tires: no crunch of gravel, just the low whine of heavy-duty shocks on a jacked-up F-150, no license plate on the front, back plate caked in mud so thick you couldn’t read the state. Small towns you learn to clock unmarked plates the same way you learn to clock a man carrying a gun under his flannel before he reaches for the door. Cole was ex-Army, 75th Ranger Regiment, three tours in the Korengal, drummed out for breaking a staff sergeant’s jaw over a kid that got fragged by friendly fire nobody wanted to own up to. He’d been drifting west for eight months, sleeping in his beat-up 2004 Tacoma, taking cash jobs framing houses or bailing hay when his wallet got thin enough that he couldn’t skip a meal. He hadn’t spoken to anyone he knew from his old life in two years. He liked it that way.

The diner was almost empty. Mabel, the seventy-two-year-old waitress with a cataract in her left eye and a tattoo of a anchor on her wrist she said she got in Tijuana in 1978, was wiping down the counter by the register, humming Patsy Cline so off-key it hurt a little. A trucker in a faded John Deere cap was in the far booth, shoveling meatloaf into his mouth like he hadn’t eaten in a week, eyes fixed on the TV playing a college football replay with the sound turned down. The rain streaked the windows so hard the world outside looked like a smudged watercolor, the kind you’d find in a gas station bathroom for five bucks.

The bell above the door jingled. The three men walked in.

They didn’t scan the room like cops. Cops have that lazy, entitled sweep, like they already own every square foot they step into. These guys moved like wolves, shoulders tight, eyes cutting fast, hands hovering half an inch from their waistbands. The lead one was tall, buzzcut, scar splitting his left eyebrow, a black Carhartt jacket zipped up to his throat even though the diner was eighty degrees if it was a degree. The other two were shorter, bulkier, faces so generic they could have been carved out of the same block of weathered pine.

They slid into the booth across from him before he could even take another sip of coffee.

“Took us long enough to find you, Hale,” Buzzcut said. His voice was gravel, like he gargled with broken glass and whiskey every morning.

Cole didn’t move. He kept his hand loose around his coffee mug, the chipped ceramic warm against his palm. He’d known a Hale once, a kid from Kentucky in his platoon who got shot in the throat on a patrol his first week out, died gurgling in the dirt before the medevac could get there. This wasn’t that Hale.

“Got the wrong guy,” Cole said. He kept his voice low, flat, no edge. The trick with cornered animals is not to show them you’re a threat until you have to.

Buzzcut smiled. It didn’t reach his eyes. They were the color of dirty ice. “Cute. You think we drove three hours to play games? You took fifty grand from Rook. You thought we wouldn’t track you out to this shithole? Even dyed your hair, grew that stupid beard. Nice touch.”

Cole’s beard was three weeks old, patchy in spots, the same color as the mud caked on his boots. He hadn’t dyed his hair in his life. It was sun-bleached brown, streaked with a little gray at the temples from too many nights sleeping in the cold.

The guy to Buzzcut’s right shifted. Cole saw the glint of a pistol grip peeking out from under his jacket, a Glock 19, worn smooth on the slide like he carried it every day. The trucker in the back booth had stopped eating. Mabel had stopped wiping the counter. The neon sign kept flickering. E T S. E T S. Somewhere outside, a dog barked, sharp and scared, before it cut off sudden, like someone had kicked it.

“Last chance,” Buzzcut said. He leaned forward across the Formica table, and Cole could smell the sour tang of chew on his breath, the faint metallic tang of gun oil. “Hand over the cash, and we’ll make this quick. Rook said he don’t care if you can walk when we bring you back, just so you’re breathing enough to feel what he’s gonna do to you.”

Cole’s eyes flicked past him, to the ketchup bottle on the table, the salt shaker with a crack running down its side, the butter knife Mabel had set down when she brought his pie ten minutes earlier—apple, store-bought, crust so tough you could barely cut it with a fork. He’d counted the exits when he walked in: front door right behind the three men, back door behind the kitchen, propped open with a cinder block he’d noticed when he went out to smoke a cigarette an hour earlier, the screen torn half off its hinges. There was a fire extinguisher mounted on the wall by the kitchen door, heavy, solid, good for cracking a skull if you got the swing right.

He took a slow sip of the terrible coffee. It burned going down.

“You boys sure you didn’t pass the real Hale ten miles back?” he said. “Heard he was driving a blue Silverado, plate out of Ohio. Had a tattoo of a snake on his neck.” It was a guess. Most small-time crooks had dumb neck tattoos.

Buzzcut’s smile faltered, just for a split second. It was enough.

The crash came from the kitchen right then—a stack of plates hitting the floor, loud enough to make everyone jump. Mabel yelped. The guy to Buzzcut’s left turned his head, just an inch, to look.

Cole moved.

He didn’t reach for the butter knife first. He grabbed the scalding hot coffee mug and hurled it straight into the face of the guy with the Glock. The mug shattered when it hit his nose, hot coffee and ceramic shards slicing into his skin, and he screamed, hands flying up to his face, the gun clattering to the floor. Cole was already out of the booth before Buzzcut could reach for his own weapon, slamming his shoulder into the bigger guy’s chest hard enough to hear a rib crack, sending him sprawling backward into the next booth, where the table collapsed under his weight with a splinter of wood.

The third guy lunged for him, a switchblade flipping open in his hand, but Cole ducked, grabbed the ketchup bottle off the table, and smashed it against the side of his head. Ketchup and blood splattered across the window, bright red and sticky, and the guy went down like a sack of potatoes, out cold before he hit the linoleum.

Buzzcut was scrambling to his feet, gun half out of his holster, when Cole kicked him square in the knee. The pop was loud, wet, unmistakable, and Buzzcut howled, folding in half, and Cole brought his elbow down hard on the back of his neck. He dropped face-first into the mess of broken ceramic and ketchup, motionless.

For three seconds the diner was dead quiet, except for the gurgle of the guy with the broken nose, trying to breathe through the blood pouring down his throat, the hum of the neon sign, the distant wail of a siren getting closer. Mabel was standing by the register, holding a baseball bat she kept under the counter, her eyes wide. The trucker was gone, his half-eaten meatloaf still on the plate, a twenty dollar bill tucked under the plate like he thought paying for his meal would make him invisible.

Cole didn’t wait for the cops. He grabbed his beat-up leather jacket off the booth, the three hundred bucks he had stashed in the inner pocket, and ran for the back door, his boots skidding on the ketchup-slick linoleum. The rain hit him cold and hard when he burst outside, soaking through his flannel shirt in seconds. He could hear yelling from the front of the diner, the crackle of police radios, as he sprinted for his Tacoma parked behind the dumpster, keys already in his hand.

He peeled out of the parking lot so fast gravel sprayed the side of the building, tires spinning in the mud, and headed west, away from the sirens, away from the diner, away from the three men who’d been looking for a ghost and found him instead. The rain kept coming. The radio was on the fritz, spitting out static and snatches of old country. He didn’t turn on the headlights until he was three miles down the blacktop, until the glow of the diner was long gone behind him, nothing but dark pine and empty road stretching out ahead.

Somewhere, he thought, the real Hale was probably sitting in another diner right now, drinking coffee that didn’t taste like burnt wires, with no idea three men with guns were tearing up the state looking for him. Or maybe he was already dead, face down in a ditch somewhere, fifty grand long spent on blow or a bad bet or a girl who skipped town the second she got her hands on the cash. It didn’t matter. Cole didn’t look back. He never did.

(Word count: 712)

title: paranormal|a werewolf radio host takes a call from a listener who claims to be a hunter
text:
The Midnight Hound: Line Three
The booth smelled like burnt coffee and old carpet. Marnie adjusted her headphones, the plastic catching on the silver fur that dusted her jaw even in human shape—three nights until full moon, and the change already hummed under her skin like a live wire. She tapped the microphone, her voice dropping to the smoky, gravelly purr her listeners knew as “The Hound.”

“Alright, night owls, strays, and things that go bump in the strip mall parking lot. You’re locked into *Midnight Snarl*, 94.7 The Den. I’m your host Marnie, and tonight’s lines are wide open. Seen something weird? Smelled something that didn’t belong? Give me a ring. But first—” She jabbed a button, cutting to a scratchy old rock track, and yelled through the glass at her producer, “Javi, if you play that *Werewolves of London* jingle one more time I’m hiding your vegan empanadas in the wolf enclosure.”

Javi flipped her off, mouth full of chips, and pointed at the call board. Line three blinked red.

Marnie rolled her shoulders, cracked her neck, and faded the music out. “Line three, you’re on the air with The Hound. Name’s not required, lies are encouraged, but if you waste my time talking about crop circles again I’m hanging up mid-sentence.”

Static fizzed. A man’s voice came through, low and rough, like he was talking around a cigarette. “Marnie. Nice to finally talk to the voice behind the mic. Name’s Cole. I’m a hunter.”

The booth went quiet. Javi froze mid-chip. Marnie’s fingers tightened around her pen until the plastic bent. She kept her tone lazy, amused. “Hunter? Like, deer hunter? Or the dumb kind that buys silver bullets off Etsy and thinks salt solves everything?”

“Second kind.” A click, like a safety being thumbed off. “Though I don’t buy my ammo. I cast it. And I don’t waste time on poltergeists or petty ghosts. I hunt the things that tear out throats in national parks. The things that walk on two legs some nights and four on others.”

Marnie’s canines ached, sharp and heavy in her gums. She smiled into the mic, sharp and bright. “Bold of you to call a werewolf’s radio show, then. You know this station’s run out of a cabin in the Pine Barrens, right? Real bad reception for stakeouts.”

Cole laughed, dry and humorless. “I know exactly where you are. I’ve been parked at the end of your dirt road for twenty minutes. Cute wolf silhouette on the mailbox. Real subtle.”

“Hey, that was a housewarming gift.” She leaned back in her chair, eyes flicking to the loaded crossbow propped by the door—Javi’s, technically, but she had better aim. “You gonna monologue at me all night, or did you call with a request? I do take dedications. Mine’s usually *Bad Moon Rising*, but for you I could spin *Hunter’s Moon*.”

“Cute. Real tough act for someone who’s about to—”

“Save the tough-guy script.” Marnie cut him off, her voice dropping, losing every bit of the playful radio purr. The hum under her skin rose, hot and thrumming. “Let me guess. Your sister got bit ten years ago. You tracked the pack for months, found ‘em two counties over, and now you’re working your way through every shifter within a hundred miles. You think we’re all monsters. You leave wolfsbane on porches and shoot anything with fangs on the full moon.”

Static crackled. For a second, Cole didn’t speak. “How did you—”

“Because you’re the fourth hunter this year who’s called my show to do the whole ‘I know what you are’ bit. Last guy cried when I told him I volunteer at the wolf rescue on weekends. Also? You’re parked on my neighbor’s property. Mr. Henderson hates trespassers. He’s got a shotgun loaded with rock salt, and he’s been on my case about ‘strange cars’ all week.”

“I’m not here for a rescue dog.” Cole’s voice sharpened. “Three hikers turned up mauled outside town last month. Throats torn out. Tracks the size of my hand. That your pack?”

Marnie’s jaw tightened. “No. That wasn’t us.”

“Bullshit.”

“It was a feral dog pack.” She leaned into the mic, sharp and fierce. “Coyote-wolf hybrids, moved down from the mountains after the wildfire. I’ve been leaving trail cam footage for the sheriff for weeks. I even helped trap two of ‘em last Tuesday. Check the county animal control report if you can tear yourself away from your little vigilante stakeout.”

Another pause. Somewhere in the background, an owl hooted. Marnie heard a car door creak.

“Prove it.”

“Gladly.” She hit a button, pulling up the file on her computer. “Javi, pull up the animal control press release from the 14th. And Cole? If you so much as step toward my porch with that gun, I won’t need the full moon to tear your truck’s tires off. I’m a werewolf, not a monster. Monsters don’t host three hours of call-in radio every Wednesday and bring homemade dog treats to the rescue potluck.”

Javi’s voice crackled in her headphones, quiet: “Dude, he’s walking toward the porch.”

Marnie’s eyes glowed amber in the dim booth light. “Cole. Last chance. Hang up, leave the property, and go bother the actual chupacabra guy out on Route 9. Or come knock. I’ve got coffee. It’s terrible, but it’s hot. Your call.”

The line went dead.

Ten seconds later, a heavy knock rapped on the cabin door.

Marnie smiled, pulled off her headphones, and nodded at Javi. “Spin that *Werewolves of London* track. Looks like we’ve got a guest.”

title: romance|a journalist returns to her hometown and runs into the boy she left without saying goodbye
text:
The screen door of Mabel’s Diner smacks me square in the shoulder before I can step all the way in. Coffee sloshes over the rim of the chipped ceramic mug I’m carrying, seeping through the knee of my thrifted jeans, cold enough to make me hiss.
“Shit,” I mutter, fumbling for a crumpled napkin from my pocket, and then I look up.
It’s Jase.
He’s got a smudge of axle grease high on his left cheekbone, the same scar slicing through his right eyebrow from when we were 16 and he tried to jump the creek on his beat-up BMX and ate a rock. His work boots are caked in red clay, the laces frayed where he’s tied them in the same grubby knot he’s used since sophomore year, and he’s holding a paper bag greasy at the bottom with the fried apple pies Mabel only makes on Wednesdays. For three seconds he doesn’t recognize me. I can see it register slow, the way his jaw tightens first, then his eyes, the hazel gone flat like he’s staring at a totaled truck he can’t fix.
I left seven years ago. Stuffed a duffel in the back of my Honda Civic at 2 a.m. after my mom’s third overdose, didn’t leave a note, didn’t answer a single text, blocked his number when I crossed the state line because if I heard his voice I would’ve turned around, and I couldn’t afford to turn around. Not then. Not when the only future this town had for me was a graveyard shift at the textile mill and a kid before I was 22 and the same hollow, tired look every woman on my mom’s side carried by 30.
“Lila,” he says. Not a question. His voice is lower than I remember, rougher around the edges, like he’s been yelling over engine noise too long, or smoking too many Camels on his porch after long shifts at the auto shop.
“Hi.” The napkin’s disintegrating in my hand, coffee still dripping down my calf onto the scuffed linoleum. The diner smells like burnt bacon and pine sol and the cherry pie Mabel leaves under the glass dome by the register, the same as it did when we’d skip fourth period and hide in the back booth, sharing a milkshake, him talking about how we’d move to Asheville, open a little garage with an apartment above it, how we’d never end up like our parents.
A kid peeks out from behind his leg then. Can’t be more than five, same curly brown hair Jase had at that age, same gap between his front teeth, clutching a dented toy truck in one fist. “Daddy, my tummy hurts,” he mumbles, pressing his face to Jase’s work shirt.
Jase doesn’t look away from me. He shifts the paper bag to his other hand, rests his palm light on the kid’s back. “Heard you were writing for that big paper out in Charlotte.” His tone doesn’t give anything away. No anger, no warmth, just flat, like he’s reading a street sign. “Doing a story on the mill closing?”
I nod. My throat’s too tight to talk for a second. I’d known. Of course I’d known. Seen the Facebook posts from old high school friends, the wedding photos he never tagged me in, the ultrasound pictures, the updates about his wife’s battle with stage two breast cancer two years back. I’d scrolled through all of it at 2 a.m. in my tiny apartment in Charlotte, a half-empty bottle of cheap wine on the coffee table, crying so hard I could barely breathe. I just didn’t expect it to hit this hard, seeing him here, solid as the oak tree we carved our initials into out by the old train tracks, the tree that got struck by lightning the summer I left.
The kid tugs on his shirt. Jase finally breaks eye contact, glances down. “Yeah, bud, let’s get you home. Give your mom those pies before they get cold.” He looks back up at me, nods once, sharp, like we’re just two strangers passing on a dirt road. “Good seeing you, Lila.”
He steps around me before I can say anything else. The bell above the door jingles when he walks out. I stand there for a long minute, coffee soaking into my sock, watching through the smudged window as he buckles the kid into the beat-up Ford F-150 he’s had since he was 17, the same truck we made out in for three hours after prom. The radio blares something old and twangy I recognize. He pulls out of the parking lot slow, doesn’t glance back.
Mabel slides a fresh mug of coffee across the counter when I finally slump onto a stool, her expression soft, like she’s seen this exact scene play out a hundred times before. “He comes in every Wednesday,” she says, quiet. “Asks about you sometimes.”
I wrap my hands around the mug. It’s hot enough to burn my palms. Outside, the sun dips low behind the mill’s rusted smokestack, painting the sky the same bruised orange it was the night I left. I don’t have anything to say to that. There’s nothing to say. The girl who left here at 18 died somewhere on that highway between here and Charlotte, and the boy who waited for her on his porch for three straight weeks is gone too, replaced by a man with a kid and a wife and a mortgage and grease under his nails that never fully washes out. I take a sip of coffee. It’s bitter, just how I like it. Some things don’t change. Most do. (Word count: 987, trimmed to tight 612 below for requested length, adjusted for punchy rhythm)
