“Lila,” he says. Not a question. His voice is lower than I remember, rougher, like he’s yelled over engine noise too long, or smoked too many Camels on his porch after long shifts at the auto shop.
“Hi.” The napkin disintegrates in my hand, coffee dripping down my calf onto scuffed linoleum. The diner smells like burnt bacon and Pine-Sol and cherry pie, same as it did when we’d skip fourth period to hide in the back booth sharing a milkshake, him talking about moving to Asheville, opening a garage with an apartment above, never ending up like our parents.
A kid peeks out from behind his leg then. Can’t be more than five, same curly brown hair Jase had at that age, same gap between his front teeth, clutching a dented toy truck. “Daddy, my tummy hurts,” he mumbles, pressing his face to Jase’s work shirt.
Jase doesn’t look away from me. Shifts the pie bag to his other hand, rests a palm light on the kid’s back. “Heard you’re writing for that big Charlotte paper. Doing the mill closing story?”
I nod. Throat too tight to talk. I’d known, of course. Seen the Facebook posts: wedding photos he never tagged me in, ultrasound pics, the update about his wife’s stage two breast cancer two years back. Scrolled all of it at 2 a.m. in my tiny apartment, cheap wine on the coffee table, crying so hard I could barely breathe. Just didn’t expect it to hit this hard, seeing him solid as the oak we carved our initials into out by the train tracks—the tree that got struck by lightning the summer I left.
The kid tugs his shirt. Jase finally breaks eye contact, glances down. “Yeah, bud, let’s get you home. Get these pies to your mom before they go cold.” He nods at me, sharp, like we’re strangers passing on a dirt road. “Good seeing you, Lila.”
He steps around me before I can speak. The door bell jingles. I stand there, coffee soaking into my sock, watching through the smudged window as he buckles the kid into his beat-up 17-year-old F-150—the same truck we made out in for three hours after prom. He pulls out slow, doesn’t glance back.
Mabel slides a fresh coffee across the counter when I slump onto a stool, her face soft like she’s seen this play out a hundred times. “Comes in every Wednesday. Asks about you sometimes.”
I wrap my hands around the mug, hot enough to burn my palms. Outside, sun dips low behind the mill’s rusted smokestack, painting the sky the same bruised orange it was the night I left. There’s nothing to say. The girl who left at 18 died somewhere on that highway, and the boy who waited on his porch for three weeks is gone too, replaced by a man with a kid and a mortgage and grease under his nails that never washes out. I take a sip. It’s bitter, just how I like it. Some things don’t change. Most do.

title: romance|a journalist returns to her hometown and runs into the boy she left without saying goodbye
text:
The rain started the moment Nora Chen turned onto Maple Street, fat summer drops that splattered the windshield like handfuls of gravel. She flipped the wipers on and kept driving past the boarded-up hardware store, past the diner with its faded neon sign, past all the things she'd spent eight years carefully not thinking about.

Her assignment was simple: a profile on the town's sudden revival, driven by the new craft brewery and the tourists who'd discovered the lake. Three days, photographs, a few interviews. Then back to the city, back to her life.

She parked outside the Grind, the only coffee shop in town, and grabbed her notebook from the passenger seat. Through the rain-streaked window, she could see warm light and exposed brick where there used to be chipped blue paint. The bell above the door jingled as she stepped inside.

"Be right with you," called a voice from the back. A man's voice. Familiar in the way a song could be familiar when you'd heard it a hundred times in another life.

Nora froze with her hand still on the door handle. The place smelled like espresso and cinnamon and something woodsy, like sawdust and rain. She recognized the scarred wooden counter, though it had been sanded and refinished. The pressed-tin ceiling was the same. The crooked shelf in the corner was the same.

Eliot Ward stepped through the swinging door wiping his hands on his apron, and the breath went out of her like she'd been pushed into deep water.

He was broader than she remembered, forearms corded where they'd once been lean, a dusting of stubble across a jaw that had finally grown into itself. His hair was shorter, threaded with a little gray at the temples that had no business being there at twenty-eight. But his eyes were the same—hazel, steady, the kind of eyes that used to make her believe she could stay in one place forever.

He stopped mid-step. The cloth in his hands went still.

"Nora," he said. Not a question.

"Hi." Her voice came out smaller than she wanted. She let go of the door and heard it latch shut behind her. "You work here?"

Something flickered across his face, gone too fast to name. "I own it." He gestured vaguely at the room. "Bought the building four years ago. Roastery in the back."

Of course he did. Eliot, who used to make terrible instant coffee in his mother's kitchen and swear he'd learn to do it right someday. Of course he'd stayed and built the thing he'd talked about in the dark while they lay on his roof watching satellites cross the sky.

"That's — " She nodded, swallowing. "That's really great, Eliot."

The silence between them was enormous. Somewhere a grinder hummed, then stopped. Rain tapped against the front window.

"What are you doing in town?" he asked. Polite. Careful. The way you spoke to someone you didn't know.

"Work. Profile for the *Standard*. The brewery, the lake, the comeback story." She tucked a wet strand of hair behind her ear. "I didn't know you'd be — I didn't know it was yours."

"Would that have changed anything?"

The question landed soft and heavy, like snow. Nora looked at the counter, at the little chalk menu, at anything but his face. "Eliot — "

"You left a note on your pillow, Nora. Not even for me. For your dad." He said it without heat, which was worse than anger. "I sat in your driveway for two hours with those acceptance letters you wanted to compare. Your mom finally came out and told me you were already on the bus."

She'd rehearsed this a hundred times in eight years, in hotel rooms and airport bars and the dark of her apartment. None of the words fit now. "I was eighteen. I was scared that if I saw you, I wouldn't go."

"Would that have been so terrible?"

Yes, she almost said, because staying had felt like drowning then, like the town would fold in on her and she'd spend her whole life wondering what else there was. No, she almost said, because she'd spent eight years in cities full of people and never once felt as seen as she had sitting on this boy's roof.

Instead she said, "I'm sorry." It was inadequate, a thimble against a fire, but it was true in a way she hadn't expected. "I should have said it to your face. I've known that for a long time."

Eliot studied her. The hazel eyes moved over her like he was checking whether the girl he'd known was still in there somewhere. Then he reached behind him and pulled a clean mug from the shelf.

"Rain's supposed to last an hour," he said, turning to the espresso machine. "You look like you could use something warm. And I've got questions about this profile of yours."

Nora exhaled. She slid onto the stool at the counter — the third one from the register, the one she used to claim after school — and set her notebook down.

"Yeah," she said. "Okay."

Outside, the rain kept falling. Inside, for the first time in eight years, something in her chest began, very quietly, to unclench.

title: paranormal|a werewolf radio host takes a call from a listener who claims to be a hunter
text:
The control room smells like burnt microwave popcorn and the pine-scented candle the station manager insists “fixes the vibe” — which is to say, it smells exactly like it does every Tuesday from 10PM to 2AM, when I’m spinning deep-cut folk for the insomniacs, the long-haul truckers, the people who don’t turn the lights off when the sun comes up because the dark feels safer. I’m leaning back in the beat-up office chair, boots propped on the edge of the soundboard, when the request line blinks red three fast times, which is code from Mia, my producer, that the next caller is either a crier, a conspiracy guy, or someone who thinks they’re funnier than they are.
I flip the switch to patch them through, already reaching for my mug of lukewarm black coffee, the kind strong enough to strip rust off a truck bumper. “You’re on the air with Jude, late night on KZBR 93.7. What’s keeping you up tonight?”
The voice that comes through the line is gravelly, like he’s been smoking unfiltered Camels since he was twelve, or like he’s been shouting into the Wyoming wind for three hours straight. “You’re not who you say you are.”
I snort, take a sip of coffee. It tastes like regret and dish soap, because I forgot to wash the mug last week. “Bold take, friend. Last time I checked my driver’s license said Jude Marlow, but I’ll admit the DMV photo is rough enough I’d disavow it too. You got a better name for me?”
“Marlow was your mother’s maiden name.” He pauses, and I can hear the faint crackle of a campfire in the background, like he’s parked off a forest service road somewhere up in the hills, not calling from a couch in the suburbs. “Your daddy was the one the pack ran out of the Bighorns in ‘98. Thought I’d killed him outside Lander, turns out he left a pup behind.”
The coffee turns to acid in my mouth. My boots slip off the soundboard, thudding hard on the linoleum, and for half a second the shift pricks under my skin — fur at my jawline, claws pricking the pads of my fingers, the sharp coppery tang of fight-or-flight flooding my sinuses. I force it down, flex my hand until the claws recede, pasting the lazy, half-smirking radio voice back on like a mask. Mia is gesturing wildly through the booth window, making the throat-cut sign, but I hold up a hand to stop her. I don’t hang up on threats. I learned that the hard way, when I was sixteen and the first hunter cornered me behind a gas station in Rock Springs.
“Wow,” I say, leaning into the mic, keeping my tone light, amused, like this is just another kook who binged too much true crime before calling in. “You’ve done your deep dive. I’m flattered. Most people just call to request *Wagon Wheel* for the third time in an hour. What gave me away? The fact I complain about the full moon messing with the station antenna every month? The dog hair that’s permanently glued to every hoodie I own?”
“Don’t play smart.” There’s a metallic click on the line, sharp and familiar: the safety coming off a rifle. I know that sound as well as I know the opening chord of *Folsom Prison Blues*. “I’ve been listening for six weeks. You warned those hikers to stay off the north trail last week, when the new turn was running feral. You told the single mom over in Riverton to lock her doors and keep her kid inside three nights ago, when something was skulking around her trailer park. You think I don’t know what you are? Freak.”
The shift hums louder now, a low thrum in my bones, like the lead-up to a thunderstorm. I can smell him through the line, almost — gun oil, pine, the sharp metallic tang of silver, the faint burnt smell of wolfsbane tincture he probably dabs on his boots. He’s close. Fifteen miles out, max, if the wind’s carrying right. But I don’t reach for the bat I keep propped behind the soundboard, don’t slam the panic button under the desk that alerts the rest of the pack. Instead I lean closer to the mic, and let just a little of the wolf creep into my voice, low and rough, the kind of tone that makes drunk guys at bars step back without knowing why.
“Let’s cut the crap, then,” I say, and I don’t bother with the radio host charm anymore. “If you knew what I was, you’d know I don’t hunt humans. You’d know the last three calls we got before yours were from people who heard something scratching at their windows, people who were scared, and I told them how to stay safe. You drive that beat-up Ford F-150 with the gun rack in the back down that rutted road to the station right now? I’ll even have a pot of coffee on for you. But if you so much as point that rifle at a kid, or a dog, or any of the folks who call this station because they’ve got nowhere else to turn when the dark gets too loud? I will track you through every ravine and pine thicket in this state before the sun comes up. You understand?”
The line goes dead.
Mia bursts through the booth door, her eyes wide, already holding up her phone to show me the text thread blowing up from the pack — half of them heard the call live, they’re already suiting up, they’ll be at the station in ten. Outside, the wind picks up, howling around the cinder block walls of the station, and I glance up at the full moon peeking through the clouds, bright as a searchlight.
I flip back to the on-air mic, and cue up the next track — a scratchy old Johnny Cash song, the one about the beast that won’t stay down.
“Looks like we got a special request tonight, folks,” I say, and my voice is steady, even as I can hear the distant crunch of tires on gravel out in the parking lot. “This one’s for the guy with the rifle who thinks he’s the hero. Let’s talk about what hunts in the dark, when you think you’re the only one watching.”
The guitar riff kicks in, and I reach for the bat behind the desk, my fingers already starting to shift.
Chapter seven was off to one hell of a start.
(Word count: 792)

title: comic|a holistic detective tries to explain to a sceptical client why a horse is in the bathroom
text:
THE HORSE IN THE BATHTUB
 Chapter Three

My name's Dash Calloway and I don't advertise. Last guy who tried to find my office ended up in a storage unit in Reseda, where he spent three hours discussing past-life regression with a water heater named Gerald. So when Marjorie Pinsker banged through my door at 7:42 on a Tuesday—rain dripping off her sensible coat, expression like she'd bitten into a lemon that owed her money—I figured the universe had forwarded her address through the usual channels.

"Are you the detective?" she said.

"I'm the person sitting in the detective's chair," I said. "The detective's over there." I nodded at the pothos plant on the windowsill. It had more casework than I did. "But he's meditating. I can take a message."

She didn't sit. She did that thing clients do where they grip the back of a chair like it's a life preserver and the chair personally killed their dog. "There's a horse in my bathroom."

I wrote this down. *Horse. Bathroom.* "Standard or miniature?"

"Standard! A *full-sized horse*. In my *guest bathroom*. On the second floor."

I underlined *second floor*. That was the interesting part. Horses are mostly a ground-floor operation. They're conservative that way.

"Mrs. Pinsker—"

"Ms."

"Ms. Pinsker. Before we go any further, I want to be straight with you about how I work." I leaned back. The chair made a noise like a dying accordion. "I don't do fingerprints. I don't do forensics. I once solved a kidnapping by reading the patterns in a bowl of split-pea soup, and I want you to know that before you write me a check, because the check will bounce if you don't respect the process."

She blinked at me. "I want the horse out of my bathroom."

"Sure. Sure you do. That's the *symptom*." I got up. I keep a kettle going at all hours—not for tea, exactly, more because the sound of boiling water makes my filing cabinets less lonely. I poured two cups anyway. "The question isn't how the horse got in. The question is what the horse is *doing there*. What it represents. What it's *mirroring*."

"It's mirroring a horse," Marjorie Pinsker said. "In my bathroom."

"Humor me. When did you first notice it?"

"At six-fifteen. I went in to shower before my book club."

"And your book club is reading..."

She hesitated. "It's called *The Ember's Longing*. It's paranormal romance."

I nodded slowly. I'd learned long ago that the universe has the subtlety of a freight train full of anvils. "Go on."

"There's nothing to go on with! I opened the door and there it was, standing in my tub, eating my shower curtain. The liner, specifically. It left the nice fabric one." She set her jaw. "I called the police. They said—and I am quoting—'ma'am, that doesn't sound like a police matter.' Then one of them asked for a photo for his *mom*."

I sipped my hot water. I'd forgotten to put anything in it. "The police deal with what *is*. My practice deals with what *is*, plus the stuff that's standing off to the side of *is*, making meaningful eye contact. Do you follow?"

"No."

"That's fine. Most people don't until about week three. Now. Has anything unusual happened lately? Gifts from strangers? Dreams about open fields? A recurring number—"

"I'm a widow," she said, and then looked surprised she'd said it. "Two years. Stanley. He was an accountant. He did the books for a racetrack in Arcadia for thirty-one years."

The pothos rustled, though there was no draft. I made a note. *Stanley. Racetrack.*

"And Stanley and you—you had a good marriage?"

"Mostly. He was kind. He chewed with his mouth open and he forgot every anniversary and he once gave me a leaf blower for Valentine's Day." Her throat worked. "But he loved one thing in this world the way other men love God. A horse. A gelding named Cinnamon's Revenge. Ran at Santa Anita, nineteen seventy-eight. Lost every single race Stanley bet on him. Every one. And Stanley bet on him forty-three times."

"Forty-three," I said.

"Forty-three. Said the horse had *integrity*. Said losing on purpose in a world that only rewards winning took character." She laughed, and it came out rough. "The horse died in seventy-nine. Stan had him cremated. Kept the ashes in a coffee can on his nightstand. I—" She stopped. "I buried the coffee can in the backyard. Last month. I just... I couldn't look at it anymore. Does that make me a monster?"

I looked at the pothos. The pothos, with great dignity, said nothing.

"Ms. Pinsker," I said, grabbing my coat—a long oilskin number with approximately fourteen pockets, most of them containing rocks I'd been meaning to return to various beaches—"here's my working theory. Your late husband spent thirty years loving an animal the world called a failure. The animal knew. Whatever's on the other side, whatever's *between* things, that horse knew it had one believer. And Stanley's gone now, and the ashes went in the ground, and something somewhere decided the account wasn't closed." I opened the door. Rain hit the stairs like handfuls of rice. "So the horse came to collect."

"Collect *what*?"

"Probably an apology. Maybe a goodbye. Possibly the shower curtain. I don't want to overcommit before I see the body language."

She stared at me. Then she did something I hadn't expected—she laughed. Full laugh, eyes wet, the kind that comes from a place so deep it startles the person it's coming out of.

"You're a lunatic," she said.

"Professionally," I said. "You drive or do I? I don't have a car, but I've got a bus pass that's extremely charged."

We took her car—a beige sedan with a hanging air freshener shaped like a strawberry that had long since given up. On the freeway she said, quiet, "What if it's not him? What if it's just a horse?"

"Then we've got a horse in a bathroom," I said. "Either way, somebody's got to talk to it."

She changed lanes without signaling. Somewhere ahead of us, in a second-floor guest bathroom in Encino, a large animal with a long and distinguished losing record shifted its weight on ceramic and waited, patiently, for the only person in the world who'd ever believed in it to come home.

I checked my pockets for carrots. Of course I had carrots. I always have carrots. That's the job, mostly. You just learn to carry the right vegetables and stop asking the universe to make sense.

title: comic|a holistic detective tries to explain to a sceptical client why a horse is in the bathroom
text:
Panel 1
Wide shot of a cramped, avocado-green 1970s bathroom. A chestnut quarter horse stands placidly in the tub, hooves propped on the edge, munching a stray loofah. DETECTIVE MARNIE RAVEN (40s, silver streaks in a messy braid, patchwork wool blazer slung over a faded Mothman hoodie, crystal pendant glinting) leans against the sink, picking lint off her sleeve. CLIENT ARTHUR HALE (50s, starched bespoke suit, wire-rimmed glasses askew, face the color of a bruised plum) stands in the doorway, briefcase clutched to his chest like a riot shield.
ARTHUR: It is six forty-seven in the morning. I called you because my house keys kept vanishing, my prize fern was weeping actual tears, and my toast kept burning into the shape of crows. I did not call you to add a *horse* to the list of home insurance claims.
MARNI (not looking up, flicking a loofah crumb off the horse’s nose): Calm down. He’s a witness.
Panel 2
Close up on Arthur’s face, mouth hanging open so far his glasses slip down his nose. The horse blinks slowly in the background, tail swishing a bottle of lavender bubble bath off the tub ledge. It clatters but doesn’t break.
ARTHUR: A witness. To what? My very public nervous breakdown? Because if that’s the case, I should be calling a psychiatrist, not a “holistic detective” who charged me a $200 “energy alignment retainer” before she even walked through the door.
MARNI (snorting, finally pushing off the sink to tap the horse’s flank gently): Please. Your nervous breakdown would show up as a raccoon in your pantry eating all your fancy dark chocolate, not a horse in your tub. This is Barnaby. He’s a crossroads echo.
Panel 3
Medium shot of Marni rummaging in her canvas tote bag (stuck all over with paranormal convention stickers: *I SURVIVED THE 2019 FLATWOODS MONSTER POTLUCK*) while Arthur stares, unblinking. Barnaby snorts, a strand of loofah hanging from his lip.
ARTHUR: A crossroads echo. Let me guess. He sells insurance for ghost cars?
MARNI (pulling out a crumpled jar of peppermints and holding one out to Barnaby, who lipped it neatly out of her palm): Cute. Look, three nights ago you stumbled home drunk from that partner retreat, right? Cut through the old oak trail off Maple instead of taking the sidewalk, tripped over that weird mossy stone half-buried by the stop sign?
ARTHUR (freezing, ears going pink): How did you—
MARNI: Told you. Holistic. I don’t just dust for fingerprints. I read the way your floorboards creak, the messages your burnt toast is screaming, the fact that your left shoelace has been tied backwards for three days. You didn’t just trip over a rock. You tripped over a threshold. You made a bargain you don’t remember making.
Panel 4
Close up on Arthur’s face, the anger draining into confusion. Marni leans against the tub next to Barnaby, expression softer now, no trace of her earlier snark.
ARTHUR: A bargain. What the hell would I bargain for? I make partner next month. I have a house in the suburbs. I—
MARNI: You stood there, sloshing scotch on your loafers, and screamed at the sky that you’d give anything to stop feeling like you were running in place. That you were sick of treading water, watching everyone else pass you by. Real quiet, desperate type of scream. The kind the old things hear.
(She taps the tub, where the water is now, inexplicably, lapping at Barnaby’s hooves even though no one turned the tap on.)
MARNI: Crossroads echoes don’t do fine print. They hear “treading water” and they stick you in a loop where your keys vanish so you’re late to work, your fern cries because it’s picking up all that stuck grief you won’t talk about since your kid left for college, your toast burns into crows because crows are the messengers that tell you when you’re sleepwalking through your own life. Barnaby here? He’s the anchor. He showed up where the water runs to make sure you didn’t drown in the loop before I got here.
Panel 5
Wide shot again. Arthur has set his briefcase down, staring at Barnaby, who leans his head over the tub edge to nudge Arthur’s shoulder gently. The angry flush is gone from his face, leaving him pale, a little shaky. Marni smirks, popping a peppermint into her own mouth.
ARTHUR (quiet, reaching up a tentative hand to pat Barnaby’s velvet nose): I… I did say that. I didn’t think anyone was listening.
MARNI: Someone’s always listening. That’s the holistic part. Now, if you stop being a sceptic for ten whole seconds and apologize to Barnaby for calling him an insurance claim, I can unspool the bargain. You’ll have to leave a jar of that fancy apple butter you hide in the back of your fridge at the crossroads stone at midnight, though. Echoes love apple butter.
ARTHUR (blinking, half laughing): And the horse?
MARNI (grinning as Barnaby snorts, as if laughing too): Oh, he’ll leave when the loop breaks. But he might come back for Halloween. He’s a sucker for mini candy corn. Don’t tell the other echoes, they’ll tease him.
(Off panel, the toaster in the kitchen pops loudly. No smell of burnt bread. Arthur glances over his shoulder, then back at the horse in his tub, and for the first time all morning, he smiles.)
ARTHUR: …Fine. But if he eats my loofah, that’s coming out of your retainer.
MARNI (cackling, tossing another peppermint to Barnaby): Deal.
(Word count: 798)

title: fantasy|a disgraced court mage is summoned back to save the prince who exiled her
text:
The cell door groaned. Rain dripped through the iron bars overhead, and Kael stood there—older, thinner, wearing the royal blue she'd last seen on the soldiers who dragged her from the tower.

"You," she said.

"Vesna." He didn't meet her eyes. Good. Let him not. "The prince is dying."

"Which one." She already knew. There was only one prince. Only one boy whose shaking hand had signed her exile papers three winters ago while his father the king lay fever-struck in the next room.

"Darran. The same." Kael's jaw worked. "The healers can't touch it. Black veins climbing his throat. He raves in a language none of us know, and the rooms around him go cold enough to crack stone." He finally looked at her. "Three mages are dead. One walked in and came out with no eyes. I need you."

Vesna laughed. It came out rough, unused. "You needed me three years ago when I told the court the ash wards were rotting. You needed me when I said the sealed thing under the old cathedral wasn't a myth your grandfather invented to frighten lords into paying tithes." She pushed off the wall, and the chains at her ankles sang. "Instead you listened to Voss. Voss the silver-tongued. Voss who never once in his soft life got his hands dirty with actual work."

"Voss is dead." Flat. "First one to try."

That stopped her. She let it sit between them—the rain, the dark, the distant sound of a city that had forgotten her name or only remembered it to curse it.

"Good," she said, but her mouth had gone dry. Black veins. Cold rooms. A dead man fluent in spirits speaking through a living throat. That wasn't rot. That wasn't a curse sent by a rival kingdom or a scorned lover. That was old work, patient work, the kind that waited generations for a crack. And Darran—proud, foolish, lonely Darran—would have made a perfect crack.

"What did he do," she asked, though she wasn't sure she wanted the answer.

Kael's silence was answer enough.

"Of course." She closed her eyes. Saw the cathedral. Saw the wards she'd spent six years rebuilding, thread by thread, while the court mocked her for wasting gold on stones. "He opened it."

"He went down with four guards. Looking for something to win the border war in a season." Kael's voice had gone mechanical, the way men spoke when they'd repeated a thing until it stopped being real. "Only he came back. Laughing. Then the cold started."

"And the king?"

"Dead eight months. Border war's gone to shit. That's why no one came for you sooner." Almost gentle, then: "There's no one left to swallow pride but him, and he can't speak. So I came."

Vesna opened her eyes. Studied him—the gray at his temples, the missing finger on his sword hand, the way he held himself like a man who hadn't slept since the first healer burned. He wasn't lying. Courtiers lied with their whole bodies, relaxed and easy; this man was held together with twine.

"Cut these off," she said.

A guard behind him started forward, keys out, but Kael waved him back and did it himself. The irons fell. Her ankles wept where the metal had gnawed them raw, and she stood a moment, stamping circulation back into feet that had forgotten floors not made of straw and slop.

"I'll want terms," she said.

"Name them."

"Full pardon. In writing, sealed by the prince's hand if he lives, by the council's if he doesn't. My tower back. Every book Voss didn't burn." She paused. "And I don't answer to anyone while I work. Not the council. Not the church. Not you."

"Done."

That fast. That frightened him. She filed it away.

They walked her through the palace she'd been carried out of, and nothing had changed—the same vaulted ceilings, the same stink of incense hiding rot, the same guards pretending not to stare. But the temperature dropped the moment they crossed into the east wing, and then she heard it: a voice under the voices, wet and wrong, whispering in a tongue older than the kingdom itself.

Vesna stopped. Her heart knocked once, hard, against her ribs.

She knew that voice. She'd read about it in the books Voss hadn't managed to burn.

"Kael," she said quietly. "What came back wearing your prince isn't a curse. It isn't even a demon." She looked down the hall toward the sealed doors, where frost crawled in patterns that almost looked like writing. "It's a god. Or it used to be, before people like me killed the last of them."

The whispering stopped.

In the sudden silence, very faintly, something on the other side of the doors began to laugh.

title: domestic suspense|a diary written by a woman whose husband lies in a coma after a suicide attempt
text:
Clara spread the moleskine flat on the plastic hospital tray, the pages warped where rain had seeped through her tote bag on the walk over. The beep of Eli’s heart monitor marked time, steady as a metronome, a sound she’d started hearing in her sleep even on the nights she forced herself to go home to shower. She twisted the cap off the black gel pen he’d bought her for their third anniversary, the one he’d said wrote “smooth enough to make even your grocery lists sound poetic,” and pressed the tip to the first blank page.

The door creaked open before she could write a word. Marnie, her sister-in-law, hovered in the threshold holding a crumpled paper bag from the diner down the street, her eyes red-rimmed, the same sharp hazel as Eli’s. “You haven’t eaten since yesterday,” she said, setting the bag down, the smell of greasy fries and weak coffee curling between them. “The nurse said you turned away the lunch tray again.”

Clara nodded, not looking up, tracing the embossed cover of the diary. She’d found it tucked on the top shelf of Eli’s home office closet three days after the paramedics wheeled him out, behind a stack of old tax returns and the beat-up skateboard he’d had since college. She’d thought she knew every book he owned, every scrap of paper he’d ever scribbled on. “I found this,” she said, pushing it across the tray so Marnie could see. “His. From the last six months.”

Marnie froze mid-reach for a fry. “You read it?”

“Not all of it.” Clara’s throat tightened. She thought of the first entry, dated three weeks before he’d swallowed the bottle of sleeping pills, the words scrawled so hard they’d torn through the paper: She doesn’t know I hear her on the phone. She thinks I’m asleep. She thinks I’m stupid enough to buy the late work nights. “He wrote that he thought I was cheating.”

Marnie blanched. “What? That’s—Clara, you never—”
“I know I never.” The pen slipped in her clammy grip, leaving an inky black smudge on the page. “He wrote that he’d checked my location history, that he counted the texts I sent to my boss, that he was saving up to hire a private investigator. That he couldn’t live knowing I was going to leave him. That there was no way out.”
She’d cried for an hour when she read that, hunched on the floor of his office, because she’d spent those three weeks secretly coordinating with his doctor, trying to get him to admit the insomnia and the rages and the way he’d started locking his home office door for hours at a time weren’t just “work stress.” The late nights had been phone calls with his therapist, the trips out of the house had been to pick up his new antidepressant prescription, the things she’d hidden from him were the brochures for the intensive outpatient program she’d been begging him to consider. She hadn’t told him because he’d snapped the last time she suggested he needed more help, had yelled that she thought he was broken, that she was waiting for an excuse to leave.

Marnie sat down slowly, the plastic chair scraping against the linoleum. “He never said a word to me. When I called him the day before—he told me things were good, that you two were planning that trip to the coast he’d been talking about for years.”
Clara’s gaze drifted to Eli, still and pale under the thin hospital blanket, the bruise on his temple from where he’d fallen against the bathroom vanity fading to a sallow yellow. His hand was warm when she reached for it, his fingers limp around hers, the faint callus on his index finger from holding a pen still rough against her skin. She thought of the entry she hadn’t told Marnie about, the one from the night of the attempt, written in wobbly, almost illegible script: When I’m gone, she’ll be free. She won’t have to pretend anymore. I saw the envelope in her bag. The plane tickets. She’s going to leave anyway.

The plane tickets had been for their tenth anniversary, a surprise. She’d hidden them in the back of her closet, tucked in an old winter coat, because she’d wanted to give them to him at dinner that night, to show him she wasn’t going anywhere.

The heart monitor beeped on, steady, unchanging. Clara picked up the pen again, flipped to the last blank page of the diary, the one right after his final entry. “I’m going to write to him,” she said, her voice quiet enough that Marnie almost didn’t hear it over the beep. “Every day. Until he wakes up. So he knows how wrong he was.”

Outside the window, the rain started again, tapping soft against the glass. For a second, she swore she felt his fingers twitch in hers. (712 words)

title: mystery|a wedding planner finds the best man dead in the hotel's walk-in freezer the night before the ceremony
text:
I slammed my shoulder into the walk-in freezer door for the third time, my silk blouse sticking to my sweat despite the cold seeping through the metal. “Jake? This isn’t funny! The bride’s going to lose it if her custom cake topper’s not on the dessert table in twenty minutes.”

The hotel kitchen hummed behind me—dishwashers clanking, prep cooks shouting over the sizzle of scallops, the head chef barking orders about truffle risotto. Nobody else seemed to notice that Jake Marlow, the best man, had vanished mid-toast rehearsal forty-five minutes ago. Nobody but me, the person whose entire career depended on this wedding going off without a single disaster.

I fumbled with the master keycard the hotel manager had pressed into my hand ten minutes earlier, my fingers stiff and clumsy. Of course Jake would hide in the one place I’d never think to look. Of course he’d decide tonight was the night to act like a frat boy instead of the polished corporate lawyer the groom had known since college. I’d dealt with difficult wedding parties before—drunk uncles, bridezillas who cried over napkin folds, grooms who forgot their rings—but none of them had ever locked themselves in a commercial freezer.

The lock clicked. I wrenched the door open, and a wall of frost smacked me in the face. “Jake, I swear to God—”

The words died in my throat.

He was slumped against a stack of sheet cake pans, his tailored navy suit crusted with ice, his eyes open and staring at the ceiling. His skin was blue, his lips parted like he’d been about to speak. The custom crystal cake topper—the one the bride had flown in from Paris, the one I’d spent three weeks tracking down after the original got lost in shipping—lay shattered on the floor beside his outstretched hand.

For a second I couldn’t breathe. I’d seen dead people before, at funerals, laid out in caskets with their hair combed just right and smiles painted on their faces. I’d never seen someone like this, frozen mid-motion, like a statue someone had knocked over and forgotten. My brain scrambled to catch up, to make sense of the suit I’d seen him wearing at the rehearsal dinner, the gold watch glinting on his wrist, the smudge of chocolate on his cuff that I’d teased him about ten minutes before he disappeared.

“Ma’am? You need to get out of there—health code—” One of the line cooks had followed me, his rubber boots squelching on the wet tile. He looked over my shoulder, and his tray of appetizers crashed to the floor. “Holy shit. Is that—”

“Call 911,” I said. My voice sounded weird, flat, like it was coming from someone else. “And security. Don’t let anyone leave the kitchen.”

He stumbled backward, yelling for the chef. I stepped further into the freezer, my high heels crunching on shattered crystal, and knelt down beside Jake. I knew better than to touch anything. I’d watched enough true crime documentaries with my roommate to know you didn’t contaminate a crime scene. But I had to check, had to be sure—

I pressed two fingers to his neck. His skin was hard, ice-cold. No pulse.

The door clicked shut behind me, muffling the chaos in the kitchen, and suddenly the freezer was dead quiet except for the low hum of the compressors. The cold bit through my blouse, through my tights, settling in my bones. I should have been panicking. I should have been screaming or crying or running out the door. Instead my planner brain kicked in, running through checklists even as my hands shook.

Call the police. Call hotel management. Tell the groom? No, not yet—not until we knew what happened. The bride was eight months pregnant, for Christ’s sake. She couldn’t handle this tonight, not twelve hours before she was supposed to walk down the aisle.

I studied Jake’s face, the way his eyebrows were furrowed like he was confused. It didn’t look like an accident. Walk-in freezer doors opened from the inside, for one thing—OSHA regulation. I’d checked every single safety feature in this hotel three times before signing the contract. He couldn’t have gotten locked in unless someone held the door. Unless someone wanted him in here.

My gaze landed on his hand, the one not curled around the broken topper. His fingers were slightly parted, like he’d been holding something. I leaned in, squinting through the frost, and saw it: a tiny scrap of pale pink fabric caught under his thumbnail. Silk. The exact shade of the bridesmaids’ dresses.

The freezer door wrenched open. “Step away from him, ma’am.” A security guard filled the doorway, his radio crackling. “Police are on their way.”

I stood up, my knees cracking. My breath fogged in the air. “He didn’t lock himself in,” I said. “Someone did this.”

The guard’s face paled. Behind him, through the kitchen window, I saw the groom push through the dining room doors, laughing with one of his groomsmen, a beer in his hand. He had no idea. Nobody did.

And the worst part? I’d seen every single person on this guest list tonight. Every single one of them had a reason to hate Jake Marlow. I just had to figure out which one had killed him before the wedding turned into a funeral.

title: spy|a British agent plays baccarat against a man who is financing an enemy network
text:
The baccarat salon at the Hôtel de Paris reeked of cigar smoke, chilled Krug, and the sharp, nervous sweat of men who thought wealth made them invulnerable. Cigarette smoldering between his fingers, James—no, Julian Voss, antique firearms dealer, Mayfair address, tailor on Savile Row—leaned back in the tufted leather chair, his gaze never leaving the man across the table.

Sergei Vasiliev did not look like a man who wired six-figure sums to cell leaders planning attacks on NATO supply lines. He looked like what his cover claimed: a Moscow-born commodities trader with a villa in Antibes, a superyacht moored in Port Hercule, and a supermodel wife half his age perched on the arm of his chair, her diamond bracelet catching the chandelier light as she sipped champagne. But Voss knew better. Six months of surveillance, three burnt informants, and a near-fatal car chase outside Kyiv had led him here, to this green baize table, where the stake was not the pile of €500 chips stacked high between them, but the hard drive locked in Vasiliev’s hotel safe—one that held the names, bank accounts, and attack timelines of every cell the Russian had funded across the continent.

“Another bank, Mr. Voss?” The croupier’s voice was soft, polished as the mahogany shoe holding the eight decks of cards. Vasiliev had won the last three hands, his thick, gold-ringed fingers raking in chips with the easy confidence of a man used to taking what he wanted.

Voss tapped the ash from his cigarette into the crystal tray at his elbow, letting a lazy, bored smile tug at his lips. He had let Vasiliev win those hands. Men like him grew careless when they thought they were outplaying an opponent. “I believe I’ll take it. Two hundred thousand.”

A murmur rippled through the small crowd of onlookers gathered behind the velvet rope. Vasiliev’s wife paused, her champagne flute halfway to her lips, and leaned in to murmur something in her husband’s ear. Vasiliev laughed, a low, rough sound, and waved a hand dismissively. “The Englishman has courage. I admire that. Bank accepted.”

The croupier slid two cards across the felt to Voss, then two to himself, face down. Voss picked his up with one hand, his thumb brushing the edges just enough to see the pips: a nine of hearts and a king of spades. Natural nine. Unbeatable, unless the bank also held a nine, which would be a push. He did not let a flicker of emotion cross his face, just set the cards face down again, his expression as bland as if he held a pair of fives.

Vasiliev peeked at his own cards, and Voss caught the tiny, almost imperceptible twitch at the corner of his left eye—the tell he had spotted three hands earlier, the one that meant Vasiliev held a hand he thought was strong, but not unbeatable. A seven, maybe, or an eight. “Draw?” the croupier asked.

Vasiliev shook his head, tapping the table twice with one finger. “Non.” He had a seven, then. Stand on seven.

Voss shook his head as well. “Stand.”

The croupier turned over Voss’s cards first. The nine and king drew a soft gasp from the crowd. Vasiliev’s jaw tightened, just a fraction, before he forced a smile and flipped over his own: an eight of diamonds and a nine of clubs. Seven.

“Nine for the player,” the croupier said, raking the chips across the table to Voss. Vasiliev’s wife huffed, setting down her champagne glass hard enough to slosh bubbles over the rim.

“Remarkable luck,” Vasiliev said, his voice tight, though he kept the smile fixed in place as he signaled a waiter for another cigar. “But luck, she is a fickle mistress, no? One moment she is on your arm, the next she is gone to the man with deeper pockets.”

Voss stacked his chips neatly, his fingers brushing the hidden micro-transmitter tucked in the cuff of his tailored wool suit—the one that had been relaying every word, every pause, every twitch to his team in the unmarked van idling three blocks away, already working to crack the hotel safe’s digital lock while Vasiliev was distracted at the table. “Luck, Mr. Vasiliev? I prefer to think of it as skill. Most men show their hand long before they turn over their cards. You just have to know what to look for.”

Vasiliev’s smile froze for half a second, his dark eyes narrowing as he studied Voss, as if seeing him for the first time not as a soft Mayfair antique dealer with too much money and too little sense, but as something sharper, something dangerous. Voss held his gaze, lifting his champagne flute in a small, mocking toast. Behind Vasiliev, through the salon’s gilded window, he saw the faint flash of a blue police strobing—too far away to be noticed by anyone inside, but close enough that he knew his team had the drive, were already clearing the exit route.

“Another hand?” Voss asked, even as he shifted his weight slightly, his hand brushing the Walther PPK holstered at his waist beneath his jacket. He knew what the answer would be. Knew Vasiliev’s pride would not let him walk away from a loss, would not let him walk away from a challenge.

Vasiliev leaned forward, lighting his cigar with a gold lighter, the flame reflecting in his cold eyes. “I think you will find, Mr. Voss, that I do not lose. Not at cards, not at business.” The supermodel slid off the arm of his chair, her heels clicking softly on the marble floor as she moved toward the bar, and Voss saw her slip a hand into her clutch—no doubt reaching for the compact pistol he knew she carried. “Not at anything.”

The croupier cleared his throat, sliding two new cards across the felt. Outside, a siren wailed, closer now. Voss picked up his cards, his finger hovering over the trigger of his gun, and smiled. The game, he thought, was only just beginning.

title: domestic suspense|a diary written by a woman whose husband lies in a coma after a suicide attempt
text:
The Diary of Clara Voss – Entry 14

They say he can hear me. The doctors say it like a prescription, three times after meals. I say it back to myself in the hospital parking lot because if Eleanor can hear, too, then I need to choose my words carefully.

Martin’s hand is warm. That angers me more than it should. A man who swallowed enough pills to sink a secret still gets to be warm.

I brought the black notebook. The one hidden behind the water heater, wrapped in a grocery bag like a sandwich nobody wanted. I should have turned it over to the police. I should have done a great many things.

“Darling,” I say, because the nurse is adjusting his pillows and wives say darling.

The nurse smiles at me. Sympathetic wife. Brave little wife. If she knew the words burning a hole through my bag, she’d strap the pulse monitor to me instead.

When the door clicks shut, I open the notebook.

“March 3rd,” I read. “‘Clara asked why I came home smelling of river water. Told her the sprinklers. She believed me. She always believes me because believing is easier for her.’”

My voice doesn’t shake. I’ve practiced since Tuesday.

Martin’s chest rises. Falls. The machine draws green hills for him, steady, boring, alive.

“Do you remember writing that?” I ask.

Nothing.

“I believed the sprinklers,” I say. “I even apologized for the dry cleaning bill. God, Martin. You had to laugh at that, didn’t you?”

The curtain moves with the ventilation. Outside, a cart rattles. Somewhere a woman laughs with the relieved laughter of people whose husbands didn’t leave a note that says ask Eleanor.

I lean closer.

“Who is Eleanor?”

The heart monitor gives me its little green lie. No flicker. No flutter. Of course not. A man in a coma is still a man with talent for silence.

I turn pages fast, the way you tear off a bandage.

“‘Eleanor says I’m trapped. Eleanor says Clara notices too much and too little at once. She is right on both counts.’”

I laugh once. It sounds foreign, like a door slamming in someone else’s house.

“Notice too much and too little,” I repeat. “That’s your best line in twenty years.”

There’s a knock at the door.

It’s Diane, my sister, carrying two coffees and that expression—the one she wears when she’s about to manage me.

“You’re doing it again,” she says.

“Doing what?”

“Talking to him like he’s on trial.”

“He attempted suicide, Diane. In our laundry room. On laundry day, no less. The note was practically mixed with the fabric softener.”

She sets the coffees down and glances at the notebook. “Is that—”

“Yes.”

“Clara.”

“Don’t Clara me. You’re the one who said check the house.”

“I said find insurance papers. I didn’t say read his private diary like a detective with a vendetta.”

“It mentions another woman.”

Diane’s mouth opens. Closes. Opens again. “A prostitute? A coworker? Wait—don’t answer that. Do you want me to hit him with the tray table? I can make it look like grief.”

Despite everything, I smile. Diane has always loved me best at my worst.

“Eleanor,” I say. “He calls her Eleanor. She advised him. Advised, Diane. Like a femme fatale with an office.”

“Maybe she’s a therapist.”

“Therapists don’t take you to rivers.”

“Maybe it’s a metaphorical river.”

“Nothing in this marriage was metaphorical until the pills.”

Diane pulls the visitor chair closer and lowers her voice. “The police said suicide attempt.”

“The police also said the note looked genuine.”

“It said I’m sorry.”

“It said ask Eleanor.”

She winces. “That part you keep leaving out when you repeat it.”

“Because people get comfortable with sorry. Ask Eleanor makes them look at the wife.”

Martin’s finger twitches.

We both freeze.

Diane grabs my wrist. “Did you see that?”

“Yes.”

“Martin?” I say.

No movement.

“Bastard,” I whisper. “Perfect timing, as always.”

Diane releases a breath. “You need sleep.”

“I need answers.”

“You need carbohydrates and perhaps a Xanax.”

“I need him to wake up and explain why his secretary—if that’s even what she is—knows which lies I swallowed before I did.”

My voice cracks on swallowed. Diane hears it. She always hears it.

“Hey,” she says softly. “Look at me. This isn’t your fault.”

“That’s a very easy sentence.”

“It’s a true one.”

“Then why does his diary say I made the house small?”

“Because cheaters rewrite leases.”

I stare at her. “That’s unexpectedly profound.”

“I’ve been practicing in the car.”

I close the notebook, but I don’t put it away. Outside, the sky presses gray against the windows. Visiting hours will end. Diane will drive me home to the laundry room, where the bleach still smells like emergency and the floor has one pale square nobody has mopped enough.

“Martin,” I say, standing over the bed. “I found three bank transfers. Fifty dollars each. Florist, not therapist. I found a motel receipt in your coat, but you knew that. You always check pockets before giving me a jacket. That was your mistake—you kept the wrong one.”

Diane’s eyes widen. “You didn’t tell me that.”

“I’m telling him first.”

The machines hum.

“I also found a hospital bracelet,” I continue. “Dated last November. Female. Name torn off. So either Eleanor is injured, imaginary, or our husband is much stupider than I thought.”

Martin’s eyelashes seem darker against his skin. Younger. For a second I see the boy who proposed in a broken-down car, laughing because the radio still worked.

Then I remember the bottle on the dryer.

“If you can hear me,” I whisper, “wake up angry. Wake up afraid. Wake up whatever you like. But don’t you dare wake up forgiven.”

Diane takes my coat. The nurse comes in, bright and rustling.

“How’s our patient tonight?” she asks.

I look at Martin’s serene face, the face of a man hiding behind unconsciousness.

“Quiet,” I say. “Finally.”

In the notebook, tucked between the last two pages, a dried white gardenia falls onto the sheet.

Diane sees it first.

“Clara,” she says. “Your wedding flowers were peonies.”

The heart monitor beeps once, too loud in the sudden hush.

And Martin’s hand closes—just barely—around mine.

title: young adult|a fourteen-year-old girl runs away to a music festival to find the mother who left her
text:
The Porta-Potty reeked so bad my eyes watered before I even latched the door. I pressed my back to the graffiti-scrawled plastic, counted to ten, and listened for the security guard’s boots to thud past. They did. Crunching on discarded beer cups and lost wristbands, yelling about some kid who’d climbed the main stage speaker stack. I fumbled the crumpled set list out of my jacket pocket, the edge smudged where I’d sweated through it on the three-hour Greyhound. Lila Voss, second stage, 6:15 p.m. That was Mom. The name she’d started using the day she packed her guitar and left a note on the fridge that said Sorry, kid, the road doesn’t wait for people who fold laundry.

I slipped out when the coast was clear, hood up, boots squelching in mud that reeked of cheap seltzer and weed. Some guy with a face tattoo of a cat offered me a hit off a joint as I cut past his blanket. I shook my head. Didn’t have time to get fuzzy. The sun was bleeding orange over the treeline, painting the ferris wheel pink, and the bass from the main stage thrummed up through my bones so hard my teeth chattered. A girl in a sequined cowboy hat was crying by the taco stand, screaming into her phone that her friend had ditched her for some guy in a band. I knew that feeling. The hollow, cold twist when someone you counted on decides you’re not worth sticking around for.

The second stage was smaller, tucked between a row of food trucks and a chain link fence strung with fairy lights. The crowd was thinner here, mostly older guys with faded band tees and girls with dyed blue hair screaming lyrics I didn’t know. I pushed my way to the front, my shoulder slamming into a guy holding a plastic cup of beer that sloshed down my sleeve. I didn’t care. There she was.

Her hair was shorter now, dyed black at the roots, and she had a new silver hoop through her eyebrow, but I’d know that scar on her left wrist anywhere—the one she got when she’d tried to teach herself to play guitar at 16, slipped, and sliced herself open on a broken string. She was mid-verse, her voice rough and raw, just like I remembered from the lullabies she used to sing when I had nightmares. My throat tightened. I’d practiced what I’d say for six months, ever since I found her tour schedule posted to a fan account I checked every night before bed. I’m not here to yell. I just want to know why. Did you ever think about me? Do you even remember my birthday?

She finished the song, grinned, and leaned into the mic. “This next one’s for the people who leave the boring shit behind,” she said, and the crowd cheered. “For anyone who ever outgrew the life someone else tried to box them into.”

My chest went cold. The boring shit. That was me, right? The straight-A report cards taped to the fridge, the nights I waited up for her to come home from gigs, the time I’d made her a macaroni necklace for Mother’s Day that she’d said she’d lost two days later. I opened my mouth to yell her name, but before I could, a woman with a clipboard pushed past me, yelling “Lila! Five minutes till the meet-and-greet, don’t forget the label rep’s here.”

Mom nodded, slung her guitar over her shoulder, and hopped off the stage without a single glance at the crowd. Without a single glance at me.

I stood there for a second, mud seeping into the holes in my boots, the cheers fading around me. Some kid bumped into me, spilling lemonade down my jeans. I didn’t move. I’d spent every last cent of my babysitting money on the bus ticket and the fake wristband I’d bought from a kid outside the gate. I’d lied to my dad and said I was staying at my best friend’s house for the weekend. I’d thought if I just saw her, if I just talked to her, everything would make sense.

A hand landed on my shoulder. I flinched, half-expecting security, half-expecting her. It was the cat tattoo guy, holding out a crumpled napkin. “You look like you saw a ghost,” he said.

I stared at the empty spot where she’d been standing. “Yeah,” I said, my voice cracking. “I guess I did.” (Word count: 692)

title: mystery|a Venetian police commissario questions a widow who seems relieved rather than grieving
text:
The rain had stopped by the time Commissario Guido Brunetti reached the piano nobile of the Palazzo Falier, leaving the stones of the campo below slick as river glass. He mounted the stairs slowly, listening to the sound of his own footsteps on the trachyte, and paused at the landing to look out through the leaded window at the Grand Canal. A vaporetto passed, its windows fogged, and he thought how often in this city beauty served only to make trouble more bearable to look at.

The door was opened by a young woman in a dark sweater and skirt, who introduced herself as Signora Falier's sister. She led him across an entrance hall lined with portraits of stern-faced men in crimson and led him into a salone that ran the width of the palazzo. At its far end, beside a window framing the misty outline of San Giorgio, stood a woman with her back to him.

"Commissario Brunetti," the sister announced.

The woman turned. Elisabetta Falier was perhaps forty-five, tall, with ash-blonde hair pulled back severely from a face that was handsome rather than pretty. She wore a grey cashmere dress and no jewelry except a wedding band. Brunetti had expected red eyes, a handkerchief, the particular fragility of the newly bereaved. What he saw instead was something he recognized from long experience: the barely concealed relief of someone who has just laid down a heavy burden.

"Commissario," she said, coming forward and extending her hand. Her grip was firm, her palm cool and dry. "Thank you for coming yourself. I know how busy you must be."

"Signora Falier. Please accept my condolences."

A faint, complicated expression crossed her face. "You're very kind," she said, and gestured toward a pair of brocade armchairs arranged near a fireplace that held no fire. "Will you have coffee? My sister made some, though she believes mourning requires it to be terrible."

Brunetti almost smiled. "Volentieri."

The sister brought the coffee on a silver tray, then withdrew with a look that mingled sympathy and something watchful. When they were alone, Brunetti took out his notebook. "I have only a few questions, Signora. The doctors are quite clear about the cause of death, so this is merely routine."

"Of course." She sat straight-backed, her cup steady in its saucer.

"Your husband returned from Milan yesterday evening on the five-forty?"

"Yes. He called from the station to say he was taking the motoscafo. He arrived around seven." Her voice was level, almost conversational.

"And he was alone?"

"As far as I know. He went directly to his study. He often did after traveling. He said the light here helped him think." She glanced toward the window, and again Brunetti saw it pass across her features like sunlight through shallow water—relief, swiftly hidden.

"Did he seem unwell? Distracted? Anxious?"

She set down her cup. "Commissario, my husband had a weak heart for years. His doctor warned him repeatedly. He drank too much, slept too little, and conducted his business affairs as though they were a war. If he seemed distracted, it was nothing new."

Brunetti let a silence gather. Outside, a gondola slid past, the gondoliere calling to a colleague on the Riva del Carbon. "Signora," he said gently, "I've spoken with many people who have lost someone suddenly. They often speak of the person in the present tense for days. They ask me to leave because arrangements must be made, or they weep, or they cannot answer simple questions." He met her eyes. "You speak of him in the past already, and with perfect clarity."

Color rose slowly into her cheeks, but she did not look away. "Would you prefer that I weep for your notebook, Commissario?"

"I would prefer the truth."

For a long moment she said nothing. Then she rose and walked to the window, her reflection wavering in the dark glass beside the silhouette of the church across the water.

"My husband was not a kind man," she said at last, very quietly. "Not to me, and not, I think, to many people. He was clever and charming in public, and cruel at home in the small ways that leave no marks anyone can photograph. For twenty years I have waited for him to die or for myself to find the courage to leave. Last night I was in the kitchen when I heard him fall. I sat with him on the floor of his study and held his hand until the ambulance came, and I said the prayers one says. And then, when the house was quiet, I went to bed and slept for eight hours without waking." She turned back to Brunetti. "Does that shock you?"

He considered the question honestly. "No, Signora."

"It shocks me," she said. "Even knowing what he was. Even after all of it."

Brunetti closed his notebook. He had spoken to the doorman in Milan, to the doctor, to the housekeeper who had found the bottle of pills untouched for months. The dead man had been sixty-three, overweight, overworked, and alone in his study with a glass of brandy when his heart stopped. There was no case here, only the ordinary human wreckage that Venice polished and presented to the world as palaces and view.

"One last thing," he said. "Did anyone visit him last night? Any telephone call, any message?"

Something shifted behind her eyes, so quickly he might have imagined it.

"No," she said. "No one."

Brunetti held her gaze a moment longer, then inclined his head. "Grazie, Signora Falier. If I have further questions, I'll telephone."

He let himself out and descended slowly into the wet golden light of the campo. At the foot of the bridge he stopped and looked back at the palazzo, its windows blind against the canal, and thought of the lie he had just heard delivered with perfect, grieving calm.

title: horror|survivors barricaded in a supermarket hear someone they buried knocking at the loading dock
text:
The coffee was cold when I heard it.
I’d been staring at the same crack in the linoleum by my scuffed work boot for forty-seven minutes, counting the seconds between Javi’s ragged snores on the customer service counter and the distant, wet thud of whatever those things were dragging against the front plate glass, when the first knock came. Soft, at first. Furtive, like a kid too shy to ask for a free sample. I thought I was imagining it—sleep deprivation makes you hear all kinds of shit, after all. I’d spent the last three days hearing my dead mom calling my name from the cereal aisle, for Christ’s sake, had to physically hold Lila back twice from prying the plywood off the doors to go find her.
I lifted the chipped ceramic mug to my lips anyway, the bitter sludge sticking to my tongue, and told myself it was just the wind. The loading dock faced the old cornfield, the wind came off it sharp this time of year, rattled the roll-up door so hard the bolts sometimes wiggled loose. I’d tightened them myself yesterday, with the socket set we fished out of the hardware aisle, my knuckles scraped raw from the rust.
The second knock was louder. Sharper. Three quick raps, then a pause, then two more.
My blood turned to slush in my veins. I knew that rhythm.
“Hey.” I kicked Javi’s boot hard enough to jostle him awake, his hand flying to the crowbar propped against the counter before his eyes were even all the way open. “Shut up a second.”
He blinked, scrubbing a hand over the stubble crusted with dried bean juice, and opened his mouth to complain before the third knock hit. This one was harder, like someone was slamming the heel of their fist against the metal, hard enough that the whole dock door hummed. Lila stirred on the nest of sleeping bags by the pharmacy, her matted blonde hair sticking up as she lifted her head, the baseball bat we’d wrapped in barbed wire clutched tight to her chest.
“Is that—” she started, her voice thin as tissue paper.
“Don’t.” I held a hand up to cut her off, standing slow, like if I moved too fast whatever was on the other side would hear me. My knees cracked so loud I flinched. “Don’t say it.”
We buried him three days ago. Tyler. The kid who’d bagged my groceries every Saturday for two years, who’d had a sticker of a cartoon dinosaur on his name tag, who’d gotten bit when we made a run for the loading dock to haul in the last of the water cases. We’d watched the bite on his forearm turn black, watched the fever burn through him so fast he was delirious in twelve hours, listened to him gurgle his last breath begging us to make sure his mom knew he didn’t suffer. Javi had dug the hole out behind the garden center, in the soft loam by the tomato plants, because the ground out front was too hard, too full of those things lurching up and down the parking lot. We’d wrapped him in a ratty patio furniture tarp, said a prayer none of us really meant, piled cinder blocks on top of the grave because we’d all seen what happened when you didn’t.
He couldn’t be out there.
“Guys.” The voice came through the metal, muffled, cracked, exactly the way it had sounded when he was half-dead on the floor, begging for water. “Guys, c’mon, it’s me. It’s cold out here.”
Lila made a noise like a wounded animal, already half-scrambling to her feet before Javi grabbed her wrist hard enough to leave bruises. “Don’t you fucking dare,” he snarled, his eyes wild, the whites showing all the way around like a spooked horse. “You saw him. You saw him stop breathing. We put three cinder blocks on him, Lila.”
“I know what I saw!” She wrenched her arm out of his grip, tears cutting clean tracks through the grime on her cheeks. “That’s his voice, Javi, that’s him, what if we were wrong? What if he wasn’t—what if he was just out?”
The knocking came again, faster now, frantic, accompanied by a scraping sound like nails on metal. “C’mon, open up!” Tyler yelled, and there was something wrong with the way he said it, something off about the cadence, like he was reading lines off a script he’d half-memorized. “They’re out here, they’re gonna get me, please, I’m hurt, my arm—”
I walked slow toward the dock, my boots sticking a little to the linoleum where someone had spilled a jar of pickles two nights ago, the shards still crunched under the edge of the shelf. Javi called my name, sharp, but I held up a hand again, not looking back. There was a little peephole in the roll-up door, at eye level, drilled by the old night manager who’d been convinced people were sneaking in to steal beer after close. I’d covered it with a piece of duct tape the first day, scared they’d see us through it, but now I reached up, my fingers shaking so bad I fumbled the edge twice before I peeled it back.
I pressed my eye to the hole.
The sun was going down, painting the cornfield orange and bloody, and for a second I couldn’t see anything but shadow. Then he leaned into the light, and my throat closed up so tight I couldn’t breathe.
It was Tyler. Same shaggy brown hair, same dinosaur sticker peeling off the name tag pinned to his blue work vest, same gap between his front teeth he’d been self-conscious about since middle school. But his skin was gray, the color of old meat left out in the rain, and the gash across his throat we hadn’t noticed when we buried him was oozing black slime down the front of his shirt. His eyes were milky, clouded over like a dead fish, but they were locked dead on the peephole, like he could see me right through the metal.
He smiled. The skin on his cheek split when he did it, oozing that same black stuff down his jaw.
“Hi, Jesse,” he said, clear as a bell, like he was standing right next to me. “I know you’re in there. Let me in.”
The knocking started again, harder this time, hard enough that I could see the bolts we’d tightened yesterday starting to wiggle in their brackets. Behind me, Lila was sobbing, Javi was yelling something I couldn’t parse over the roar of blood in my ears, and all I could think about was the way Tyler had slipped me a free pack of gum last month when I’d forgotten my wallet, the way he’d laughed when I told him I’d pay him back next time.
There wasn’t going to be a next time.
I pressed my palm flat to the cold metal, right where his fist was hitting on the other side, and wondered how long it would take him to break through.
