title: young adult|a fourteen-year-old girl runs away to a music festival to find the mother who left her
text:
Chapter 7

The bus exhaled a cloud of diesel fumes and rumbled away, leaving Maya alone at the edge of a field that throbbed like a second heartbeat. She was fourteen years old, twenty-two miles from home, and her backpack contained one change of clothes, a toothbrush, and forty-three dollars in crumpled allowance money. Somewhere beyond the chain-link fence, her mother was singing.

Not literally, Maya corrected herself, gripping the frayed straps of her backpack. Her mother wasn't on stage. But three years ago, Eleanor Voss had packed a single suitcase, kissed Maya's forehead while she slept, and vanished into a life that apparently included folk festivals and a phone number that never answered. The ticket confirmation in Maya's pocket—found in an old email account her mother hadn't fully signed out of—proved she was here. *Willow Creek Folk Fest. Weekend Pass.*

The entrance line moved like a sluggish river. Maya kept her head down, adjusting the sunglasses she'd borrowed from her father's nightstand. A security guard glanced at her ticket barcode, then at her face, and she held her breath until the scanner chirped green and he waved her through.

Inside, the world unfolded in chaos and color. Tie-dye tapestries draped between food trucks. A man on stilts strode past in a velvet coat. The air smelled like fried dough, dust, and sweet smoke she didn't want to identify. Music layered upon music—a fiddle workshop somewhere to her left, a drum circle to her right, and from the main stage, a woman's voice carried over the crowd like something wild and half-tamed.

Maya's throat tightened. It wasn't her mother's voice. That wasn't why she'd come.

She checked her phone. 11:47 AM. Her father would think she was at the library. She had until six before he'd start calling.

She began near the merch tents, scanning faces with an intensity that made her temples ache. Women with her mother's hair—chestnut, usually loose past the shoulders. Women with her mother's laugh, bright and sudden. Each one turned out wrong, and each wrong face felt like a small, stupid death.

By noon the sun burned overhead. Maya bought a lemonade and sat on a fallen log near a cluster of food trucks, studying the festival map though she already knew it by heart.

"You look like you're solving a crime."

A girl perhaps a few years older than Maya had dropped onto the log beside her, carrying a paper tray of loaded nachos. She had a silver ring through her eyebrow and a camera hanging around her neck.

"Just meeting someone," Maya said carefully.

"At a festival? Good luck. I've been trying to find my boyfriend for two hours." She held out the nachos. "I'm Jules."

"Maya." She took a chip because it seemed polite. "Do you know where the artisans' field is? The smaller stage?"

Jules pointed with a tortilla chip. "Past the ferris wheel, follow the path through the willows. Why, someone playing?"

"Someone I need to talk to."

The answer came out steadier than she felt. Jules studied her for a moment, then nodded. "For what it's worth, the best talks at festivals happen there. Nobody can hear you over the banjos."

Maya found the path and followed it through curtains of hanging willow leaves. The main crowd noise dimmed. The smaller stage sat in a natural bowl of grass, ringed by craft booths and shade trees. Maybe fifty people sat on blankets. A trio played a slow acoustic song, and between verses, Maya scanned every face.

She saw her on the third pass.

Eleanor Voss sat cross-legged near the back on an embroidered blanket, wearing a denim jacket Maya didn't recognize, hair shorter than she remembered, pinned back with two thin clips. A woven bag rested beside her. She was alone, turning a paper cup between her hands, and she looked—Maya searched for the right word—ordinary. Smaller than memory allowed.

For a long moment, Maya couldn't move. Three years of unanswered letters, of birthdays passing in silence, of her father's careful, closed expression whenever her mother's name surfaced. All of it condensed into a pressure behind her sternum.

Then Eleanor looked up.

Recognition crossed her face slowly, like clouds clearing. Her lips parted. The paper cup tilted, and a little water spilled onto the blanket unnoticed.

"Maya?" Her voice was barely audible over the music.

Maya walked down the slope, backpack bouncing against her shoulders. She stopped a few feet away, close enough to see the fine lines around her mother's eyes, the faint tremor in her hand.

"You left your email logged in," Maya said. Her voice cracked on the last word. "On the old laptop. I've been checking it for two years."

Eleanor set the cup down with exaggerated care. "You came alone."

"I'm fourteen. I took the bus."

"Jesus." Eleanor pressed her fingers to her mouth. Her eyes glistened. "Maya, I—"

"Don't." The word came out sharper than Maya intended. Around them, a few heads turned. She lowered her voice. "Don't say you're sorry yet. I haven't decided why I'm here."

Her mother nodded slowly. She shifted on the blanket and gestured, tentative as though offering something fragile, to the empty space beside her.

"Then stay," Eleanor said. "Even if it's just for the song."

Maya looked at the patch of blanket, at the woman who had once known every fear she'd ever had and had chosen to leave anyway. Somewhere behind them, the fiddle began a new melody, thin and searching.

She sat down, leaving a careful foot of space between them. Not forgiveness. Not yet. But she had forty-three dollars, a return ticket she hadn't bought, and six hours before anyone would notice she was gone.

The song stretched on, and for the first time in three years, Maya let herself look at her mother without looking away.

title: comic|a holistic detective tries to explain to a sceptical client why a horse is in the bathroom
text:
The Horse in the Guest Bath
The first thing I noticed about Marnie Hollis was that she was holding a can of wasp spray like it was a loaded .38, and her left sock was inside out, neon pink fuzz sticking up where the cuff should’ve been. The second thing I noticed was the horse.
It was in her guest bathroom, the one with the seashell-shaped soap dish and the wallpaper printed with tiny lighthouses, the one she’d told me over the phone she’d only used twice since moving in three months ago, once when her cousin’s kid had a stomach bug and once when the master bath toilet backed up during a thunderstorm. The horse was a chestnut, white blaze down its nose, standing half-turned like it had been mid-trot when it decided to duck in for a pee. It was eating the hand towel that had been hanging on the towel ring.
“Vic,” Marnie said, her voice tight enough to pluck, “I called you because my ex kept leaving dead goldfish in my mailbox, and I thought you did that woo-woo detective stuff that doesn’t involve cops asking me stupid questions about restraining orders. I did not call you to explain why there is a 1,000-pound farm animal in my half-bath.”
I leaned against the doorframe, pulled a crumpled bag of lemon drops out of my jacket pocket, and offered her one. She batted my hand away. The horse chewed the towel like it was a fancy appetizer, made a soft rumbly noise in its throat.
“First off,” I said, popping a lemon drop into my own mouth, “he’s 920 pounds, I weighed him with the aura scale I keep in my truck. Second off, this is related to the goldfish. You want the long version or the version that doesn’t make you want to spray me in the eyes with that Raid?”
“There is a version of this that doesn’t end with me calling animal control and then a realtor?”
“Probably not, but hear me out. Your ex, Gary? The one who sells essential oil blends out of his van and says he’s a reincarnated Sioux warrior even though his mom lives in Skokie and he’s afraid of house cats?”
Marnie’s jaw tightened. “We don’t talk about the cat incident.”
“Right, well, Gary didn’t just leave those goldfish to be a dick. He bought a curse off a lady he met at a Phish show in Deer Creek. Twenty bucks, plus a half ounce of that lavender stuff he swears cures testicular cancer. The curse was supposed to make ‘all the baggage you left with him come home to roost.’” I nodded at the horse, who had finished the hand towel and was now sniffing curiously at the toilet plunger. “Turns out the curse lady was half-asleep when she wrote it, because ‘roost’ sounds like ‘roan’ if you’re stoned on mushroom chocolates and the guy next to you is blowing a vuvuzela. Roan is a horse color. In case you didn’t know.”
Marnie stared at me. She stared at the horse. The horse lifted its tail and deposited a pile of manure directly on her lighthouse-patterned bath mat, neat as you please.
“Are you fucking with me,” she said, flat as a pancake.
“Wish I was. I talked to the curse lady this morning. Name’s Starlight, legally it’s Brenda, she lives in a trailer outside Aurora and collects vintage My Little Ponies. She felt terrible, said she’ll refund Gary his twenty and send you a free bottle of patchouli room spray if we don’t report her to the Better Business Bureau. Problem is, the curse is sticky. We can’t just haul him out to a farm, because every time we try to lead him across the threshold, he pops right back in here. Tried it twice already before you got home. The kid from the stable down the road thought I was having a stroke.”
I nodded at the scuff marks on the tile, the faint scratch along the doorframe where the horse’s hoof had caught when we’d tried to tug him out with a lead rope. Marnie blinked a few times, set the wasp spray down on the hall table, and reached for the lemon drops. She took three, popped them all in her mouth at once.
“So what you’re telling me,” she said, slow, like she was picking her way through a field of broken glass, “is that my dipshit ex tried to curse me, the curse lady misspelled a word, and now I have a horse living in my guest bathroom because of… homophones?”
“Pretty much. Also, the horse’s name is Kevin. Starlight says he’s from a farm outside Rockford, he got struck by lightning last week, he was between bodies, the curse latched onto him. He’s pretty chill, all things considered. Doesn’t bite. Likes peppermints.”
As if on cue, Kevin nickered, craning his neck to sniff at Marnie’s outstretched hand. She flinched, then relaxed a little when he huffed warm air against her wrist, soft as a blanket fresh out of the dryer. Down the hall, the grandfather clock she’d bought at an estate sale chimed four. Somewhere outside, a kid yelled for their dog.
“Wait,” she said, after a minute, “if the curse was supposed to bring back my baggage, why is it a horse? I didn’t leave a horse with Gary. I left a vintage record player and a really nice cast iron skillet and a hoodie that had my college logo on it.”
I shrugged. “Baggage doesn’t always look like what you think it does. Maybe you left a part of yourself that wanted to run away and live on a farm when you were 12 and your parents made you quit horse camp to go to math tutoring. Maybe Gary’s got so much unprocessed bullcrap floating around him the curse grabbed the nearest thing that looked like freedom. I don’t make the rules, I just untangle the messes. Also, for what it’s worth? The goldfish were fine. Starlight said they were just regular feeder fish, they’re living in her aquarium now, she named one after Gary.”
Marnie stared at Kevin for a long time. He’d given up on the plunger and was now nudging at the toilet lid, like he was trying to figure out how to lift it. She sighed, so deep her shoulders hunched up to her ears.
“I don’t have any peppermints,” she said.
“I got some in the truck.”
“Fine. But if he eats my good bath towels, you’re buying me new ones. And if Gary shows up here? You get to explain to him why there’s a horse in my house, and then you get to help me beat his ass with the plunger.”
“Fair,” I said.
Kevin whinnied, like he approved. Somewhere down the block, a car backfired. I didn’t tell her that the curse had a second clause, that when we got Kevin out in three days, once the magic wore off, she’d wake up with that old horse camp urge in her chest so strong she’d sign up for lessons by the end of the week. I didn’t tell her she’d end up buying Kevin from the farm six months later, that he’d live in the little pasture she’d rent out past the suburbs, that she’d bring Gary the cast iron skillet back just to watch him gape when she told him why the horse had showed up in the first place. People don’t hire holistic detectives to hear the ending ahead of time. They hire us to stand there with them while the horse eats the hand towel, and not look at them like they’re crazy when it does.
I turned to head out to the truck for the peppermints, and heard Marnie snort. When I looked back, she was scratching Kevin between the ears, and he was leaning into it like a big fuzzy dog, half-closing his eyes.
“Hey Vic,” she said, “if this curse thing works out, think we can send a horse to Gary’s van? His bathroom’s way smaller than mine.”
I grinned. “I’ll ask Brenda.”

title: fantasy|a half-vampire girl and her dog travel from village to village hunting the undead for money
text:
Here's your continuation:

---

The mud sucked at Wren's boots as she stepped into Hargrove. Rain dripped from the eaves, turning the main street into a shallow creek. Biter padded beside her, his black coat matted, ears forward. He didn't bark. Never did. Not when it mattered.

The village looked like all the others. Tight shutters. Pale faces peering through cracks. Smoke from chimneys that didn't quite cut the smell—rot, wet wool, fear.

"She's here," someone muttered.

Wren didn't look. She knew the drill. They'd whisper. Cross the street. Clutch their children. Half-vampire wasn't something these folks understood, and understanding wasn't something she was selling.

The alderman waited outside the tavern. Fat man with a bad eye and worse teeth. He held a cloth to his face despite the rain.

"Took you long enough," he said.

"Got here when I got here." Wren dropped her pack on the porch. Bitter sat, alert. "Where is it?"

"Old mill. North road. Took another one last night. Miller's boy. Fourteen." The alderman's jaw worked. "Dragged him out through his window. Screams woke the whole street, but nobody—" He stopped. Swallowed. "Nobody moved."

"Smart."

He flinched like she'd struck him.

Wren unbuckled her pack. Inside: three ash stakes, iron-headed mallet, a jar of salt mixed with shaved silver, oilskin wraps of garlic enough to strip paint. She kept the crossbow loaded over her shoulder—bolt heads filed to points, soaked in holy water she'd traded a bottle of good whiskey for outside Carthmere.

"Coin first," she said.

"The agreement was after—"

"Coin first. I don't hunt on credit and I don't argue. Fifty silver or I walk."

His mouth opened. Closed. He produced the pouch from inside his coat, like pulling a tooth. Wren hefted it. Bit one coin. Good enough.

"The thing in the mill," she said. "How old?"

"Old. Been there since before my grandfather. But it never came into the village before. Not until—"

"Until now." She slung the pack again. "Biter. Come."

The dog stood.

They took the north road at a jog. Rain came down harder, finding the gap between Wren's collar and skin. She didn't mind. Cold kept her honest. Her mother's blood—the vampire half—preferred warmth. Preferred a lot of things Wren didn't let herself think about.

The mill rose out of the grey like a broken tooth. Wheel motionless, water black beneath it. Door hanging open on a single hinge.

Biter growled low in his chest.

Wren dropped to one knee, fingers brushing the mud. Drag marks. Two sets—something going in, something being pulled. Blood thinned by rain, but her nose caught it anyway, sweet and bright beneath the rot. Her teeth ached. She pressed her tongue flat behind them and breathed through her mouth.

*Not yours. Never yours.*

She pulled a stake and the mallet. Nodded to Biter. "Wait."

Inside, the mill was all shadows and rot-sweet air. Floorboards groaned. Something creaked overhead, slow and steady, not quite the rhythm of the building settling.

Wren lifted the crossbow and climbed.

The top loft was dark. Not empty-dark. *Occupied*-dark. She could feel it the way other people felt weather in their knees.

The thing hung from the rafters like a sleeping bat, but it had the boy. White skin. Too still. Wren set her jaw, planted her boots, and put the bolt where the heart should be.

It screamed.

The fight lasted four minutes that lasted an hour. It came off those rafters faster than anything dead should move, and Wren cursed—loud, steady, professional—as she rolled aside and drove the stake in with the mallet. Once. Twice. On the third strike the thing locked rigid, then sagged, and the mill was just a mill again, full of rain and old wood and a boy who wasn't coming home.

She knelt. Closed his eyes with two fingers.

"I'm sorry," she said. She didn't say it often. It never helped. She said it anyway.

Outside, Biter was waiting. Wren leaned against the mill, breathing hard, and pulled a strip of dried meat from her pocket. Tore it in two. Half for him. Half for her. The rain ran down her face and she let it.

South by morning. Another village. Another thing that shouldn't exist.

She spat blood—her own, from where she'd bitten through her lip—and looked down at the dog.

"Come on," she said. "We've got work to do."

title: fantasy|a disgraced court mage is summoned back to save the prince who exiled her
text:
The frost on the Windspire battlements crunched under Elara Voss’s scuffed work boots, sharp as broken glass. Three years scrubbing tavern taps and mending farmers’ plows with threadbare magic hadn’t softened the edge of the old resentment; when the royal summons had arrived, sealed with the stag crest of the House of Lyr, she’d almost tossed it in the hearth. But the courier had been a girl of sixteen, white-faced and stammering that the prince was dying, and Elara had found herself slinging her worn leather satchel over her shoulder before she could think better of it.

The guards at the chamber door didn’t meet her eyes as they stepped aside. They’d been there the day Kael had banished her, had stood silent while he’d called her a traitor for daring to warn him that the shadow-binding charm he’d commissioned to win the border war would feed on his own life force, faster than he could outrun it.

The room reeked of burnt myrrh and the cloying, cold tang of corrupted magic. Kael lay on the canopied bed, his once-bronzed skin gray as ash, the black veins of the charm snaking up his neck to pool under his jaw. His council healers clustered by the hearth, their robes crisp, their hands empty, when Elara shouldered past them.

“You took your time.”

The voice was a rasp, but it was still him—still that sharp, unapologetic tilt she’d once known better than her own. Elara dropped her satchel on the bedside table with a thud, ignoring the flinch of the head healer behind her. “I was halfway across the kingdom when your messenger found me. You didn’t exactly leave me with a royal postern key when you exiled me. Remember? You said if I ever stepped foot in the Spire again, you’d hang me from the south turret.”

Kael’s mouth twitched, the ghost of the boy who’d snuck her honey cakes from the royal kitchens when they were both twelve, before the crown had settled heavy on his shoulders. “I was angry. You told the entire court the charm I’d spent a year forging would kill me before I turned twenty-five.”

“It will kill you before the moon sets, if you keep interrupting me.” Elara fished a shard of moonstone and a vial of rowan sap from her bag, her fingers brushing the faint, silvery scar on her wrist—the mark of the oath she’d sworn when she’d taken the post of court mage, to protect the heir of Lyr no matter the cost. She’d thought she’d burned that oath out of herself the day she’d walked out the gates, but it had hummed under her skin every mile of the ride north. “You knew the price. You just thought you were too important to pay it. That I was being hysterical when I begged you not to bind it to your bloodline.”

“I had to end the war.” Kael coughed, flecks of black spattering the linen sheet pulled up to his chest. “The raiders were burning villages. Children were freezing in the border holds. What was I supposed to do? Wait while your ‘safe’ magic took another year to muster?”

Elara didn’t answer. She pressed the moonstone to the center of his chest, muttering the old counter-curse she’d scribbled in the margins of her grimoire the night after he’d banished her, the one she’d told herself she’d never use. The shadow charm writhed under his skin, lashing out to singe her wrist, and she hissed, pouring more of her own magic into the stone until her vision spotted at the edges. The black veins receded, slow as retreating tide, and Kael’s gasp turned from rattle to real, ragged breath.

When she pulled her hand away, her sleeve was smoldered through, the burn on her wrist blistering. Kael stared at it, then up at her, the arrogance gone from his face for the first time since she’d known him. “I’m sorry,” he said, quiet enough that only she could hear. “For the exile. For not listening.”

Elara capped the rowan sap, wiping her stinging hand on her threadbare trousers. The council was murmuring behind her, already talking of reinstating her quarters, of back pay, of a royal apology at the next feast. She thought of the tavern, of the regulars who brought her apple pie, of the quiet life she’d built where no one asked her to clean up the messes princes made when they thought they were invincible.

“Save it,” she said, nodding at the faint black thread still wrapped around his ring finger—faint, but not gone. “The curse isn’t fully broken. It’s tied to that stupid pride of yours. Next time you decide to play with magic you don’t understand? Don’t send for me. I won’t come.”

She slung her satchel back over her shoulder, but she didn’t move for the door. Outside, the first star pricked through the frost-fogged window, and Kael laughed, weak but real, and for a second, the three years of anger felt thin as spun glass.
